Body: At the left of the composition the horses of a quadriga are shown coming through a gate. Behind them are a warrior in a Corinthian helmet and a Scythian archer. In the center of the composition Athena stands facing left. She holds a spear in her right hand, and a shield in her left hand. The shield is decorated with a border in added red and a leg in added white. Athena wears an aegis with snaky edges, and a helmet with a very tall crest. Under the shield of Athena crouches an old man whose age is rendered through baldness and the use of added white for his hair and beard. The old man faces to the right wrapped in a mantle and gesturing with his right hand. At the right of the composition, a warrior holds a small child in his right hand over his shoulder about to dash it to the ground. The warrior wears a corslet over a chitoniskos, a Corinthian helmet, and a sword at his waist. He holds his shield which is seen in back view on his left arm. His two spears lean against a tripod on a three step base at the far right of the scene.

Shoulder:The walls of Troy. The crenelated line of the battlements of the walls of Troy are placed along the break in the vase from the body to the shoulder. Soldiers and women are shown in the openings of the crenellations. At the left of the composition, facing right, a Scythian archer prepares to draw his bow. Next to him a soldier facing right is partially obscured behind a crenellation. In the center of the scene, a warrior faces left, carrying a shield shown in profile view and wearing a Corinthian helmet with a tall crest. In the next opening, two figures are shown. An old man, depicted with beard and hair in added white, faces left and gestures down at the scene below. In front of and partially obscuring the old man is a warrior standing up from behind the protection of the battlements. He faces left and has his helmet pushed up in order to drink from a horn held in his right hand. In the next crenellation two women, wearing fillets are shown watching the action below and gesturing. At the extreme right of the composition, there are two more women shown. The background of this scene is filled with the branches of the tree that grows in the scene on the body of the vase.

The identification of the scene or scenes on this vase is very problematic. To begin with, are the shoulder and the body two separate scenes or are they meant to be read as one scene? The answer to this question determines how one reads the scene on the body. Wiencke 1954 interprets the decoration of the vase as a series of independent scenes; the chariot on the left separate from the scene of killing on the right, and the battlements scene on the shoulder. He interprets the scene on the right of the body as the Ilioupersis with Priam crouching in horror as Neoptolemus kills Astyanax. Mota 1957, 28-29 reads the scene on the shoulder as the Trojan celebration when the Greeks falsely withdraw, and the body as the Ilioupersis. However, several features suggest that the scenes on the body and the shoulder go together. Shapiro 1991 has pointed out how the painter uses the structure of the vase to convey architecture of the city, bonding vase structure and decoration, and he emphasizes the mourning gestures of the women, which link them to the scene below. Also the repeated breaking of the border between the two scenes leads the viewer to see them as one. Reading the shoulder and body as one scene, Boardman 1974, following Beazley 1986, interprets the vase as Achilles killing Troilos in front of the walls of Troy. Such an interpretation calls for the viewer to understand a compression of distance, with Priam as not present at the killing but actually far away. The vase appears to blend elements of the iconography of both Achilles and Troilos, and Neoptolemos and Astyanax as Dugas 1937, 24 suggested. The artist probably intended to depict Achilles and Troilos for the use of the figures on the battlements is very unusual (a scene of combat from the battlements can be found on Malibu 84.AE.38 and would fit better with this story, but he does not follow the standard iconography for the killing). The image of a warrior with a child grasped by the ankle belongs firmly to the death of Astyanax. Troilos is shown usually as killed by a sword.

The Antiope Group is a subdivision of the Leagros Group, contemporaries of the red figure Pioneers. Hydriai are the favorite shape for the workshop and scenes from the Trojan war are a favorite theme. The full picture field and the team of horses emerging from the frame of the picture are standard typical of compositions by the Leagros Group.
artifact.inscriptions: There are extensive nonsense inscriptions on both the shoulder and body of the vase.

artifact.name: Munich 1615A
artifact.summary: Side A: Hermes flying, carrying the infant Herakles. Side B: Chiron.
artifact.other_bibliography: LIMC, III, Cheiron, no. 100; LIMC, V, Hermes, no. 383; LIMC, IV, Herakles, no. 1665
artifact.date_description: The dates assigned to this vase vary widely. CVA, Munich 9 gives 510/500, but LIMC, V, Hermes, no. 383 dates the vase 480/470.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Candelori Collection.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Hermes flying, carrying the infant Herakles. Hermes moves to the right, looking back over his right shoulder. He carries the infant Herakles in his left arm and carries his kerykeion in his right hand. The bearded god wears a chitoniskos and a mantle. He also wears a petasos with a folded-brim and winged boots. The tip of a scabbard can be seen at Hermes' left side. The flying motion is conveyed by the use of a knielauf schema and winged boots. The infant Herakles is wrapped in a mantle and wears a fillet in his hair. Both figures are labelled.

Side B: Chiron. The centaur Chiron is depicted as a creature having the rear portion of a horse and the forelegs and torso of a human. The head and face of Chiron is human and bearded, but with the addition of horse ears. He wears a himation with decorated border which covers the transition between the equine and human parts of the body. Over his left shoulder, he carries a branch, a regular attribute, on which is shown his hunting catch, two birds and two rabbits. He gestures with his right hand. A dog accompanies the centaur, standing behind him. Chiron faces right.

The painter makes use of a great deal of added color. Added red is used on Hermes' mantle and chitoniskos, the brim of the petasos, part of the winged boots, and on his beard; on the mantle and fillet of Herakles; and on the hair, beard and himation of Chiron. Added white is used to decorate the garments of Hermes, Herakles, and Chiron. It is also used for the crown of Hermes' petasos, and details of the rabbits and the dog.

This representation of Hermes delivering the infant Herakles to Chiron to be raised is probably unique. A white-ground lekythos Copenhagen, National Museum 6328, depicting Hermes carrying an infant to Chiron, probably is meant to represent the infant Achilles, rather than Herakles. The tradition of Chiron educating Herakles is preserved in literature in Schol. Theokr. 13, 7/9b. The iconography of the scene appears to be derived from the much more common representation of Hermes carrying the infant Achilles to Chiron.
artifact.inscriptions: Side A has four dipinti. &epig-rough;*E*R*M*E*S, Hermes, is written diagonally retrograde to the left of the figure of Hermes, and &epig-rough;*E*R*A*K*L*E*S, Herakles, over the infant's head. At the bottom of the scene under Hermes, *X*A*I*R*E *S*U, welcome. *K*A*L*O*S &epig-rough;*O *P*A*I*S, the boy is beautiful, is placed vertically to the right of Hermes.
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora.

artifact.name: Munich 1575
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles kitharodos, with Athena. Side B: Frontal chariot.
artifact.other_bibliography: LIMC, IV Herakles no. 1439, and pp. 814-817; Boardman 1975, 1-12; Schauenburg 1979, 49-76; Shapiro 1989, 159; Hafner 1938, no. 97.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Candelori collection.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles kitharodos with Athena. Herakles stands at the left of the composition, facing right, playing the kithara, with his left foot resting on a bema. Athena stands at the right on the other side of the bema. Herakles wears a lionskin, belted at the waist, with the head drawn up. Under the lionskin, he wears a short chiton with a decorated border. He carries a quiver on his back and a short sword on his left side. Athena faces left. She wears a peplos, the aegis without gorgoneia, but with snaky edges, and an Attic helmet with a high crest. She carries a spear in her left hand, resting the end of the spear on the platform. She gestures with her right hand closed in a fist.

Side B:Frontal chariot. The four-horse chariot carries a warrior and a driver. The four horses are shown in frontal view with the heads of the two outer horses facing outwards, and those of the inside horses facing inwards. The driver, the figure on the left, faces left. He is depicted as unbearded, wearing a long chiton and a fillet in his hair. He carries a kentron. The warrior, behind and to the right, facing right, is bearded, wears a Corinthian helmet with a high crest, and carries two spears.

Theokr. 24, 109-110 mentions Herakles learning to play the kithara as part of his education. Scenes of Herakles kitharodos become popular in Attic vase-painting in the period circa 530-500. They usually show the hero mounting the bema, and almost always include Athena. The scene of Herakles kitharodos appears to have no mythological or ritual connections. Boardman 1975, 10-11 was the first to suggest that the scene has political implications. He sees an overall increase in scenes depicting Herakles in the second half of the sixth century B.C. and the creation of a new iconography as being due to an identification of Peisistratos with Herakles. In this interpretation the Herakles Kitharodos motif is connected with the introduction of recitals at the Panathenaia.
artifact.inscriptions: Side B. *M*N*E*S*I*L*A *K*A*L*E, "Mnesilla is beautiful", over the left horse of the frontal chariot.
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora.

artifact.name: Munich 1562
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and the boar<lb>Side B: Dionysos and woman reclining<lb>Floral on the neck<lb>Palmette complex under the handles
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Munich 8, pl. 376; LIMC, V, Herakles no. 2117 and 47-48; Carpenter 1986; Johnston 1979, Type 1D, 17; LIMC, III, Dionysos no. 758.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Candelori collection.
artifact.condit: The glaze is chipped, especially on Side A.
artifact.graffiti: Trademark scratched under the foot *A*Q*T*I.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles and the boar. Herakles occupies the center of the composition, holding the boar upside down over his left shoulder. Herakles leans forward threatening to drop the animal on Eurystheus who hides in a pithos set in the ground. Herakles is bearded and wears a corslet over a chitoniskos. He carries a quiver on his back, a sword at his waist, and his club rests against the rim of the pithos. The figure of Eurystheus is damaged, but appears to have been bearded. He holds his arms out pleadingly to Herakles. Herakles is accompanied by human and divine onlookers. Iolaos stands at the right of the composition, facing right, but looking back over his shoulder at the action. He is bearded and wears a corslet over a short chiton with a decorated hem. A sword hangs at his waist and he holds two spears in his right hand. At the left of the composition, Hermes and Athena are seen as the hero's protectors. Hermes stands facing left, gesturing with his right hand. He wears a short decorated chiton with a mantle wrapped over one shoulder, and a petasos. He is bearded. Athena also stands facing left but she looks back over her shoulder at Herakles, gesturing with her raised right hand. Athena wears an embroidered peplos and a snaky-edged aegis, as well as a helmet with a tall crest. She holds a spear in her left hand. Athena's flesh is painted white. Added dots are used throughout the scene as ornamentation. Herakles, Eurystheus, and Iolaos are labelled.

Archaic Attic art emphasizes the fact that Herakles had to capture the Erymanthean boar alive. Artists represent the hero carrying off the subdued boar rather than the actual struggle. This emphasis on the live capture is found in the most complete ancient reference to the story, Diod. Sic. 4.12.1-2, which also has the tradition of Eurystheus hiding in the pithos. The actual delivery of the boar to Eurystheus, rather than scenes of Herakles carrying the boar on his way back, are most popular from the mid sixth century on.

Side B: Dionysos and woman reclining. At the right of the composition, Dionysos, bearded and with long locks of hair, reclines facing left with his left elbow resting on a pillow. His lower body and one shoulder are wrapped in a decorated mantle and he wears an ivy wreath. He holds a kantharos in his right hand. Four round, flat loaves of bread are placed in front of Dionysos. At the left a woman reclines in the same posture with her left elbow resting on a pillow, but she turns her head back to the right and looks at Dionysos. She also has her lower body and one shoulder wrapped in a mantle, leaving the rest of her torso bare, and wears a red fillet in her hair. The upper part of the composition is filled with a large, spreading vine, the trunk of which rises from the center of the scene. The vine is filled with bunches of grapes and four small satyrs clamber about in it picking the harvest. Added white is used for the flesh of the woman, the kantharos, the bread, and various ornament.

The precise interpretation of this scene is somewhat difficult. Scenes of Dionysos reclining with a woman are generally interpreted as Dionysos and Ariadne on Naxos, as this vase has been described in CVA, Munich 8 and LIMC, III, Dionysos no. 758. Carpenter 1986, 114, n. 67, however, calls into question whether Ariadne, a divine wife, would be shown bare breasted, and prefers to see such women shown reclining in a Dionysiac context as maenads.
artifact.inscriptions: On Side A three figures are labelled. *E*R*A*K*L*E*O*S, Herakles, is placed to the right of the figure curving around Iolaos' head. *E*U*R*U*S*Q*E*U*S, Eurystheus, is painted above and to the right of the figure's head. *I*O*L*E*O*S, Iolaos, is painted to the right of the figure.
artifact.painter_mod: Attributed to the circle of the

artifact.name: Munich 1493
artifact.summary: Scenes in Hades. Side A: Herakles and Kerberus. Side B: Sisyphos and small winged figures (amyetoi) pouring water into a leaky pithos.
artifact.other_bibliography: LIMC, V Herakles no. 2604 and pp. 96-100; Schauenburg 1958, 48-78; LIMC, I Amyetoi, no. 2 and pp. 736-738; Van Straten 1975, 563-571; Boardman 1975, 1-12; Felten 1975; Shapiro 1989. For the Nekyia of Polygnotos, Stansbury-O'Donnell 1990.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Candelori collection.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles, at the left of the composition moving right, drives Kerberus in front of him. Herakles wears a belted lionskin over a short chiton with a decorated border. The lion's head covers his own and the hero is bearded. He carries a quiver on his back. Herakles carries his club in his right hand which he raises over his head threatening the monster. His left hand grasps the chain holding the dog. Kerberus is depicted as a monstrous dog having two heads, a long mane whichcovers both necks and continues down the back, and a snake for a tail. Kerberus moves to the right in front of Herakles, with one head looking back at him. Although this depiction of Kerberus does not follow descriptions of the beast in literature (Hesiod [Hes. Th. 310-312] describes Kerberus as having fifty heads and Sophocles [Soph. Trach. 1098] as having three), the portrayal with two heads and a snaky tail is the usual iconography in Attic vase-painting. Other Archaic wares routinely portray Kerberus with three heads. Depictions of Herakles and Kerberus begin in Attic vase-painting in the mid sixth century B.C. The scene in which Herakles drives Kerberus before him, rather than leading him, is found only in black figure. This vase is unusual in that it shows only Herakles and the dog, without Athena or Hermes. The artist has used added red for the chiton, belt, quiver, and beard of Herakles and the collar of the dog; and added white for alternating locks of the mane.

Side B: This side of the vase depicts two scenes taking place in Hades. At the left of the composition, four small, unbearded, winged figures, wearing short belted chitons, carry hydriae to fill a very large half-buried pithos. The figures are placed symmetrically around the pithos, two at the base and two at the mouth pouring water from their hydriae into the pithos. At the right, Sisyphos, naked and bearded, rolls the rock, emphasized by the artist's use of added white, up the hill.

The scenes on the two sides of the vase appear to be related. Depictions of Sisyphos have been collected by Schauenburg 1958. The small winged figures are best interpreted as amyetoi, the souls of those uninitiated in the mysteries. Plato (Plat. Gorg. 493) tells of the uninitiated in Hades eternally filling a leaky pithos. The depiction of the amyetoi in Greek art is very rare, known only on three Attic vases from the Archaic period and the fifth century painting of the Nekyia by Polygnotos in the Lesche of the Knidians at Delphi. Pausanias (Paus. 10.31.9) records that in the painting Polygnotos labels the water carriers in Hades as the uninitiated. The depiction of the Amyetoi with Sisyphos in Hades, as on the Munich amphora, is also found in the later painting by Polygnotos. The combination on the Munich amphora of the scene of those punished in Hades with Herakles and Kerberus has been interpreted as an intentional contrast. van Straten 1975 argues that the two sides of the vase are meant to contrast the varying fates of the initiated versus the uninitiated in the underworld, following a tradition that Herakles was an Eleusinian initiate. Boardman 1975 connects certain changes in Herakles and Kerberus iconography in the late sixth century with Peisistratean political propaganda.
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora.

artifact.name: Munich 1478
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Apollo - Struggle for the tripod. Side B: Dionysos and satyrs. On neck, floral.
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Munich 7, pls. 356, 2, 357, 358; von Bothmer 1977, no. 138; Gialouris 1953, 293-321; B. Cohen 1978, no. A16; Shapiro 1989
artifact.date_description: B. Cohen 1978, no. A16 places this work in the artists' mature period.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Candelori collection
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles and Apollo struggle for the tripod. Herakles moves to the right, looking back at Apollo who pursues him. Herakles swings his club above his head with his right hand and grasps the tripod in his left. He wears the lionskin belted over a short chiton with a sword and a quiver over his shoulder. The artist has attempted to show a back view of Herakles, as is indicated by the dorsal mane on the lionskin. Apollo moves to the left after Herakles, clinging to the tripod with his right hand and grabbing the end of Herakles' club in his left. Apollo is depicted as unbearded, with a wreath in his hair, wearing winged boots. The figures are labelled.

The theme of the struggle for the tripod becomes popular in the last quarter of the sixth century. While this depiction of the scene shows only the combatants, the favored Attic composition adds two onlookers, Artemis and Athena. Shapiro 1989, 63 points out that in this period in these struggle for the tripod scenes, a new iconography of Apollo becomes popular, which had only limited use previously, that is the depiction of Apollo in a short chiton with a bow, rather than in a long garment with a kithara.

The Lysippides Painter depicts the struggle for the tripod on this vase and on Munich 2080. There is a marked similarity in the rendering of several features on these two vases: the movement is from left to right, Apollo grabs Herakles' club, Herakles is shown in back view, and Apollo wears winged boots. (Although winged boots are most commonly associated with Hermes or Perseus, Gialouris 1953, 315 has pointed out that other heroes and deities do wear them occasionally.) The Lysippides Painter has a clear and distinct iconography for the struggle for the tripod. von Bothmer 1977, 56 has seen the lack of correspondence between the iconography of these vases and the earliest surviving versions of the myth by the Andokides Painter, New York 63.11.6 and Berlin F 2159, as evidence that the black figure Lysippides Painter and the red figure Andokides Painter are not the same artist.

Side B: Dionysos and satyrs. In the middle of the composition, Dionysos stands facing right. He wears a long chiton with a diagonal mantle and a wreath in his hair. He holds a kantharos in his right hand. At the left a satyr, facing right, plays the double flute. At the right another satyr, facing left, carries a wineskin.
artifact.inscriptions: On Side A both figures are labelled: *A*P*O*L*O[..]*S, Apollo, over his head, and [[*E*R*A*K]*L*E*S, Herakles, to the right of his head. [*K]*A*L*O*S, [he is] beautiful, is painted between the legs of Apollo. *K*A*L*O*S, [he is] beautiful, is painted between the legs of Herakles. To the right of the legs of Herakles is painted *P*O*R*A*D*X*S, Pordax (transposed to Poradchs). This kalos name appears on another vase by the Lysippides Painter in Reggio.
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora.

artifact.name: Munich 1439
artifact.summary: Side A: Equestrian accompanied by a group of bearded men. Side B: The like. Under one handle, man pursuing woman; under the other, two men.
artifact.other_bibliography: ABV, 240, no. 20; Karo, JHS 19 (1899) 162, no. 34; H.W. Burkhardt, Reitertypen auf griechischen Vasen, 17.
artifact.dimensions: H. 0. 39 m., diameter of rim ca. 0.162 m., diameter of foot 0.13 m.
artifact.collection_history: Formerly Collection Candelori.
artifact.comparanda: Munich 1444; ABV, p. 239, Group I.
artifact.primary_citation: <bibl>CVA, Munich MAK 7, p. 40-41, pl. 337, 1-2 and pl. 336, 3</bibl>.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A group consisting of an equestrian with two bearded companions moves to the right. The bearded man on horseback wears a headband and a red chiton. He has tied an animal skin over this garment. The band and the seams of the chiton are decorated with white dots. His right hand is holding a spear. The horse has white teeth and its mane is tied up. Red lines mark the mane, the chest, and the muscles on its hind legs. Above the horse is a bird in flight, its wing and tail feathers indicated in white. The bearded men on foot are both nude except for a short mantle. They are both carrying wreaths in their right hands, their left arms are slightly raised. They wear necklaces and headbands with dotted decoration and their mantles show dotted rosettes and red dots. A nude man walks in front of them carrying a small mantle, similarly patterned as the others, over his left arm. Two smaller figures occupy the space below the handle: first another nude, bearded man, who has his hair tied up in a knot and wears the same attire as the previous man, raises both hands in pursuit of a girl. Her arms are raised and she wears a black and red peplos, its seams decorated with white dots. Red paint marks the straps of her sandals, the necklace and armbands, and the headband.

Side B:This scene shows only a few variations on the opposite group. The equestrian is lacking the animal skin tied over the chiton. Behind his two companions another bird in flight is painted below the handle. The bearded man walking in front of the group with the horseman wears also a red chiton with white-dotted seams, an animal skin tied over it, and a red Phrygian cap. In front of him two men are facing each other; their hands are raised. Both have red hair, which is tied up, and they wear the dotted headband and mantle.

artifact.name: Munich 1437
artifact.summary: Side A: Gigantomachy. Side B: Gigantomachy.
artifact.other_bibliography: Gerhard 1840-1858, p. 26, note 23 i.
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.47 m., diameter of rim ca. 0.16 m.
artifact.collection_history: Formerly Collection Candelori.
artifact.comparanda: Munich 1438; Vatican 365; CVA, Altenburg, 1, 21; ABV, 312, 5.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A divine warrior is driven into battle in a quadriga with a goddess as charioteer. He places one foot into the chariot and thrusts his lance against an opponent already lying on the ground. The divine couple can be identified as Zeus and Hera, or Ares and Aphrodite. Gerhard also suggests Iris as a possibility. The goddess wears a partially red painted peplos, the god a short chiton with dotted decoration along the seams. The fallen titan wears a red crested helmet. In the center behind the group stands Athena in fighting position; she protectively holds her round shield in front of her and raises her spear against a fallen giant wearing a Corinthian helmet and greaves. The chariot is met by a giant carrying a spear pointing down and a Boeotian shield marked with a triskeles circled in red. He is equipped with red greaves, a chiton with grid pattern, a harness with dotted decoration, and a Corinthian helmet. Set off behind him is the next group of fighters. A god holding his spear in a horizontal position attacks a giant already fallen to the ground. He is trying to protect himself with his round shield against the oncoming blow while defending himself with a rock. Also to this group belongs another giant, who is slightly hidden behind the handle. He raises his spear to a horizontal position, ready to attack.

Side B: The central figure of the scene is a goddess, probably Athena, striding to the right. She is wearing a crested Attic helmet and holds her spear horizontally in pursuit of a fleeing giant, who is looking back at her. He wears greaves, a short chiton with dotted decoration, and a harness with incisions indicating the backward twist of his upper body. Behind the group Poseidon has speared his opponent and threatens to smash him with a huge rock (the island Nisyros). Red marks indicate the irregularities on the rock. The pair of fighters to the right of the group is hardly preserved. The god is depicted in attack position with raised spear and protective round shield. He is wearing greaves, a short, partially red chiton with white dotted decoration along the seam, and a red helmet. Only a part of his opponent's round shield and his turned left foot remains. The following group surrounds the handle. To the left, a divine warrior pushes against his fallen opponent who tries to protect himself with his white, round shield.

artifact.name: Munich 1433
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Nessos<lb>Side B: Centauromachy. Below: Floral, and three rows of animals
artifact.other_bibliography: J.D. Beazley and F. Magi, La Raccolta Benedetto Guglielmo nel Museo Gregoriano Etrusco, (Rome 1939), p. 26; D. v. Bothmer, Ancient Art from New York Private Collections, p. 170, 5; ABV, 95 IV. 98, 37; Brommer 1960, p. 119, A7.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Canino.
artifact.comparanda: Munich 1432 (v. Bothmer); ABV, 102, no. 103; Vatican G13; Louvre E 833.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A, shoulder: Herakles battles Nessos. Herakles pursues the centaur brandishing his sword in his right, his left fist extended forward. Nessos attempts to flee to the right, holding a white stone in his left. Deianeira slips from his back and runs towards Herakles with her arms raised. The hero wears a short white chiton, the lion's skin loosely pulled over his head. Deianeira wears a belted peplos, decorated with white dots along the seam, on top of a long garment with figurative central panel showing white sphinxes with extended wings. Nessos wears a white wreath; his chest is rendered in red.

The central group is flanked on the left by two centaurs. The first brandishes a huge white stone; he also wears a white wreath. His chest is depicted with a red beard and red chest, his hind legs are outlined in white. The second centaur holds a smaller stone ready to be hurled; only his chest is painted in red. They are complemented on the right by a group of three figures facing the central battle scene. The first is a woman dressed in a chiton and a red mantle, its seam decorated with white, partially missing dots. She is followed by an older man holding a staff. Slightly balding, his beard and hair is rendered in white; he wears a red mantle over a chiton and a red headband. The last figure is another woman dressed in a long garment painted red below the waist. She holds a wreath in each hand. The skin was painted in white; the color is now lost. From the left handle a lotus blossom grows on a long, curved stem. The background cover readable, but meaningless inscriptions.

Side B, shoulder: Centauromachy in three groups. The central group consists of a centaur brandishing a tree trunk above his head, flanked by two attacking warriors. The centaur is turned to the left, his head facing backwards. His mouth is open and the bent right front leg indicates a first stumbling. He is rendered with a red beard and red chest, wearing a wreath with formerly white wreaths. The two warriors are shown in Chalcidian helmets with white crests, belted swords and round shields. The right shield is painted in red, the left was possibly white. The left warrior wears a red armor over a short chiton decorated with a grid pattern. Between his legs are two straps visible which could indicate a poorly executed skin. The right warrior wears a tight red garment longer than the previous with small sleeves and a wide seam. Two spirals with white dots on the chest possibly recall an armor. To the left of the central group a bearded warrior pursues a fleeing centaur. The warrior is nude, except for a Corinthian helmet, sword belt and shield, his spear raised in attack. The fleeing centaur is turned backwards and clasps a white (?) rock in both hands. His hair, beard, and outlines of muscles are rendered in red. To their right another centaur is pleading with his opponent. In the typical gesture of begging for mercy he places his fingertips onto the forehead and chin of the warrior who is pressing on to him with raised spear, his shield protectively held in front of him. The centaur's hair, beard and detailing of the body are red; the wreath in his hair was possibly white. The Attic helmet and round shield of his opponent was once white. He also wears a red armor and a chiton with incised decoration. All centaurs appear to be defeated. In the background, meaningless inscriptions.

Upper Animal Frieze A: The distribution of the animals does not....
artifact.inscriptions: Meaningless painted inscriptions on panels A and B.

artifact.name: Munich 1428
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Nessos. Side B: Horsemen.
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Munich, MAK 7. 32, p. 24-25, pls. 323,1-2 and 322, 3-4; ABV, p. 98, 40.
artifact.other_bibliography: von Bothmer, Ancient Art from New York Private Collections., 169, no. 2.
artifact.dimensions: H 0. 363 m., diameter of rim ca. 0.15 m., diameter of foot 0.11 m.
artifact.collection_history: Formerly Collection Candelori.
artifact.comparanda: Munich 1429
artifact.graffiti: Meaningless inscriptions on the background of panel A.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles fighting the centaur Nessos. Herakles pursues the fleeing centaur with raised sword. He is wearing the lion's skin over a white chiton. His scabbard is fastened with a white strap to his back. The centaur has fallen under the onslaught and raises his right hand in a gesture of submission, holding Deianeira in his left arm. She also raises her right hand. Her peplos is decorated along the hem with white dots. Behind Herakles stands Athena, leaning on her spear. She is rendered with red hair, wearing a high crested helmet and a mantle with red lining over a long garment with red top. To the right of Nessos a second centaur is watching the battle. His beard, hair and chest are painted red and he holds a tree in both hands, prepared to fight.

The space behind Athena is occupied by a group of two youths and a young girl. The girl in the center stands with both hands raised, holding a wreath in her left. The members of the group are dressed in chiton and mantle, which are carelessly painted in red. The skin of the women is rendered in white.

The background of the panel is marked by meaningless inscriptions.

Side B: Four equestrians, who are nude and beardless, gallop to the right. The first three horsemen are followed by a group of birds in flight. Three riders hold the reigns tightly in both hands; the second in line holds the rein only in his left, his right placed behind him onto the back of the horse. The chest of the first two horsemen and the necks of the horses are carelessly painted in red. The mane of the second horse from the right is painted in white.

Two animal friezes circle the amphora above and below the panels.

Upper Animal Frieze A: Antithetical sphinxes are flanked by two lions whose heads are turned backwards. The tongue of the left lion is visible. The left lion is also part of the next group below the handle, consisting of two antithetical swans with curved necks and bowed heads placed between antithetical lions. The remaining part of B is occupied by antithetical swans between antithetical sirens. Below the right handle of B is painted a bird in flight.

Lower Animal Frieze A: A stag is flanked by panthers.

Animal Frieze B: The frieze is not centered. Two antithetical stags flank a panther.

artifact.name: Munich 1416
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Iolaos in chariot, with Athena and Hermes<lb>Side B: Komos
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Munich 1, pls. 50-51; Johnston 1979; LIMC, IV, Herakles no. 1414 and 810; Carpenter 1991; Boardman 1972, 57-72
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Canino collection.
artifact.graffiti: Graffito under foot, Johnston 1979, Type 2B 40.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles and Iolaos in chariot with Athena and Hermes. At the left of the composition, Herakles and Iolaos are mounted in the car of the chariot. The figure of Iolaos is almost completely covered by that of Herakles placed in the foreground. Only Iolaos' Corinthian helmet with high crest and his arms holding the reins, and a kentron and club in his right hand are clearly visible. Herakles wears a short chiton, the lionskin with the head drawn up over his own, a mantle over one arm. He carries a spear in his right hand. Athena stands in the middle of the composition with her lower body obscured by the horses of the quadriga. Her torso is frontal and she looks at Herakles on the left. She wears a snaky aegis and a helmet with a tall crest. She holds a spear in her right hand and gestures with her left. Her shield is seen in profile view propped against her side under the horses. At the right of the composition Hermes stands facing left at the head of the team, carrying the kerykeion. He is wrapped in a mantle and also wears boots and a petasos. All figures are labelled.

Scenes of Herakles in a chariot are very popular in the last quarter of the sixth century. Often, if Athena is driving the chariot, such scenes are interpreted as the Apotheosis of Herakles. However, with scenes such as the one on this vase where Iolaos drives and Athena merely looks on it is unclear whether one should interpret the scene as an allusion to a specific journey. Boardman 1972, 62-63 sees a political allusion in representations of Herakles in a chariot in which Iolaos is shown holding Herakles' club. He believes that the ancient viewer would have connected this image with the club-bearing bodyguards of Peisistratos.

Side B: Komos. Five bearded, wreathed komasts wearing tainia around their necks dance and play music. The figure at the left, wearing only boots, moves to the right leaning forward slightly, while looking back over his shoulder. The figure next to him on the right also moves to the right, singing and playing a barbiton. This figure and the other three figures to the right all wear a sort of loincloth. The figure in the middle of the composition faces right with his head thrown back, playing a kithara. As well as the loincloth, this figure carries a small mantle over his left arm and wears boots. The figure second from the right dances, sings, and plays krotala. He faces left toward the kithara player. At the right of the composition another figure wearing boots moves to the right with his head thrown back, playing the double flute. All figures are labelled.
artifact.inscriptions:
On Side A, the figures are labelled *I*O*L*E*O*S, Iolaos, under Herakles' spear; &epig-rough;*E*R*A*K*L*E*S, Herakles, downwards in front of Iolaos' club; and *A*Q*E*N*A*I*A, Athena, under the horses. *K*A*L*O*S, [he is] beautiful, is painted over the heads of the horses. Between Athena's arm and the horse's mane some letters are preserved *S*E[]*O*I*S.

On Side B, the figures are labelled from left: *M*I*L*I*X*O*S, above the figure; *T*E*L*O*K*L*E*S, beside the figure's barbiton; *M*U*S*A*O*N, over the head of the figure to the right; *D*I*O*D*O*R*O*S, behind the figure; and *X*R*E*M*E*S, in front of the figure.

artifact.name: Munich 1410
artifact.summary: Side A: Two warriors fight over body while two women look on. Side B: Amazons and warrior.
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Munich 1, pls. 41, no. 2, 42, nos. 1-3, 52, no. 4; Johnston 1979; von Bothmer 1957; LIMC, I, Antilochos I, 835-837; Bohr 1982
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Candelori collection.
artifact.graffiti: Trademark under the foot of Johnston 1979, Type 39A, 1
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: In the center of the composition, two warriors fight with spears raised over the body of third warrior, while two women look on. The warrior on the left moves to the right holding his spear in his right hand and wearing his shield, shown in rear view, on his left arm. He wears a Corinthian helmet pushed up on his head with a kerykeion ornament, a chitoniskos, a corslet, a chlamys, and greaves. The warrior on the right moves to the left. He too is bearded and has a helmet with a crest pushed back on his head. He wears a nebris over a short chiton, greaves, and a sword at his waist. His shield, shown in frontal view, has cutouts at the sides, and is decorated with a gorgoneion, a lion, and a snake. In between the feet of these warriors lies the corpse of a third. He wears a corslet over a short chiton, greaves and a Corinthian helmet with a tall crest. His head is shown twisted completely around, and his shield in profile view lies on his chest. An eagle flies between the two warriors. On each side of this central fight, a woman wearing an elaborately decorated peplos and mantle, and holding a long staff stands watching.

The battle of Achilles and Memnon over the body of Antilochos, related in the lost epic poem the Aethiopis, was a very popular scene on Attic black figure vases. The figures of the composition are often labelled allowing identification of the warriors and of the two women as their mothers Eos and Thetis. However, the scene often appears as on this vase without inscriptions identifying the figures. In this context, the scene may have been meant to be understood as Achilles and Memnon or it may have become a generic battle scene.

Side B: Amazons and warrior. At the left of the composition, a warrior faces left, wearing a helmet and greaves, and carrying a spear and a shield with a bird shield device, which obscures his body. In the middle of the composition, an Amazon leads a horse to the right. She wears a Scythian cap, a mantle, and she carries two spears. At the right, an Amazon moves to the right looking back over her shoulder. She wears a short chiton, greaves, a sword at her waist, and a helmet with a tall crest. She carries a spear in her right hand and carries her shield on her left arm.

von Bothmer 1957, 91 has shown that beginning in the mid sixth century Amazons begin to be depicted in Attic vase-painting doing standard warrior activities, such as arming, leading horses, carrying dead comrades. Compositions such as this of an Amazon leading a horse accompanied by a male warrior are very popular.

The Painter of Munich 1410 uses a lot of added color. Women's flesh is white and added red and white are used throughout the composition. The painter executes a battle scene almost identical to that on side A of this vase on Karlsruhe 61.89.

artifact.name: Munich 1385
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles killing the lion. Side B: A woman between two youths, flanked on either side by two hoplites.
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Munich, MAK 1, p. 17-18, pls. 18.3 and 25.1; ABV, p. 310.
artifact.other_bibliography: CVA, Munich, MAK 1, p. 17-18, pls. 18.3 and 25.1; ABV, p. 310; Beazley, BSA 32, 1931-32, 13, 25; Langlotz 1932, no. 248.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles killing the Nemean lion, thrusting his sword into the lion's chest. To his left watches a youth wearing a chiton and a mantle decorated with flowers, as well as a woman dressed in a chiton and a peplos. She also wears earrings and a necklace. The spectators to the right include a bearded older man, dressed similarly to the youth on the left, and a hoplite. A few details are rendered in white, such as the woman's skin, the lion's teeth, the handle of the sword, and the lower edge of the hoplite's helmet. The majority of the details are painted in red.

Side B: The central figure is a woman wearing a peplos and a hooded mantle drawn over the back of her head. She is flanked by two youths dressed in a chiton and a mantle with floral decoration. The group is framed by two hoplites. Their shield devices consist of three lines, an eye, and a pentagram. White paint marks the woman's skin, the shield devices, and the crests of the helmets. As in the other panel, the remaining details are rendered in red.

Above the panels runs a frieze of pendant lotus buds. Red lines decorate the rim, neck and foot of the amphora. Rays set off in white paint extend from the foot.
artifact.inscriptions: A cross, painted in red, marks the bottom of the amphora's foot.

artifact.name: Mount Holyoke 1967.BS.II.11
artifact.summary: Tondo: woman playing krotala and dancing.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by the Mount Holyoke College Art Museum (1967 BS II.11)

Height: 3 5/8 in. (9.2 cm.); Diameter: 9 7/8 in. (25 cm.)

Broken and repaired.

Inside: a woman, playing castanets (krotala) and dancing, runs to the right, her head turned to the left over her shoulder. She wears a peplos, bracelets, and a fillet in her hair. Around the tondo near the border is inscribed *K*A*L*O*S *K*A*L*O*S (beautiful, beautiful). A reserved line forms the tondo.

Red: the inscription, bracelets, and fillet.

Attributed to Oltos [Beazley] ca. 525 - 500 B. C.

Oltos, whose name is known from his signature as painter on two kylikes, was a contemporary of the Andokides Painter, the inventor of the red-figure technique (see Boston 01.8037). On this vase, the new technique is seen in its early stages. The use of added color is reduced, resulting in a more sober color scheme. The figure is outlined with relief lines and occasionally with a contour stripe. Inner details are painted with firm black relief lines. The figure is thus spotlighted against the black background. This kylix belongs with the early to middle work of Oltos (see Bruhn 1943).

Bibliography: Hesperia Art Bulletin 39 (1967) no. A 13; E. Finkenstaedt, "A Red-Figure Kylix by Oltos at Mount Holyoke College," AJA 72 (1968) 383, pl. 129; Para., 328, no. 127 ter.

artifact.name: Mount Holyoke 1932.BS.II.5
artifact.summary: Woman, youth and maid.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by the Mount Holyoke College Art Museum (1932 BS II.5)

Height with lid: 6 3/4 in. (17 cm.)

Broken and repaired; missing pieces restored and painted; some repainting on design areas.

Woman, youth, and maid. To the right of a large door a woman is seated holding a ball of wool in her hand. In front of her is a wool basket above which is draped a piece of cloth. Next, a youth leaning on a staff extends an arm with a ball of wool. In his other hand is a piece of cloth. Lastly, a maid carrying a mirror and a piece of drapery, runs to the right towards the door. The mirror's top, the hanging drapery, and the drapery of the youth are partly restored. On the lid, laurel wreath and tongue pattern.

White: balls of wool, wool in basket, fruit of laurel.

Attributed to the Veii Painter [Beazley]ca. 470 - 460 B. C.

The Veii Painter was a member of the Penthesilea workshop. His early work, of which this is an example, is characterized by the lively but careless drawing found on the lesser works of the Penthesilea Painter.

Bibliography: ARV2, 906, no. 109.

artifact.name: Mount Holyoke 1929.BS.II.4
artifact.summary: Side A: goddess and woman. Side B: king.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by Mount Holyoke College Art Museum (1929 BS II.4)

Height: 13 in. (33 cm.)

Broken and repaired; some restoration and repainting in drapery. Under foot, graffito. Said to be from Volterra.

Side A: goddess and woman (Hera and Hebe?). On the left, a woman, possibly Hebe, the cup bearer of the gods. She wears a himation over her chiton and extends her right hand with an oinochoe. On the right, a goddess, possibly Hera, with lotus-tipped scepter and phiale. She wears a himation, chiton, and diadem.

Side B: king (Zeus?). A bearded man wearing a himation stands to right holding a lotus-tipped scepter.

On A, a strip of meander pairs alternating with saltires; on B, a strip of simple rightward key.

Attributed to Polygnotos [Beazley] ca. 450 - 440 B. C.

The style of Polygnotos is ultimately derived from that of the Niobid Painter (cf. Mount Holyoke 1932.BS.II.5), but it has much that is new in it: the lines are longer and more fluid, the figures softer and fleshier, the whole drawing broader and less archaic (Beazley 1918, 171). The figures on this vase have a certain nobility but are very schematized, and our identification is uncertain. The name of Polygnotos is known from his signature on five vases. Two other artists contemporary with him sign with the same name, and as Beazley suggests, all three may have taken the name from the famous mural painter, Polygnotos of Thasos (ARV2, 1027). The school of Polygnotos was large; the Christie Painter (Harvard 1970.108) was one of his most able associates.

Bibliography: ARV2, 1031, no. 44.

artifact.name: Mount Holyoke 1925.BS.II.3
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles regaled by Athena. Side B: same.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by Mount Holyoke College Art Museum (1925 BS II.3)

Height: 6 13/16 in. (17.2 cm.); Diameter: 8 11/16 in. (22 cm.)

Broken and repaired.

Side A: Herakles regaled by Athena. Herakles, in a lion skin with his club between his knees and his quiver at his waist, sits on a stone seat. One hand is raised in greeting, one extended with a phiale. Athena, in chiton, himation, and Attic helmet, approaches from the right and extends her oinochoe to fill his cup. At the left is Hermes playing flutes. Behind Herakles is a dwarfed tree with branches extending in the background.

Side B: the same, except the tree trunk is not visible.

Under the handles, bearded goats; around the lip, a double row of dots between bands; below, red and black alternating tongues between lines.

Red: the brim of Hermes' pilos, his beard, belt, and shoes; the edge of Herakles' lion skin, his belt; Athena's hair; ornaments on the drapery; the wine; the fillet at the base.

White: Athena's flesh, helmet crest; Hermes' hat and chiton; dots on the edges of Herakles' cup, the meander on his rock seat; the fruits of the tree; the goat's horn, his belly, and mouth.

Attributed to the Theseus Painter [Vanderpool] ca. 500 B. C.

The Theseus Painter, so named because he often chose the deeds of Theseus for his subject, was above all a painter of skyphoi, most of which can be dated by their style as ca. 500 B. C. (Haspels 1936, 163). Four others are known showing Herakles regaled by Athena (ABV, 519). The subject is probably Herakles resting after one of his twelve labors. Athena, his patron, brings him wine or nectar to refresh him. Many vases are known showing Herakles with Athena and Hermes, but Athena serving the hero wine does not appear until the beginning of the fifth century (Beazley 1961, 56).

Bibliography: Mount Holyoke College, Nancy Everett Dwight Foundation Catalogue ill.; E. Vanderpool, "The Rectangular Rock-cut Shaft," Hesperia 15 (1946) 289-290; ABV, 519 (with no. 18).

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.85
artifact.summary: Woman and youth at a tomb.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. No. 183.
artifact.condit: The surface and the color of the vase appear to be in very good condition, but Beazley indicates that the vase was restored.
artifact.decoration_description:
On the body of the vase, a woman and a youth are depicted on either side of a tomb. The woman approaches the tomb from the left, carrying an offering wrapped in a cloth. She wears a belted chiton and a scarf in her hair. The figure is rendered completely in outline except for her hair painted in solid brown and the scarf in purple. The cloth covering the offering which the woman carries still bears traces of green paint and the hem is purple. The tomb has a stele topped with a palmette finial, and the stele is bound with red fillets. The youth stands to the right of the tomb with his right hand on his hip, wrapped in a himation which shows traces of dark paint. A wreath hangs in the field behind his head. This scene at the tomb is surmounted by a grayish meander enclosed in red lines. The decoration on the body does not encircle the vase but stops at the sides. The mouth, neck, handle, and lower body of the vase are glazed. The top of the foot is glazed while the sides are reserved. The shoulder is decorated with palmettes.

The white ground technique, which first becomes popular in the experimental stage of Attic vase painting in the 520's, consists of covering the natural reddish ground of the clay with a thin white "slip" of ultra-refined clay, which remains white after firing. In the earliest usage of this white ground technique, decoration in the standard black-figure technique of silhouette with incision and added color would then be placed against this lighter background. By the early fifth century, many painters switch to an outline technique. As can be seen on this lekythos, artists using this technique enliven figures drawn in outline with areas of solid added color. From its inception until the mid fifth century, white ground is used primarily for small vases, such as lekythoi, pyxides, and alabastra, and for small areas of larger vases. After the middle of the fifth century, white ground is used only rarely for vases other than lekythoi. With these white ground lekythoi of the second half of the fifth century, there is also a change in iconography; the subjects depicted now being almost exclusively funerary.

The iconography of this vase is fairly standard for late fifth century funerary lekythoi. The most common scene found on such vases is the visit to the tomb, and the most frequently depicted visitor is a young woman. The youth on the right of the stele may be a male relative accompanying the woman, or he may represent the dead man himself.
artifact.shape_description: The "standard cylindrical shape" lekythos developed at the end of the sixth century and continued to be produced until the beginning of the fourth.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.84
artifact.summary: Four people at a tomb.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. No. 181.
artifact.condit: The surface is quite worn on the left side of the vase.
artifact.decoration_description:
On the body of the vase four people are depicted at a tomb. Two women approach the tomb from the left. The first woman on the left is poorly preserved but it appears that she once held something in her right hand. She wears a dark himation over her chiton. The woman second from the left wears a similar himation and also appears to have a fillet in her hair. The center of the composition is occupied by the tomb with its stele. The stele is topped by a palmette and acanthus finial. A young man without a beard and a child stand at the right of the stele. He wears a red himation over a chiton and carries two spears. The child also wears a red himation. The mouth, neck, handle, and lower body of the vase are glazed. The top of the foot is glazed while the sides are reserved.

The white ground technique, which first becomes popular in the experimental stage of Attic vase painting in the 520's, consists of covering the natural reddish ground of the clay with a thin white "slip" of ultra-refined clay, which remains white after firing. In the earliest usage of this white ground technique, decoration in the standard black-figure technique of silhouette with incision and added color would then be placed against this lighter background. By the early fifth century, many painters switch to an outline technique. As can be seen on this lekythos, artists using this technique enliven figures drawn in outline with areas of solid added color. From its inception until the mid fifth century, white ground is used primarily for small vases, such as lekythoi, pyxides, and alabastra, and for small areas of larger vases. After the middle of the fifth century, white ground is used only rarely for vases other than lekythoi. With these white ground lekythoi of the second half of the fifth century, there is also a change in iconography; the subjects depicted now being almost exclusively funerary.

The iconography of this vase is fairly standard for late fifth century funerary lekythoi. The most common scene found on such vases is the visit to the tomb, and the most frequently depicted visitors are young women. The man on the right of the stele may be a male relative accompanying the women who tend the grave, or since he is depicted as a warrior with spears, he may represent the dead man himself.
artifact.shape_description: The "standard cylindrical shape" lekythos developed at the end of the sixth century and continued to be produced until the beginning of the fourth.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.83
artifact.summary: Man and woman at a tomb.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. No. 179.
artifact.decoration_description:
The body of the vase shows a man and a woman at a tomb. The center of the composition is occupied by the tomb and its stele, bound with fillets rendered in matte red. A woman approaches the tomb from the left, carrying a basket, decorated with a leaf pattern on the side, with more fillets. The woman is rendered in outline and her hair appears to have had a light yellowish wash. She wears a chiton with unusual sleeves. A young man without a beard approaches from the right, holding an oil container in his right hand. He too is rendered in outline except for the solid, bright red himation covering his chiton. His hair is indicated by a yellowish brown wash. A small, winged, naked female figure hovers in the air between the stele and the woman's head. This scene at the tomb is surmounted by a grayish stopped meander enclosed in red lines. The decoration on the body does not encircle the vase but stops at the sides. The mouth, neck, handle, and lower body of the vase are glazed. The top of the foot is glazed while the sides are reserved. The shoulder is decorated with a tongue pattern and palmettes.

The white ground technique, which first becomes popular in the experimental stage of Attic vase painting in the 520's, consists of covering the natural reddish ground of the clay with a thin white "slip" of ultra-refined clay, which remains white after firing. In the earliest usage of this white ground technique, decoration in the standard black-figure technique of silhouette with incision and added color would then be placed against this lighter background. By the early fifth century, many painters switch to an outline technique. As can be seen on this lekythos, artists using this technique enliven figures drawn in outline with areas of solid added color. From its inception until the mid fifth century, white ground is used primarily for small vases, such as lekythoi, pyxides, and alabastra, and for small areas of larger vases. After the middle of the fifth century, white ground is used only rarely for vases other than lekythoi. With these white ground lekythoi of the second half of the fifth century, there is also a change in iconography; the subjects depicted now being almost exclusively funerary.

The iconography of this vase is standard for late fifth century funerary lekythoi. The most common scene found on such vases is the visit to the tomb, and the most frequently depicted visitor is a young woman, sometimes accompanied by a male relative, as on this vase. The basket of fillets carried by the woman is also a common feature. The small winged figure on this vase is somewhat atypical. In general terms, this figure is an eidolon, representing the dead person. The term eidolon, however, is usually applied to fully represented figures in epiphany scenes, which become especially popular during the Peloponnesian War. The figure on this vase is part way between such representations and the very small, winged, hovering, mosquito-like figures, rendered in black silhouette, which also represent the dead (sometimes called psychai in order to differentiate them), as on Athens, NM 1926.
artifact.shape_description: The "standard cylindrical shape" lekythos developed at the end of the sixth century and continued to be produced until the beginning of the fourth.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.81
artifact.summary: Ivy-berry tendril
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson Collection. Harvard Inv. No. 175.
artifact.condit: Discoloration from oxidation.
artifact.decoration_description:
The primary decoration of this vase is an ivy-berry tendril on the middle of the body. This decorative zone is flanked above and below by lattice work and a key meander. The decoration on the body does not encircle the vase but stops at the sides. The mouth, neck, handle and lower body of the vase are glazed. The shoulder is decorated with rays, and the foot is semi-reserved.

Pattern lekythoi, ranging from the late sixth through the fifth century, represent a mass-produced, less expensive alternative to figured lekythoi, produced at the same time, by the same artisans. The decoration of these patterned vases can include a variety of geometric and natural designs, with palmette chains being the most frequently used motif. Ivy-berry tendrils on pattern lekythoi are most common in the second half of the fifth century.

The white ground technique, which first becomes popular in the experimental stage of Attic vase painting in the 520's, consists of covering the natural reddish ground of the clay with a thin white "slip" of ultra-refined clay, which remains white after firing. In the earliest usage of this white ground technique, decoration in the standard black-figure technique of silhouette with incision and added color would then be placed against this lighter background. Later there is a switch to an outline technique. From its inception until the mid fifth century, the white ground technique is used primarily to decorate small vases, such as lekythoi, pyxides, and alabastra, and small areas of larger vases. After the middle of the fifth century, white ground is used only rarely for vases other than lekythoi.
artifact.shape_description: The "standard cylindrical shape" lekythos developed at the end of the sixth century and continued to be produced until the beginning of the fourth.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.79
artifact.summary: Man between lions<lb>On shoulder: hare and hound.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 171.
artifact.decoration_description:
On the body of the vase, a man stands facing right between two lions. The man is bearded, and wears a long chiton with himation. The two lions are placed heraldically looking back over their shoulders. On the shoulder of the vase, a hound chases a hare to the right. The mouth, neck, handle, lower body, and foot of the vessel are glazed.

The Dolphin Group decorates shoulder lekythoi and other small shapes, generally in a non-narrative animal style carrying over from the earlier sixth century. They favor symmetrical compositions as seen here. Boardman 1974, 183 has suggested that many of the vases of the Dolphin Group may actually be Euboean rather than Attic.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.76
artifact.summary: Dionysos and maenad.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 164.
artifact.condit: Part of the surface is scaled off
artifact.decoration_description:
The main decoration of the vase is placed in a panel. Dionysos reclines at the right of the composition facing left toward a maenad who stands playing the kithara. Dionysos reclines on a kline leaning on his left elbow. In his right hand he holds a kantharos. His torso is bare, but a himation is wrapped around his legs, and he wears a wreath. The maenad, standing at the left of the composition facing right, wears a chiton and himation. A dog lies under the kline. Vines fill the field behind the figures. The lip of the vessel carries ivy tendrils and the neck, palmettes.

The Painter of Sevres 100 decorates oinochoai and is related to the Athena Painter. The majority of his vases carry Dionysiac themes. The scene with Dionysos reclining appears to derive from representations of Herakles reclining, which become popular shortly after the middle of the century. The kantharos replaces the drinking horn as the most common attribute of the god in the 540's.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.75
artifact.summary: Side A: Combat between cocks. Side B: Combat between cocks.
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.123 m., D. with handles 0.27 m., D. without handles 0.209 m.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 162.
artifact.decoration_description:
On Side A, two naked youths rush at one another. They each carry a club, swung back ready to deliver a blow, and have what appears to be a cloak over the other arm. The depiction of the combatants closely resembles that used on other cups, for example the Hermogenean skyphos (Mississippi 1977.3.70) which shows Herakles and the lion. A draped youth stands at the left watching. This battle is placed between cocks, and in turn the whole scene is framed by palmettes which grow from the handles. A nonsense inscription is placed between the combatants. Side B is the same except the spectator and the inscription are lacking.

Little Master cups are a favored cup form beginning in the mid sixth century. They are decorated in a distinct miniaturist style. On band cups such as this, the handle zone is reserved and decoration, generally comprised of one to three figures, is placed in its center. Palmettes almost always grow from the handles.
artifact.inscriptions: A nonsense inscription is placed between the combatants on Side A.
artifact.shape_description: The Little Master cup becomes the most popular cup form in the middle and the third quarter of the sixth century. The shape is distinctive for its offset lip and high foot. There are two forms of Little Master cup, the lip cup and the band cup. The lip cup has a reserved lip, clearly articulated from the bowl. The band cup has a glazed lip which forms a gradual transition from the bowl.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.73
artifact.summary: Europa.
artifact.sources_used: Robinson 1956, no. 5; Zahn 1983, 25-37 and no. 24; LIMC, IV, Europe I, no. 34 and 89-92
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.272 m., D. with handle 0.164 m., D. without handle 0.141 m.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 156.
artifact.decoration_description:
In a panel framed by dicing, a running meander and black strokes, Europa rides the bull to the right. She is seated side-saddle on its back and grasps a horn with her left hand. Europa wears a peplos and mantle, and a wreath in her hair. The bull wears a red fillet around its neck. The artist has rendered the sea in a sepia wash with added white waves. Also a tree branch growing out of the left frame indicates the land left behind.

The story of Europa and the bull was most popular in the period from circa 530-490. Often there is a problem of identification with scenes showing a woman seated on a bull, since maenads are also shown as riding bulls. In this instance, the artist's rendering of the sea leaves no question as to the identification of the woman as Europa.
artifact.painter_mod: Influenced by the workshop of the

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.71
artifact.summary: Departure Scene. On shoulder: Herakles and the lion. Predella of lions and boars.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 151. Robinson purchased the vase in 1929 from the Schiller collection, Berlin.
artifact.decoration_description:
On the body of the vase, a bearded man leading a horse to the right stands at the center of the composition. He is wrapped in a chlamys and carries a spear. At the left, a woman wearing a peplos holds out both hands, gesturing toward the departing man. At the right, a naked youth stands facing the man, gesturing with his right hand. On the shoulder of the vase, Herakles, at the left, moves toward the lion. Herakles wears a short chiton, a corslet, and a chlamys. He has his quiver over his shoulder, and carries his club in his right hand back ready to hit the lion. Iolaos, wearing a short chiton and chlamys, and holding a club, crouches at the right of the composition. In the predella, two sets of lions and boars confront one another.

The first labor of Herakles was to subdue a lion living near Nemea. Diodorus Siculus (Diod. Sic. 4.11.3-4) stresses that the lion was invulnerable to iron weapons. Most artists choose to illustrate Herakles strangling the lion, as a variety of literary sources relate the myth: the Diodorus passage cited above, Theok. 25, 266-271, and Apollod. 2.5.1. The painter of this skyphos chose to illustrate an episode related by Theok. 25, 253-261, that before Herakles strangled the lion, he knocked it senseless with his club. The schema with the lion prepared to spring and Herakles with his club finds its greatest popularity in the last quarter of the sixth century. In such scenes, the general composition for a fight or battle, as on Mississippi 1977.3.75, is applied to Herakles and the lion.

Although this vase is listed in the museum records as being attributed to the Acheloos Painter, Beazley placed this vase in the Manner of the Antimenes Painter. This latter attribution may be more accurate. Certain features of the vase, especially the depiction of a departure scene and the use of a predella, are not typically found in the Acheloos Painter's work, but are frequently found in the work of the Antimenes Painter and those in his manner — to which group it is attributed by Beazley (ABV, 277, no. 12).

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.70
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and the Nemean lion<lb>Side B: the same
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Robinson I, pl. 24; LIMC, V, Herakles, no. 1898, and 31-33; Moore & Philippides 1986, 59; Boardman 1974
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 150.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles and the lion. Herakles moves to the right, naked, with a chlamys draped over his left arm, attacking the lion which springs at him. He holds a club in his left hand, pulled back behind his body ready to bludgeon the animal. Side B has the same general scene but with differing details. On this side, Herakles holds the club in front of his body, and the lion is not leaping.

The first labor of Herakles was to subdue a lion living near Nemea. Diodorus Siculus (Diod. Sic. 4.11.3-4) stresses that the lion was invulnerable to iron weapons. Most artists choose to illustrate Herakles strangling the lion, as a variety of literary sources relate the myth: the Diodorus passage cited above, Theok. 25, 266-271, and Apollod. 2.5.1. The painter of this skyphos chose to illustrate an episode related by Theok. 25, 253-261, that before Herakles strangled the lion, he knocked it senseless with his club. The schema with the lion prepared to spring and Herakles with his club finds its greatest popularity in the last quarter of the sixth century. In such scenes, the general composition for a fight or battle, as on Mississippi 1977.3.75, is applied to Herakles and the lion.
artifact.shape_description: The Hermogenean skyphos has a deep bowl tapering at the foot, low flaring foot, and an offset lip. The lip is glazed, as is the body, except for two reserved bands. As on a band cup, decoration is limited to the handle zone, and generally consists of a small figural scene flanked by palmettes growing from the handles.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.69
artifact.summary: Side A: Dionysos in a donkey-cart preceded by a man and a goat. Side B: the same.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 149.
artifact.decoration_description:
On Side A, Dionysos is seated in a cart, drawn to the right, by two donkeys. The god wears a long chiton and himation, and an ivy wreath in his hair. He holds a grape vine, bearing clusters of grapes and blossoms in added white, in his left hand. The cart has two wheels and is of the type often seen hauling cargo, definitely different from the normal chariots used by the gods. The harnesses of the donkeys are rendered in added red and have leaf decoration in added white. A man moving to the left, looking back over his shoulder precedes the cart. He too wears an ivy wreath. He also wears a short chiton in added white, and a himation with added red dots. A goat precedes this man in turn. Side B is the same, only the added white is better preserved and there is some decoration on Dionysos' cart. An ivy tendril within lines of glaze decorates the lip of the cup. The handles are glazed. The lower body receives alternating red and black strokes above a black foot. The underside of the foot has concentric circles.

The theme of Dionysos in a donkey-cart is fairly unusual. The god is connected with donkeys early in Attic art with depictions of Dionysos sending Hephaistos back to Olympus mounted on one. In late black figure vase-painting, particularly in the early fifth century, scenes of Dionysos mounted on a mule become more common. The scene of Dionysos in a cart, like this one and Athens, Agora P26648 are related to the scenes of Dionysos mounted, with the emphasis being on Dionysos' pastoral/agricultural connections.

The Theseus Painter decorated a great many skyphoi and was the principal artist of the "White Heron group". The skyphoi by the Theseus Painter tend to be earlier than his lekythoi, probably dating to before 500.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.68
artifact.summary: Side A: Combat. Side B: Boxing match. Interior: Youth running to the right.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 148.
artifact.decoration_description:
On Side A, two armed warriors fight between spectators. The warriors are naked except for greaves and a Corinthian helmet. Each warrior has a sword at his waist, and brandishes a spear and a round shield. The shield device of the warrior on the right is a tripod. The spectators, four on the left and three on the right, are alternately naked and draped. On Side B, there is a similar composition with two boxers fighting in the middle of a crowd of spectators. The boxer on the left is older and bearded. Both boxers are naked and their hands and wrists are wrapped in leather thongs for protection. The treatment of the nine spectators is the same as on Side A. The tondo on the interior of the cup carries a naked youth running to the right and looking back over his shoulder.

Siana cups follow two systems of decoration. The "overlap" system treats the body and the offset lip as a single decorative zone. This is the system seen on the Mississippi cup, and is the earliest type of decoration for Siana cups. A "double-decker" system, which treats the body and the lip as separate zones, appears later in the workshop of the C Painter.
artifact.shape_description: The Siana cup develops from the Komast cup. The basic changes being a higher lip and foot. The shape appears to have been created circa 575 by the C Painter, and it continues in use until circa 525.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.65
artifact.summary: Side A: Dionysos between eyes<lb>Side B: Warrior and youths between eyes (Departure scene?)<lb>Shoulder: A, seated man with two youths; Dionysos and satyrs; B, battles<lb>Under handles: satyr
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 140
artifact.decoration_description:
On the body of Side A, Dionysos, holding an ivy branch in his right hand and a kantharos in his left, moves to the right between a pair of eyes. He wears a long chiton, a himation wrapped diagonally over one shoulder, and a wreath. On the shoulder of Side A, the center of the field carries a pair of eyes with a nose. Figural scenes then flank this central motif. On the left, a seated man is flanked by naked youths. The man is bearded, dressed in a long chiton and himation. He wears a fillet in his hair and holds a staff in his left hand. The youths both move to the right, with the forward figure looking back over his shoulder. On the right, Dionysos is seated between dancing satyrs. He holds a drinking horn in his right hand. On the body of Side B, a warrior moving right stands between two youths, with the scene again placed between a set of large eyes. The unbearded youths are wrapped in himatia and face the warrior. The warrior wears a short chiton, a corslet, a sword at his waist, greaves, and a Corinthian helmet with a bit of his beard showing out from the bottom. He carries a spear in his right hand and a Boeotian shield on his left arm. On the shoulder of Side B, there is again the central motif of eyes and nose, but both flanking scenes are fights. On the left, two warriors move to the right, attacking a falling warrior. All the warriors wear corslets, short chitons, greaves and Corinthian helmets, and carry a spear and a shield. On the right, a single warrior moving to the right attacks a falling warrior. The portrayal of the warriors is the same as on the left.

On the body of the vase, the area under the handles is filled with a running satyr carrying an ivy branch in each hand. The subsidiary decoration on the vase is fairly elaborate. The scenes on the body of the vase are separated from the shoulder by two lines. The shoulder scene is bounded on the top by a zone of tongue pattern. The neck is decorated with addorsed palmettes. The lower body is decorated with a simple key maeander running left, above a zone of lotus buds, above a zone of rays.

The Antimenes Painter decorated a large body of vessels, especially neck-amphorae and hydriae, in the last third of the sixth century. Several features of this vase are typical of his work, while certain others make this vase unique. The use of eye decoration is most frequently found on cups, but does occur on a small number of other shapes. The Antimenes Painter decorated a series of neck amphorae with eyes and Dionysiac scenes. Dionysiac scenes are common in the artist's repertoire, and the depiction of a seated Dionysos as on the shoulder of Side A was especially favored by the Antimenes Painter. In his depiction of Dionysos, the Antimenes Painter uses both the drinking horn and the kantharos, which began to replace the drinking horn in the 540s, as an attribute of the god. Also typical of the painter's style is the choice and placement of the subsidiary decoration. This Mississippi vase is exceptional, however, in that it has eyes on both the body and the shoulder. It appears to be a combination of two types of vases decorated by the Antimenes Painter. The first is the Dionysos mask between eyes (also with satyrs under the handles) placed on the body of the vase, like London B 266. The other type features decoration between eyes in an enlarged shoulder zone with the rest of the body glazed, like Louvre F 202. One example of this type, New York 64.11.12, either by the Antimenes Painter or close to him, has the eyes and a nose in the middle and scenes to the side, like the Mississippi vase. The Mississippi vase is the only instance of the Antimenes Painter combining these two decorative schemes.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.64
artifact.summary: Side A: Warrior between horsemen. Side B: Departure scene.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. no. 139.
artifact.decoration_description:
On Side A, a warrior stands in the center of the composition, facing right. The warrior appears to wear a very strange square hemmed chiton, which extends below his round shield. He also wears a Corinthian helmet and greaves. The shield carries five white balls as a shield device. Two horsemen shown frontally flank the warrior. They wear white chitons and greaves. Robinson 1956 interprets these figures as the Dioskouroi. The painter may well have intended them as such, but this is not certain. The Dioskouroi acquire identifying attributes relatively late, thus precise identification in Archaic art can be difficult. Riders are very popular in Attic vase painting of the sixth century, and not all pairs of riders were meant to represent the Dioskouroi.

On Side B, A young woman stands at the left of the composition facing right. She wears a decorated peplos and himation, and has a fillet in her hair. A spear leans against her shoulder. She gestures with her left hand toward the departing figure at the right. A bearded man wearing a long chiton and himation stands in the center, facing right. He holds a spear or staff in his left hand. On the right, a youth moves to the right looking back over his shoulder. He wears a fillet in his hair, a short chiton, and a mantle. He also holds a spear.

The neck of the vase is decorated with addorsed palmettes. A running meander above a zone of rays decorates the lower body of the vase. The area under the handles is filled with a palmette and lotus bud motif.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.63
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and the Boar. Side B: Woman between warriors.
artifact.collection_history: Once in the Robinson collection. Harvard Inv. 137.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles and the boar. In the center of the composition Herakles stands facing right, carrying the boar on his left shoulder. He rests his right foot on the rim of the pithos, within which Eurystheus cowers, raising his arms in supplication. Herakles is naked except for his sword. Herakles carries the boar with its head toward the rear. Iolaos stands at the left of the composition, facing right.
