Side B: battle. The scene is arranged in three groups. Nearest handle A/B a nude warrior moves to the right, long spear in his right hand, shield with apron on his left. His head is protected by a Chalcidian-type helmet and he fights a pair of warriors, also nude, who face him. One opponent, brandishing a sword, his left side under a shield, has fallen to his knees. He and the mate standing behind, who has come to his aid, also wear the Chalcidian-type helmet; the latter's has a crest and above the visor a floral design. The standing warrior wields a long spear and his shield has a snake emblem. A pair of combatants is next, one draped, one not. The nude man runs to the left, but has turned to parry the attack of the draped warrior who has his sword drawn. The chlamys or mantle has a broad stripe around the edge. The nude warrior's left is protected by a shield (device: tripod) which has an apron elaborately decorated with bosses and ranks of zigzags. The last pair, at handle B/A, again has a draped warrior battling one who is nude. The former wears a pilos, a cone-shaped helmet, the latter, as much as is preserved, carries a shield and, in his right hand, a long spear which, running under the handle and through the palmette, leads the viewer to the other side of the vase, to more battle (For palmettes, see Oberlin 67.61).

Under each handle an arrangement of palmette fans back to back, with abutting scroll tendrils at the center of the configuration: under B/A the top fan has eleven petals, the bottom one, nine; under A/B only the top fan is well-preserved and it has ten petals. The tondo is surrounded by a border of meanders, running left, punctuated approximately at the cardinal points, by dotted (raised) cross-squares; the cross-square near the bull's head is juxtaposed, mistakenly, onto a meander design. A meander pattern of similar design borders the exterior pictures below, one dotted cross-square, approximately in the center, on each side. Light brown glaze (tondo): the glaze in raised droplets for the knobs on Theseus' club; sheath and hilt of sword (not raised). Side A: scabbard of fallen warrior, sword hilt of first draped warrior near handle A/B. Side B: three bosses in relief (two above the ear and one at the join of the visor to the helmet) on the Chalcidian-type helmets; four rows of five bosses each on the shield apron of the nude warrior in the central group (bosses in high relief) and on the shield above for the tripod emblem (in relief); for the snake emblem (in relief) and the crest on the helmet of the second standing nude warrior.

Yellow dilute glaze: tondo: Theseus' rib cage, abdominal musculature, muscles of thighs, arms and neck, pubic hair; tassels on sword hilt; for the bull: strokes accentuating the rolls of flesh on the neck, the hairs inside the ear, wash on the forehead, tendons in the leg and chest; exterior: musculature of warriors as for Theseus.

Dark brown dilute glaze: tondo: for hero's hair and detail of his breastbone; exterior: wash for the inside of shields, beards, zigzags on shield-aprons, hair.

The attribution to the painter was made recently by Dietrich von Bothmer. The Penthesilea Painter was prolific (about 200 vases assigned), with the quality of his production occasionally superb, often competent, and sometimes disturbingly poor. The Elvehjem kylix is one of his best. Frequently the exterior of his cups is of lesser quality than the interior or tondo. His magnificent name-vase in Munich (Munich 2688: ARV2, 879, no. 1) has, on the exterior, a design of arming youths, drawn hastily. In quite remarkable style the interior depicts Achilles slaying the Amazon Queen, Penthesilea. The painter's artistry on the Madison cup is excellent, inside and out.

This decorator worked in white-ground as well as red-figure and he also is versatile in the choice of shapes he decorates, among them: plaques, a bobbin (toy?), a kylix without a foot, one with a cover, and another with an especially deep bowl. Likewise, his art is as ready to portray touches of humor as it is the reality of terror. A bewildered Paris tries to evaluate the beauty of three goddesses, each of whom makes "different" eyes at him, on a charming white-ground pyxis in New York (New York 07.286.36: ARV2, 890, no. 173). A bull seems to envision his fate as sacrifice on the interior of a cup at Oxford (Oxford 1931.12: ARV2, 884, no. 73). His best work exhibits monumentality, expressiveness in the characterization of his figures and an uncommonly wide range of color — in the case of the Elvehjem kylix, through the use of glazes. These virtues were learned no doubt from familiarity with mural painting. The design in the tondo of the Madison cup was perhaps inspired by contemporary sculpture, the metope with Herakles and the Cretan bull from the temple of Zeus at Olympia.

The sculptor of the metope and this decorator were faced with a dilemma: in a restricted space how does one design a hero of human scale proportionate to a beast, which, legend told, was of enormous size. Much like the pose of the Cretan bull at Olympia, the painter has lowered the bull's head, has exaggerated the rolls of flesh on the neck and compressed the powerful body. The viewer left to reconstruct the body fully extended would see the size worthy of the hero's special strength. Theseus was a hero of Athens, and like its hero, Athens had been terrorized by Persia on the plains of Marathon; Athens, like Theseus, had checked a threat and pestilence. As Louise Clark informally suggests, the bull may indeed be a fitting symbol for Persia; it is often depicted crowned at Persepolis. Coincidental to the victory over the Persians, the bones, allegedly of Theseus, were discovered on Skyros in 476 B.C. and piously moved home to Athens. The pictures on the exterior of the kylix may be stock, "the shirts against the skins." Mrs. Clark mentions informally that the nudity of one team may suggest an ambush. Pallas, Theseus' uncle, was anxious to secure the Athenian throne for his sons and in order to achieve this, Theseus was to be killed at ambush while sleeping. Laos, a herald, betrays the plot to Theseus who, feigning sleep, rises and defeats his enemies.

The Madison vase seems later in the painter's career. The head in three-quarter view is similar to the head of the man attacking a boar, represented in the tondo of a kylix assigned to the Penthesilea Painter now at The Metropolitan Museum (New York 41.162.9: ARV2, 882, no. 39). Dietrich von Bothmer recognized that the fragment from the Louvre (Louvre CP 11504/B) belongs with this cup; the fragment came to the Louvre in 1868, from the collection of the Marchesa di Campana.

There is a kylix by the Penthesilea Painter at The Art Institute of Chicago (Chicago 1889.27, from Cervetri, ARV2, 884, no. 77) which has as the interior scene a young man paying off a prostitute, and on the exterior, youths and women.

"The rope sketched by the Penthesilea Painter in the tondo was probably painted in red, now gone. For the subject of I, cf. ARV2, p. 880, no. 15 (now augmented). The Louvre fragment Louvre CP 11504 came to the Louvre in 1861 with the collection of the Marchese Campana (not '1868' and 'Marchesa di Campana'). It is no. 14 in ARV2, p. 880." (Letter of Dietrich von Bothmer to Warren G. Moon, 15 Feb. 1980)

(unpublished)

W.G.M.

artifact.name: Madison 1976.143
artifact.summary: Winged female figure walking right.
artifact.collection: Elvehjem Museum of Art, University of Wisconsin-Madison
artifact.essay_text:
The Painter of Palermo 4ca. 480-470 B.C.Lent by the Elvehjem Museum of Art, University of Wisconsin-Madison; gift of Mr. and Mrs. Arthur J. Frank (1976.143).

The Vase: h. 29 cm; max. d. 9.0 cm; d. of mouth 5.2 cm; d. of foot 6.9 cm. Intact; brush marks and slight streaking of glaze, misfiring on the reverse of body and foot; minor pitting and flaking under handle. Type 2 lekythos with fillet and incision between body and foot. Inside of neck glazed; pouring surface, edge and underside of foot reserved. The resting surface is flat except for a small, shallow conical depression at the center. Small vent above left wing of figure.

Decoration: Winged female figure strides right, carrying a fillet (in applied white, now faded) in her outstretched arms. The wings of the female extend onto the shoulder of the lekythos. The figure is positioned on a groundline composed of an uneven arrangement of pairs of stopped meander-patterns (r.), separated by a single cross-square, the corners filled (dotted) with an additional cross-square at the right end of the line. A thin band of close vertical strokes, with a reserved line above, accentuates the flare at the base of the neck. The figure wears an Ionic chiton and short himation, some of the folds of which, on the left sleeve and on the overfold, are in yellow dilute; the right sleeve is decorated with rows of x's between groups of pleats, the hem is bordered with a band of dots. Her hair is bound up with a dotted band. The tops of the wings are dotted. Around her right arm is a spiral bracelet. Thick relief lines: right thumb, lower edge of left sleeve, eyebrow, nape of neck, scalloped edges (top and bottom) of overfold and upper edge of right wing. The hair is outlined in reserve. Except in a few areas the figure is outlined in relief, giving sharp separation from the field. The figure's hands are reversed.

The concept of Nike, who the winged figure surely is, may have been accepted by the middle of the sixth century, because of the Panathenaic games, or before. The first Nike actually to be named on a vase is not until 530 B.C., on a Nikosthenic amphora now in Rome (Isler-Kerényi 1969, p. 32). She is a personification who brings the message of victory from the gods to the recipient, with great speed because of her gift of flight. In early Greek literature and thought, her identity and genealogy are confused: in Hesiod (Hes. Th. 383-384) she is the daughter of the Titan, Pallas, while in the Orphic Hymn 88, 4f., Ares is named as her father. In Bacchylides (Bacchyl. 11.4ff. she is a messenger of Zeus, the ultimate giver of victory, later, she became the embodiment of victory herself, eventually to be worshipped as a goddess (first at Elis in the mid-fourth century B.C.). Some feel her origin in Greek art can be traced to Near Eastern influence where winged mythological types are more common (Akurgal 1966, 183-195). In red-figure vase-painting, she appears frequently after the Persian Wars, ca. 479 B.C., visible clarion of civilization's defeat of the Persian barbarian. On these vases she is often shown carrying prizes to the victor — amphora, fillet, tripod or wreath — or, in some instances, sacrificial implements so that the recipient may return in proper measure the favor that the gods have bestowed (cf. the Nikai on the column krater, Chicago 1889.16). For a most recent discussion of Nike: Isler-Kerényi 1969.

This is certainly the lekythos which is added to the work of the Painter of Palermo 4 in Para. It has been claimed that the vase was painted by the Pan Painter, who is careless and clumsy at times, but never like this; the line alone could not be his. Two standard-type lekythoi near the Pan Painter, Oxford 313 and Oxford 314 (ARV2, 560, nos. 6 and 7), may have prompted the attribution: the maeander and cross-square borders, the winged Nikai, chitons decorated with x's and upper wings dotted, spiral bracelets, hair similarly bound up, the long lines of the chins. They are of course contemporary, and so is a lekythos in Palermo recalling the Triptolemos Painter (ARV2, 367, below) to whom Beazley saw a resemblance in the Oxford vases (CVA, GB 3, Oxford 1, pl. 33). The Triptolemos Painter has connections with Douris, and so does the Cartellino Painter whose lekythos, Athens 1633 (ARV2, 452, no. 4), has a flavor of the Elvehjem one, although it is decorated somewhat differently. The decoration of the Athens lekythos is typical of the so-called BL Class, from a large long-lived workshop which produced both black-figure and red-figure lekythoi — that of the Athena and Bowdoin Painters. One of the characteristics of BL decoration is the band of bars on the neck instead of the more usual tongues. The bars on the Elvehjem lekythos, and on others by the Painter of Palermo 4, and the resemblance in style to the Bowdoin Painter's own work (cf. Kurtz 1975, pl. 15) make it likely that the Painter of Palermo 4 had some connection with that shop, although Beazley had not actually formed the painter's oeuvre by detaching it from the Bowdoin Painter, as Arias implies in EAA, v, 873 (see J.D. Beazley, Greek Vases in Poland [Oxford 1928] 18f. and 79, addendum to p. 19). Another contemporary artist who painted lekythoi of the BL type is the Providence Painter. His Nike on a lekythos in (New York 07.286.67: ARV2, 641, no. 90) spreads her wing across the shoulder of the vase like the Elvehjem Nike does. This was habitual for winged figures on lekythoi with undecorated shoulders (Caskey & Beazley, 41).

The Elvehjem lekythos is a small window with a big view onto a major workshop of lekythos painters with which some of the most important artists of the time can be linked, no matter how different their styles. The view includes a glimpse of the interactions in the potter's quarter of Athens, which must have been a close but not closed community.

For reversed hands: M. Robertson, JHS 74 (1954) 229-230. For the Painter of Palermo 4, ARV2, 310. For relationships between the Triptolemus Painter and Douris, ARV2, 360; between Douris, the Cartellino Painter, and the Bowdoin Workshop, Kurtz 1975, 25, between the Providence Painter and the Bowdoin workshop, Kurtz 1975, 43.

Bibliography: Ars Antiqua AG Lucerne, Auktion (June 1966) no. 77, and pl. XIV; Para., 358, above, no. 4 bis.

W.G.Moon, L.Berge

artifact.name: London F 90
artifact.summary: Demeter and Kore (?) in a chariot drawn by two Erotes; surrounded by satyrs, maenads, and Aphrodite (?).
artifact.other_bibliography: P.E. Corbett "The Burgon and Blacas Tombs," JHS LXXX (1960) 52-60, pl. IV, 4
artifact.collection_history: Blacas Collection, 1867
artifact.decoration_description:
In the center of the composition is a chariot drawn to the right by two Erotes. They have curly hair, fillets decorated with trefoils, white cross-belts, and belts with white studs. They hold the reins between them, and the further one looks back at the other. In the chariot are two female figures (Demeter and Kore?), wearing fillets decorated with trefoils, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, embroidered chitons and himatia. The nearer one holds a goad in her right hand and the reins in both hands. Behind the chariot is a maenad dancing to the left, with her hair flying behind her. She wears the same type of fillet, jewelry, and a chiton, and carries a thyrsos in her left hand. Before her is a seated maenad, wearing earrings, necklace, bracelets, and a long embroidered chiton. She holds a string of beads. In front of the horses is a female figure seated on a rock to the right. She is attired similarly to the other seated woman, but her chiton is embroidered with stars, and she holds a string of beads in both hands. Before her, on a slightly higher level, is a maenad dancing to the left. She wears earrings, a necklace, bracelets, and a chiton. Her left hand is extended, in her right she holds a flower. Above her head is a satyr seated to the right, looking back. He wears a wreath and holds a string of beads in his hands.

On the upper row, on the left of the satyr, is an Eros to the left, wearing a wreath. He places his right arm on the shoulder of a female figure seated to the left, who looks back at him. She is dressed like the other females, and holds a string of beads in both hands. Beneath the Eros is an ivy plant. Next is an Eros moving away to the left and looking back. He wears a wreath, earrings, necklace, bracelets, and a short embroidered chiton with a wave pattern border, and holds a white fillet in each hand. On the left is a youthful satyr seated to the left, looking back, wearing a wreath and holding something in his left hand. Before him is an Eros wearing a fillet decorated with trefoils, and holding out a phiale with fruit in his right hand.

On the lower row, under the handle on the left, is a youthful satyr advancing, wearing a fillet decorated with trefoils, and holding a flower in his left hand and a thyrsos in his right. Next is Aphrodite (?) seated to the left, with a beaded cap, necklace, bracelets, a long embroidered chiton with a wave pattern on the breast, and sandals. Her right hand is held up as if beckoning to an Eros, who has curly hair, a fillet with trefoils, and a flower in his right hand, and is about to climb onto her knee. Behind her is a maenad dancing to the right, with her hair in a bunch, wearing a fillet with trefoils, earrings, a necklace, bracelets, and a similar chiton with wave pattern. She holds a thyrsos in her left hand, and her right is extended. Before her are a rabbit and a crouching satyr, who wears a wreath and holds out a kantharos in his right hand. Next on the right is a female figure moving away, looking back, with her hair pulled back, earrings, a necklace, and an embroidered chiton. She holds a tympanon. Under the handle is a maenad dancing to the right, wearing a beaded fillet, necklace, bracelets, and an embroidered chiton. She holds a thyrsos, and extends her other hand to a satyr, who has a wreath and a thyrsos in his left hand. He moves away from her, looking back and extending his right hand to her. The ground is indicated throughout by white lines and flowers are scattered about.

The lip of the vessel is decorated with egg-and-dart, as is the neck (here it is larger and more sloppy). Below the figures is a meander and checker pattern.

"Petty style, imitating the Meleager Painter" (ARV2, 1417.1)

artifact.name: London F 68
artifact.summary: Side A: Cult initiation of Herakles to the Mysteries. Side B: Dionysos and Hephaistos.
artifact.other_bibliography: B. Otto "Marsyas im Thiasos" Jahrbuch der Staatlichen Kunstsammlungen in Baden-Württemberg 12 (1975), 27, fig. 8; I. Scheibler Griechische Töpferkunst. Herstellung, Handel und Gebrauch der antiken Tongefässe (Munich, 1983) 64, 67, fig. 63.; Parke 1977, fig. 31; E. Simon 1983, pl. 8.1; E. Simon "Neue Deutung zweier eleusinischer Denkmäler des vierten Jahrhunderts v. Chr." AntK 9(1966) 89, 90, fig. 5; LIMC, III, pl. 469, Dioskouroi 169; Metzger 1965, 39, no. 27
artifact.comparanda: For initiation scene, compare to Naples 91083 (Bianchi 1974, 9).
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: The initiation of Herakles and the Dioskouroi into the mystery cult. On the far right, Triptolemos is seated in his winged car drawn by two white serpents. He is nude, with his mantle partly draped over his shoulder, and wears a laurel wreath in his hair. Holding up his right hand, he appears to be speaking to Persephone, who stands before him, half turned to the left. She holds a torch in her right hand, and looks over her shoulder at Triptolemos. She wears a white chiton with a cloak wrapped around her waist, a wreath in her hair, a necklace, armlets, and sandals. Her body is also painted white. In front of her Demeter is seated, with her body turned to the left but looking over her shoulder at Triptolemos. She wears a sleeveless chiton fastened at the shoulders, a wreath in her hair, earrings, a necklace, and armlets. She holds a sceptre in her right hand, and her body is painted white. Behind and above her is Artemis, also wearing a sleeveless knee-length chiton, lace-up boots, and a wreath in her hair. She holds a torch in her right hand, and gestures with her left towards Triptolemos. At the same level in the background as Artemis, but standing on the other side of Persephone, is Hekate. She wears a knee-length chiton similar to Artemis' and a wreath in her hair, and she also holds a torch in her right hand. She is leading one of the Dioskouroi forward from the far right. He is nude, with a cloak thrown over his shoulder, and holds a kind of fasces (painted white) decorated with projecting knobs, probably made of tied together palm branches. In front of him is a star. Corresponding to this figure on the far left of the composition is the other Dioskouros, moving forward towards the center. He carries the fasces, and his cloak is wrapped around his lower body and flung over his shoulder. He does not have a star in front of him. Below him, in the foreground, is Herakles, who moves toward the center of the scene. He holds a club in his left hand, and the fasces in his right. He looks back and upward, over his shoulder, as he strides forward. Above Persephone's head, and meant to be represented as far away, is an uneven line of a mountain, and above it an architrave and columns of a Doric building (probably meant to represent the Temple of Demeter at Agra, Catalogue, 57). The architecture is painted white. The identification of the two figures leading in the Dioskouroi and Herakles (Artemis and Hekate), have been suggested to be Iacchus and Eumolpos (or Eubuleus) instead (Bianchi 1974, 24).

The Cult of the Mysteries was one of the most important cult celebrations in Athens, and for reasons of politics as much as religion, the initiation of Herakles and the Dioskouroi was a favorite theme (Simon, Festivals, 28). Triptolemos is depicted because he was the mortal chosen by Demeter to bring grain to mankind; the chariot he sits in was her gift to him. Eumolpos was the ancestor and founder of one of the Athenian clans, the Eumolpidai, and Iacchus is thought to have been Dionysos in another guise (Simon, Festivals, 32). Iacchus has been described as "Semele's son and giver of wealth (schol. Aris. Frogs 479).

Side B: Dionysos and Ploutos recline on a kline while Hephaistos walks toward them. In the center of the scene is a vine, under which Dionysos and Ploutos recline on a kline, covered with a panther skin and embroidered pillows. Dionysos is seated on the left, and turns his head to the right to look at his companion. He holds a thyrsos in his right hand, and props himself up with his left elbow. His long hair is encircled with an ivy wreath and a diadem, and a mantle covers the lower half of his body. His companion, Ploutos, is beardless, and has short hair bound with a laurel wreath. A mantle also covers his lower body, but he is nude from the waist up. He looks towards Dionysos, and holds a keros (drinking horn) with both hands. To the left of Dionysos, and slightly behind him, is a woman dressed in a chiton with black border and wearing earrings and armlets. Her hair is bound up in a bun at her neck, and she wears an ivy wreath. She holds a flat basket of fruit in her left hand, and extends her right over Dionysos' head as if she were placing something on it. In the upper left corner of the composition a woman sits with her body to the left, but looks to the right. Her hairstyle is the same as the other woman's, and she wears a sleeveless chiton. She holds a dish of fruit with her right hand, and with her left she pulls the hem of her chiton over her shoulder. Below her is a satyr bringing a dish of fruit to Dionysos; a nebris (fawn skin) hangs from his left arm, and he wears an ivy wreath in his hair. On the far right, Hephaistos walks in, supported by another satyr. This satyr also wears an ivy wreath, and carries a torch in his right hand. Hephaistos has his right arm slung around the satyr's shoulders, and walks unsteadily. He wears an ivy wreath, and a cloak over his shoulders. He carries a pelekys (double-edged axe) over his left shoulder. In the center of the composition, below Dionysos, a small Eros runs bent over to the right; he holds a string in his hands, the other end of which is held in the beak of a running duck or swan.

artifact.name: London F 65
artifact.summary: Side A: Lovemaking scene. Side B: Three youths.
artifact.other_bibliography: K. Schauenburg "Frauen im Fenster," RM 79 (1972) 6, pl. 8.2
artifact.condit: Fragments missing on Side A.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: On the left, a youth is seated in a chair, in profile to the right. His cloak is thrown over the chair seat and back, and he is nude, wearing only a wreath in his hair. He drapes his right arm over the chair back, and his left above his head, in a relaxed attitude. In front of him stands a boy, also nude and wearing a wreath in his hair, who is about to climb onto the youth's lap. He steadies himself with his right hand on the chair back, while he uses the staff in his left hand to help himself up. His left foot is on the chair seat. The purpose for this maneuver is made clear by the youth's erection; they are about to engage in homosexual sex. To the right of these two is a Doric column, painted white, and then a bearded man wearing a mantle wrapped around his waist and a wreath in his hair. He stands with his left hand on his hip and watches the goings-on. To his right is a woman standing in a doorway, the upper part of which is open. She leans her elbows on the sill, and also watches the youth and boy. Keuls (293) suggests that because this is not a "typical" homosexual love scene (a youth and a mature man), it depicts male prostitution. The architectural setting and the two people watching would tend to confirm that.

Side B: Three draped youths are in conversation. They are all completely covered in himatia, and wear thin wreaths or fillets in their hair. The one on the left stands with his body frontally, and head turned to the right. The center figure is in profile to the right, and the third is in profile to the left, gesturing with his right arm and speaking to the other two.

The upper band of decoration is an olive wreath, the lower is meanders and crossed squares.

artifact.name: London F 582
artifact.summary: Swan standing on a flower, surrounded by tendrils
artifact.condit: There are chips in the paint at the rim.
artifact.decoration_description: The design is in white and yellow paint on a black ground. A swan stands to the right, with its wings spread. It perches on a flower, the tendrils of which spread to either side, over the body of the vase. The swan is painted white, with yellow bill and legs. The wings are picked out with yellow. The neck of the vase is encircled by white vertical lines, and a row of yellow dots.

artifact.name: London F 473
artifact.summary: Side A: Seated Eros<lb>Side B: Seated woman
artifact.condit: The knob of the vessel is missing, and the surface is badly chipped, especially on Side B.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A winged Eros is seated on a rock (?). He is in profile to the right, sitting in a slumped-over position. He has a necklace or chain of some type looped over his left shoulder, then down across his chest and under his right arm. He wears bracelets and anklets painted white, and a white wreath in his hair. His wings are also highlighted with white paint. He holds a phiale containing white fruit or eggs in his left hand.

Side B: A woman sits on a chair which has crossed legs. Her legs are in profile to the right, but she twists her upper body around to look toward the left; her right arm is stretched out behind her in this turn, and a necklace dangles from her hand. In her left hand, she holds a platter. She wears a mantle which is only draped around the lower part of her body, and her hair is held up in a bun.

The shoulder of the vessel is decorated with ivy leaves outlined in white, with incised stems and clusters of berries (a favorite decorative pattern of this painter, Trendall 1967, 597). The upper border of the figural panel is two rows of alternate checks, and the lower border is a wave pattern. There are palmettes under the handles.
artifact.shape_description: Skyphoid pyxis.

artifact.name: London F 303
artifact.summary: Side A: Symposium. Side B: Dionysiac scene.
artifact.collection_history: Temple Collection, 1856.
artifact.condit: Some of the figures are restored, and the flower knob is damaged.
artifact.comparanda: This vase provides links with the "H.A.," Varrese, and Dublin Situla Painters. The woman bending forward holding the wreath—cp. to Varrese Painter's Taranto 8922, Basel Antikenmuseum s. 33, and Zürich Univ. 2654. (Trendall & Cambitoglou 1978, 334)
artifact.decoration_description:
Around the body is a frieze divided into two scenes: Side A: A symposium is depicted. In the center of the composition is a couch with a mattress on the top, placed on raised ground, on which recline three youths to the left. The youth on the right is looking back. They all have drapery over their lower limbs, and their left arms rest on embroidered cushions. The one on the left wears a fillet in his hair, the one on the right, a wreath. The middle one wears two fillets twisted, one is white and decorated with flowers. The youth on the left holds a branch, the one on the right a phiale, and the middle one holds a kylix with one finger, as if playing kottabos (a drinking game). In front of the couch are two tables, on one is a kylix, on the other a kantharos, a pomegranate, and other fruit. Between the tables is a situla with a fillet around it, and to the left of the tables is a flat basket ornamented with a meander, in which is fruit. On the left is a female figure to the right, with her hair in a knot behind and falling in curls to her shoulders. She wears earrings, a necklace, an embroidered chiton, an undergarment with yellow sleeves, and white shoes. She is playing a double flute. Behind her a female figure approaches, with similar hairstyle and jewelry, but also bracelets. In her right hand is an Apulian sistrum, and in the left she holds a dish of fruit. On the right of the banqueters is a female figure to the left, with the same clothing and jewelry as the flute-player. In her left hand she holds a phiale, from which she sprinkles incense on an incense burner in front of her. Behind her a youthful satyr approaches, with a fillet ornamented with trefoils, a white kantharos in his left hand, and a situla in the right, on which is painted a seated female figure in yellow. Between these two figures, and between the two on the left, are vines spreading over the scene; in the field is a rosette. The ground lines are indicated by white dots.

Side B: In the center of the composition Dionysos is seated to the left, looking to the right. He wears two fillets twisted together, sandals, and his drapery lies under him. He holds a wreath in his right hand, a thyrsos in his left. Before him to the left stands a female figure with her left foot on raised ground, holding out a wreath with both hands. Her hair is bound up; she wears a radiated cap, earrings, bracelets, a sleeveless chiton and sandals. Below Dionysos are two phialae, a large basket, and a myrtle twig; behind, on a lower level, is a youthful satyr. He wears a fillet, and carries a thyrsos in his left hand. With his right he offers Dionysos a white kantharos with black bands. On the left is a youthful satyr to the right, wearing a fillet and sandals, and carrying a torch in his left hand. Before him is a tall plant. Behind him is a female figure to the right, similar to the woman offering the wreath. She holds out a tympanon with her left hand, and a white bell (?) is her right. Above are two rosettes, and the ground line is indicated by white dots.

On the cover, between two bands of egg-and-dart pattern, is a frieze of figures. First is a seated female, holding up the open lid of a box. Her hair is gathered up under a cap, and she wears earrings, a necklace, bracelets, a chiton and himation, and shoes. At her side is a fan, on which is painted a white palmette. Before her are a rosette and a flower. Next is a female figure running to the right, dressed as the seated woman. She holds out a wreath in her left hand, and before her, in the field, is a tendril. Eros runs to the right, looking back. His hair is tied back in a bunch, and he wears a necklace, bracelets, sandals, and holds a fillet in both hands. Before him is a plant. Next is a female figure seated to the left. Her hair is pulled back, and she wears earrings, a necklace, bracelets, a chiton and himation, and shoes. She holds up a mirror in her right hand. Lastly, a female figure runs to the left, wearing earrings, a necklace, bracelets, a long chiton and himation, and holding out an embroidered fillet in her right hand.

Around the lip of the vessel is an egg-and-dart pattern, around the neck, ivy. On the shoulder is a radiated tongue pattern and egg-and-dart, while below the figural designs are meander and checker patterns. The stand is fluted; around the top of it is an egg-and-dart pattern, and around the foot is an ivy wreath. On the top of the cover is a plastically modelled flower, the edges of the petals are very broken.

artifact.name: London F 284
artifact.summary:
Side A: Young warrior and his horse in a naiskos, with male and female offering bearers around
Side B: Visitors to a tomb
artifact.sources_used: H. Lohmann Grabmäler auf unteritalischen Vasen (Berlin 1979) 214, no. A339, pl. 20, 2; M. Schmidt, A.D. Trendall, and A. Cambitoglou Eine Gruppe apulischer Grabvasen in Basel (Basel 1976) 54-57
artifact.other_bibliography: Robrertson 1975, 483, 486, pl. 152b
artifact.collection_history: Hamilton Collection
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: In the center of the composition is a naiskos with two Ionic columns, a timbered ceiling, and pedimented roof. It stands on a base decorated with scrollwork. Inside the naiskos stands the statue of a nude young man, wearing a cloak around his shoulders. He stands before his horse, which is in profile to the left, holding a wreath with his right hand, and a spear in his left hand; he rests his left elbow on the horse's back, above which is a cuirass. Outside of the naiskos, to the left, sits a youth wearing a pilos and fillet, with a pear and shield. Near him stands a woman, bending forward, holding a mirror and a wreath. To the upper right of the naiskos, a nude youth sits. He holds two phialae in his right hand, a branch in his left, and he wears a wreath. He is sitting to the left, on top of a cloak. Below him a woman stands to the left, holding a situla in her right hand and an oinochoe in her left. On the neck of the vessel is a female head in three-quarter view to the right, surrounded by scrolls and flowers.

Side B: People are bringing offerings to a grave. A large stele tied with a red fillet is in the middle of the composition. It is set on a base decorated with scrollwork. On either side, in the upper left and right, sits a nude youth to the left. They both wear fillets in their hair, and are seated on their mantles. The youth on the left holds up a large box in his right hand, and a wreath in his left. The youth on the right also holds a box in his right hand, but a situla in the other. Below each is a woman wearing a sleeveless chiton, with her hair bound up in a bun. The woman on the left wears earrings, a necklace, and bracelets. She holds a tympanum and a bunch of grapes. The woman on the right holds a basket and ivy wreath.

The mascaroons are decorated with female heads which have white curly hair and skin on Side A, and dark hair and skin on Side B. Around the shoulder of the vessel is a radiate band pattern, under which is a band of egg-and-dart. Below the figural scene is a meander band. Under the handles are palmettes.

The style of the Lycurgus Painter is closely associated with the Underworld Painter, especially in the treatment of draped women and the rendering of faces. The pattern work (especially the flowers and scrolls on the neck) are more like those of the Patera and Ganymede Painters (Schmidt, 54).

artifact.name: London F 272
artifact.summary:
Side A: Centaurs at the wedding feast of Peirithoös, the lovesickness of Phaidra
Side B: Dionysos with satyrs and maenads
artifact.sources_used: H.R.W. Smith Funerary Symbolism in Apulian Vase-Painting (Berkeley, 1976) 187-188; Trendall 1976, color pl. A; Richter 1966, 27, 61, figs. 113, 327; Trendall 1989, pl. 195
artifact.other_bibliography: E. Bielefeld Zur griechischen Vasenmalerei des 6. bis 4. Jahrhunderts vor Christus (Halle 1952) fig. 45; K. Schauenburg "Göttergeliebte auf unteritalischen Vasen," Antike und Abendland 10 (1964) pl. 2, fig. 4; M. Grant and J. Hazel Who's Who in Classical Mythology (London 1973) 330; Williams 1985, pl. 69
artifact.collection_history: Fittipaldi Collection, afterwards in possession of Prince Napoleon Bonaparte.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: The upper register depicts what might be the lovesickness of Phaidra. In the center is a large couch, the legs of which are inlaid with palmettes, volutes, and Gorgoneia, while along the front are spirals and other patterns. On the couch is a mattress with a lozenge pattern and an embroidered purple cushion at each end. Beneath it is a large low stool with inlaid patterns in white, yellow, and purple. In front of the couch are two female attendants who stand facing each other. The attendant on the left holds up a large white fan in her right hand, and extends her left to to the other woman, whose hands are placed behind her head. The first wears earrings, a double necklace, a long chiton and overblouse which falls to her hips. She also has sandals, and her hair is gathered under a close-fitting cap. The other wears earrings, a double necklace and long, transparent chiton. She has shoes, and her hair rises in a mass over her forehead and falls loosely on her shoulders. On the left is Phaidra, seated on a four-legged cushion to the right, with a downcast face. Her legs are crossed, and her hands are clasped on her right knee; her feet rest on a footstool. Her hair is gathered up under a veil, and she wears earrings, a double necklace, bracelets, a long chiton, and sandals. Behind her and above her head hangs a sistrum tied with a purple fillet. Before Phaidra hovers Eros to the left, represented on smaller scale with long hair and sandals, holding out a fillet. Behind Phaidra is a nurse standing to the right, with white hair, a long girt chiton and himation. The nurse's right hand supports her chin, and her left is extended. On the right is a paidagogos standing to the right, with white hair and a beard, a short girt chiton, bordered himation, high boots with white tops turned out, and a crook in his left hand. His right hand is extended as if he were conversing with the female figure facing him. She wears earrings, a necklace, a veil, a long chiton and himation. Her right hand is placed under her chin. Above, behind the paidagogos, hangs a cista, on which are painted human figures in white.

The lower register of Side A depicts the combat between the Lapiths and the Centaurs at the wedding feast of Peirithoös. A centaur advances from the right, wearing a wreath and panther-skin draped over his shoulders and knotted in front. He carries a branch in his left arm, and seizes Laodameia by the left arm and around her neck. She has just stepped down from a chair, which has very ornamented legs and a cushion (similar to the couch decribed above). Laodameia has long hair and wears a diadem, earrings, triple necklace, long transparent embroidered chiton, and sandals. Her right foot is placed on a footstool, and she looks back at Peirithoös, who advances and seizes the centaur's right arm. He is nude and beardless, with short curly hair, a chlamys thrown over his left arm, and a sword in the right. Above each of them their names are inscribed: *L*A*O*D*A*M*E*I*A ("Laodameia") and *P*E*I*R*I*Q*O*O*S ("Peirithoös"). Behind Peirithoös is a female figure retreating and looking back, with a white fillet in her hair, long bordered chiton with an overblouse, and a broad scarf floating behind. She also wears sandals, a bracelet on her right arm, and she extends both hands in astonishment. On the right, Theseus advances. He is beardless, with a chlamys over his left arm, his left hand extended to seize the centaur, whom he is about to strike with a club in his right hand. Above him his name is inscribed *Q*H*S*E*U*S ("Theseus"). Behind him is a female figure retreating and looking back. She has a veil on her head, her hair is tied in a knot with a fillet, and she wears earrings, a double necklace, bracelets, a long chiton and himation, and sandals. Below the centaur is a yellow situla. The ground-lines of both scenes are indicated by white dots. Smith (187) notes that in the myth the briade's name was Deidamia or Hippodamia, not Laodameia.

Side B: In two scenes, Dionysos reclines on a couch, surrounded by his followers. On the upper level in the center of the composition, a youthful Dionysos is seated to the left, looking back. He wears a fillet, anklets, sandals, and his drapery is thrown down beneath him. He holds a phiale in his right hand,and a thyrsos head downwards in his left. Above him is a cluster of grapes, and on the left a tree. Beyond the tree is a female figure seated to the left, looking back. Her hair is tied in a knot with string, and she wears a radiated open cap, double necklace, a bracelet on her right arm, a long girt chiton fastened on the shoulders, and sandals. She holds a thyrsos in her right hand tied with a fillet, and a wreath in her left. On the right is a similar female figure, looking back (she wears a bracelet on her left arm, no girdle, and a tympanon in her left hand).

On the lower level, Dionysos reclines to the left on a kline with embroidered hangings in the center of the composition. He is beardless, with long hair, a wreath, and a himation over his lower body. His left leg is doubled up under him, and he rests his left elbow on a purple embroidered cushion and holds a white kantharos in his other hand. At his feet, a female sits on the kline, facing him. Her hair is tied back with a string under an open cap radiated in front, and she wears a double necklace, bracelet on her left arm, a long chiton, a himation over her lower limbs, and sandals. On her lap is a tympanon, and in her right hand she holds out a small white prochoös. Behind her is a youthful satyr, wearing a fillet, carrying a large krater with both hands. It is fluted at the top and bottom, and has three human figures painted on it, in white and yellow. In front of the couch is Pan, represented in smaller scale, beardless, and with goat's legs. He moves to the left, with a branch in his right hand, and a dish of fruit in his left. Behind him to the right is an incense burner. Behind Dionysos stands a female figure with hair as the last, wearing earrings, a necklace, bracelets, a long chiton, and an overblouse. She holds up a wreath in her right hand to crown Dionysos, and in her left is a thyrsos.

Above the scenes, along the rim, is a laurel wreath. Below, the vase is fluted.

artifact.name: London F 271
artifact.summary: Side A: The madness of Lycurgus<lb>Side B: Pelops and Hippodameia
artifact.other_bibliography: M. Floriani Squarciapino, "Pelope ed Ippodamia nel frontone orientale di Olimpia," ASAtene n.s. XIV-XVI (1952-1954) 131-140; O.J. Brendel, "Der grosse Fries in der Villa dei Misteri," JdI 81 (1966) 206-260; L. Séchan, Études sur la Tragédie grecque dans ses rapports avec la céramique (Paris 1926) 452; M. Borda, Ceramiche apule (Bergamo 1966) 107, color pl. 7
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: The madness of Lycurgus is depicted. The composition is arranged in two rows of figures, one over the other. In the center of the lower scene stands Lycurgus. He is about to kill his wife, whom he has thrown down and his holding by the hair with his left hand, while he pushes her down further with his left knee. In his right hand he brandishes a double-edged axe. His hair and beard are shaggy and disheveled, and his chest and stomach are covered with hair. He wears a panther skin cap, a chlamys thrown over his shoulders and fastened in the front with a circular brooch, and high, lace-up boots. His sword hangs at his left side, suspended by a shoulder-belt. His wife has fallen with her left leg doubled under her. She raises both hands above her head, and tries to loosen his grip with her right hand. Her hair is disheveled, and a stream of blood flows from the wound above her left breast. She wears earrings, armlets, a double necklace, a chiton, embroidered peplos, and sandals. Her chiton is belted at the waist and fastened at the right shoulder, leaving her left shoulder and breast uncovered. Behind Lycurgus, to the left, is a youthful male looking on at the scene. He raises his left hand as if chastising Lycurgus, and his right is placed at the back of his head in a gesture of despair. He has moderately long hair and whiskers, but no beard. He is nude except for a chlamys flung over his left arm, and high, lace-up boots. A sword hangs suspended from a shoulder strap on his left side. Behind him is a (shorter) paidogogos, advancing slowly and carrying a crooked staff in his right hand. His hair amd beard are white, amd his face covered with wrinkles. He wears a knee-length chiton, belted at the waist, a chlamys which hangs over his left arm, and high lace-up boots. Under his chiton he wears a tight-fitting long sleeved top, decorated with a lozenge pattern, each lozenge containing a white spot. To the right of Lycurgus, a male and female carry away his dead son. The female is closest to Lycurgus, and looks toward him with an expression of sorrow. She wears earrings, a necklace, a chiton which is belted at the waist, a tight-fitting blouse under the chiton, which is decorated with zigzag and horizontal lines, and shoes. She holds the dead body with both hands. The head of the dead youth falls backwards, and his right arm hangs down lifelessly. Blood flows from a wound in his right side, and a chlamys is thrown over his body. The male supports his legs; he also looks towards Lycurgus. He wears a sword, chlamys, and high lace-up boots. Both he and the dead youth have disheveled hair and whiskers, but no beard. In the center of the upper scene, above Lycurgus, is a winged figure, probably Lyssa. She hovers in the air, partially surrounded by a triple radiate circle, and with her right hand points a kentron (goad) at Lycurgus. Around her left arm are twined two snakes; she wears a cap, earrings, a necklace, and a long embroidered chiton (which rises up to her knees in her rapid descent). Two shoulder belts cross her breast diagonally, and her chiton has a belt decorated with white studs. On the ground below her (but still above Lycurgus' head) are a hydria lying on its side and a flower. Behind her are a male and female group; the male is probably Ares. He is seated on a stool, holding a spear in his left hand and looking sorrowfully on the scene. The female stands on the far left of the composition. She is stooping forward, resting her left foot on rising ground and moving both hands as if speaking to him. Her hair is bound up, and she wears earrings, a necklace, armlets, an embroidered chiton, and sandals. On Lyssa'sr right is Apollo, seated in three-quarter position to the left on a throne. He is beardless, and his hair falls over his shoulders in long ringlets. He wears a laurel wreath and a chlamys is thrown over his lap. In front of him is an altar with a burning offering. In his left hand he holds a heptachord lyre, and he raise his right to the side of his head. His head is turned towards Hermes, on the right. Hermes stands in profile to the left, with his right foot resting on a rock. He holds out his right hand, as if addressing Apollo, while in his left he holds the caduceus. His petasus (cap) is painted white, and hangs behind his head. He holds his chlamys over his left arm, and wears high boots with wings on them.

Side B: The contest for Hippodameia is depicted. The composition is again arranged in two groups of figures. In the lower register, a large basin on a pedestal (both painted white) occupies the center of the scene. In front of it and on lower ground is Pelops, seated on rocks. He is nude and beardless, wearing high lace-up boots and sitting on his mantle which is thrown over a rock. He looks to Hippodameia on the left, while supporting his left elbow with his right hand, which rests on the pommel of his sword. He seems to address Myrtilos on his right with the gesture. Between him and Myrtilos is a tall Ionic column (it reaches into the upper scene), with a tripod on top. Part way up the column hangs a bucranium, with a fillet. Myrtilos, wearing high lace-up boots, a chlamys, and a petasus (cap), stands to the far right of the lower scene. His left foot is turned to walk away, and he holds a chariot wheel as he looks at Pelops. Both he and Pelops have whiskers, but no beard, and curly hair. Between them, near the column, is a tall flower. Hippodameia stands to the left of Pelops. Her hair is bound up, and she wears earrings, a double necklace, armlets, an embroidered chiton with looped up sleeves, a bordered peplos, and sandals. Her right hand is on her hip, and her left extended to Pelops. Behind her is another female, either Hera or Sterope (Hippodameia's mother), who pushes her forward with her left hand. Her hair falls in long ringlets over her shoulders, and she wears a diadem, earrings, a double necklace, armlets, an embroidered chiton and peplos, and sandals. Her peplos is pulled over the back of her head, and her right arm and hand arm hidden in it. In front of her, on the ground, is a flower. In the upper scene, Aphrodite is seated above Hippodameia. She sits in three-quarter profile to the left, on a stool with meander decoration. She wears a cap from which her hair projects in a mass behind, and a veil at the back of her head. She wears earrings, a necklace, armlets, a chiton with looped up sleeves, an embroidered peplos, and sandals. She rests her left hand on the stool, and holds a corner of her veil with her right. Before her to the left stands Pan, leaning forward with his left foot raised on a rock and holding a laurel branch tied with a sash in his right hand. He is youthful, wearing a wreath of reeds and having a short tail. On the other side of Aphrodite, above the basin, is Eros. He is seated on a rock, on which his chlamys is spread, and he holds a myrtle wreath towards Aphrodite, but looks to Myrtilos. He wears a cap, shoulder belt, and sandals. To the far right, above Myrtilos, is a female figure. She is perhaps a local nymph; seated on a decorated cista, she looks toward Hippodameia. Her hair is bound up, and she wears earrings, a double necklace, armlets, a chiton, an embroidered peplos, and sandals. Her chiton has looped up sleeves, and has slipped off of her right shoulder.

Around the rim of the vessel are palmettes. The area below the figural section is fluted.

artifact.name: London F 197
artifact.summary: Side A: Departure of a warrior<lb>Side B: Youth and woman
artifact.sources_used: J. Beazley "Groups of Campanian Red-Figure," JHS 63 (1943) 78; Williams 1985, p. 64, fig. 73; Trendall 1966, pl. 13a; F. Weege "Oskische Grabmalerei" JdI XXIV(1909) 151, fig. 23
artifact.other_bibliography: Trendall 1989
artifact.comparanda: The veiled woman on Side A is very much like those on the bell kraters Louvre K 261 and Santa Maria Capua Vetere 72.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A woman offers a warrior a drink at his departure. The woman stands in profile to the right, her left foot forward and her weight resting on the right leg. She wears a chiton with sleeves to the elbow, and a mantle is draped over head head. She holds a skyphos in her right hand, and an oinochoe in her left. In front of her face is a circular floral pattern, while above that, hanging from the border decoration at the shoulder of the vessel, is a half circle painted white. The warrior stands frontally, with his head turned to the left, looking at the woman. He holds a spear in his right hand, and balances a shield on the ground with his left. He wears breastplate of three circles and a plumed helmet (typical of native Oscan warrior—see F. Weege, Oskische Grabmalerei, JdI XXIV (1909), 150, figs. 21, 22 for examples) which are both painted white. His short chiton is decorated with dots, perhaps representing an animal skin.

Side B: A youth and a woman are represented.

The lip of the vessel is decorated with a radial band pattern, the neck with a large palmette, and the shoulder with another radial band pattern. The lower border is a wave pattern, and there are palmettes under the handles.
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora with twisted handles.

artifact.name: London F 194
artifact.summary: Side A: Woman, Naiad, River-god (Man-faced bull) and Eros<lb>Side B: Two draped youths<lb>Neck, A: Siren; B: Female head
artifact.collection_history: Blacas Collection
artifact.comparanda: The Siren's head on the neck of the vessel can be compared to that on London F 250.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A woman stands with her head in profile to the right, holding an oinochoe in her right hand and a mirror in her raised left. She wears her hair in a bun, with a wreath on her head, a necklace, bracelets, and a long sleeveless chiton, girt at the waist. To the right is a laver set on a base, with several laurel branches growing around it, and a propped-up phiale. Eros hovers over it, facing right, with his right foot touching it and his left one raised (apparently resting on a rock behind the laver). He holds out a wreath over the bull rider's head, and a fruit and necklace in his other hand. He is nude, but wears a wreath, bracelets, and strings of beads over his left shoulder and around his right thigh. Next, a man-faced bull walks to the left. It has the body and horns of a bull, with a bearded man's face. On it is seated a woman, wearing a sleeveless chiton, necklace, and wreath in her hair, which is also in a bun. She daintily holds one of the bull's horns with her right hand, and balances a hydria on her knee with the other. Above her head to the right is a veiled head in a window, looking at the scene. A fillet hangs from the window. The oinochoe, mirror, laver, bull's horns, veiled face, and hydria are painted white. It has been suggested that this is Dionysos in the form of a bull, bringing Semele (his mother) back from Hades (Walters, 99). The veiled face is similar to those from Greek sepulchral reliefs, and is suggestive of the Underworld. On the neck of the vessel is a Siren in profile to the left, with hair in a bun, wearing a wreath and a necklace. Above and below it are phialae.

Side B: Two youths stand facing each other. They wear wreaths and himatia. The one on the left has a branch in his right hand and a fruit and necklace in his left. The other youth holds fruit. Between the two figures is a tendril, and above that, a window. Behind each youth is a fillet and a phiale. On the neck of the vessel is a female head to the left, with hair in a bun, wearing an embroidered cap, beaded fillet, and necklace.

On the neck of the vessel is a wave pattern. On the shoulder is a flower with leaves on either side (Side A) and a tongue pattern (Side B). Below the handles are palmettes, and running below the figural design on both sides is a wave pattern.

artifact.name: London F 189
artifact.summary: Side A: Two comic actors in costumes and masks on an elevated stage<lb>Side B: Two youths
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Gr. Brit. 2, Brit Museum 2; Trendall 1966, pl. 14b, p. 11; Walters 1893, 97, 98
artifact.other_bibliography: Williams 1985, p. 64, fig. 74b; Trendall 1989, 202, 203
artifact.collection_history: Castellani Collection, 1873.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Scene from a comedy. A high stage is supported by a Doric column and two pilasters, from which hang two purple fillets and four vine branches. On it a father drags his son home from a banquet. The father is on the right; he has a mask with short, stiff, white hair, a beard and moustache. He wears a jerkin and leggings, over which is a short white chiton with yellow stripes and a purple border, and an embroidered mantle is wrapped round his body and over his left arm. He wears a purple phallus and has a padded stomach, which is the standard equipment of comic actors. In his left hand he carries a hooked stick, and he walks to the right, looking back, while grabbing his son's wrist with his right hand. The son wears a mask with black hair and beard, and a wreath. He carries a lantern in his right hand, and a phiale (drinking vessel) and purple fillet with yellow spots in his left. He wears clothes similar to his father's. Behind him is a swan, pecking on the ground.

Side B: Two youths stand facing each other. The one on the left has long curly hair, in which is a wreath. He wears a long chiton and himation with a dotted border, sandals, and carries a staff. The other wears a fillet, and his clothing is similar to the first. In his right hand he holds a fillet and a white fruit or ball, in his left is a staff. Between them a fillet hangs on the wall.

The himatia borders are typical of Python's style (Trendall, 203, fig. 17).

The upper border is a laurel wreath, the lower is a wave pattern. Palmettes are below the handles.

artifact.name: London F 179
artifact.summary: Side A: Dionysiac scene. Side B: Thiasos.
artifact.sources_used: Trendall 1989, pl. 86; T.B.L. Webster Monuments Illustrating Tragedy and Satyr-Play (London, 1962): 81, no. LVI, pl. 5c; A. Trendall Phylax Vases (London, 1967): 96.
artifact.other_bibliography: G. Schneider-Herrmann Red-figured Lucanian and Apulian Nestorides and their Ancestors (Amsterdam, 1980): fig. 50, 50a; J. Charbonneaux Grèce Classique (Paris, 1969): fig. 352
artifact.comparanda: Webster (81) notes that a dramatic mask of an elderly woman's head is unusual, and cites two other examples where it appears: Naples 2858 and London 1958.2-14.1.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Dionysiac scene. On the left, a maenad in a long, black bordered chiton stands on a higher level (really on top of one of the palmette decorations). In front of her, beginning at ground level, a grapevine grows, twisting around a white vertical pole, and then growing to the right, to cover the head of Dionysos. A young, nude, beardless satyr with a cloak draped around his shoulders reclines against the vine, and wraps his right arm around it. In his left hand, he holds a white kantharos. A small olive tree grows in the field just above the cup, and also one at the groundline, directly below. On the grapevine hangs a white painted dramatic mask of an elderly woman's head, with furrowed cheeks and wearing a veil. In the center of the composition, Dionysos sits on a cloak, in a three-quarter view. He is beardless, nude, with long curly hair and a band wrapped round his head. He and the satyrs wear short boots. Behind and to the right of him stands a little satyr, who leans casually on the god's shoulder. Below them on the groundline a deer reclines. To the right, a maenad in a short embroidered chiton and cap, pelt, belt, and lace-up boots stands frontally. She turns her head to look at Dionysos. Under her, there is one more olive tree on the groundline, to the right of the deer. To the far right stands a nude satyr with a Pan-pipe. He is bearded and has white hair. On Side A, the neck of the vase is decorated at the highest level with an elaborate maeander, below that an olive wreath, below that a black band, and below that a tongue or ray pattern. On the shoulder is a palmette band, and lower down a spiral pattern. Webster (81) notes that a dramatic mask of an elderly woman's head is unusual, and cites two other examples where it appears: Naples 2858 and London 1958.2-14.1.

Side B: Thiasos. On the left stands a maenad, in a similar position to the left hand maenad on Side A. She wears an elaborate embroidered gown and cloak, and a wreath in her hair. She holds a shield in her left hand. Below and to the right of her sits a young, nude, and beardless satyr. He balances an amphora on his left shoulder and holds a thyrsos in his right hand. Above and to the right of him, in the center of the composition, a youth stands, apparently balancing himself on the seated satyr's leg with his right foot. The youth is nude, although he has a cloak draped over his left arm. He also carries a large bell krater with that hand. Over his head, maybe hanging on a wall, is another cloak or piece of cloth. Lower down and to the right is a maenad. She wears a wreath in her hair, and her gown is unfastened at the right shoulder, exposing her breast. She holds a situla and runs to the right, looking back. On the right and higher up sits a youth in three-quarter view to the right; he also looks back and raises his left arm toward the center youth. He has a cloak draped about him, wears a wreath in his hair, and holds a lyre. The neck of the vase on this side is decorated at the top with an olive wreath, below that a spiral pattern, next an ivy pattern. On the shoulder is a tongue pattern, then egg and dart. The handles on both sides are decorated with pinwheel-striped rotelles, and an ivy pattern. Under the handles are palmettes, and the border below the figural panel is a maeander and crosses.

artifact.name: London F 174
artifact.summary: Side A: Departure of a warrior<lb>Side B: Four draped youths
artifact.other_bibliography: Trendall 1974, 48, no. B51; A. Cambitoglou and A. Trendall "Addenda to Apulian Red-Figure Vase Painters of the Plain Style," AJA 73 (1969): 423-433; N. Moon "Some Early South Italian Vase Painters," BSR 11 (1929): 30-49
artifact.comparanda: Side B, the animal leg in background: Matera 9978 (no. 63)
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: On the left, a man stands leaning with his right hand on the border, and with his left supports a shield balanced on the ground. His right leg is crossed casually in front of his left. He wears a short embroidered chiton, leggings, and lace-up boots, all of which are traditional Oscan costume. He looks towards a woman at the center of the composition, who is walking in profile to the right. She wears a long crinkly peplos with an overfold to her knees (the portrayal of this type of dress is characteristic of the painter); her hair is bound up in a scarf. She pours an offering from the vessel she is holding (which is a nestoris, an Italian vessel shape) into the phiale held by the youth at right. He is dressed in Oscan costume, like the first man, and is leading a horse off to the right.

Trendall (1989, p. 24) notes that this is one of the first Apulian vases to show people wearing native costume. The representation of the nestoris is also unusual.

Side B: Four draped youths. On the left, a youth is shown frontally, with his head in profile to the right. His right hand is on a staff, and his left on his hip. He wears a himation draped to leave his chest and right shoulder free. An animal leg (?) is suspended on the wall in the background. It is also present in the composition of Matera 9978 (no. 63), but there is no explanation for it. To the right a youth wearing a diadem stands in profile to the left, as if in conversation with the first character. He is wrapped in a himation with a black border, so that only his feet and head show. On the wall to the right is a set of hand weights. The third youth to the right wears a himation like the first. He stands frontally, with head in profile to the right. His right arm is extended, and he holds a staff. His left hand is on his hip. A cross-shaped object is suspended from the wall to his right. The last youth stands in profile to the left. He is completely wrapped in a himation like the first one.

The rim of the vessel is decorated with a olive wreath border, while the neck has an ivy and berry pattern. The upper border of the figural scene is a tongue pattern, while the lower is a maeander and crosses. In the center of the composition on Side A, hanging from the upper border, is a semicircular pattern decorated with rays and a spiral pattern. The vertical borders are a pattern of checks.

The Sisyphus Painter is "A highly competent draughtsman, but his larger compositions lack unity, being often arranged in studied groups, which seem to be inspired by sculptural originals, like the Parthenon and Phigaleia friezes." (Trendall 1966, p. 19).

artifact.name: London F 159
artifact.summary: Side A: Sacrifice of Iphegenia<lb>Side B: Adonis, a man and two women
artifact.other_bibliography: FR, 165, fig. 80
artifact.comparanda: This vase reflects the influence of both the Iliupersis Painter and the Painter of Athens 1714. Cp. reverse to Leningrad 586 (no. 6) and also vases in subgroup of Copenhagen 335.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Sacrifice of Iphigenia. In the center of the scene is a square altar with two steps. To the right of the altar stands Iphigenia; with her head bowed she looks up in trepidation at the altar. Her hair is loose and flowing over her shoulders and she wears armlets and a chiton. Behind her and almost concealed is a deer standing on its hind legs, which was substituted for her as a sacrificial victim. Behind the altar stands Calchas, the priest. He wears a mantle wrapped around his waist and draped over his left arm, and holds out the sacrificial knife towards the head of the deer. In his left hand he holds a sceptre. Above him hang two garlanded bucrania. On the left of the altar is a youthful beardless attendant, stooping forward with a basket of fruits and branches in his left hand, and an oinochoe in his right. he wears a mantle which is wrapped around his waist and looped over his left arm. Above and to the right of him is Apollo, seated on a chlamys which is thrown over a rock. He is beardless and holds a laurel branch in his right hand. His body is in three-quarter profile to the left, but he turns his head to the right to watch the sacrifice. On the far left is a female standing at ground level, who holds a flower (?) in her left hand, and rests her right on her hip. Her hair is in a bun, and she wears a necklace, armlet, a chiton, and a peplos. On the far right Artemis stands in the middle field (level with the top of the altar). In her right hand she holds a bow, and in her left two spears. Her hair is drawn back and held in place with a diadem, and she wears earrings, a necklace, armlets, a knee-length chiton, a black bordered chlamys fastened at the breast with a circular brooch, and high, lace-up boots. The chiton is belted and has straps criss-crossing her breast.

Side B: Two youths and two women. In the center is a youthful seated male (Adonis?), looking to the right and holding two spears in his left hand. He is nude, and seated on a chlamys. Above his head hangs a shield with a star decoration. To the right stands a youthful male, who holds a staff in his right hand, and has a chlamys draped over his left arm. He and Adonis wear diadems. Next to him is a female holding a phiale. She wears earrings, a necklace, an armlet, and a chiton. To Adonis' left is a female holding up a mirror, who also wears earrings and an armlet.

On the neck, Side A, are two griffins with palmette between. On the handles are gorgon masks, with white faces and brown eyes and hair. At the lower attachments the handles terminate in swans' heads.

This vase reflects the influence of both the Iliupersis Painter and the Painter of Athens 1714. Cp. reverse to Leningrad 586 (no. 6) and also vases in subgroup of Copenhagen 335.

artifact.name: London F 157
artifact.summary:
Side A: The ambush of Dolon
Side B: Two woman presenting wreaths to two youths.
artifact.other_bibliography: W.B. Stanford and J.V. Luce The Quest for Ulysses (London, 1974): 27, fig. 13; F. Lissarrague "Iconographie de Dolon le loup," RA 1 (1980): 11, 27, fig. 10; P. Levi Atlas of the Greek World (New York, 1984): 127
artifact.condit: On both sides, the figures are restored in places.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: In the center of the composition between two leafless tree trunks is Dolon. His lower body is turned to the left, while he looks over his shoulder to the right. His legs are slightly bent and he appears to be tiptoeing. He has a moustache and whiskers, and wears a skin hat, a spotted skin knotted around his neck, and leggings. Under the skin cloak, he has a short chiton, and a quiver decorated with a wave pattern hangs at his left side. He holds a knotted spear in his right hand, which he is pointing at Diomedes, and in fright is just letting go of a bow held in his left hand. To the left, Odysseus steps out from behind one of the trees. His left hand is on Dolon's shoulder, and he prepares to drive him through with the sword in his right. Odysseus is bearded, and wears a pilos (cap), chlamys, and lace-up boots (endromides). On the right, Diomedes comes out from behind the other tree. He stretches out his right hand to seize Dolon, and in his left he holds two spears. He is bearded, and wears a crested helmet with cheek pieces, decorated with a crouching wolf, a chlamys, and lace-up boots. The mantles of Odysseus and Diomedes are decorated with black borders; Odysseus' also appears to be lined with spotted skin. The scene is bordered by two more tree trunks at the far edges.

Dolon was the only son of Eumedes, a Trojan herald. He went to spy on the Acheans at the encouragement of Hector, who promised him Achilles' horses as a reward. However, he was caught and killed by Odysseus and Diomedes. Trendall (11) thinks that this vase ". . . gives a burlesque version of a heroic theme, the ambush of Dolon as described by Homer (Hom. Il. 10.338 ff.), and may well have been influenced by the paintings of Zeuxis of Heraklea, who was famous for his caricatures." The figures are represented in very graceful positions, almost like a ballet (D'Agostino 1974, 258).

Side B: Two women offer wreaths to two youths. On the right is a youth clad in a mantle, in profile to the left. Before him stands a woman with her hair bound up in a diadem, wearing a necklace, and a belted chiton. She faces the youth, and holds up a wreath in her right hand, while in her left is an embroidered sash. Behind her in profile to the left is a naked youth. His left hand rests on his hip, and he reaches forward with his right to receive a wreath from the other woman. Her hair is long and curly, and she also wears a necklace and chiton, as well as a peplos. She offers the wreath with her right hand. All of the figures wear sandals.

On both sides, the upper band is a painted olive wreath, below which is an egg-and-dart pattern. The lower band is another egg-and-dart pattern, under which is an acanthus and palmette design.

artifact.name: London E 439
artifact.summary: Side A: Dionysos Mainomenos. Side B: Satyr playing auloi.
artifact.sources_used: Smith 1896, 233; J. Maffre "Quelques scènes mythologiques sur des fragments de coups attiques de la fin du style sévère," RA 2 (1982) 203- 205, fig. 6; D. Paquette L'Instrument de Musique dans la Céramique de la Grèce antique (Paris, 1984), 39, fig. A4
artifact.other_bibliography: H. Kenner Das Phänomen der verkehrten Welt in der griechische-romischen Antike (Bonn, 1970), 121, fig. 34; LIMC, III pl. 312, Dionysos 151
artifact.comparanda: In shape and style, compare to a vase in the Pomerance Collection ARV2, 298 and 1643 (Philippaki, 53)
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Dionysos Mainomenos ("the frenzied Dionysos"). Dionysos walks to the left, his hands held above his head. In his right hand, which is raised before him, he holds the hindquarters of a fawn (or kid) which he has torn in half. He holds the forequarters in his other hand. He looks downward with his eyes wide open and staring. An ivy wreath is in his hair, and he wears a loose-fitting, crinkly chiton which falls in even folds below the red belt at his waist. A spotted panther's skin flung around his shoulders, with the paws tied at the neck. His feet are clad in high, laced boots.

While it is common to see maenads, the followers of Dionysos, tearing up animals, it is unusual to see the god himself doing this (Maffre, 204).

Side B: A satyr walks to the right, playing auloi. He wears an ivy wreath in his hair, which falls in long ringlets on his neck and over his bald forehead. In front of his face is the inscription *K*O*M[*O*S] ("song").

At the mouth of the vessel are two rows of dotted egg-pattern, on the shoulder are tongues. The lower border on both sides is a meander alternating with cross-squares. The decoration is Nolan style, but the small palmette at the base of the handles is not orthodox (Philippaki, 54).
artifact.inscriptions: On Side B, in front of the satyr's face is the inscription *K*O*M[*O*S] ("song").

artifact.name: London E 437
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Acheloos<lb>Side B: Satyr and Maenad.
artifact.sources_used: G. Ahlberg-Cornell Herakles and the Sea Monster in Attic Black-figure Vase-painting (Stockholm, 1984): 100, 105, fig. 37; Boardman 1975, fig. 54; Bruhn 1943, 113-114; Philippaki 1967, 2, pl. 2
artifact.other_bibliography: LIMC, 1 pl. 50, Acheloos 245; Schefold 1978, fig. 195; Poliakoff 1982, pl. 24; Birchall & Corbett 1974, 34; R. Flacelière and P. Devambez Heraclès, images e rècits (Paris, 1966): pl. 16; J. Charbonneaux Grèce Archaique (Paris, 1968): 315, fig. 361; Gerhard 1840-1858, pl. 115
artifact.condit: Broken and restored. Side B is very damaged with many fragments missing.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles and Acheloos fight. Herakles, nude and wearing a wreath in his hair, is to the left and partially hidden by Acheloos, whom he is grabbing in a wrestling hold. He grabs Acheloos by the horn with one hand, and has the other hand at his throat. With his left foot he straddles the snake body of Acheloos. Acheloos' body from the breasts up is human (or satyr, with pointed ears and snub nose), but the rest of him is a Triton, with scales and dorsal fins. He grabs Herakles' wrists and tries to free himself, unsuccessfully. There is the inscription *F*A*N*F[*A*I*O*S] *E*P*O*I*E*I ("Pamph[aios] made [me]"). Bruhn (113) also notes the inscription &epig-rough;*E*R*A*K*L*E *A*X*E*L*O*I*O ("Herakles, Acheloos") on Side A, and *O*R*E*I*Q*U*A ("Oreithua") on Side B, but no one else notes this and it is not visible in photographs. Herakles and Acheloos is a rare subject on red figure vases, but common on late sixth century black figure ones. Oltos is unique in showing Acheloos as half-satyr, half-triton (Philippaki, 2). It is also suggested that portraying him with a bull's horn and a Triton body is actually showing all at once the successive phases of his transformations (Ahlberg-Cornell, 100).

Side B: A dancing maenad is shown, wearing a chiton, himation, and animal skin. She carries a tree, crotalon (castanet) and ivy wreath. Opposite her is a flute-playing satyr.

At the shoulder on both sides, tongues and an ivy pattern. At the base there are rays, and around the handle attachment points are tongues and palmettes.
artifact.inscriptions: Side A: *F*A*N*F[*A*I*S] *E*P*O*I*E*I ("Pamphaios made [me]"). Bruhn (113) also notes the inscription &epig-rough;*E*R*A*K*L*E *A*X*E*L*O*I*O ("Herakles, Acheloos") and *O*R*E*I*Q*U*A ("Oreithua") on Side B, but no one else notes this and it is not visible in photographs.

artifact.name: London E 432
artifact.summary: Side A: Artemis attacking a fawn. Side B: Three youths.
artifact.other_bibliography: E. Simon Der Götter der Griechen (Munich, 1969): fig. 143; J. Overbeck Griechische Kunstmythologie: besonderer Theil (Leipzig, 1871-1889): pl. 21, 27; M. Bieber "Attische Reliefs in Cassel," AM 35 (1910): 10, pl. 3; Schefold 1934, pl. 1, b
artifact.collection_history: Blacas Collection.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Artemis stands in the center of the composition, her body turned to the right in a three-quarters view. She holds a deer (white with black spots) by its ear with her left hand, and brandishes a torch in her raised right hand. The deer's head is raised, and its hind legs collapse beneath it. Artemis wears a peplos with a black border, which is belted at the waist. To the left, Zeus is seated, with his head in profile to the right, observing the scene. He holds an upright staff, and has long curly hair and a beard. His mantle is draped to leave his chest and right arm free. To the far right is Apollo, who is nude except for a chlamys draped around him. He has long, curly tendrils of hair, and he leans on a staff with his left arm. Between Apollo and Artemis is a Nike with spread wings. She is wrapped in a mantle around her waist and left arm. She touches Artemis' head with her left hand.

Side B: Draped youths face each other. In the field is a ball(?).

Below the figural band is an egg-and-dart pattern. Above is the same, with a band of checks over that. On the rim is also an egg-and-dart pattern. Under each handle is a palmette on an inverted palmette.

artifact.name: London E 424
artifact.summary: Side A: Peleus accosting Thetis. Side B: Dionysos with Satyr and Maenad.
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1989, 191, 192, fig. 390; D. Brinkerhoff "Hypotheses on the History of the Crouching Aphrodite Type in Antiquity," JPGM Journal 6-7 (1978-1979) 83-96.
artifact.other_bibliography: Simon & Hirmer 1976, 157, 158, pl. LII; Williams 1985, 60, 61, fig. 67; Henle 1973, 21, fig. 13; Folsom 1976, pl. 64
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Peleus capturing Thetis. In the center crouches the nymph Thetis. She is nude, with a blue-green cloth draped over her knees. Her hair is bound up in a scarf. Peleus, to the left, grabs her right arm. He is also nude, except for a chlamys and a cap on his head. A sea monster has entwined itself around his right leg. Above and to the right of Peleus' head hovers Eros. These three main characters are surrounded by Nereids, who show various levels of surprise and fright at Peleus' appearance. The one on the far left wears a chiton with black border. She looks towards the main scene and raises her hand in fright. Above her to the right sits another Nereid. She wears a himation draped to leave her right arm and shoulder free, and her hair is pulled up in a scarf. She looks down more calmly on the scene. To the right of Thetis a woman in a black bordered chiton walks to the right, looking down at Thetis, while on the far right a nude woman crouches on the ground, holding her garment in her hands. Between these two, near the ground level, is a small leaping dolphin, while above, the last Nereid flees to the upper right hand corner of the composition. She is also nude, and carrying her garment. There is gold paint used for Peleus' hat, Thetis' hairband, and also some of Eros' wings. Blue is used for the remainder of the wings, green for drapery over Thetis' knees. Eros and Thetis have white skin.

Thetis was a sea nymph who could change her form, and to win her love, Peleus first had to capture her. He is shown here grasping her arm as she bathes at the seashore. The sea monster coiled around his leg was the artist's way of representing the nymph changing form. Brinkerhoff (91) says that "The crouching Thetis shows a turned head, a twist to her body, and a raised left leg on which the left elbow rests, all foreshadowing the position of the Hellenistic statue. . . " The pose of the fleeing nymph on the right was probably inspired by wall-painting.

Side B: Dionysos between a satyr and maenad.

The rim of the vessel is decorated with an egg and dart pattern, as is the neck just above the figural panel. The band below the panel is a maeander and check pattern.
