artifact.name: London E 410
artifact.summary: Sides A and B: Birth of Athena.
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1975, 194, fig. 355; Smith 1896, 214, 215; LIMC, II pl. 550, Artemis 1275, pl. 745, Athena 358; Richter 1966, fig. 105
artifact.other_bibliography: Schefold 1978, 21, fig. 7; Gerhard 1840-1858, pl. 3-4; A.H. Smith 1910, 7
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Poseidon stands on the left, in profile to the right. He wears a chiton and himation, a diadem in his hair, and holds a trident in his right hand. Above his head is the inscription *P*O*S*E*I*D*W*N ("Poseidon"). Behind him a winged Nike moves rapidly forward and extends her right hand before her in an expression of amazement. Her hair is bound up with a double diadem, and she wears a chiton with sleeves over which is a bordered outer garment. To Poseidon's right is Hephaistos, wearing a short sleeveless chiton and carrying his axe slung over his left shoulder. He wears a purple wreath in his hair, and has a chlamys thrown over his shoulder. He runs to the left, and looks back at Zeus. His hand is raised to his face and he points to Athena with surprise. Over his head is the inscription &epig-rough;*E*F*A*I*S*T*O*S ("Hephaistos"). Zeus is seated frontally in the center of the composition. He wears a sleeveless chiton and peplos with a thin black border near the bottom. His hair is gathered up under a laurel wreath, and his beard is long and pointed. In his left hand he holds a scepter, while with his right he gestures towards Poseidon and Hephaistos in surprise. The legs of his throne are richly decorated with palmette, star and lozenge patterns, surmounted by Ionic capitals. His feet rest on a transverse rail. Athena (under life size) has just sprung out of his head, and stands on her left leg with the right one kicked out behind her. She is fully dressed, wearing a crested helmet, peplos, and aegis. She also carries a spear. Above each character are their names, *Z*E*U*S ("Zeus") and *A*Q*E*N*A ("Athena"). To Zeus' right is Eileithyia, who looks round at him as she moves away and gestures in surprise. She wears a diadem which holds up her hair, a chiton and a short overgarment reaching her hips. Above her head is the inscription in retrograde *H*I*L*E*I*Q*U*A ("Eileithyia"). To her right is Artemis, advancing toward the center of the scene. She raises her right hand with a gesture of surprise, and holds a bow in her left. She wears armlets and a chiton with a short overgarment reaching her waist. Her hair is bound up in a triple diadem, with a hairnet below to hold the ends of it. Over her head is inscribed *A*R*T*E*M*I*S ("Artemis").

Side B: the same scene is continued. Behind the Nike is a youthful male figure (Apollo?). He is beardless and his hair is bound up with a wreath, although three ringlets fall in front of his ear. He wears a mantle which leaves his right arm and shoulder free. Behind him is Dionysos, wearing a chiton with sleeves and a peplos. He carries a thyrsos in his left hand, and wears an ivy wreath in his hair. Over his head is the inscription *D*I*O*N*U*S*O*S ("Dionysos"). A middle-aged, balding man is behind him. He has a beard and wears a wreath in his hair. He also wears a mantle which leaves his right arm and shoulder free, and holds a staff in his right hand. Back-to-back with this figure is Hades. He has a white beard and hair, and wears a bordered mantle. He also holds a staff in his right hand.

The figural panels are bordered by an upper horizontal band of palmettes, and a lower band of meanders and crosses.

This vase has been described as being "remarkable for the beauty of its drawing" (Catalogue, 215), but a less complimentary view was taken by Boardman (194), who said the "florals are atrocious, the figures little better."
artifact.inscriptions: Over the heads of the appropriate characters, names are inscribed: *P*O*S*E*I*D*W*N ("Poseidon"), &epig-rough;*E*F*A*I*S*T*O*S ("Hephaistos"), *Z*E*U*S ("Zeus"), *A*Q*E*N*A ("Athena"), *H*I*L*E*I*Q*U*A ("Eileithyia"), *A*R*T*E*M*I*S ("Artemis"), and *D*I*O*N*U*S*O*S ("Dionysos").
artifact.painter: Painter of the Birth of Athena

artifact.name: London E 41
artifact.summary: Side A: Theseus abducting Antiope. Side. B: Man (or youth) and woman between two mounted youths. Int: Theseus and rescued maiden(?)
artifact.sources_used: B. Cohen 1978, 379 ff., pl. 86, 2,3; J. Neils "The Loves of Theseus: An Early Cup by Oltos," AJA 85 (1981), 177-179 pl. 40-41, fig. 1, 3, 4; Smith 1896
artifact.other_bibliography: Williams 1985, 38, pl. 44; LIMC, I, pl. 683; Schefold 1978, fig. 205 (1)
artifact.condit: Broken and restored.
artifact.comparanda: Oxford 1927.4065 Same scene with addition of Poseidon and charioteer.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Theseus carrying away Antiope, the Queen of the Amazons, in a quadriga. Theseus has long hair bound with a myrtle wreath, and wears a chlamys and cuirass. He stands in the chariot, holding in his left hand the reins and two spears, and in his right, which is restored, the reins and a goad. Over the horses is the partial retrograde inscription [*Q*E*S*E]*U*S ("[These]us"). Theseus' left arm supports Antiope, who wears a Phrygian cap wreathed in myrtle and terminating in a spike, earrings, a jerkin reaching the hips, and tight-fitting pants. At her left side her quiver is hung from a shoulder belt, and her jerkin is ornamented with parallel, indented lines and bordered with a meander pattern. Her belt also has a meander pattern, and her pants are decorated with spots. She leans over the arm of Theseus, turning away from him and looking backward; in her left hand she holds her bow, and in front of her face is the inscription *A*N*T*I*O*P*E*I*A ("Antiope"). Behind her advances Perithoos, armed with a Corinthian crested helmet, a round shield, a cuirass over a short chiton, greaves and two spears. He is bearded and has long hair. His chiton is embroidered, bordered with a meander pattern and fringed. He raises his right hand toward Antiope, and in front of him is inscribed retrograde *P*E*R*I*Q[*O]*O*S("Perith[o]os"). Behind him is Phorbas, armed with a Corinthian crested helmet, a cuirass over a short chiton, a sword hung at his left side, and greaves. In his left hand he holds a spear, he is looking back over his shoulder, and in front of him is the retrograde inscription *F*O*R*B*A*S ("Phorbas").

Side B: Two figures, a man and a woman, flanked by youths on horseback. The man, on the left, leans forward on his staff and extends his left hand to address the woman. His head is missing, and he wears a mantle which leaves his right arm uncovered. The woman wears a chiton and peplos, armlets and sandals. Her head is also missing. She stretches out her right hand toward the man, and in her left she holds a flower. Both youths are nude; behind the one on the right is the inscription *X*A*X[*R]*L*L*I*O*N ("Cachrylion"). These figures are described in the 1870 British Museum Catalogue (279) as the Dioskouroi taking leave of their parents, Leda and Tyndareus, while Neils (179) thinks that Theseus and Helen are depicted.

Int.: A female stands on the right, holding a flower. On the left stands a beardless man with long hair, playing a lyre. He wears a vine wreath in his hair, and a mantle which leaves his right arm uncovered. In front of his head is the inscription *X*A*I*R*E *S*U ("Greetings to you"). The female has long hair looped up in a diadem, a necklace, armlets, and sandals. With her left hand she raises the chiton she is wearing above her ankle. Beazley (AR) thinks that these two are Theseus and one of the rescued maidens, and cites the François vase for comparison. In this case, the female is more likely to be Ariadne.

According to Neils (178) this is the earliest Attic representation of Theseus abducting Antiope, as it pre-dates the pediment of the Temple of Apollo Daphnephoros in Eretria. Oltos painted this scene at least one other time; a later cup (ca. 510 B.C.) at Oxford (Oxford 1927.4065) depicts the same actors, with the addition of Poseidon and a charioteer. The British Museum cup was made towards the end of the early part of his career. His earlier horses have red-glazed manes and tails, and no body markings except the lines of the shoulders and cheek, "they bring to mind the products of a cookie cutter" (Cohen, 378). These horses are more detailed, and their temperaments seem to agree with the individual scenes; those in the abduction scene are very spirited, tossing their heads back, while those on the reverse are calm.
artifact.inscriptions:
Side A: Over the horses is the partial retrograde inscription [*Q*E*S*E]*U*S ("[These]us"). In front of Antiope's face is the inscription *A*N*T*I*O*P*E*I*A ("Antiope"). In front of Perithoos is inscribed retrograde *P*E*R*I*Q[*O]*O*S ("Perith[o]os"). In front of Phorbas is the retrograde inscription *F*O*R*B*A*S ("Phorbas").

Side B: Behind the youth on the right is the inscription *X*A*X[*R]*L*L*I*O*N ("Cachrylion").

Int.: In front of the man's head is the inscription *X*A*I*R*E *S*U ("Greetings to you").

artifact.name: London E 382
artifact.summary: Side A: Satyr negotiating with hetaira. Side B: Telephos, Orestes, and Agamemnon.
artifact.sources_used: LIMC, I pl. 192, Agamemnon II; E. Keuls "Male-Female Interaction in Fifth-Century Dionysiac Ritual as Shown in Attic Vase Painting," ZPE 55 (1984) pl. 19.12; E. Keuls "The Conjugal Side of Dionysiac Ritual and Symbolism in the Fifth Century B.C.," Mededelingen van het Nederlands Instituut te Rome 11 (1985) pl. 4.23
artifact.other_bibliography: Keuls 1985, 365, fig. 305; G Penso La Medecine Romaine, L'Art d'Esculape dans la Rome Antique (Paris, 1984), pl. 45; C. Bauchhenss-Thüriedl Der Mythos von Telephos in der antiken Bildkunst (Würzburg, 1971)
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Satyr and hetaira. She stands in profile to right, holding her right hand out, palm up. She wears a chiton and a long cloak over it. Her left arm is wrapped around the cloak. Her hair is up in a bun, held in place with a diadem or scarf. The satyr is in profile to the left, facing the woman. He is nude, and touches his genitals with his left hand while pointing to the woman with his right. Keuls suggests that he is negotiating for sex with the woman, and she also notes that in general satyr/hetaira scenes are depicted as being less violent than satyr/maenad scenes (Keuls, "Conjugal," 29).

Side B: Telephos is seated on an altar, holding the child Orestes. On the left, Agamemnon enters. He is nude, with a cloak thrown over his arms. He holds a spear in his right hand and his left is held out in supplication. Telephos is also nude, with a cloak thrown over his shoulders. His left thigh is bandaged, and he holds a spear in his right hand. Both adult men are bearded.

Euripedes based a drama on the story of Telephos, who received the wound in his thigh from Achilles, while defending Mysia from the Greeks. The wound could not be cured until the one who wounded him healed him. In order to convince the Greeks to help him, Telephos (on the advice of Clytemnaestra) grabbed Orestes and threatened to kill him if he didn't receive aid. Odysseus interpreted that the "one who had wounded him" was actually Achilles' spear; after anointing the wound with rust from the spear, Telephos was saved. In this depiction, Telephos is shown in a non-threatening way, carefully holding the child. It is interesting to note that both Sides A and B depict "bargaining," albeit in two very different forms.

There is a band of maeanders as the upper and lower border for the panel.

artifact.name: London E 38
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Busiris. Side B: Banquet scene. Interior: Man with flute and dancing girl in leopard skin.
artifact.sources_used: A. Bélis "Charnières ou Auloi?" RA 1 (1988): 109-118, fig. 3.; Boardman 1975, fig. 75; B. Cohen 1978, pl. 95.2; Schefold 1978, 134, fig. 172; Robertson 1975, pl. 78, ab
artifact.other_bibliography: Birchall & Corbett 1974, fig. 32; J. Maffre "Quelques scènes Mythologique sur des fragments de coupes Attiques de la fin du style sévère" RA 2 (1982) 215 fig. 14; D. Paquette L'Instrument de Musique dans la céramique de la grèce antique, Etudes d'organologie Paris, 1984; Brommer 1974, II pl. 11a; Keuls 1985, 164, fig. 137; Durand 1986, 112, fig. 30; LIMC, III, pl. 128, Bousiris; Schefold 1978, fig. 172
artifact.comparanda: Side B, position of third banqueter: kylix by Douris London E 49. Int., woman's panther skin: silens on red figure kylix by Epiktetos RISD 25.077, also a black figure kylix with a warrior wearing a pelt Villa Giulia and Heidelberg 18.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles, Busiris, and four Egyptian attendants. In the center of the scene stands Herakles. He wears a lion skin and short chiton, and a quiver hangs at his left side. He is bending forward to grab Busiris by the arm, while he raises his club with his right hand to hit him. Busiris lies cringing on the ground before the altar. He raises both hands in supplication, and he is bleeding from his cheek and head. To the left, two attendants run away from the scene, looking back over their shoulders. The furthest one carries the makhaira or sacrificial knife, while at his feet is the kaneon (offering basket). Next to him, the other servant wears a mouthpiece for the flute, and is carrying the flute case on his back. On the right hand side, two more servants run away, and also look back. The furthest one has apparently dropped a cithara, which lies on the ground at his feet. Next to him, the other servant is carrying an oinochoe. The Egyptians (including Busiris) wear chitons and wreaths; their heads are shaven and their features very Nubian. Above the scene is the inscription *P*U*Q*O*N *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Python made [me]").

This scene relates the story of the death of the Egyptian king Busiris, who was told by the Cypriot prophet, Phrasius, that in order to stop the famine in the land he would have to sacrifice all strangers entering the kingdom. After sacrificing the first stranger (Phrasius himself) Busiris attempted to kill Herakles, who broke lose from his bonds and killed the king instead.

Side B: Symposion or banquet scene. On the left stands an auletrix (flute player). She wears a scarf covering her hair, earrings, and a chiton and peplos. Before her, a bearded man reclines on his left elbow on a dining couch, his left hand casually draped over the side. He flings his head back, and supports it with his right hand bent behind his neck. His drinking cup sits on the ground in front of the flute girl. To the right stands a nude boy holding an oinochoe, with which he fills the drinking bowl of the second banqueter. This man is balding, and has a scarf tied around his forehead like a fillet. He holds a kylix out to the boy with his right hand, while extending his left hand toward him. The boy is touching the man's left arm (perhaps to hold him off?). At the far right, a third banqueter is shown from the back; only the head of his dining couch is visible. He too is reaching out with his drinking cup for the boy to give him more wine. Above their heads is the inscription *E*P*I*K*T*E*T*O*S *E*G*R*A*F*S*E[*N] ("Epiktetos painted [me]"). The rather creative pose of the third banqueter is echoed in a cup by Douris London E 49, which is probably somewhat later.

Int.: A flute player with double flutes plays for a dancing woman (maenad or hetaira). She is holding krotala (something like castanets), and dancing wildly; she wears a scarf in her hair, a very short chiton with embroidered border, and a panther skin. The flute player is beardless, and he is nude except for a chlamys flung over his far shoulder. He seems to be beating the time of the music with his left foot.

Epiktetos also painted a very early kylix in the Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design (RISD 25.077) which shows silens and maenads wearing pelts; this has definite Dionysiac connotations. However, another kylix (black figure) by this artist shows a warrior wearing a pelt very similar to that worn by the maenad in the British Museum cup Villa Giulia and Heidelberg 18.
artifact.inscriptions: Side A: *P*U*Q*O*N *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Python made [me]"). Side B: *E*P*I*K*T*E*T*O*S *E*G*R*A*F*S*E[*N] ("Epiktetos painted [me]").

artifact.name: London E 372
artifact.summary: Side A: Athena and Erichthonios. Side B: Two youths running (should have been Herse and Aglauros, but they are male).
artifact.other_bibliography: Kron 1976, pl. 7.3; LIMC, II, pl. 754 Athena; C. Kardara "H Zoforos tou Parthenos o Kyrios Mythikos tes Pyren kai to Panellenion Programma tou Perikleoys," ArchEph 1982, 22- 23, fig. 9
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: At left, Athena stands in profile to the right. She holds a spear in her right hand, and a helmet in her left. Her hair is wrapped in a scarf, and she wears a chiton fastened at the shoulders. On the right is a pile of rocks (?), on which sits a basket. The wicker lid, decorated with olive wreaths, has been thrown off and is lying on the rocks. Two snakes emerge from the rocks, near the base of the basket. A small child, dressed in a cloak thrown over his shoulder, is seen from the waist up in the box. He looks towards Athena and waves with his right hand.

The child is Erichthonios, son of Athena and Hephaistos. The myth was that the virgin Athena went to visit Hephaistos at his forge. He made advances to her and she ran away, disgusted. However, some of his semen spilled on the ground, and Erichthonios was born from that. Athena then took the baby and gave him to the daughters of Kekrops, Herse and Aglauros, for safekeeping, as is told in Eur. Ion 20ff. Athena had entrusted the baby Erichthonios to them, on the condition that they not open the basket in which he was kept with the two snakes. They did, and as punishment Athena drove them both mad, and they threw themselves off the heights of the Acropolis.

Keuls (123) suggests that the box in which Erichthonios sits is a substitute for Athena's non-functioning womb.

Side B: Two youths are depicted running. They should have been Herse and Aglauros, daughters of Kekrops, but they are male.

The upper border of the figural panel is a band of olive branches, the lower border is a band of maeanders and crosses.

artifact.name: London E 370
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Deianeira with the poisoned shirt<lb>Side B: woman
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1989, fig. 7; A. Greifenhagen "Zeichnungen nach attisch rotfiguren Vasen im Deutschen Archäologischen Institut, Rom" AA 2 1977, 208, fig. 7
artifact.other_bibliography: Birchall & Corbett 1974, fig. 36; B
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: To the left is Herakles, walking to the right. He is nude, and carries his lion skin flung over his left arm. His right arm is extended to receive the garment from Deianeira. She stands in profile to the left, offering the garment with her right hand. She wears a peplos of crinkly fabric, and a cloak with black border over it. On the ground between the figures lies Herakles' club.

Side B: A standing woman wearing a peplos.

On both sides there is a horizontal border with an egg-and dart pattern above and below the figural panel.

artifact.name: London E 363
artifact.summary: Side A: Achilles receives new armor<lb>Side B: Youth (Achilles?) and women holding armor
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1975, fig. 332; LIMC, I, pl. 110, Achilleus 515; V. Slenoferova "Zwei seltene Vasendarstellungen wohlbekannter Sagen" AK 29 (1986) pl. 14, 3-4.
artifact.other_bibliography: C. Isler-Kerényi Lieblinge der Meermädchen, Achilleus und Theseus auf einer Spitzamphora aus der Zeit der Perserkriege. Zürcher Archäologische Hefte 3 (Zürich 1977) 28, fig. 11
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: To the far left stands Athena, in a scale breastplate, helmet and chiton. She holds a lance and gestures with her right hand to Achilles. In front of her stands a Nereid holding a helmet and lance. She wears a chiton with an overblouse extending to her waist, and a scarf in her hair. In the center of the composition sits Achilles, mourning the death of his friend Patroklos. He is seated on a chair to the left, his head bowed. his upper body is wrapped in a cloak which partially covers his head, and he is wearing a diadem. Underneath the cloak a short embroidered chiton is visible. He holds a staff in his left hand. Thetis stands to his left, her arms wrapped around his shoulders. Her hair is bound up in a diadem, and she wears a long chiton and over it a cloak decorated with circles. To the right of this scene, another Nereid stands, her right hand covering her mouth as though she were moved by Achilles' suffering. She wears a chiton and an overcloak pinned at the left shoulder. With her left hand, she balances a shield upright on the ground. The shield design is of a woman (Athena?). The nereid's hair is pulled up in a scarf. Behind her stands an old man, possibly Phoinix, wearing a himation.

Side B: To the left stands a Nereid, holding a sword and helmet. In front of her is a youth (Achilles?) in profile to the right. He is wearing a long himation and a cloak which partially covers his head. His right arm is hidden under his clothing, and in his left hand he holds a spear. He is facing another Nereid, who holds greaves (?) in her left hand. Behind her stands a third woman, holding a quiver (?). All of the women wear long chitons; the center woman also wears a cloak over her right arm, and a scarf in her hair.

Palmettes decorated the lower handles, and the bottom border of the figural pattern has a band of maeanders.

artifact.name: London E 34
artifact.summary: Int.: Nude girl with washbasin.
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1975, 61, fig. 109; R. Burrows and P. Ure "Excavations at Rhitsóna in Boeotia," BSA 14 (1907-1908), 294, fig. 19a
artifact.other_bibliography: E. Gjerstad et al. Greek Geometric and Archaic Pottery Found in Cyprus (Stockholm, 1977), pl. 74.6
artifact.decoration_description:
Int.: A nude girl (probably a hetaira) bends over to pick up or put down a washbasin. She is shown in profile to the right, and wears her hair tied up in a scarf with a symposiast's wreath around it. The basin she is holding appears to be made of metal. It has four handles around the rim, and three legs with lions' feet terminals.

An inscription runs around the tondo behind her back, &epig-rough;*E*R*M*A*I*O*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Hermaios made (me)").

Hetairai were common subjects of drinking cups such as this kylix. See for example the kylix from Rhitsóna with a similar scene (Burrows, 226-318).
artifact.inscriptions: An inscription runs around the tondo behind her back, &epig-rough;*E*R*M*A*I*O*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Hermaios made (me)").

artifact.name: London E 336
artifact.summary: Side A: Menelaos (or Ajax) seizing Helen (or Kassandra). Side B: Draped bearded man.
artifact.other_bibliography: LIMC, II, pl. 182, Apollon
artifact.condit: Surface badly abraded in some areas, especially the lower body of Menelaos/Ajax.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A woman rushes towards a statue of a nude youth, while a man grabs her from behind by her hair. The statue is a typical kouros type; a nude standing youth with his arms by his sides, probably in this case depicting Apollo. It is roughly two-thirds life-size, and is placed on a platform. The woman runs up to it, almost seeming to trip over the platform. Her arms are extended to grasp at it, while her head is being pulled back by the tug at her hair. She wears a belted chiton with a cloak, and her hair is loose and flowing over her shoulders. The man behind her is a warrior; he wears a crested helmet and greaves (the middle part of his body is missing), and carries a spear and shield with a wolf (or lion?) shield device. He steps up on the platform with his right foot and grasps the woman's hair with his right hand. He appears to be gritting his teeth, and looks rather ferocious.

This scene has been interpreted either as Helen seized by Menelaos (Boardman, 61) or the rape of Kassandra by Ajax (Simon, 123).

Side B: A draped, bearded man stands, holding a staff.

artifact.name: London E 313
artifact.summary: Side A: Zeus with thunderbolt<lb>Side B: Semele
artifact.other_bibliography: Hoppin 1919, 60; Beazley 1918, 38; Beazley 1925, 80; Johnston 1979, 120; Kaempf-Dimitriadou 1979, pl. 12.1,2; LIMC, pl. 281, Aigina 3; Birchall & Corbett 1974, fig. 4-5; Keuls 1985, 54, fig. 34
artifact.date_description: This is a "late" Nolan amphora
artifact.collection_history: ex. Blacas Coll.
artifact.graffiti: Underneath the foot is an incised *B.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Zeus striding to the right, holding a lotus sceptre in his left hand and hurling a thunderbolt in the form of two lotus buds joined by a bar. He wears a himation and mantle which are actually typical of female dress in Late Nolan amphorae (Kurtz, 86).

Side B: Semele (?) runs to the right and looks back with a gesture of fear. She wears a bracelet on each wrist, and her dress is similar to that of Zeus.

Below the design on each side there is a band of broken, stopped meanders alternating with patterned squares (crosses and dotted saltires). Underneath the foot is an incised *B.

artifact.name: London E 3
artifact.summary: Ext. Side A: Ithyphallic satyr warrior with drinking horn. Side B: Ithyphallic satyr warrior with oinochoe and trumpet. Int.: Horseman.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robertson 1975, pl. 70c; Schefold 1978, fig. 74, 75; Simon & Hirmer 1976, pl. 97
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired.
artifact.decoration_description:
Ext. Side A: Both Sides A and B are executed in red figure. Between the eyes and palmettes with open fronds is a running satyr. He is carrying a pelta (shield) and a rhyton (drinking horn), and wearing an ivy wreath. He crouches as he runs. There is a horizontal inscription, *E*P*I*K*T*E*T*O*S ("Epiktetos").

Side B: Eyes and palmettes as on Side A. Another satyr, carrying a pelta and oinochoe, runs to the left. He looks over his shoulder and blows a trumpet as he runs. The inscription on this side is *E*G*R*A*S*F*E*N ("drew [me]").

Interior: The interior is done in black figure. A horseman is depicted, riding to the right. He wears a cloak and wreath, and is carrying two spears. The lower pleated edge of his short chiton just shows from under his cloak. The horse is shown in a lively position, rearing up slightly, with its mouth open. Although riding bareback, the horseman does hold reins. There is an inscription running around the tondo: &epig-rough;*I*S*K*U*L*O*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Hischylos made [me]").

Epiktetos' red figure work is well drawn, "An exquisite balance of line and detail" (Boardman, 58). This is particularly apparent on Side B, where the satyr is turned in a rather inventive position, so that the viewer sees his back. This and the crouching pose of the first satyr exemplifies Epiktetos' early interest in the study of anatomy (Cohen, 427).
artifact.inscriptions:
Side A: *E*P*I*K*T*E*T*O*S ("Epiktetos").

Side B: *E*G*R*A*S*F*E*N ("drew [me]").

Int.: &epig-rough;*I*S*K*U*L*O*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Hischylos made [me]").

artifact.name: London E 271
artifact.summary: Side A: Terpsichore with Mousaios and Melousa<lb>Side B: Youths and a woman
artifact.other_bibliography: M. Wegner Musikgeschichte in Bildern II Musik des Altertums, 4, Griechenland (Leipzig, 1963)1963, 47, fig. 22; Richter 1970c, fig. 138; D. Paquette L'Instrument de Musique dans la céramique de la grèce antique, Etudes d'organologie (Paris, 1984) 11, fig. 1b
artifact.condit: Face of Mousaios slightly restored.
artifact.decoration_description: Side A: The poet Mousaios and the Muses Terpsichore and Melousa. Mousaios stands to right, he is laurelled and beardless, wearing a mantle which leaves his right arm and shoulder free. His right hand rests on a straight laurel branch, and in his left he holds a tortoiseshell lyre. Above his head his name is inscribed *M*O*S*A*I*O[*S]. Terpsichore is seated on a chair, and plays on a fourteen-stringed harp. Her head is inclined toward the harp in a three-quarter view. She wears a diadem in her hair, and a chiton and peplos. Over her head is the inscription *T*E*R*Y*I*X*O*R*A. On the left stands Melousa, fitting a mouthpiece to her aulos (flute). Her hair is covered by a cap surmounted by a topknot, and she wears a chiton. In front of her face hangs a kithara, while above her head is the inscription *M*E*L*E*L*O*S*A. Side B: A female figure standing between two youths. The female's head is covered by a linen veil, and she wears a chiton and peplos. She stretches out her right hand to the youth on the left, as if addressing him. Both male figures are beardless, wear mantles, and hold staffs in their right hands. The one on the left wears a wreath.
artifact.inscriptions: In the field above the figures' heads are the inscriptions: *M*O*S*A*I*O[*S]; *T*E*R*Y*I*X*O*R*A, *M*E*L*E*L*O*S*A.
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora with twisted handles

artifact.name: London E 270
artifact.summary: Side A: Rhapsode reciting. Side B: Flute player.
artifact.sources_used: Beazley 1974, 15, no. 13.; A. Bélis " Auloi grecs du Louvre," BCH 108 (1984) 114, fig. 5; A. Bélis "La Phorbéia," BCH 110 (1986) 206, fig. 1; Boardman 1975, fig. 138; D. Kurtz " Beazley and the Connoisseurship of Greek Vases," GVGetMus 2 (1985) 244, fig. 6; R. Ling The Greek World (Oxford, 1976) 108
artifact.other_bibliography: Beck 1975, pl. 14.78; J. Davidson "Notes on the Panathenaea," JHS 78 (1958) 37, fn. 22.; M. Wegner Musikgeschichte in Bildern II Musik des Altertums, 4 Griechenland (Leipzig, 1963) 33, fig. 11; Webster 1972, 61 pl. 5b; D. Paquette L'Instrument de Musique dans la céramique de la grèce antique, Etudes d'organologie (Paris, 1984): 21, fig. IIb; Bieber 1961a, 5, fig. 9; R. Browning The Greek World, Classical, Byzantine, and Modern (London, 1985),160
artifact.collection_history: Ex. Coll. Canino
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A rhapsode stands in profile to the right. He wears a loosely draped himation, and his right shoulder is exposed. His right arm is extended in front of him, resting on his staff. He is reciting poetry, as we see the words come out of his mouth &epig-rough;*O*D*E*P*O*T*E*N*T*U*P*I*N*Q*I("As once in Tiryns . . ."). He stands on a platform, on which is inscribed *K*A*L*O*S *E*I ("You are beautiful").

Side B: A flute player walks toward the right. He is dressed in a himation which flutters out behind him, and a sleeveless overshirt decorated with a checker pattern. This same pattern is seen on the shirt of another flute player ; a fragment of a volute krater Würzburg inv. 4781 shows only the arm of the musician, and he is wearing a long sleeved checkered shirt.

Both panels have a lower border of stopped meanders alternating with patterned squares (crosses and dotted saltires).
artifact.inscriptions: Side A, the rhapsode is reciting, &epig-rough;*O*D*E*P*O*T*E*N*T*U*P*I*N*Q*I("As once in Tiryns . . ."). He stands on a platform, on which is inscribed *K*A*L*O*S *E*I ("You are beautiful").
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora with twisted handles

artifact.name: London E 266
artifact.summary: Side A: Aging reveler carrying barbiton<lb>Side B: Young reveler
artifact.sources_used: J. Beazley "The Master of the Berlin Amphora," JHS 31 (1911) 281, pl. 11-12; Kurtz 1983, 76, 79, 86; D. Paquette L'Instrument de Musique dans la céramique de la grèce antique, Etudes d'organologie (Paris, 1984):183.; Williams 1985, 41
artifact.other_bibliography: Beazley 1930, pl. 14; F. Frontisi-Ducroux and F. Lissarrague "De l'ambiguite a l'ambivalence un parcours Dionisiaque," Annali Napoli 5 (1983) fig. 6,1
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: An older man, nude except for a cloak draped over his shoulders, walks to the right and looks over his shoulder. He carries a barbiton (stringed instrument) in his left hand. He seems to be distracted by something behind him, and so is not playing the instrument; however, his fingers are poised on the strings and he holds the plectrum with his right hand. He holds a walking stick under his left arm. "His lithe body is strangely both tense and languid; his muscles and sinews are taut, but his down-turned head and slightly flexed knees impart a sense of languorous grace." (Williams, 41). The lower border is a band of stopped meanders alternating with patterned squares (crosses and dotted saltires).

Side B: A young reveler walks to the right. He holds a staff in his right hand and a kylix in his left. He wears a wreath in his hair and a cloak draped about his shoulders. The border below his feet is a meander pattern.
artifact.shape_description: Neck amphora with twisted handles

artifact.name: London E 258
artifact.summary: Side A: Achilles<lb>Side B: Briseis
artifact.other_bibliography: LIMC, III, pl. 139, Briseis
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired; some pieces are missing.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Achilles stands, facing right. He holds a spear in his right hand and his shield is slung over his left arm so that the inside is turned toward the viewer. He is dressed for battle; he wears scale patterned armor on his torso, a leather skirt under which is a short chiton, greaves and a crested helmet (it is impossible to tell if it is a Corinthian helmet, because the front part is lost).

Side B: Briseis stands facing right. She holds a flower to her nose with her left hand, and her right rests on her waist. She is dressed in an ornate chiton of crinkly fabric and an overmantle. This last is decorated with swastikas and dots, and has a meander border. She wears earrings and a diadem.

Briseis was the prize of Achilles, and was taken from him by Agamemnon. Because of this slight to his honor, Achilles refused to continue fighting in the Trojan War. Homer describes the parting of Achilles and Briseis in the Iliad:

". . . and Patroclus gave ear to his dear comrade, and led forth from the hut the fair-cheeked Briseïs, and gave her to them to lead away. So the twain went back beside the ships of the Achaeans, and with them, all unwilling, went the woman. But Achilles forthwith burst into tears, and withdrew apart from his comrades, and sate him down on the shore of the grey sea, looking forth over the wine-dark deep ... (Hom. Il. 1.345-350)
artifact.shape_description: Belly amphora Type C

artifact.name: London E 255
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Apollo fighting for the tripod<lb>Side B: Man with crab on shield, man in leopard suit, old man with staff
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1975, fig. 45; E. Knauer Die Berliner Andokides-Vase (Stuttgart, 1965) pl. 10; Walters 1851, 238, 239
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Contest of Herakles and Apollo for the tripod. The hero, who has seized the tripod with his left hand, is about to deal Apollo a blow with the club in his right. The god, who also grasps the tripod with his left hand, passes his right hand round to take an arrow from the quiver which hangs at his left side. Herakles is bearded and wears a diadem but no clothing. Between his legs is the inscription *D*E*X*I*O*I ("receive the blow" or better "take that!"). Apollo has long hair looped up with a diadem and falling in ringlets on his cheek. He is also nude. Between his legs is the inscription *A[*P*O*L]*L*O*N ("Apollo"). Behind him Artemis is advancing to his assistance. She wears an embroidered cap, a chiton looped up at the sleeves and belted to keep the right thigh bare, and then over this a peplos or chlamys. She stretches forward her left arm as if to shoot, and with her right hand draws an arrow from her quiver. In front of her is the inscription *A*R*T*E*M*I*S ("Artemis"). Behind Herakles stands Athena, holding a spear in her right hand, and a helmet decorated with a meander pattern in her left. Her hair is looped up in a diadem, and she wears the snake aegis, chiton with looped up sleeves, and a peplos over it. In front of her is the inscription *A*Q*E*N*A[*I]*A ("Athenaia") and *P*A*L*O*N ("shake it!"), addressed to Herakles as he is wrestling for the tripod.

Side B: A youthful warrior standing between an Amazon and an aged male. The warrior is armed with a Corinthian crested helmet, a cuirass, a round shield emblazoned with a crab, and a sword. He wears a chiton that reaches his hips. He stands facing left, and raises his right hand to his helmet. The Amazon wears a Phrygian cap, with long flaps hanging down over the breast, and a tight-fitting, embroidered jacket and pants, belted at the waist. A quiver hangs at her left side, and she holds a single-edged battle axe in her right hand, and a bow in her left. Her hair falls out loosely from under her cap, and she looks down at a dog seated in front of her.

In front of the Amazon's head is the inscription *G*E*X*G*O*G*X, and behind *K*I*S*I. Over the dog *X*G*E. . . *S*I. The aged man behind the warrior holds a staff in his right hand. He is bald, and wears a myrtle wreath, a mantle drawn over the back of his head like a veil and sandals. In front of him is the inscription *X*E*X*G*I*O*X*E*X*O*G, and behind, *X*E*L*E*I*O*P*X*I*O. These last five are nonsense inscriptions.
artifact.inscriptions: In the field around the figures, *D*E*X*I*O*I ("receive the blow" or better "take that!"), *A[*P*O*L]*L*O*N ("Apollo"), *A*R*T*E*M*I*S ("Artemis"), *A*Q*E*N*A[*I]*A ("Athenaia"), *P*A*L*O*N ("shake it!"), *G*E*X*G*O*G*X, *K*I*S*I. *X*G*E . . . *S*I. *X*E*X*G*I*O*X*E*X*O*G, *X*E*L*E*I*O*P*X*I*O. These last five are nonsense inscriptions.

artifact.name: London E 241
artifact.summary: Body: Feast of Adonis. Eros and Pan, women gathering incense, dancing, and one woman playing the flute.
artifact.other_bibliography: Boardman 1989, 193, pl. 404.
artifact.comparanda: Berlin F 3248; St. Petersburg 928
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: Beazley identifies this as the Feast of Adonis. Eight figures are depicted. In the center on the third rung of a ladder a partially clad woman stands (possibly Aphrodite?). She is dropping something into a kylix held by a woman with plaited hair standing on the ground to the left. To the right of the ladder is a small tree with berries, and next to that a woman dances to the right with her head thrown back and lower face veiled with a scarf. On the far right a woman is dancing and playing castanets; she moves to the right but looks back over her shoulder. Between these two women flies an Eros who is playing flutes. On the far right another heavily draped woman is dancing, while next to her at a higher level a woman plays the flutes. Above both of these women is a small, goat-legged dancing Pan.

The paint is white with yellow details laid on for flesh, gilding for details, red for wreaths, and pink and blue for drapery. The hair is drawn with fine brown lines over brown wash.

Below the design and around the lip of the vessel is an egg pattern motif. A palmette is beneath each side handle, and at the back there is a pattern of six palmettes.

The Feast of Adonis appears as a topic on several other vases, most notably St. Petersburg 928, which is also from the Apollonia group. This vase depicts eight figures, two of which are erotes. There is no dancing, but rather the harvesting of myrrh, one of the main activities of the feast.

artifact.name: London D 58
artifact.summary: A youthful warrior being carried off by Sleep and Death.
artifact.other_bibliography: Beazley 1938; Felten 1971, 86, fig. 1; Simon & Hirmer 1976, pl. 204; Folsom 1976, pl. 50
artifact.condit: Parts of the design are restored.
artifact.comparanda: Two similar lekythoi by the Thanatos Painter: Munich 2777 and Berlin F 3160.
artifact.decoration_description:
On the shoulder of the vessel is an egg-pattern and palmettes, under which is a meander. In the center of the main scene is a slender stele set on a base with two steps; near the top above an egg moulding is drawn a Corinthian helmet with a long plume. Above the shaft and the base are several fillets, painted red. The eyeholes of the helmet are painted red. Before the stele, two nude winged figures, probably Thanatos and Hypnos (Death and Sleep), are bringing a dead warrior to the tomb. The figure at the left bends over, holding the legs of the dead person. On the body of the former are red marks (plumage?). He has straight hair, a curly beard, and wears a wreath. The youthful standing figure on the right is painted red, and he holds the dead person from behind, under the arms. His hair is curly. The dead youth wears a cuirass, painted with ornaments in detail, and a small red mantle which hangs over both arms from behind. His hair is curly and rather long. The whole scene is drawn in fine lines of light brown glaze, except for the wings which are added in coarser lines of dull black. There are some traces of the preliminary sketch with a dull point.

"The scene itself is most poetically conceived, no doubt carrying out the suggestion of the scene in the Iliad (16. 671) where Thanatos and Hypnos carry the body of Sarpedon to Lycia for burial" (Fairbanks, 258).

There are two similar lekythoi by the Thanatos Painter Munich 2777 and Berlin F 3160. Hesiod (Hes. Th. 763 ff.) and Pausanias (Paus. 5.18.1) both give descriptions of the brothers Sleep and Death (Kurtz 1975, 211).

artifact.name: London B 610
artifact.summary: Side A: Athena standing between 2 Doric columns. Side B: Pancration, 3 athletes, man with palm branch.
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Great Britain, British Museum 1925, 4; Moore & Philippides 1986, 140; Beazley 1986, pl. 103.1, 3
artifact.other_bibliography: Williams 1985, 62, fig. 71.; Beck 1975, pl. 39.209; N. Yalouris and others Athletics in Ancient Greece, Ancient Olympia and the Olympic Games (Athens, 1977) 228, fig. 129; R. Patrucco Lo Sport nella Grecia antica (Florence, 1972) 313, fig. 151; N. Eschbach Statuen auf Panathenäischen Preisamphoren des 4. Jhs. v. Chr. (Mainz, 1986) 139, fig. 72-73, pl. 34; V. Olivová Sports and Games in the Ancient World (London, 1984) 142.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Athena stands, facing right, holding a shield in her left hand and a spear in her upraised right hand. The shield is turned so that the shield-device cannot be seen. She wears a belted chiton, a high crested helmet, and a cloak is draped over her shoulders. On either side of her is a Doric column, surmounted by a Nike statuette. Running down the shaft of the left column is the inscription *N*I*K*H*T*H*S *A*R*X*W*N ("Niketes [being] archon"). The inscription running down the shaft of the right column reads *T*W*N *A*Q*H*N*H*Q*E*N *A*Q*L*W*N ("One of the prizes from Athens").

Side B: Pancration (wrestling match). On the left, a nude athlete stands frontally, his right hand on his hip, and his left arm extended at his side. To the right, 2 nude athletes are engaged in a wrestling match. The one on the left is bearded. His left arm is wrapped around his opponent's face, and his right is raised to deliver a punch. His opponent bends forward and attempts to pull away the arm wrapped around his face. Behind them, to the right, stands a bearded man wearing a white wreath in his hair and a himation. He holds a palm branch in his right hand.
artifact.inscriptions:
Side A: running down the shaft of the left column, *N*I*K*H*T*H*S *A*R*X*W*N ("Niketes [being] archon").

Running down the shaft of the right column, *T*W*N *A*Q*H*N*H*Q*E*N *A*Q*L*W*N ("One of the prizes from Athens").

artifact.name: London B 607
artifact.summary: Side A: Athena standing between 2 Ionic columns. Side B: 3 boxers, Nike with palm branch.
artifact.sources_used: Beazley 1986, pl. 102, 1-2; CVA, Great Britain, British Museum (London 1925) 3; Moore & Philippides 1986, 139
artifact.other_bibliography: Beck 1975, pl. 38.202; J. Swaddling The Ancient Olympic Games (London, 1980) 65.; N. Yalouris and others Athletics in Ancient Greece, Ancient Olympia and the Olympic Games (Athens, 1977) fig. 125; Poliakoff 1982, pl. 5; R. Patrucco Lo Sport nella Grecia antica (Florence, 1972) 237, fig. 107; R. Ling The Greek World (Oxford, 1976) 18; G. Majno The Healing Hand, man and wound in the Ancient world (Cambridge, MA, 1975) 173, fig. 4.29; N. Eschbach Statuen auf Panathenäischen Preisamphoren des 4. Jhs. v. Chr. (Mainz, 1986) 132, fig. 70-71, pl. 33.1-2; M.I. Finley and H.W. Pleket The Olympic Games, the First Thousand Years (London 1976) pl. 21; V. Olivová Sports and Games in the Ancient World (London, 1984) 139.
artifact.condit: Series of holes running along breaks suggest it was repaired in antiquity.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Athena stands, facing right, holding a shield in her left hand and a spear in her upraised right hand. The shield is turned so that the shield-device cannot be seen. She wears a belted himation and a high crested helmet. On either side of her is an Ionic column. The one on the left supports a statuette of Athena holding a branch, on which is perched an owl and a trophy stand. Running down the shaft of this column is the inscription *P*U*Q*O*D*H*L*O*S *A*R*X*W*N ("Pythodelos [being] archon"). The column on the right is surmounted by a figure of Triptolemos in a winged chariot, behind which is a sheaf of corn. The inscription running down this shaft reads *T*W*N *A*Q*H*N*H*Q*E*N *A*Q*L*W*N ("One of the prizes from Athens").

Side B: On the left, a boxer stands in profile to the right. His left hand is raised to his mouth and he tightens his caestus (leather straps) with his teeth. To the right, 2 boxers are engaged in combat. The one on the left throws a punch with his left hand, while his right arm is slightly bent, having ineffectively blocked his opponent's punch. The latter has thrown out his left arm while leaning back slightly, thereby gaining the advantage of not being hit in the face. Behind him, to the right, stands Nike holding a palm branch. She wears a white chiton and a dark cloak over it. She holds a palm branch in her right (?) hand. The Nike standing on this side suggests that the second pugilist is winning.
artifact.inscriptions:
Side A: running down shaft of left column, *P*U*Q*O*D*H*L*O*S *A*R*X*W*N ("Pythodelos [being] archon").

Running down shaft of right column, *T*W*N *A*Q*H*N*H*Q*E*N *A*Q*L*W*N ("One of the prizes from Athens").

artifact.name: London B 605
artifact.summary: Side A: Athena standing between 2 Doric columns<lb>Side B: 2 athletes, a bearded man holding palm branch.
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1974, 169, fig. 304; CVA, Great Britain, British Museum 1925, 3; Moore & Philippides 1986, 17.
artifact.other_bibliography: Simon 1969, 191, fig. 174.; Jüthner 1968, 333, fig. 75; LIMC, II, pl. 719, Athena 140; Beazley 1986, p. 99.2
artifact.comparanda: Hildesheim 1254; Hildesheim 1253 These both have the same shield device of Harmodios and Aristogeiton.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Athena stands, facing left. On her left arm is a shield, bearing the shield-device of Harmodios and Aristogeiton. Her right arm is raised, and she holds a spear in her right hand. Her himation is heavily embroidered, and she wears a high crested helmet. On either side of her is a Doric column, surmounted by a cock. Running down the side of the column on the left is the inscription *T*W*N *A*Q*H*N*H*Q*E*N *A*Q*L*W*N ("One of the prizes from Athens").

Side B: On the left, a nude athlete stands in profile, facing right. He reaches up with his right hand to touch the shoulder of the figure in front of him. This man, also an athlete, stands frontally, but his head is turned to the right. He holds 2 spears in his left hand. To the right of him stands a bearded man in profile, facing left. He holds a staff in his right hand, and wears an himation and a wreath (?) in his hair. His left arm is bent slightly and tucked under his clothing.

Moore dates this to ca. 403, because of the use of the Ionic alphabet which was officially adopted that year, and also the appearance of Harmodios and Aristogeiton as a shield device. As tyrant slayers, they represented the restoration of democracy (Moore, 17).
artifact.inscriptions: Side A: running down shaft of left column, *T*W*N *A*Q*H*N*H*Q*E*N *A*Q*L*W*N ("One of the prizes from Athens").

artifact.name: London B 590
artifact.summary: Interior: Hoplite blowing a trumpet
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1974, fig. 169; D. Callipolitis-Feytmans Les Plats attiques à figures noires (Paris, 1974), pl. 72.4; H. Walters "Hischylos" JHS 29 (1909) 103-119, pl. xi
artifact.other_bibliography: D. Paquette L"Instrument de Musique dans la céramique de la grèce antique, Etudes d'organologie (Paris, 1984), 77, T4; A. Bélis "La Phorbeia," BCH 110 (1986) 205-218, 216, fig. 15; H.R.W. Smith 1929, 35
artifact.decoration_description:
Int.: Hoplite blowing trumpet. In a reserved field, the hoplite runs to the right, raising a trumpet to his lips with his left hand. He wears a high crested helmet, a short chiton belted at the waist, a cloak, and greaves.

Walters (108) characterizes this work as careful, though not mannered drawing, with a generally restrained composition and sparing use of accessory colors, which is symptomatic of later stages of black figure vase painting.

artifact.name: London B 52
artifact.summary: Body: Hunter carrying game, standing between 2 men with staffs.
artifact.other_bibliography: F.L. Bastet, BABesch 41 (1966) 84-85, fig. 5; von Bothmer 1960, 75, 80; Langlotz & Schrader 1939, 38, n. 35.; Rumpf 1953, 50-51, pl. 12, 10; Walters 1893, 65
artifact.date_description: "This olpe stands somewhat apart from the others painted by the Amasis Ptr. and may well be the earliest." von Bothmer 1985, 139
artifact.comparanda: London B 421; Bristol H 803
artifact.graffiti: Several scratches at the top of the handle could be the remains of a graffito.
artifact.decoration_description:
Ext.: A hunter, carrying game and accompanied by his dog, stands between 2 men holding staffs. The hunter wears a fringed leather cap and a short belted chiton, also fringed. He carries the game (a fox and an hare) on a lagobolon, or yokelike stick, on his left shoulder. He walks to the right, his dog beside him on his left side. In front of the hunter stands a bearded man with short red hair, holding a staff in his right hand. His left arm is bent under his himation. Behind the hunter, another short haired man, wearing a himation, stands facing right. He holds a staff in his right hand. The clothing of all 3 men is decorated with red dots and dot-rosettes. The dot-rosettes have a red center and white petals.

The theme of this vase is the return of a successful hunter, as seen on a lip- cup inscribed by Tleson as potter, now in the British Museum, London B 421, and a chous attributed to the Amasis Painter, Bristol H 803, in the City Museum of Bristol (von Bothmer 1985, 138-139).

The figural panel is on one side of the vase, beginning to the right of the handle and ending opposite the handle. It is bordered at the top by an ornamental strip of seventeen upright black buds with dots in the interstices. On the side to the left of the handle are two reserved spandrels with a black disk between them, which might represent an apotropaic eye.
artifact.shape_description: Trefoil mouth

artifact.name: London B 507
artifact.summary: Body: Foundry scene; two men at a forge.
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1974, fig. 285; K.D. White Greek and Roman Technology (London, 1984) 37, fig. 28; G. Zimmer Antike Werkstattbilder (Berlin, 1982) 20, fig. 11
artifact.other_bibliography: P. Zancani Montuoro " La scure. Martello da S. Sosti" AttiMGrecia N.S. 9-10 (1968-69) 44, pl. 12a; A. Burford Künstler und Handwerker in Griechenland und Rom (Mainz, 1985) pl. 29; J.Z. Ziomecki Les Répresentations d'Artisans sur les Vases Attique (Wrocaw, 1975) 57, fig. 19
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired; some pieces missing.
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: A foundry scene is depicted. In the center is a tall, tubular-shaped forge. On the left a bearded man crouches. He has taken a piece of heated metal from the forge with pliers, and holds it on the anvil in front of him. With his left hand he gestures to his assistant, who is standing on the other side of the forge. The assistant stands facing left, leaning on a large hammer with his right hand. In the background, various other tools hang on the wall; a pair of pliers, a hammer, and the handle of another tool.

Also in the background are the retrograde inscriptions &epig-rough;*O . . . *M*U*S *K*A[*L]*O*S . . .*D*O*K*E*I *N*A*I ("Ho . . .mus is beautiful, truly!"), and also three meaningless inscriptions.

It has been suggested that the bearded master is actually Hephaistos (White, 37), but there is nothing about him to suggest divinity, and daily life scenes like this were common on vases of the period; see for example Boston 99.527, depicting a butcher in his shop.
artifact.inscriptions: In the background are the retrograde inscriptions &epig-rough;*O . . . *M*U*S *K*A[*L]*O*S . . .*D*O*K*E*I *N*A*I ("Ho . . .mus is beautiful, truly!"), and also three meaningless inscriptions.
artifact.shape_description: Trefoil mouth oinochoe

artifact.name: London B 502
artifact.summary: Body: Escape from the cave of Polyphemos.
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1974, fig. 255; O. Touchefeu-Meynier Thèmes odysséens dans l'art antique (Paris, 1968) 52, no. 127
artifact.other_bibliography: B. Fellmann Die Antiken Darstellungen des Polyphemabenteuers (Munich, 1972) 127, FL 37; B. Van de Wijer Iconologisch onderzoek van het Polyphemusavontuur in de griekse, romeinse en etruskische Kunst (Leuven, 1982) no. 160
artifact.condit: Some paint losses around the ram's horn.
artifact.comparanda: Athens, NM 1085 An oinochoe by the same painter with a similar subject, except here Polyphemus holds a club.
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: Polyphemos reclines on the ground, while Odysseus makes his escape under the ram. The giant lies in the lower right hand corner of the panel, propping himself up with his left arm. He is nude, with a long scraggly beard and hair. His left leg is extended, while his right is pulled up toward his body. He reaches out toward the ram with his right hand, and seems just about to touch Odysseus. Behind the giant is a vine tree, the branches of which fill the background. On the left, the foreparts of the ram are visible, and it seems to be walking toward Polyphemos. Clinging underneath is a bearded man, definitely Odysseus.

The panel has vertical borders of dots, and the upper border is upright bars.

The story of Polyphemos is told by Homer (Hom. Od. 9.105-566). The giant Polyphemos was blinded by Odysseus and his men, so that they could escape from his cave. This depicts the moment after the blinding, when the wounded giant lets all of the sheep out of his cave, not knowing that Odysseus and his men were clinging underneath them. The figure depicted must be Odysseus, because he was the only one who used a ram, instead of a female sheep, for his escape.

artifact.name: London B 492
artifact.summary: Body: Herakles and the Erymanthian boar, Athena.
artifact.other_bibliography: Birchall & Corbett 1974, fig. 23.
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: To the left is Herakles, wearing the lion skin and carrying a bow and quiver. He has grasped the boar by its left rear leg and lifted its hindquarters off the ground. This has caused its front legs to buckle under it, and it appears to be in a very helpless position. To the right stands Athena. She is wearing her snake aegis and a high crested helmet. She holds her spear in her left hand and gestures toward Herakles with her right.

The panel is bordered vertically by bands of ivy leaves, and there is a horizontal band at the top of upright bars. Athena's skin, the boar's tusks and belly, the teeth of Herakles' lion skin and details of his chiton are picked out in white paint. The boar's neck, the rosettes on Athena's robe, and the pattern on Herakles' chiton is decorated with red paint.

Cohen notes that Herakles wide and bushy mustache is typical of the Lysippides Painter's early period, as seen also on the figures of Louvre F 294.

artifact.name: London B 475
artifact.summary: Maenad on a bull
artifact.graffiti: Inscribed on the base is an *E with an additional line on its top bar, and a circle with a wiggly line through it.
artifact.decoration_description:
A Maenad is seated on a bull. She faces right, and looks back over her shoulder. She has long hair, bound with a diadem, and wears a necklace and embroidered sleeved chiton. She is playing crotala (castanets). In the field is a vine branch.

On the rim of the vessel is a checker pattern. On the neck are alternating palmette and lotus flowers, and below that, pomegranate buds.

artifact.name: London B 436
artifact.summary: Side A: Merchant vessel and war ship sailing towards each other. Side B: Similar to Side A. Int.: Gorgoneion.
artifact.sources_used: Walters 1893, 229, n. B436; Boardman 1974, fig. 180; Morrison & Coates 1986, 35, fig. 26; Casson 1971, 128; Morrison & Williams 1968, 109, Arch. 85; J. Harrison "Odysseus and the Sirens—Dionysiac Boat Races—a Cylix by Nikosthenes," JHS VI (1885) 29
artifact.other_bibliography: O. Höckmann, Antike Seefahrt (Munich 1985) 55, fig. 43; E. Afsmann "Nautisch-archäologische Untersuchungen," JdI VII (1892) 53; R. Williams "Notes on Supplementary Plates LXXXV-LXXXVIII," Greece and Rome XVIII (1949) 144, pl. LXXXVIII, 4c; L. Casson "Hemiolia and Triemiolia" JHS LXXVIII (1958) 14-16, pl. V, VI; R. Williams "Early Greek Ships of Two Levels," JHS LXXVIII (1958) 127, pl. XIVe
artifact.collection_history: From the Blacas Collection
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A merchant vessel is facing right, approached by a war ship. The merchant vessel is rigged with a mast and sail, and it has an apotropaic eye painted on its bow. At the stern is a landing-ladder, and a steersman with the steering oars. Along the sides are lattice-work bulwarks. The sails are furled. Sailing towards it is a war ship with mast and sail. Its prow is in the form of a boar's head, and it has a high fore-deck, steering oars and a landing ladder at the stern. The bulwarks are the same as the merchant ship's. Eight figures can be seen rowing the upper set of oars (there are at least as many people on the lower deck) and the sail is fully extended, giving the impression that the boat is moving "full steam ahead."

Side B: A similar design as Side A. The merchant vessel has unfurled sails in this scene, while the people in the war ship are standing up; one is holding onto the end of a sail, and the other two are hauling on ropes. The war ship is towing a smaller boat, to the right, which has an apotropaic eye painted on the prow. The surface of the sea is indicated with a wavy line.

Interior: A Gorgoneion is depicted, with curly hair, a protruding tongue, and tusks.

This was originally interpreted as a boat race scene (Harrison, 29), but it is more likely that it depicts a pirate ship overtaking a merchant vessel. Side A is the first part of the story, where the pirate ship races toward the unsuspecting boat, using all of its oarsmen and sails. On Side B, it has reached its prey; the pirates have leapt up from their oars and are pulling down the sails as they prepare to board the merchant vessel. The latter, realizing too late what is happening, is attempting to escape under sail (Casson 1971, 128).

artifact.name: London B 432
artifact.summary: Sides A and B: Gigantomachy. Athena attacking fallen giant. Int.: Potter in his workshop.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Athena attacks a fallen giant (Enkelados, according to Walters). Athena and the giant are shown between the painted "eyes"; she is on the left, and lunges toward the giant on the right. She wears a helmet and carries her shield in her left hand; she is dressed in an embroidered peplos and chiton. The giant is in a half sitting position, with his right leg flexed. The background is filled in with tree branches.

Side B: Same as Side A, but the giant has a Corinthian helmet and a white embroidered chlamys. Under each handle, a dolphin is depicted.

Int.: A potter sits at his potter's wheel. Above him are stacks of vases on a shelf, four kylikes and a jug. In the exergue is a dog. Drawing and incising on all the vase is extremely crude.

artifact.name: London B 425
artifact.summary: Ext. Side A: Zeus, Poseidon, and Hades between Pegasi. Side B: Demeter, Hermes, Persephone, Pluto (or Dionysos?), vine branch. Int.: Nike.
artifact.sources_used: D.A. Amyx "Xenokles in Seattle," AJA 66 (1962): 229-232.; CVA, Great Britain 1, British Museum 1, 1926, 5.
artifact.other_bibliography: R. Blatter "Eine neue Töpfersignatur des Xenokles," Antike Welt 19 (1988): 57.
artifact.condit: broken and repaired
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: On the left, a winged horse (Pegasos) walking toward the right. In front of the horse stands a male figure, identified as Zeus, also walking to the right and raising his hand before him. He appears to be gesturing to the next person, who stands facing him. This figure holds a trident in his right hand and is identified as Poseidon. To the right of Poseidon stands Hades, walking left and in profile. He holds something (?) in his hands. Behind him is another Pegasos, facing left.

Side B: A female figure stands on the far left; she gestures with her left hand and moves toward the right. The CVA identifies her as Demeter, while Beazley calls her a generic goddess. Hermes, wearing winged boots and carrying the caduceus, walks to the right. In front of him is a female, either Ariadne (Beazley) or Persephone (CVA), who stands in profile to the right. She is reaching out to another figure who hands her a kantharos. This figure is Dionysos, and the vine branch behind him to the far right is his attribute. Below the figural band on each side is the horizontal inscription *C*E*N*O*K*L*H*S *E*P*O*I*H*S*E*N ("Xenokles made [me]").

Int.: Nike, running to the right.
artifact.inscriptions: Below the figural band on each side of the exterior is the horizontal inscription *C*E*N*O*K*L*H*S *E*P*O*I*H*S*E*N ("Xenokles made [me]").

artifact.name: London B 424
artifact.summary: Ext. Side A: Introduction of Herakles to Olympos. Side B: Birth of Athena.
artifact.sources_used: Boardman 1974, 60, fig. 123; J. Henle Greek Myths, a Vasepainter's Notebook (Bloomington, 1973) 77, fig. 38; Schefold 1978, 16, fig. 3, 35
artifact.other_bibliography: R. Bianchi Bandinelli L'arte dell'antichità classica (Turin, 1976) n. 285; Simon 1969, 217, fig. 200
artifact.condit: The interior has been repainted with a black-glaze relief.
artifact.comparanda: Basel 103.4 depicts a similar Birth of Athena scene, with Hephaistos fleeing.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles' arrival at Olympos. On the left, Herakles, wearing his lion skin and armed with a bow, strides to the right. Athena walks in front of him. She grasps his left wrist with her right hand, and with her left hand reaches out before her to the seated Zeus, apparently about to touch his beard in an imploring gesture. Athena wears a belted peplos and aegis with snakes. Zeus is seated on a small throne. He holds a staff in his right hand, and reaches out to Athena with his left. Under the figural band runs the horizontal inscription *F*R*U*N*O*S *E*P*O*I*H*S*E*N *X*A*I*R*E *M*E*N ("Phrynos made me. Hail!").

Side B: The birth of Athena. Zeus sits on a throne, facing right. Both of his hands are raised in a gesture of surprise or pain; in his right hand he clutches the thunderbolt, and his left hand is raised towards Hephaistos. From his head sprouts the head and upper torso of a (slightly under life-size) Athena. She carries her shield in her right hand and spear in the left. In front of these two stands Hephaistos; his legs are turned in profile to the right, and he seems to be walking in that direction, but twists his upper body back to look at Athena and Zeus. He gestures toward them with his right hand, and holds his axe in his left.

This scene depicts the moment after Hephaistos has hit Zeus on the head with his axe to assist in the birth of the goddess, and is now fleeing the scene. This event is also depicted on an amphora of Group E which is roughly contemporaneous (ca. 550 B.C.), Basel 103.4.

Below the figural band on this side is the horizontal inscription *X*A*I*R*E *K*A*I *P*I*E*I *M*E *N*A*I*X*I ("Hail and drink me, verily!").
artifact.inscriptions:
Side A: *F*R*U*N*O*S *E*P*O*I*H*S*E*N *X*A*I*R*E *M*E*N ("Phrynos made [this]. Hail!").

Side B: *X*A*I*R*E *K*A*I *P*I*E*I *M*E *N*A*I*X*I ("Hail and drink me, verily!").

artifact.name: London B 421
artifact.summary: Int.: Hunter carrying a fox and hare, accompanied by dog.
artifact.other_bibliography: Hoppin 1919, 387; Boardman 1974, 60.
artifact.collection_history: ex. Blacas Coll.
artifact.comparanda: London B 52; Bristol H 803
artifact.decoration_description:
Ext. Side A: No exterior decoration except palmettes at handles and the horizontal inscription *T*L*H*S*W*N *O *N*E*A*R*X*O*U *E*P*O*I*H*S*E*N ("Tleson son of Nearchos made [this]").

Int.: The hunter is shown running to the right. Over his left shoulder he carries a lagobolon, or yokelike stick, on which are hung a red fox and a black hare. He has red hair and a red beard, and is dressed in a short chiton with a checked pattern of crosses and rosettes. A white dog runs beside him, on his right side (closest to the viewer).

Bérard notes that the representation of hares often has erotic connotations, for they were given as love gifts (Bérard 1989, 75). In this case, however, the scene is simply the return from a successful hunt.
artifact.inscriptions: *T*L*H*S*W*N *O *N*E*A*R*X*O*U *E*P*O*I*H*S*E*N ("Tleson son of Nearchos made [this]").

artifact.name: London B 39
artifact.summary: Two hoplites fighting, two youths on horses.
artifact.sources_used: Amyx 1988, 269, 330, 403, 601; F. Lorber Inschriften auf korinthischen Vasen. DAI Archäologische Forschungen 6 (Berlin 1979) no. 105; Payne 1939, no. 1399
artifact.other_bibliography: Williams 1985, p. 29, fig. 33; Benson 1953, List 108, no. 12; R. Arena "Le iscrizioni corinzie su vasi" Memorie della Accademia dei Lincei ser. 8, v. 13, (Rome 1967) 96, no. 50
artifact.condit: Paint flaking on rim and neck.
artifact.decoration_description:
On the handle is a plastically modeled spotted snake, which divides at the top to lie along the rim. On the lip of the vessel are white rosettes with red centers. The neck, foot, and lower body of the vase are black, while the upper border of the figural panel is decorated with a tongue pattern.

On either side of the main scene is a nude youth on a horse, facing towards the center. On the far side of each rider we can see the black outline of the warriors' horses, held by the youths. The horses which the youths ride are white and wear bridles. Behind each of the youths is a flying bird.

In the center, the two hoplites are fighting. Both wear Corinthian plumed helmets, greaves, and body armor. They carry shields and spears. The hoplite on the left stands up, lunging forward with his left leg. His shield is held in his left hand so that the interior, which has a scale pattern, is visible. He holds his spear up above his head with his right arm, and has poked the other warrior in the thigh with it. This warrior has almost fallen to his knees, but is still attempting to escape. His body is almost completely hidden by his shield, which is decorated with a Gorgon's head. He holds his spear ineffectively in his right hand, his back to the viewer as he looks over his shoulder at his attacker. Between his legs is the nonsense inscription *O*G*Av*R*F in retrograde. Between the heads of the two warriors is another nonsense inscription *N*O*P*I*O*E*S, also retrograde.
artifact.inscriptions: Between the legs of the warrior on the right is the nonsense inscription *O*G*A*N*R*F in retrograde. Between the heads of the two warriors is another nonsense inscription *N*O*P*I*O*E*S, also retrograde.
artifact.shape_description: Trefoil mouth oinochoe w/ plastic decoration (snake)

artifact.name: London B 380
artifact.summary: Ext. Side A: procession of hoplites leading horses. Side B: Perseus, Hermes, and Athena in flight; 3 Gorgons pursuing. Int.: hoplite charging.
artifact.sources_used: M. Moore and M.S.P. Philippides, Attic Black-figured Pottery (Princeton, 1986), 62, 63.; CVA, 1926, Great Britain, British Museum (London, 1926) 3-4
artifact.other_bibliography: Boardman 1974, 32; Kauffmann-Samaras, A. "Le 'Peintre C,' peintre novateur de la céramique attique, dans la collection du Louvre," La revue du Louvre 5/6 (1987):340-355.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired.
artifact.decoration_description:
Ext. Side A: Procession of 5 hoplites walking left, each leading a pair of horses. The hoplites are armed with helmets, shields, and spears. Their shield devices are (l-r) a crescent, Gorgoneion, drinking-horn, Gorgoneion and poplar leaf.

Side B: Perseus, Hermes, and Athena in flight, with 3 Gorgons pursuing. The last Gorgon on left is the decapitated Medusa, with a horse's head springing from her neck. Behind the first and last Gorgon is a nude standing youth.

Int.: A hoplite armed with Corinthian helmet, shield and spear. His left leg is raised, as if running, and he moves towards the right.

Under the foot of the vessel is a spike.

artifact.name: London B 376
artifact.summary: Side A: Two large eyes, with a nose between. Side B: The same as Side A. Under each handle are two confronting satyrs.
artifact.other_bibliography: Richter & Milne 1935, 30
artifact.collection_history: Canino Collection
artifact.condit: One of the handles is narrower than the other, having served for suspension of the cup.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Two large eyes are depicted, with a nose (or ivy bud?) in between. The center and outlines of the eyes are painted black, the ground is white,and there are purple rings are the pupils.

SideB: decorated the same as Side A.

Under each handle are two confronted satyrs plaiting two vine branches which spread over the sides of the vase, enclosing the eyes. Around the nipple at the base is a row of dots, and a tongue pattern in purple and black.
artifact.shape_description: The vessel is in the shape of a woman's breast (Greek masto/s).

artifact.name: London B 364
artifact.summary: Body in black<lb>Lower zone of neck, side A: Herakles and Kyknos; side B: Fight, with chariots
artifact.other_bibliography: Perrot & Chipiez, 1882, (10) 257, 263, fig. 168; Pfuhl 1923, fig. 256.
artifact.condit: Fragments missing from neck and shoulder.
artifact.comparanda: Williams (p. 34) compares it to metal prototypes like the bronze vase in the British Museum London GR 1980.10-29.1, which is also signed on the rim.
artifact.decoration_description:
The entire body of the vase is painted black, with a pattern of rays in the reserved area near the base. The handles are decorated with an ivy pattern on Side A, and a spiral chain on Side B. A maeander and addorsed palmette chain are above the figural band on the neck, while the inscription *N*I*K*O*S*Q*E*N*E*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Nikosthenes made [me]") is on the rim.

The figural decoration is on the neck of the vessel. Side A: Hermes, Iolaos, Herakles, chariot with charioteer, Eris, Athena, Ares, Zeus, Phobos and Kyknos with chariot.

Side B: Battle scene with chariot.

Williams (p. 34) compares it to metal prototypes like the bronze vase in the British Museum (London GR 1980.10-29.1), which is also signed on the rim. The black painted body may suggest a metal prototype. D. Kurtz (as cited in the CVA) has pointed out a bronze version published in Hornbostel 1977, 91f., no. 63; and also that the placing of the signature on the lip of the British Museum vase reflects the practice with metal vases.

Kyknos was the son of Ares and Pelopia, daughter of Pelias. He would prey on travelers, killing them and dedicating the spoils to his father, Ares. He did this to travelers going to Delphi, which angered Apollo who then had Herakles fight him. Herakles killed Kyknos, prompting Ares to avenge his son's death. The outcome of the story has two versions; that Athena helped Herakles to wound Ares, who ran off to Mount Olympos, or that Zeus interfered and wouldn't let them fight at all. Both Athena and Zeus appear in this version.
artifact.inscriptions: The inscription *N*I*K*O*S*Q*E*N*E*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N ("Nikosthenes made [me]") is on the rim.

artifact.name: London B 327
artifact.summary: Shoulder: Dionysiac group<lb>Body: Two heroes quarreling
artifact.other_bibliography: Williams 1985, 40, fig. 45a; Johnston 1979
artifact.condit: Paint is flaking at the rim.
artifact.graffiti: Underneath the foot is an incised monogram *D*V ##note: the delta actually has a line down the middle of it, making it look like two back-to-back triangles.##
artifact.decoration_description:
On the shoulder: Dionysiac group; Dionysos, Ariadne, satyr and maenad. In the center of the composition Ariadne and Dionysos sit facing each other. Dionysos, on the left, sits on a footstool and holds a drinking horn. Ariadne is seated on a chest or box. To the left of the main scene, Hermes stands and holds his caduceus, and a satyr chases a maenad. To the right of the main scene, the satyr and maenad composition is repeated. Vine branches are in the background.

On the body: Two heroes quarreling. There are seven nude or partially clothed men in the scene. In the center, a bearded man wearing only a chlamys strides to the right, between the two fighting men. He looks back to the left with his arms raised and mouth open; he appears to be shouting excitedly and trying to stop them. The fighting man to the left is bearded. He is brandishing his sword above his head, and in his left hand he holds the scabbard in front of him. He strides toward his opponent, who is also stepping forward. The opponent is clean shaven, with three curling strands of hair falling down on the side of his face. His right arm is hidden behind the central figure, and in his left hand he holds a sword. A nude man has grabbed each of these fighters around the waist, in a further attempt to stop them. At the furthest edges of the composition, another figure stands on each side. The one to the left is draped in a cloak and is clean shaven. He steps forward and raises his left arm to grasp the wrist of the bearded fighter and stop him from using his sword. The figure on the far right is bearded; he wears a loincloth (?) tied around his waist. He has grasped the beardless fighter's arm in the crook of his own.

The vertical borders are ivy and the lower horizontal one is palmettes.

artifact.name: London A 342
artifact.summary: "Nipple" jug with curvilinear pattern.
artifact.sources_used: R.N.L. Barber The Cyclades in the Bronze Age (Iowa City: Univ. of Iowa Press, 1987): 148, 149.; Williams 1985, 11
artifact.decoration_description: Body: Two projecting "nipples" are in the front of the vessel just under the neck; they are encircled with painted rings and dots. Under this is a painted eye with a symmetrical curl pattern below it. Around the shoulder of the vessel is a repeated pattern of four-petalled flowers within circles. The paint is a matte black-brown color.
artifact.shape_description: Distinctly local Melian style and shape.

artifact.name: London 1980.10-29.1
artifact.summary: Neck: A: Dionysos and satyrs. B: frontal chariot.
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Great Britain 15, Castle Ashby, 1979; G. Richter "A Kyathos by Psiax in the Museo Poldi-Peoli" AJA 45 (1941) 587-592; Mertens 1979, 22
artifact.other_bibliography: Mommsen 1975, 31; H.R.W. Smith 1929, 4, 38
artifact.collection_history: Ex. Coll. Castle Ashby
artifact.condit: One break across the body.
artifact.comparanda: Similarities in shape between this amphora and two others of the same class by Andokides, but painted by Antimenes Louvre F 201 Copenhagen, Thorvaldsen Museum, 38. For the field decoration of vines, as well as the figural style, see Museo Poldi-Peoli, Milan, inv. 482.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Dionysos and two satyrs. The god hurries left, looking back. He wears an ivy wreath, chiton and himation and carries a drinking horn in his right hand, and an ivy tendril in his left. The ivy spreads in the field before him, while another tendril, springing from behind his back, fills the right field symmetrically. The satyr on the left crouches raising his hands; the one on the right dances with one hand clenched, the other raised to the god. The beards of all the figures, tails of the satyrs, and dots on Dionysos' chiton are painted red. The groups of four dots on the chiton are painted white.

Side B: Frontal chariot with four horses. There is a charioteer in a long chiton looking left, the head of a warrior in a Corinthian helmet looking right. At either side stand naked youths, arms flexed with clenched hands. The helmet crest, manes of the center horses, horses' chest bands, youths' forelocks, and a stripe across the chariot body are painted red. The chiton and pendants on the chest bands are painted white.

There is an inscription in black along the plain top of the lip *A*N*D*O*K*I*D*E*S *E*P*O*I*E ("Andokides made [me]").

Beazley, (ABV) notes the similarities in shape between this amphora and two others of the same class made by Andokides, but painted by Antimenes Louvre F 201, Copenhagen, Thorvaldsen Museum, 38. All three amphora have black bodies, and this may suggest metal prototypes for this class. D. Kurtz (as cited in the CVA) has pointed out a bronze version published in Kunst der Antike (Schätze aus norddeutschem Privatbesitz) 1977, 91f., no. 63; and also that the placing of the signature on the lip of the British Museum vase reflects the practice with metal vases.

For the field decoration of vines, as well as the figural style, see Museo Poldi-Peoli, Milan, inv. 482 the kyathos attributed to the Psiax Painter by G. Richter, which depicts a reclining Dionysos flanked by two satyrs.
artifact.inscriptions: There is an inscription in black along the plain top of the lip *A*N*D*O*K*I*D*E*S *E*P*O*I*E ("Andokides made [me]").

artifact.name: London 1978.6-15.1
artifact.summary:
Side A: Nike and anabates
Side B: Three youths
artifact.other_bibliography: E. M. W. Tillyard, The Hope Vases (Cambridge 1923) pl. 31.5; Swaddling 1980, 72; British Museum Society Bulletin 34 July 1980; British Museum Occasional Papers 22 1981, 5, 38, fig. 3.
artifact.collection_history: Once Deepdene, Hope 223. Christies sale, July 1977, no. 148, then Charles Ede Ltd., GPSI vi, 1978, no. 5.
artifact.comparanda: Syracuse 16034. The other name vase, with identical scene.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Nike and anabates (victorious athlete). On the left, the Nike is shown in profile, facing right. She holds a victory wreath out to the rider with her right hand. She wears earrings and bracelets, and her chiton is decorated with a wavy black border (the folds of the drapery are typical of the Anabates Painter's early work). Towards her comes the rider on his horse. He is shown in the process of leaping off, and his feet (as well as all four of the horses' hooves!) are off the ground. He is nude, and carries a small shield. The horse wears a bridle. These two figures are rather awkward looking, particularly because, as mentioned above, they seem to be levitating in midair. Behind them is the turn-pole, with a fluted column and Ionic capital.

Side B: Three standing youths. The youth on the left is in profile to the right. He is wrapped in a himation, so that only his head and feet show.
