Under each handle, there are two heraldic lions, flanking a complex of a palmette over two tendrils in volute shape, with lotus buds and more palmettes. These lions have red manes and are turning their heads back, showing their open mouths. All of them have erect ears more appropriate for a wolf or a panther.

Below the animal friezes, a band with network decoration in black with red dots or daisies in the inner fields. Rays coming from the bottom. The rim or lip and the handles and the area underneath are black.
artifact.shape_description: The neck amphora is the most common shape in so-called Pontic ware (see Ducati 1968).

artifact.name: Malibu 89.AE.73
artifact.summary: Eleusinian deities
artifact.collection: Malibu, The J. Paul Getty Museum
artifact.collection_history: Purchased from the art market, London.
artifact.decoration_description:
A: Demeter standing profile to the right, with her left foot advanced, wearing a himation draped over her left shoulder and around her lower body, over a medium-, button-sleeved chiton, a narrow stephane, a krobylos, and a spiked pendant earring, holds grains in both hands, her left arm raised, and her right arm lowered; Triptolemos, seated 3/4-view to the right in his winged chariot (with a spotted snake profile to the right just behind the wheel), wearing a himation draped over his left arm and around his lower body, over a short-sleeved chiton, a white wreath in his hair, with a bun, hold grains in both hands, each arm bent at waist level; Persephone, labelled on the left of her body, following the curve of her drapery and interrupted by her arm), standing 3/4-view to the left, with her right foot advanced, wearing a himation draped over her left shoulder and around her lower body, over a medium-, button-sleeved chiton, and her hair in a krobylos (?), tied with two narrow taeniae, and a spiked red pendant earring, holds an oinochoe in her slightly lowered left hand, and extends a phiale in her right hand, at waist level; bearded Kalamites, standing 3/4-view to the left, with his right foot advanced, wearing a himation draped around his lower body and over his left shoulder, over a short-sleeved chiton, a fugitive white wreath in his hair, holds his clenched left fist just below waist level, and a scepter in his left hand.

B: Bearded Theos, standing profile to the right, with his left foot advanced, wearing a himation around his lower body and draped over his left shoulder, over a medium-sleeved decorated chiton, and a krobylos tied with two thin taeniae, holds a scepter upright in his slightly raised left hand, and a phiale, at waist level, in his right hand, into which a female figure (Thea? [Clinton], inscribed KALOS), pours a libation from an oinochoe held in her upraised right hand; she is standing profile to the left, with her weight on her left leg, her right leg slightly advanced, wearing a himation draped around her lower body and draped over her left arm, over a medium-sleeved chiton, and two taenia in her hair, the ends of her hair held by a swath of fabric; a bearded male figure, standing profile to the right, with his left foot advanced, enveloped in a himation wrapped around his bent right arm, his left hand extended, at waist level; Eleusis, standing profile to the right, with her left foot advanced, wearing a himation draped around her lower body and over her left shoulder, over a medium-sleeved chiton, a sakkos, a pointed pendant earring, holds an oinochoe in her upraised right hand, and a phiale at waist level in her extended left hand; bearded Hippothon, standing near frontal, turning his head profile to the right, with weight on his frontal left leg, his right leg relaxed and bent, wearing a himation draped around his lower body and over his left shoulder, over a short-sleeved chiton, and a fugitive white wreath, his hair in a bun, rests his obscured left hand on his hip, and holds a scepter upright in his upraised right hand.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 540
artifact.summary: Peleus and Thetis fighting, Nereids and Nereus
artifact.sources_used: Simon 1975b, 141; LIMC, IV, Glauke I, 4 with pl.; VI, s.v. Kymathoe, s.v. Melite I, 2 with bib; s.v. Kymatholege I, s.v. Nao, 2; s.v. Nereus 84.
artifact.other_bibliography: Langlotz 1932, n. 540, pl. 198-199; Kretschmer 1969, 202; Krieger, Die Kampf zwischen Peleus and Thetis in der griechischen Vasenmalerei, 1975, 89.182 no. 241.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Some fragments are missing, especially a large one in Peleus and Thetis group. The red inscriptions of the names of the Nereids are almost gone.
artifact.comparanda: The fight between Peleus and Thetis is represented in many Attic red-figured vases (LIMC, VI, s.v. Nereides, ns. 283-290) On Athens NM 1629 (CC1588) (ARV2, 1250, 34; 1688) the scene is almost the same
artifact.decoration_description:
On the body is represented the fight between Peleus and Thetis in presence of seven Nereids (all named: Kymathoe, Kymatolege, Nao, Melite, Psamathe, Speo and Glauke) and their father Nereus. The scene goes all around the entire vessel in a continuous frieze, but the dispositon of the nine figures allows a division into three fields or sides A, B and C. The seven Nereids and Nereus are disposed in pairs facing one another, starting from the center of side A where Peleus attacks Thetis, and spreading around the vase.

On side A, Peleus is attacking Thetis in the center of the scene. On either side, two Nereids are fleeing. Peleus grabs Thetis by the lower part of the body, holding her very tightly. Thetis seems to be trying to flee from him, extending her right arm towards her sisters gesturing for help. Peleus' body is lost, but on his head he wears a red wreath, almost worn away. He is depicted smaller than the other figures because of he is human, not divine. Thetis is taller, richly dressed in chiton and himation and wearing a crown or diadem on her head.

At left of this pair, the Nereid Kymathoe (named in an inscription above her head: *K*U*M*A*Q*O*H), clad in chiton and himation, runs to the left, turning her head back to look to the fighting couple. She has black hair tied up in the back and makes a gesture lifting her left arm. To right of Peleus and Thetis is the Nereid Nao (inscription over her head: *N*A*O; according to Kretschmer it should be read Nao, and not *S*A*O) running from the couple to the right. She is seen from the back, turning her head and extending her right hand towards her father. Her appearance is similar to her sister Kymathoe.

Side B: Nereus and two Nereids facing each other. At left stands Nereus moving to left facing his daughter Nao on side A. He is bearded, dressed in rich himation, and carries a scepter. He raises his hand to hurry to help his daughter Thetis. In the center of this side is another Nereid moving to the right. She is dressed in chiton and himation, and wears a taenia in her long black hair falling over her back. She gestures with both hands while she goes to meet one of her sisters coming from right. The third Nereid on this side is wrapped in chiton and himation, with her left hand concealed in her himation. She gestures with her right hand and her hair is black and tied up.

Side C: Three Nereids. At left, Melite (inscription over her head: *M*E*L*I*T*H) wearing a pointed crown, runs to the right with her right arm outstrechted. Next to her another Nereid, Kymatolege (inscription over her head: *K*U*M*A*T*O*L*H*G*H) going left to meet Melite, extending her right hand. She is dressed in a belted peplos and her black hair is long and falling over her back. At right, the seventh Nereid, Glauke (inscribed *G*L*A*U*K*E), moves to the right, facing her sister Kymathoe on side A. She is dressed like the others in chiton and himation one of the hands concealed and the other extended, and her hair is tied up with a band. The inscriptions are almost faded away.

All the Nereids, except one, are dressed in long chitons and himations folded in a very characteristic way making zigzag patterns on the edges, recalling the folds of the Berlin Painter, the Achilles Painter's master. The figures are well disposed, and they form a closed and perfect, comprehensive composition. The Nereids form couples and they do not run in the same directions. The frieze that comes out is perfect in its conception.
artifact.inscriptions: Over the head of each Nereid:
artifact.shape_description: Simon believes that the stand is too large and does not belong to the dinos

artifact.name: Moscow II 1, 117
artifact.summary: Anangke (Necessity)
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>Sidorova 1985 (with earlier bibliography)</bibl>, no. 43, fig. 83; N.M. Lossewa, "Attische rotfigurige Vasen des 5. Jhs. v. U.Z. in der Sammlung des Museums der Bildenden Künste (Puschkin Museum) in Moskau," Wissenschaftliche Zeitschrift der Universität Rostock 16 (1967) Gesellschafts und Sprachwisenschaftliche Reihe 7/8, 9/10, 481-82, pl. 47.1
artifact.collection: Moscow, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts
artifact.decoration_description: Winged female figure, labelled Ananke, running profile to the right, her straight left leg advanced, while her right leg is bent back, wearing a medium-sleeved belted chiton with a long kolpos, and a red sakkos, from which a single black lock of hair protrudes, bends both arms and holds her skirt in her left hand, lowered at her side, while she holds a torch upright in her right hand.
artifact.inscriptions: <Foreign lang=Greek>*A*N*A*N*L*H</Foreign>

artifact.name: Würzburg L 521
artifact.summary: Side A: Three women playing music; Eros<lb>Side B: three youths
artifact.other_bibliography: Wegner, Das Musikleben der Griechen, 1949, 20; Simon, Gnomon 44, 1972, 421.; Beck 1975, pl. 83. 404; CVA, 2, pls. 19.5-11; Moon 1983, 219, fig. 14.24; Paquette 1984, 129; Keuls 1985, 126, fig. 11.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Scene of women playing music. In the middle of the scene a woman sits on a chair, holding a lyre and flanked by women standing on either side. Eros comes flying from the right. Behind her a woman is standing at left, resting her left hand on the back of the chair. The woman at right holds in her right hand the double pipes (aulos) and in her left a cradle-kithara. She is dressed in belted peplos. Between her and the seated woman, Eros, naked and with wings, like a little child, is flying to the left into the scene. There are diverse objects around the room: a chair, an open box between the seated woman and the woman at right, and, on the wall, are hanging several objects like a taenia and a crosslike instrument of unknown meaning and use.

Side B: Three youths in the palaestra. Three young men draped in himatia talk in the palaestra. The one at left carries a strigil and the one at right opens his hand showing a astragalos (knucklebone used in games). All of them hold knotted sticks. Hanging on the wall between them is a bag for the astragaloi.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 515
artifact.summary: Death of Hipparchos. Side A: Hipparchos, Harmodios and Aristogeiton. Side B: three bodyguards.
artifact.other_bibliography: AZ, 41, 1883; Beazley, JHS 68, 1948 26ff; Brunnsaker 1977, 108f.; Philippaki 1967, 68 ff.; Etudes des Lettres, 1983, (4), 29, fig 19.; Beckel et al. 1983, 103, n.44; Boulter 1985, pls. 64-65; OHCW 1986, 34 (Boardman).
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Restored
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: The murder of Hipparchos. Harmodios and Aristogeiton are murdering Hipparchos, the brother of the tyrant Hippias. In the middle of the scene is Hipparchos, a richly dressed figure wearing a mantle, his hair arranged in locks falling over the forehead. He is being attacked from both sides. At left, seen from the back, Aristogeiton is plunging his sword into Hipparchos' body. Aristogeiton is bearded, and wears a light mantle. On the other side Harmodios, dressed in the same way as his friend, but without beard and with blonde hair, brandishes his sword in his right hand over his head. All three wear wreaths for the feast and have their mouths open as if screaming or shouting.

Side B: Three bodyguards of Hipparchos brandishing spears. The bodyguards, two youths and an older man, holding spears, are moving excitedly in all directions. The youth at left and the man wear mantles and the youth at right a cloak over his shoulders. Both youths are moving outwards and the man in the middle moves his body to the right but turns his head and extends his right arm to the left.

This is the representation of an almost comtemporary event. The murder of Hipparchos took place during the Panathenaics of 514 BC (see Hdt. 5.55, Hdt. 6.109, Hdt. 6.123, Paus. 1.8.5, Paus. 1.29.15. The picture of this vase seems to be inspired in the sculpture group erected for Harmodios and Aristogeiton in 477/476 BC in Athens (Paus. 1.8.5).
artifact.shape_description: Stamnos with lid

artifact.name: Würzburg L 511
artifact.summary: Side A: Boreas pursuing Oreithyia in presence of Athena. Side B: Two maidens fleeing to Erechtheus
artifact.sources_used: Simon 1975b, 139; LIMC, III, Boreas, no. 53; IV (add.) Erechtheus, no. 62.
artifact.other_bibliography: Langlotz 1932, n. 511, pl. 180; Classical Journal, 61, 243, fig. 5; Simon 1967, 113; Beckel et al. 1983, 109, n. 47; Archaeologischer Anzeiger 1985, 40, fig. 14; Boulter 1985, pl. 71;
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Some cracks and scratches.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Boreas pursuing Oreithyia in presence of Athena. In the middle of the scene, Athena stands between Boreas and Oreithyia. At left, moving to right, Boreas, the god of the North wind, is running with his hands outstretched, pursuing Oreithyia, the daughter of the king of Attica, who is fleeing to right. Athena is a tall figure, dressed in a pleaded belted peplos and wearing a diadem in her hair and holding a spear, leaning on her left shoulder. Boreas is bearded, wearing a short chiton, and has large wings, winged shoes and a wreath in his hair. Oreithyia is dressed in a long chiton and himation and wears a band in her hair.

Side B: Two maidens and Erechtheus. Two young women come fleeing from both sides to the centre of the scene where Erechtheus, the king of Attica, stands holding a scepter. Erechtheus is a bearded man, wrapped in a himation and wearing shoes. The maidens, dressed in chiton and himation, seem to be two companions of Oreithyia, perhaps Aglauros and Pandrosos fleeing to Erechtheus to report the events. The one at left, a short and black-haired young woman, comes walking to meet Erechtheus with her left hand extended and her right concealed in her himation. The one at right turns her head to look backwards at the scene on side A. She has the hair tied up in a sakkos or another type of hat. Her left hand is concealed in the himation and her right is lifting her dress.

The picture represents the pursuing and abduction of Oreithyia by Boreas. As is ususal in such scenes of abduction, the maiden (often a goddess or heroine) is in the company of other maidens (often nymphs), who are the witnesses to the facts. In this case Oreithyia is the daughter of Erechtheus, the legendary king of Attica. The setting of the abduction is Attica with the presence of its goddess, Athena.

The composition on both sides seems to be symmetrical.

Under the handles large addorsed palmettes with florals growing from them.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 509
artifact.summary: Side A: jumper and trainer. Side B: kitharode and man.
artifact.other_bibliography: Ebert, Zum Pentathlon der Antike, Leipzig 56, 1963, 51; Yalouris, Athletics in Ancient Greece, Ancient Olympia and the Olympic Games, Athens, 1977, 115, fig. 46; Juthner, Die athletischen Leibesubungen der Griechen., 1965, II, pl. 59; Paquette 1984, III, C15.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Good
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A scene of sport. A jumper in the middle of the scene is training with weights. He is naked and his muscles are well rendered through thin lines. Around his left ankle he wears a band, perhaps an amulet. In front of him, at his left stands his coach dressed in himation. Over his shoulder he holds a stick used to maintain discipline (rhabdos). Both of them wear a red wreath, now mostly lost. Between them there are hanging on the wall a sponge, an aryballos and a strigil, the gear of the athlete for cleaning up after exercise. Behind the jumper on the floor at right there is a pick for loosening the earth for the long jump.

Side B: Scene of music contest. In a building there is taking place the performance of a kitharode. Between two Aeolic columns, signifying a building, stands a bearded kitharode, dressed in a special kind of tunic or mantle. In his right hand he holds a plektron. In front of him at right, a bearded man sits on a stool. He holds a knotted stick and he may be a referee. Both of them wear a red wreath, almost gone.

The fact that all the figures wear a wreath and the nature of the scenes itself recalls the Panathenaic festival in Attica, which included contests in both sports and music.
artifact.shape_description: Amphora of Beazley's type C

artifact.name: Würzburg L 508
artifact.summary: Scenes of interrupted duels: Side A: Ajax and Phoinix; Side B: Hektor and Priam or Antenor
artifact.sources_used: Friis-Johansen 1967, 186, 208 and fig 76; Simon 1975b, 132; LIMC, I, s.v. Aias I, no. 43; s.v. Aithiopes, no. 10; s. v. Antenor, 12; Robertson 1975, pl. 82b; Beazley 1974b, 14,n. 4; Schmidt, in Opus Nobile: Festschrift U. Jantzen, 1969, 144 ff.
artifact.other_bibliography: FR, pl. 104; Himmelmann 1967, 2, 96 ff.; Chase 1979; HSCP 13, 1902, 88, 114; AK, 1973, 16, pl. 11.2,3; Langlotz 1932, 508, pl. 176.; CVA, 2, pls 12.1,2, 13.1-6; Snowden 1970, 51, fig 22; Beardsley 1929, no. 73; Beckel et al., 101, no. 43; Boulter 1985, pls. 51-52; BCH 110, 1986 213, fig. 14
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.date_description: A later work of this painter.
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.decoration_description:
The topic, the interruption of the duel of Ajax and Hektor, is developed on both sides of the vase. The picture is divided into two groups corresponding closely to each other. Each of them shows an old, white-haired man in a chiton and mantle, leaning on a long staff, who leads a warrior after him. The warriors follow reluctantly with hostile backwards glances.

Side A: A Greek hoplite is restrained and led away by an old man leaning on a long stick. The group is moving to the left, but both men look backwards. The warrior, who is fully armed and helmeted, opens his mouth to speak. He has long black hair falling in ringlets over his shoulder and black beard. On his right hand he holds a sword in a scabbard with a sword belt. He carries a spear and a round shield with an Ethiopian (?) as a device. The black slim figure on the shield is blowing a long trumpet and carries a sword on a scabbard. The foot of the warrior, seen from the front breaks the frame underneath: a meander band. The drawing of his armor on the body, the legs and the greaves are missing.

The warrior is drawn by his right hand by the old man dressed in chiton and himation or mantle, labelled *F*O*I*N*I*X*S, "Phoenix".

Side B: Another group of a hoplite and an old man moving to the right but turning their heads to look backwards. The hoplite is seen from his back. He is bearded and his long black hair falls down over his back in ringlets. He carries in his left hand a round shield seen from the back, showing the inner side of the shield and its handle, and a spear. In his right he carries a decorated belt. His position, the position of his feet is the same as that of the hoplite on Side A, but from the back; the two figures thus correspond symmetrically to one another. The old man who is leading him away is dressed in long chiton and himation, and has white hair and beard. His hair is gathered back in a small pony tail. He leans in a long staff. The name of the hoplite is preserved: &epig-rough;*E*K*T*O*R.

Even though the name of the warrior on side A is not preserved, he must be Ajax, and the picture represents the episode described by Homer (Hom. Il. 7.275ff.). The duel between Ajax and Hector has been interrupted by the two old men, and both warriors are going back after exchanging gifts to seal their pact. Hector holds in his hand a beautiful fringed belt, and his opponent a sword in a scabbard with a sword belt: the very gifts that Ajax and Hector exchanged according to Homer (Hom. Il. 7.303-305).

The artist, however, treats the subject with the customary license. In Homer it is the heralds Talthybios and Idaios who part the combatants. Instead, the Kleophrades Painter made two venerable old men as a mediators, calling the one on Ajax's side Phoinix, whom he must have found particularly suited to represent sober reflection. The second old man was no doubt also named, but his name is not preserved. Beazley suggested that the old man restraining Hector could be Antenor, as the counterpart of Phoinix who restrained Ajax on the other side of the vase. Later Beazley preferred to identify this person as Priam, citing an inscribed stamnos by the Triptolemos painter in a Swiss private collection (ARV2, 361, 7). The stamnos published by Schmidt presents a very unusual scene and the inscriptions appear to have caused the painter some difficulty. Thus the identification of Antenor on the amphora remains still plausible.

The apparently hostile attitude and reluctance to let themselves be parted manifested by the warriors do not correspond either to the idyllic conclusion of the duel in Hom. Il. 7.299-302, but on the other hand they match the feelings which the two heroes otherwise entertain for each other and are indeed not unhomeric.
artifact.inscriptions: Figures are labelled: *F*O*I*N*I*X*S, "Phoenix" and nearby, [*K*A]*L*O*S *E*I, "You are beautiful"; &epig-rough;*E*K*T*O[*R] "Hector" and again, *K*A*L*O*S *E*I, "You are beautiful".
artifact.shape_description: Amphora of Type A

artifact.name: New York 07.286.51
artifact.summary: Perhaps the abduction of Helen
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 7.243 s.v. Peitho no. 3, pl. 178 (N. Icard-Gianolio); <bibl>Shapiro 1993</bibl>, 190-91, 259 no. 124, fig. 149; <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 2.s.v. Aphrodite no. 1447 (A. Delivorrias); <bibl>Walter 1971</bibl>, 168-69, fig. 149; <bibl>Hamdorf 1964</bibl> 118 no. 483d; A. Greifenhagen, Griechische Eroten (Berlin 1957) 80 fig. 52; Ghali-Kahil 1955, 13; C.W. Clairmont, Das Parisurteil in der antiken Kunst (Zurich 1951) 48-49; G.M.A. Richter, "An Ivory Relief in the Metropolitan Museum of Art," <hi rend="ital">AJA</hi> 49 (1945) 268 fig. 10.
artifact.collection: New York, Metropolitan Museum of Art
artifact.decoration_description: A female figure, perhaps Hera [Clairmont] or Tyndareus [at the abduction of Helen, according to Shapiro], holding scepter to right; Peitho (labelled), standing profile to the right, wearing a himation veiled over her head, which she holds above her shoulder in her upraised left hand, and a narrow red taenia; Aphrodite (labelled), standing profile to the right, wearing a himation draped around her lower body and over her breast/left shoulder, over a medium-, button-sleeved chiton, and a sakkos decorated with small brown dots, holds her lowered, bent left arm at her side, and a flower bud in her right hand, at waist level; nude, red Eros, flying near profile to the right (his legs, back of torso and head, and most of wings preserved), wearing a narrow red taenia, bends his right arm.
artifact.shape_description: Type A

artifact.name: Würzburg L 504
artifact.summary: Departure scenes. Side A: Arming. Young warrior and woman; Side B: Man wrapped in a himation and woman holding phiale and oinochoe
artifact.other_bibliography: FR, pl. 107, 2; Langlotz 1932, 504, pls. 171-2 and 184; Pallottino 1940, 67; Johnson, AJA, 49, 1945, 491ff; Weill, BCH 86 (1962), 70 f. 81; Beckel et al. 1983,111, no. 48.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.date_description: Probably a late work of Hermonax.
artifact.condit: Good
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A scene of arming of a young warrior. He stands at left of the scene with his sword in its scabbard in his left hand, about to put it on. He has a very long hair, falling down his back and tied with a taenia or band. In front of him, facing left, is his wife (or perhaps his sister), a woman dressed in long chiton with her hair tied up with two fillets. In her left hand she holds his shield, which has a threatening snake as device. In her right hand she offers him his helmet, holding it by the cheek flaps. The helmet has a very long crest and a device in front.

Side B: Scene of departure or arming. A man with a spear is shown at the moment of leaving for the battle. He is standing at left, wrapped in a himation and holding a staff in his hand. In front of him, a woman with long hair tied with a diadem is offering him a phiale in her right hand. She holds a jug (a hydria or an oinochoe) in her left, from which she just filled the phiale. She is dressed in long chiton and himation.

The figures are over a decoration band. Under either handle there is a palmette.

The two scenes depict two different aspects of such arming and departure scenes: the more technical aspect of arming and the more ritual aspect of the libation.
artifact.shape_description: Large, with triple handles

artifact.name: Würzburg L 500
artifact.summary: The struggle over the Delphic tripod: Side A: Apollo; Side B: Herakles
artifact.sources_used: Simon 1975b, 127; Boardman 1979, fig. 145; ; LIMC, II, s.v. Apollon, n. 1027; V, s.v. Herakles, n. 2960 with plate.
artifact.other_bibliography: Langlotz 1932; Robertson 1975, pl 83c; Beazley 1930, 8. 16. n. 6
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.date_description: One of the Berlin Painter's early works.
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Good. The black glaze is worn in some areas
artifact.decoration_description:
The figures on both sides are part of the same scene: the struggle over the tripod. Side A: Apollo. A slim naked Apollo moves to the right pursuing Herakles, who is on the other side of the amphora. The god carries his himation on his outstretched left arm. He holds his bow in the same hand and an arrow is in his right hand, behind him, ready to shoot. His hair is gathered up in a womanish way. His face is beautiful and delicately drawn.

Side B: Herakles carrying the tripod. Herakles, moving to the right, is carrying Apollo's tripod over his shoulders, fleeing from the god. He is dark-haired and bearded. Besides the tripod he carries his attributes: the lion's skin like a cape over his back and left shoulder and the club in his right hand. The figures are painted directly on the black glaze that covers the whole amphora.

artifact.name: Ancona 3130
artifact.summary: The birth of Aphrodite
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>Shapiro 1993</bibl>, 199, 259 no. 125, fig. 160; <bibl>Paribeni 1991</bibl>, 46-47 pl. 14; <bibl>Arafat 1990, 30-32</bibl>; <bibl>Add2</bibl>, 303; <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 3.193, s.v. Charis no. 2 (E. Harrison); <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 2.121, s.v. Aphrodite nos. 1176, 1257 (A. Delivorrias); <bibl>Loeb 1979, 69-70</bibl>; <bibl>Roberts 1978, 46 no. 2</bibl>; <bibl>Mertens 1972, 137 no. 6</bibl>; <bibl>Webster 1972</bibl>, 268; <bibl>Walter 1971</bibl>, 169-70, fig. 150; <bibl>Para</bibl>, 429; <bibl>Simon 1969a, 40-41</bibl>; <bibl>Simon 1959, 169</bibl>; <bibl>Stella 1956</bibl>, 244; G. van Hoorn, "Satyrspielen," <hi rend="ital">BABesch</hi> 17 (1942) 7, fig. 16; R.U. Inglieri, "Pisside policroma di Numana con la genesi di Afrodite," <hi rend="ital">RivIstArch</hi> 8 (1940) 46, 49 fig. 4, 52 fig. 7AA.
artifact.collection: Ancona, Archeologico Museo Regionale delle Marche
artifact.collection_history: Found in 1919 at Sirolo-Numana, Tomba Giuletti-Marinelli (locanda Molinella).
artifact.decoration_description: A bearded nude Zeus (labelled), seated profile to the right on a throne (his lower half is missing), torso frontal, head profile to the left, both arms bent slightly and outstretched, holds in his right hand an olive branch to the left, over a low altar, and in his left hand a black scepter to the right; Hera (labelled) standing 3/4-view to the left (chest and right arm missing), wearing a chiton, a pink himation with dark red border, a white taenia, tilts her head down, and holds her left arm at waist level, and in her right hand holds a black scepter to the left; Peitho (labelled), standing frontal, head profile to the right, wearing a medium-sleeved chiton with a long kolpos, a white taenia, holds in her right hand a dress (missing), to the left, and holds in her left hand a phiale to the right; Charis (labelled) (barely preserved), running profile to the right, with weight on her forward, slightly bent, left leg, right leg pulled back; Aphrodite anodos, crouched profile to right (barely preserved, face and arms missing), left knee bent, wearing a belted, sleeved chiton, a long pony tail, a white taenia, tilts her head up; lekythos (on wall) above; nude Eros, standing near profile to the left, weight on both legs, bent at knees, right leg advanced, long curly hair bound with red taenia, reaches both arms forward (forearms missing), probably holding a red sash, part of which remains in the field between Charis and Eros.
artifact.shape_description: Type A

artifact.name: Athens, Fethiye Djami NA 1957-Aa 757 and Aa 757a
artifact.summary: The Wedding of Alkestis
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>Shapiro 1993</bibl>, 201 n. 463, 205, 259 no. 126; <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 7.247 s.v. Peitho no. 46 (N. Icard-Gianolio); <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 2.288 s.v. Apollon no. 852 (B. Lambrinudakis et al.), 735-36 s.v. Artemis no. 1440 (L. Kahil/N. Icard); <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 1.534-35 s.v. Alkestis no. 2 (M. Schmidt).
artifact.decoration_description: A chariot proceeds to the closed door of the house of Admetos: Alkestis, Admetos, Apollo, behind the horses, with laurel crown, kithara, and plektron; Artemis, wearing a peplos and a sphendone, holds torches; Hermes; Peitho, standing frontal, with her head turned to the right, wearing a chiton, a himation, and a taenia, holding a dinos (?) on her head.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 482
artifact.summary: Tondo: man carrying a hare, talking to a boy in the palaestra.
artifact.other_bibliography: Langlotz 1932, n. 482, pls. 152, 164; Wegner 1968b, 185f., 265ff.; Koch-Harnack 1983, 67, fig. 4; Beckel et al. 1983, 105, n. 45.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Good
artifact.decoration_description: The cup is only decorated inside. Tondo: A man carrying a hare talking to a boy in the palaestra. A bearded and black haired man leaning on his cane talks to a boy standing at right. The man, facing right, bends down his head to the boy and brings his left hand to his chest. He wears a himation draped under his left arm and in his right hand carries a frightened, couching hare as a love gift for the boy. The boy is facing the man and looking down. He is completely wrapped in a mantle which covers even half of his head and, like the man, wears a red band on his hair. Behind the boy there is a bench and, hanging on the wall, a sponge and alabastron, his athletic equipment marking the scene as the palaestra or gymnasium. Between the two figures there is a big leaf with tendril. There must be a love relationship between them suggested by the hare, an usual love gift. According to Simon, the leaf also suggests the presence of Eros (Simon 1975b, 134).
artifact.shape_description: For the shape, Bloesch 1940, 100, Python no. 38.

artifact.name: Tübingen F2
artifact.summary: Side A: Themis and Bendis<lb>Side B: Dog and Kephalos
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>Shapiro 1993</bibl>, 224-25, 264 no. 147, fig. 185; Oakley 1990, 35, pl. 124A; <bibl>Add2</bibl>, 316; <bibl>Boardman 1989a</bibl>, fig. 318; J. Burow, CVA Tübingen 5 (1986) 49-52, pls. 21, 22.1-6, fig. 22 (with previous bibliography); <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 3.96 s.v. Bendis no. 2 (Z. Goceva/D. Popov).
artifact.collection_history: Formerly in the Arndt Collection
artifact.decoration_description:
A: Themis (labelled), standing 3/4-view to the right, with weight on her left leg, wearing a belted, sleeved chiton with shoulder straps, a himation draped over her left shoulder and around her lower body, a black necklace, dotted-disk earrings, and a spiked crown indicated by three white vertical stripes, wears her hair in a long pony tail, with a curled lock on her cheek, bends her arms and holds in her right hand a torch to the left, and in her left arm a three-peaked kanoun to the right; Bendis (labelled) standing 3/4-view to the left, with weight on her right leg, wears boots, a short sleeveless double-chiton with a nebris over her left shoulder, and a Thracian fox-skin cap; a dog, standing profile to the left, behind Bendis, advances its right leg.

B: Dog and Kephalos (labelled), shown as a hunter; Artemis (labelled) with kanoun.

This skyphos, earlier presumed to have been Boiotian, has been conjectured by Shapiro (225) to have commemorated the arrival of the Bendis cult in Athens. In this context, Themis represents the Athenian "Custom" with which Bendis will be revered, e.g. with torches and kanouns (her attributes), as are appropriate in all Athenian religious festivals.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 480
artifact.summary: Tondo: young man offering a hare to a seated boy
artifact.other_bibliography: Langlotz 1932, n. 480, pl. 150; Koch-Harnack 1983, 70, fig. 7.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Some small modern additions on youth's body and boy's forehead. The black glaze outside is partially worn.
artifact.decoration_description:
The cup is decorated inside only and the picture is framed by a maeander.

Tondo: a young man offering a hare to a seated boy. A youth dressed in a mantle offers a hare to a seated blonde boy completely wrapped in a mantle. The youth stands at right, bending down to the boy and holding the hare by the ears with his right hand and by the rear feet with his left. He seems to carry also a long stick in his left hand, but it is not clear because of the damage of the picture. The hare seems to be a love gift (Simon 1975b).
artifact.shape_description: For the shape, Bloesch 1940, 94, Hieron no. 32.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 468
artifact.summary: Side A: eyes, satyr squatting<lb>Side B: eyes, horse to right<lb>Tondo: black figured komast
artifact.other_bibliography: Langlotz 1932, pls. 92.3, 93.1, 97. 2; B. Cohen 1978, 92.3, 93.1, 97.2; Beckel et al. 1983, 93, n. 39.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: The figure on tondo is badly damaged. The added red and white on the eyes is missing in some areas.
artifact.decoration_description:
On both sides a pair of large eyes. Under eye-brows, eyes with red pupils, black iris and a white circle in between. Between each eye and handle on either side there is a bushy fan-shaped palmette linked to each handle through a tendril.

Side A: Between the eyes, a naked satyr squatting frontally. An ithyphallic satyr is squatting frontally in an indecent position. He turns his head to left and holds a drinking horn in his right hand. He has beard, horse ears, and wears a red ivy wreath over a long curly hair falling in ringlets over his left shoulder. Over his head, in red, the signature of the painter: *E*P*I*K*T*E*T*O*S *E*G*R*A*S*F*E*N: (Epiktetos painted it.)

Side B: Between the eyes, a horse with red tail stepping to right. The black inner drawing is almost totally worn. Above, in red, the signature of the potter: *N*I*K*O*S*Q*E*N*E*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N: (Nikosthenes made it.)

Tondo: Black figured komast carrying a skyphos. A naked youth with a cloak over his shoulders is running to the right, carrying a skyphos in his outstretched right hand. On his head is a red ivy wreath.
artifact.inscriptions: On side A, over the satyr: *E*P*I*K*T*E*T*O*S *E*G*R*A*S*F*E*N: (Epiktetos painted it.) On side B, over the horse: *N*I*K*O*S*Q*E*N*E*S *E*P*O*I*E*S*E*N: "Nikosthenes made it".
artifact.shape_description: Bilingual eye-cup: outside red-figure, inside black-figure. For the shape, Bloesch 1940, 9, Nikosthenes, B no. 6. Foot type AZ (ARV2): broad and nearly flat.

artifact.name: Verona 25653
artifact.summary: A-B: The exploits of Theseus<lb>Tondo: Themis
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 6.140 s.v. Krommyo no. 8, pl. 63 (E. Simantoni-Bournia); E. Curti, "Il culto di Artemis-Bendis ad Eraclea," Studi su Siris-Eraclea (Rome 1989) 26-27; Oakley 1990, 90 no. 148 pl. 123; <bibl>Neils 1987</bibl>, 132, 169 no. 114; <bibl>Brommer 1982, 10 fig. 1</bibl>; <bibl>Harrison 1977</bibl>, 159; <bibl>Add</bibl>, 154; <bibl>Hamdorf 1964</bibl> 91 no. 219d; G. Riccioni, <hi rend="ital">CVA Verona, Museo del Teatro Romano</hi> 1 (1961) III,I 3-4, pl. 2 (with previous bibliography); B.B. Shefton, "Medea at Marathon," <hi rend="ital">AJA</hi> 60 (1956) 159-61 no. 4; P. Marconi, "Vasi Dipinti Greci al Museo Civico di Verona," <hi rend="ital">BdA</hi> 4 (1925) 553, 557, figs. 4, 6; M. Lehnerdt, "Herakles und Acheloos," <hi rend="ital">AZ</hi> 1885, 115-18, pl. 7.1.
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.045 m; Max. diam. (rim) 0.142 (excluding handles), 0.204 (including handles)
artifact.collection: Verona, Museo Archeologico al Teatro romano (Museo Civico)
artifact.collection_history: Formerly in the Allesandri Collection
artifact.decoration_description:
A: Nude Theseus advancing 3/4-view to the right, leaning back, with his left leg bent and raised, and his weight on his straight right leg, wearing a scabbard band over his right shoulder, wields an axe in his right hand and reaches out his left arm to the right, to restrain the Marathonian bull; the bull is rearing profile to the right, and raises its head and left foreleg; a female figure (Marathon?), standing 3/4-view to the right, with her head profile to the left, and her legs slightly bent (the left leg is advanced), wearing a chiton (partially missing), a himation draped around her lower body and over her left shoulder, a red sphendone, a black hoop earring, reaches her right hand forward, palm out, and holds a phiale in her right hand, which is stretched toward Theseus.

B: Nude Theseus advancing 3/4-view to the right, with his weight on his bent, forward right leg, wearing a chlamys, a scabbard band over his right shoulder, and a white taenia, holds his sword at his side in his right hand, and a rock in his upraised left hand (it is obscured by his chlamys); the Krommyonian sow, moving profile to the left, raises its forelegs; the sow is partially obscured by the old female figure (Phaia or Krommyo), who stands in front of it, profile to the left, with her legs and waist slightly bent, wearing a short-sleeved chiton with a long kolpos, and short white hair, and extended her right hand (to beseech Theseus?) to the left.

Themis: On a reserved groundline Themis (?) standing 3/4-view to the left, with her bent right leg advanced, wearing a medium-sleeved chiton, a himation around her lower body and draped over her left shoulder, long hair, and a brown band necklace with single black pendant, bends both arms, and pours a libation from an oinochoe held in her right hand over a peaked altar, and holds a 3-peaked kanoun in her left hand.

None of the characters are identified by inscription. Beazley suggested the identification of Themis, as this stemless cup is paired with an cup of identical shape and size (Verona 52) which bears Bendis on its tondo; this pairing is comparable to the representation of Themis and Bendis on the Tübingen skyphos (Tübingen F2).

artifact.name: Würzburg L 265
artifact.summary: Side A: silens making wine. Side B: Dionysos and silens dancing. Shoulder: Dionysos seated, with silens and nymphs. Lid: animal frieze.
artifact.sources_used: Arias & Hirmer 1962, 299, pl. 55; Beazley 1986, 55, pls. 54.2 and 55.2; Boardman 1979, 55, pl. 88; Simon 1975b, 95, pl. 25; LIMC, 3, s.v. Dionysos, n. 415 with plate.; Carpenter 1986, pls. 19b and 20a; Hedreen 1992, 87-88, pls. 29 a-b
artifact.other_bibliography: Enthousiasmos 1986, fig. 6; Hagenow, Aus dem Weingarten in der Antike: der Wein in Dichtung, Brauchtum und Alltag, Mainz, 1982, 211; Beckel et al. 1983, 35; von Bothmer 1985, 61, 113-115, n.19
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.date_description: The vase belongs to the mature phase, about 530 BC.
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: The glaze is worn in some areas; parts of the surface are damaged and have been repainted.
artifact.comparanda: For the scene compare another amphora also attributed to this painter Basel, Kauml; 420 Para., 65. Two silens arm in arm: Budapest 50.189 (Para., 61); Vatican 371 (ABV, 367, 91)
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Scene of winemaking. Five silens (satyrs) are involved in various aspects of the production of wine. Hairy ithyphallic silens are picking grapes and making wine. To the far right, facing left, a silen picks a bunch of grapes from a vine, which extends from the right of the picture into the center, supported by two vine poles. In front of him, a silen treads grapes in a basket, as another pours in bunches of grapes. The silen treading grapes faces left and is bending down to look at the grapes, lifting his left arm that hold or grab the tendrils or the branches of the vine. The treading basket in on a trestle platform which slopes gently towards a spout, thus collecting the liquid oozing through the basket. The juice then drains into a pithos (earthenware store vessel) sunk into the ground, of which the top is visible. On the ground under the trestle a black jug (sort of hydria) and further to the left a black kantharos. The third silen is facing right and carrying the bunches of grapes in a recipient from which they are being shot into the treading basket. A fourth silen standing to right plays double pipes, making music to accompany the work, and a fifth to the left pours water from a hydria into a large black pithos, from which only the half is visible.

Above, along the top of the panel, a miniature frieze with five satyrs and four nymphs or maenads dancing around Dionysos. Dionysos is seated on a stool facing right, with a drinking horn in his hand, while silens and nymphs dance on either side of him. The silens and nymphs move with exaggerated gestures, lifting arms and legs. Five of them are coming from left to the center, to Dionysos, and the other four are coming from right to left, dancing in front of Dionysos. The silens are naked and ithyphallic and the nymphs are dressed in decorated peplos and crowned with ivy.

Side B: Dionysos and satyrs dancing. Dionysos and four silens are dancing, playing music and -one might say- tasting the new wine. A bearded Dionysos, dressed in chiton and himation and crowned with ivy, dances in the middle of the scene. In his left hand he holds three short sprigs of ivy branches and in his right a kantharos lowered to receive wine from a silen who is pouring it out for him from a wineskin. The silen turns his mask-like face, looking round at us proudly. At left of this central group, a silen playing the aulos (double flute). At right, behind the figure of Dionysos, two others hasten up, their arms round each other's necks, holding drinking horns; the one behind drinking.

The small upper frieze has five silens and four nymphs dancing. Dressed and with the same characteristics as on side A, their dancing seems to get wilder. The silens and the nymphs form two lines: one, coming from left to right, including three silens and two nymphs, and the other, coming from right to left, with two and two. Both lines are led by a silen and meet each other.

Purple used for the hair and tails of the silens, for the flower and on the himation of Dionysos; white, which has largely gone, was for female flesh (of the nymphs), whilst a yellowish color was applied for the stream of wine flowing from the trading platform into the pithos.

The whole vase is consecrated to Dionysos. He is present in some way on both sides of the vessel. Beazley also thought in an unitary conception of the entire vase and identified the scenes on this vase as a single subject, the vintage, the obverse showing the manufacture of the wine and the reverse showing the first taste of the finished product.

The black figure vintage scenes depict two activities: harvesting the grapes and processing them, picking and treading. Most illustrate one or the other, but several show both activities which suggests that the processing of the grapes was thought to take place near the vineyard. However, this is the earliest vase on which picking and treading grapes are depicted together in the same scene, and despite of the scenes of the same type, it seems likely that depictions of the two processes developed independently.

There are many ancient representations of the vintage and sometimes the vintners are mortals, more often there are silens or satyrs. The association between satyrs and wine on Attic-black figure vases takes two basic forms. They carry wine or they are involved in its production, either picking grapes or treading them. In each of these contexts, Dionysos is sometimes included and sometimes not. Satyrs are also sometimes shown drinking or holding a drinking-vessel, but these scenes are very much the exception rather than the rule. In this vase we have everything. Besides, the representation of Dionysos dancing is very rare. Rare too to see the silens pouring actually wine from a wineskin for Dionysos. These details suggest that we are not dealing with a stock. This is the earliest picture in which Dionysos himself joins in the dance, instead of standing motionless amid the tumult and Dionysos dancing is rare in Attic-black-figure.

The silens depicted in this vase are characteristic of the Amasis painter: "Amasean breed". Fat, hairy, and swine-like, with huge necks and alert features; characteristic also is their pose, massive thighs and the shape and attitude of their phalloi. The indication of hairiness on the silens' body is fairly rare. The female companions in the dancing of this special silens are considered by Hedreen to be nymphs, instead of the almost generally accepted maenads, who he retains not to be the partners of the silens. The Amasis painter was one of the first Attic vase painters to specialize in Dionysiac scenes.

Above the foot a reserved zone filled with a zone of double rays. On both handles where they are anchored to the body, there is a reserved body, filled with vertical zig-zag lines. At handle root a palmette within a reserved patch.

Lid: On the lid, siren between sphinxes, between lions, between a siren and a swan. A frieze with different kind of animals following a pattern. There are real and fantastic animals mixed together.
artifact.shape_description: Amphora of type A with lid, but special model. The amphora is abnormal both in its general shape and its details, such as the form of the foot and the decoration of the handles. Only Berlin F 3210 (ABV, 151, 21) has the same shape. Würzburg L 282 is its correspondent lid.

artifact.name: London E 222
artifact.summary: Peitho and Himeros
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>Matheson 1995</bibl>, 214, 361 no. P 71; <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 7.247 s.v. Peitho no. 50 (N. Icard-Gianolio); <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 5.426 s.v. Himeros no. 11, pl. 300 (A. Hermary); <bibl>Shapiro 1993</bibl>, 113-14, 203, 243 no. 55, fig. 64; <bibl>Hamdorf 1964</bibl> 1964, 118 no. 483e; <bibl>Papadaki 1960</bibl> 124; <bibl>Smith 1896</bibl>, 172-73 (with previous bibliography); <hi rend="ital">CIG</hi> 8365; O. Jahn, <hi rend="ital">Peitho, die Göttin der Überredung</hi> (Griefswald 1846) 25
artifact.decoration_description: Peitho (labelled) standing profile to the left, wearing a himation draped over her left shoulder, over a sleeved chiton, and a sakkos, holds a phiale and above it a large alabastron (hung from cord by small square fastening) in her hand (her left hand is obscured by the himation). She faces a nude, winged Himeros (labelled) seated on a rock profile to the left, with his right foot slightly advanced, wearing a narrow, white taenia, who holds a torch (?) in his right hand, and rests his left hand on his lap.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 222
artifact.summary: Side A: Apollo kitharode (between columns with cocks on them) Side B: A naked man (Dionysos ?) and maenad on donkey. Below, lions and boars.
artifact.other_bibliography: Wegner, Das Musikleben der Greichen (1949), 211; Jessen, AA, 1955, 301f.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Good
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Apollo kitharode between columns with cocks on them. In the center of the scene, Apollo stands looking to the right, with a band on his head, playing the kithara. He wears a long chiton and himation. On either side there are two Doric columns with cocks. On the background there are branches and on either side, between the columns and the handles, on each palmette a raven.

Side B: Dionysos and a maenad on donkey. At left, a woman with a wreath on her head and dressed in a short chiton or dress rides a mule or a donkey towards the right. She carries a branch of grape-vines that goes all over the picture. Her face, arms and legs are white. The donkey is a big animal with the mouth painted in added white. In front of her marches a man carrying a stick. He is moving towards the right, dancing and turning his head backwards to look at the woman on the mount. He is naked except for the red ivy wreath in his head and the decorated himation or cloak over his right shoulder. Added red is used in his clothes, and his beard is also red. The woman seems to be a maenad, and the man is surely not a satyr, but may be the god Dionysos himself.

The amphora does not have the usual Panathenaic theme, but the presence of the cocks on the columns and the shape itself suggests that the amphora might have been a prize vase or may be souvenir. The themes represented belong, though, to two different worlds: Apollonean and Dionysiac. They are often found together and opposed in Greek art.

Under the handles is a decorative floral motif consisting in lotus flowers linked to four palmettes growing from the handles: two on either side, one upwards and one downwards. The motif is similar to some of the Antimenes Painter's decorations (see Würzburg L186).

Under the picture an animal frieze goes around the entire vessel. This ancient motif consists in a procession of lions and boars drawn in silhouette. Under the frieze, rays coming from the foot.
artifact.shape_description: May have been a prize vase even the shape does not correspond exactly to the Panathenaic amphorae. Beazley includes it among the Panathenaic amphorae in ABV. The Kleophrades Painter, a late Archaic red-figure vase painter, made several black-figure amphorae as prize vases for the Attic festival

artifact.name: Würzburg L 186
artifact.summary: Side A: Judgement of Paris<lb>Side B: horseman and two men
artifact.other_bibliography: Raab 1972, 166, no. 35
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Good
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: The Judgement of Paris. From left to right, the goddesses Hera, Athena and Aphrodite are led by Hermes in the presence of Paris. In first place marches Hera, as the queen of the goddesses. She is a tall figure, wrapped in a chiton and himation and holding up a flower (?) in her left hand. Her gesture suggests that she seems to be speaking. Following her, Athena wears a helmet and holds a spear in her right hand. The last goddess, as in the literary sources, is Aphrodite. All three goddesses wear chiton and himations with red bands as decorations. Hera and Athena's chitons are decorated with small stars or flowers in white. Aphrodite wears plain folded chiton. All of them have long hair tied in the back and red bands or taenias in their heads. Athena's helmet breaks the frame above the figures. The faces, hands and feet are painted in bright added white.

Facing the group of goddesses are Hermes and Paris. They are standing at right, their bodies facing right, but turning their heads to look at the trio. Their two bodies overlap. Hermes is closer to Hera, gesturing with his right hand, which breaks the frame above. He is bearded, dressed like a messenger, with kerykeion and petasos, special shoes and a mantle or chlamys. There is added red on his dress and his beard, and the top of his hat is white. Paris is also bearded, with long hair, wrapped in a chiton and himation and carrying a stick or staff. He goes to meet the divine procession. Hermes' kerykeion and Paris' staff are parallel and break the decorative palmettes growing from the handles.

The scene follows faithfully the Archaic sources which speak about the Judgement of Paris: the Iliad and the Cypria (Hom. Il. 24.25-30; Cypr. (EGF 17)).

Side B: A young horseman flanked by two men. In the middle of the scene is a horseman dressed in Thracian dress with very wide sleeves in black and white, carrying two spears. He is a young man with short hair; the hair over his forehead is red. The horse is a massive animal with a red mane. Under the horse is a dog. On either side of the youth stands a bearded man looking inwards at the young horseman. The man at right, in front of the horse, is wrapped in a himation and leans on a stick. He is standing, almost overlapping the decorative palmette above. There is some added red on his hair and his clothes. The man at left is naked except for a short mantle or cloak over his shoulders, and carries two spears. He is moving to left but turning his head to look backwards at the horseman. There is added red on his cloak, hair and beard.

The figures are drawn with incision. Only half of the body of the vase is occupied by the picture. The lower part has a simple meander band, a linked lotus-bud chain, and thick rays coming from the bottom. Under the handles a rich floral motif formed by a lotus flower pointing down linked through four tendrils with four palmettes growing from the handles, two at the top and two at the bottom. On the neck, floral ornament.

The Antimenes Painter decorated a large number of vessels, especially neck-amphorae and hydriae, in the last third of the sixth century. Several features of this vase are typical of this painter, such as the choice and placement of the subsidiary decoration.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 176
artifact.summary: Side A: Dionysos with youths and men. Side B: the like. Under the right handle, two naked men running, under the left, naked youth running. On the neck, floral.
artifact.other_bibliography: Beckel et al. 1983, 79, no. 32
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.date_description: A late work. Later ovoids tend to have larger figures and floral necks.
artifact.collection_history: From the Feoli Collection
artifact.condit: Slightly restored
artifact.comparanda: For the wheels in the floral cf. Vatican 338, ABV, 241, 24
artifact.decoration_description:
Sides A and B: the amphora shows the same scene on both sides, with the same group of five figures. Dionysos stands in the center of the scene, flanked by two naked youths, flanked in turn by two men draped in himatia. Dionysos holds a kantharos in his hand and a heavy-fruited branch of a grape-vine in his other hand. The god, looking towards right, is richly dressed with chiton and himation or mantle decorated with red dots and white rosettes. He also wears on his head an ivy wreath. On either side of Dionysos there is one figure, one youth and one bearded man walking towards right, making exaggerated gestures with their arms and turning their heads to look backwards. The one at right seems to look at Dionysos and the one at left seems to look at the man behind him. Both of them are naked except for the fillets they wear in their heads. The interpretation of the red band or stain on their chests is uncertain. On either side of them there are two standing men dressed similarly to Dionysos, but not as richly. Both are looking inwards to the center and make the same gesture with the hand.

Under both handles there are figures, something that is very common in the Affecter's works. Under the right handle, two naked running men one of them is carrying a round bowl. Under the left handle, one man or youth running naked. All of them have the same red band or stain on their chests. The Affecter frequently paints handle figures connected or not with the subject of the main scene. They are smaller figures, usually youths and men walking or running, naked or with chlamys or cloaks over the shoulders. Their identification is not clear yet. Beazley in this case tentatively proposed komasts, perhaps because of the bowl that one of them is carrying

The interpretation of the scene, repeated identically on both sides of the vase, is somewhat difficult. Beazley identified the scene as the welcoming of Dionysos by Ikarios, but there is no clue to identify any of the figures represented in this amphora as Ikarios. Neither the youths or the men have any attribute — grapevines, wine cups, thyrsoi, etc. — to identify them as part of a Dionysiac scene either; only the presence of Dionysos places the scene in this realm. Anonymous youths appear also with Dionysos in thirteen works by the Amasis Painter. The relationship between the god and the youths in some of them is not evident. Concerning Beazley's interpretation of Dionysos and Ikarios on nine vases by the Affecter, no attributes differentiate the figures Beazley identifies as Ikarios from the other stock figures greeting and departing on the Affecters's vases. There is, in fact, no evidence to support an identification of any black figure scenes as the meeting of Dionysos and Ikarios.

Dionysos appears in at least seventeen of The Affecter's vases. He always wears a lush ivy wreath; on all but one, he carries a kantharos; and on all but the latest he carries a heavily-fruited branch of grape-vine and he wears a chiton.

Most of the scenes by The Affecter seem to be simply decorative, without further significance. In this regard, Carpenter states that the figures of The Affecter are stock figures, merely decorative and repeated, used like models and patterns. The Affecter is a formalist and employs similar stock figures in the majority of his scenes. He lacks a sense of coherent narration, so that Beazley thinks that "the pictures are decoration and nothing beyond and that one can seldom tell what is going on". Furthermore, in this case, the fact that the scene is exactly the same on both sides suggests that it is simply a decorative intention.

On the neck a double floral design of palmettes and flowers.
artifact.shape_description: Affecter's standard class: echinus mouth and foot, round handles, double rays only at the base. It differs from other neck amphorae in its ovoid shape. Mommsen 1975 classifies this amphora as standard shape type I (Standardform Typ I)

artifact.name: Würzburg L 164
artifact.summary: Exterior: eyes; silens and nymphs dancing and in erotic attitudes<lb>Interior: Side A: Phineus; the Horai; Boreads pursuing the Harpies; Side B: Dionysos and Ariadne in a chariot with silens and nymphs; Tondo: Satyr's mask
artifact.sources_used: Rumpf 1927, 20, pls. 40-44; Simon 1975b, 84-84, pl. 19; Schefold 1978, 26, pls. 176 and 232; LIMC, 3, s.v. Boreadai, n. 7 (with plate), s.v. Dionysos, n. 763; Carpenter 1986, 77 and 111; Hedreen 1992, 50, 73, 77-78, 87, pl. 22
artifact.other_bibliography: Langlotz 1932, 164, pl. 27; Vojatzi 1982, n. 42
artifact.dimensions: H 0.120 m., with handles 0.155 m., D. 0.380 m.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.date_description: This vase is dated in the third quarter of the sixth century. Slight differences between authors make it range from just ca. 530 BC (Simon) to between ca. 530 and ca. 520 BC (Gaspari: LIMC)
artifact.collection_history: From Collection Feoli
artifact.condit: Some gaps filled with plain clay. Moderate damage to some figures.
artifact.comparanda:
There are some parallels for the postures of the satyrs on this cup. For the silen on the back of the animals making a lewd gesture to Dionysos see Louvre G 88 (ARV2, 48, 162). For the scene of Dionysos standing in a chariot a good parallel is a neck amphora in Bologna (Bologna 29; ABV, 285, no. 3), where Dionysos and a woman are shown standing in the car of a frontal chariot, around which a silen and a nymph dance.

The pursuit of the Harpies by the Boreads appeared in Greek art as early as the 7th century, so even individual black-figure images of a bearded wind god are usually interpreted as a Boread, not as Boreas himself, whose iconography is poorly defined in this period (see LIMC, III, s.v. Boreadai
artifact.decoration_description:
Exterior, side A: Eyes flanked by pairs of silens and nymphs in erotic attitudes. A pair of large black eyes with a nose in the middle. Between the eyebrows is the protome of a panther or lion. The eyes seem to represent the face of a satyr with two stylized pointed ears on either side. The irises of the eyes are drawn as a series of concentric circles, and have the tear duct typical of Chalcidian vases. To each side of the eyes are pairs of silens and nymphs in symplegma (erotic union). The silen at right is attacking the nymph from the rear; she is bending forwards. Like all the silens on the outside of the cup, he is naked, hairy and with horse ears and tail. The nymph is dressed, but her skirt is lifted. The silen is grabbing her by the breasts. The lower part of the legs of the silen are missing. Between the ear and the couple there is a flower. The couple at left is also in the same erotic attitude, but the position of the nymph is slightly different. The silen is identical to the one at right. The nymph is not bent so far forwards and turns her head to look at the silen behind her. Her skirt is lifted and the silen is ithyphallic. Between the couple and the handle there is a bird flying.

Exterior, side B: Eyes flanked by pairs of silens and nymphs dancing. The large clear brown eyes with a palmette in the middle seem to represent the face of a nymph. On either side of the eyes is an ear, stylized like a volute, with an earring. On either side of the ears, a silen and nymph dancing. The silens' bodies are covered with hair and they have pointed horse ears. The nymphs are completely dressed in black dresses decorated with stars or dots and with bands on the hem. In the couple at right, the nymph runs to the left lifting her right arm over her head and turns her head back to look at the silen. The silen is bearded and has horse ears and tail. Part of his left leg is missing. In the couple at left, the silen is moving to the right, extending his arms back and turning his head to look backwards. The nymph acts like the one at right, but her dress is not decorated with dots or stars. Her right arm is missing. Under the left handle area there is a bird (perhaps a screech owl) and a flower; under the other a flower.

Interior, side A: the Boreads driving away the Harpies, disgusting birds who tormented the blind Thracian king Phineus. This scene is the one that gives the name to the cup. On the right, Phineus is lying on a kline. His name was in a damaged inscription:*F[...]. In front of him is the table laden with the food which the Harpies took from him. He is reclining on his right arm against cushions piled at the head of the kline. His eyes are white, indicating his blindness, his face staring frontally at the viewer. His upper body is naked, and a himation is wrapped around his lower body and legs. Next to him at right there is a woman, standing and draped in a himation, labelled *E*R*I*X*Q*O; Simon believes that she is his wife. Behind her are growing ivy leaves. At his left, next to him, two goddesses are standing facing the left, looking away from Phineus at the Harpies. The two women are dressed in chiton and himation decorated with floral and bands. One of them carries a lotus flower which recalls the lotus flowers and buds from the friezes in Chalcidian pottery. An inscription beside them identifies them as &epig-rough;*O*R*A[*I], "Horai."

The following scene is the pursuit of the Harpies by the Boreads, who have just arrived with the Argonauts. The winged sons of Boreas, the North Wind, are flying to the right, their legs in the pinwheeling knielauf posture, the standard archaic convention for suggesting rapid movement, be it running or flying. Their names are Kalais and Zetes, inscribed beside them: [*Z*H]*T*H*S and *K*A*L*A*I*S. They are dressed identically, with chitoniskos with a maeander band on the shoulder. They are bearded, wear winged shoes and each have four wings; both brandish swords. The Boread at right, Kalais, has his left leg in front, the one at left, Zetes, has his right leg in front. His hair is tied in a krobylos. The Harpies (their name inscribed: *A*R*P[...]) are half-women and half-birds, with four large wings. They seem to be flying over the sea, represented by schematic high waves and fishes. Their legs are also in the pinwheeling position, to indicate that they are flying.

The episode is described by Apollonius Rhodius, book 2 177ff.

Interior, side B: Dionysiac scene with silens and nymphs. Dionysos and a woman veiled like a bride stand in a chariot drawn by wild animals. In the middle of the scene, a man (identified as Dionysos by inscription: [*D*I*O*N]*U*S*O*S) and a woman ride to the right in a chariot drawn by a lion, a panther and two stags. On the back of the animals a silen turns his head back to look at Dionysos and makes a lewd gesture at him. On the right a silen dances before a lion-head spout pouring forth liquid into a basin. The liquid is wine: the grapevine growing from the lion head spout shows this, as does the visible excitement of the silen and the fact that he is filling a phiale, a vessel associated with wine rather than water. Behind the group of the chariot at left, three nymphs are taking a bath at a spring, while two hairy silens hidden behind a palm tree ogle them. Over their heads a bird is flying. The fountain is small and flows among ivy leaves. The nymphs have left their cloths hanging on the wall and are naked and squatting, with their long hair falling in long curly locks. The silens are black, naked and ithyphallic.

The main problem is the identification of the woman beside Dionysos. The chariot drawn by wild animals appears in later poetic accounts of the marriage of Dionysos and Ariadne: this and the veil, frequently associated with marriage, strongly suggest that the woman standing in the chariot is Ariadne (see Hes. Th. 947-949; Pherekyd. in FGrH 3, F148. Other scholars, however, have identified the woman as Semele.) Furthermore, Hedreen sees the scene on the Phineus cup as a compendium of mythological imagery related to the life of Dionysos on Naxos, the scene of Dionysos' marriage to Ariadne. The picture has another points of contact with the mythology of Dionysos on Naxos. Several ancient writers tell us of a spring of Naxos that miraculously produced wine like the spring represented in the cup. This cup also adds further evidence to the Eastern source of the connection between Dionysos and panthers.

The identification of the women taking a bath seems fairly certain. They must be nymphs, the natural companions of the silens (satyrs). Simon, however, suggests that they are the Charites and tries to make a connection between the Horai on side A and the Charites here. The exotic setting and the perfume she claims is flowing from the fountain support her belief. However, the outstanding characteristic of these female figures is their nudity, which is rare in this period. On the other hand, the nudity, the bath and the presence of the silens strongly support the identification as nymphs. The exotic setting among the palms trees recalls the oriental origin of Dionysos. The atmosphere of the whole scene is somehow idyllic.

Hedreen likes to affirm regarding the relationship of the silens and nymphs with Dionysos. On the Phineus cup the silens and the nymphs seem to take no interest in Dionysos and Ariadne standing in their chariot, with the exception of a silen who makes a lewd gesture in the direction of the divine couple from the backs of the draft animals. The other silens are preoccupied with the wine-fountain or with the nymphs bathing at a spring, but have no time for the god.

The whole vase is unified by the presence of silens and nymphs on the exterior and on side B of the interior. It is difficult to establish the relationship between the two scenes on the interior, however, for the two scenes belong to separate myths. They do however share one detail: the presence of goddesses on both sides belonging to those always difficult to delimitate collective bodies: Nymphs, Horai or Charites.

Tondo: A satyr masque. The face of a silen in a reserved circle with black hair and beard and showing an open mouth.
artifact.inscriptions: Almost all names of the figures represented in the interior of the cup are incribed. On side A: the name of Phineus: *F[...]; the Horai: &epig-rough;*O*R*A[*I]; the Boreads, Kalais and Zetes: [*Z*H]*T*H*S and *K*A*L*A*I*S; the Harpies: *A*R*P[...]. On side B: Dionysos: [*D*I*O*N*U]*S*O*S.

artifact.name: Würzburg L 160
artifact.summary: Side A: Helen and Paris, Andromache and Hector, Kebriones riding a horse<lb>Side B: Horsemen. Birds<lb>Under the handles: man running; youth walking
artifact.sources_used: Rumpf 1927, 14, pl. 31/34: Inschriften Maler; Brommer 1973, 400,2; Arias & Hirmer 1962, 311, pls. XXVI, 75- 76; Simon 1975b, 83f, pl. 17; LIMC, 1, s.v. Alexandros no. 68, with plate; s.v. Andromache I, 4; 2, s.v. Helene, 193; s.v. Hektor 13.
artifact.other_bibliography: Schefold 1978, 199, fig. 271; CMV, GrA, 83, fig. 88; Beckel et al. 1983, 46, n. 16
artifact.dimensions: H. with lid 0.457 m. Without lid 0.379 m.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: From Collection Feoli
artifact.condit: Small gaps. The added white in the face, arms and feet of Helen and Andromache is often missing
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Two Homeric couples, Helen and Paris, Andromache and Hector, and Kebriones, Hector's squire. All the figures are inscribed. In the center of the scene, which is not symmetrically arranged, Hector takes his leave from Andromache; on the left are Helen and Paris, and on the right Kebriones with horses. From left to right, Helen, with a band on her head, wrapped in a purple himation, turns her face away from Paris who is looking at her. The white of her face is fairly well preserved. Near her legs there is the inscription of her name: (retr.) &epig-rough;*E*L*E*N*E. Next to her, Paris (Alexandros), facing to the left, is dressed like an archer, in short purple chiton carrying a bow in his hand a bow-case and quiver on his back. He wears a winged boots and is named *P*A*R*I[*S] (retr.) in the inscription in front of his head.

The next figure to the right is Andromache, who, dressed in a long chiton, opens up to her husband her purple himation which covers most of her body as well as her head. The white which covered her flesh has largely gone, leaving a dull black surface. The inscription *A*N*D*R*O*M*A*X*E (retr.) is behind her, near her legs. She is conversing with Hector who is the main and tallest figure of the composition. He faces to the left, dressed like an hoplite, with Chalcidian helmet, purple metal corslet, purple greaves, shield and carries a spear. On the shield is represented a swooping eagle as blazon. His tall helmet breaks the decoration on the shoulder. Under the helmet there is the inscription (retr.) *E*K*T*O*R. His face is contoured with incision.

Behind Hector in the right part of the vase a youth mounted on one horse and leading another. He must be Hector's squire and is called Kebriones by the inscription (retr.) *K*E[*B*R*I]*O*N*E*S. Behind him is an eagle in flight. The second horse is presumably for Hector who is leaving for the battlefield.

Side B: Two youths dressed in short purple tight-fitting chitons are galloping on horses. In the free spaces of the side there are four birds. Arias suggests that one of them seems to be a duck, the rest are birds of prey; Simon suggests they are a vulture, a swan, and two other kind of birds. Much use of the purple for details on the horses and birds which are between the horses' legs, or flying in the background. The horses are large black magnificent animals. The one at right is bending his head down.

Under the handles there are two small figures. Under the left one, a bearded nude male running; his face is contoured with incision. Under the right, a walking man wearing a purple chlamys.

There is almost no doubt about the interpretation of the scenes in this extraordinary Chalcidian krater. It was assumed that the presence of the two Homeric couples on side A set the scene in Book 6 of Homer's Iliad (Hom. Il. 6.340ff; Hom. Il. 6.484ff), the leave-taking for the battle of Paris and Hector. But probably it refers to two different moments of the Iliad. Simon, and with her most of the authors in LIMC, for example, claim that, while for Hector and Andromache this is the moment of the farewell described in Hom. Il. 6.484ff, Paris is not leaving, but arriving from the battlefield released by Aphrodite as in book 3 of the Iliad (Hom. Il. 3.427ff). In this regard Paris' winged shoes are considered a proof of the divine intervention of Aphrodite, saving him from the attack of Menelaos and bringing him safe back to Helen. Simon claims that the painter's intention was to put together in opposition two very different Homeric couples in two different and contrasting moments: Helen and Paris, with her turning her face away from him and regretting seeing him back safe from the attack of his former husband Menelaus, and Hector and Andromache at the moment he is leaving for the battle. However, their son Astyanax, an important character in this tense moment, is not present in the picture. The result is a thoughtful composition consciously asymmetric in the form and in the meaning. The figure of Kebriones, Hector's squire — in some sources his half brother — is of special interest, in that he is surprisingly represented as a horseman, instead of as a charioteer, as he is generally shown.

The representation on side B seems to be mostly decorative. This may be no more than a new interpretation of the ancient frieze of galloping horsemen, but it might also be seen as the battle that is going on while the meetings on side A are taking place.

The figures of small naked youths and men running under the handles recall the same type of figures used many times on the works of The Affecter (see the figures on Würzburg L 176). The presence of this type of figures gives a sense of continuity to the scenes on both sides which is not completely real. It seems to respond to a phase in the concept of the decoration of the entire vessel: half way between the continuous frieze and the two separated scenes, each one with a complete sense.

The lip of the krater flares out slightly and is decorated with a dense stepped pattern. The neck is black but decorated on each side with four solid circles in purple surrounded by white dots. At the junction of neck and shoulder a tongue pattern, black and purple. Underneath the figure scene a zone of linked buds and flowers of buxom type typical of Chalcidian, then vertically sloping zig-zag lines, followed by rays springing from the base the foot. The disk is black on its top surface and purple on the upper third of the side. The rest of the side is reserved. A thick fillet painted purple at junction of body and foot.

Lid: On the lid is painted an old animal motif. From the center outwards rays, then linked flowers and buds, then a circular frieze consisting of seven large black boars moving to the left. It recalls the old animal friezes on the Chalcidian vases, but the trick of overlapping two of the animals changes the impression and turns it from a simple frieze to a living, running flock of boars. Much purple and incision. Filling rosettes.
artifact.inscriptions: Beside each figure on side A the correspondent name: (retr.) &epig-rough;*E*L*E*N*E, (retr.) *P*A*R*I[*S], (retr.)*A*N*D*R*O*M*A*X*E, (retr.) *E*K*T*O*R, (retr.) *K*E[*B*R*I]*O*N*E*S
artifact.shape_description: This is one of the four different types of kraters most frequently used in the Chalcidian production. Lid with knob fashioned in the shape of a small vase. The handles are stirrup-shaped rather than columns, and their peculiar form occurs also on Corinthian and Laconian kraters

artifact.name: Würzburg L 131
artifact.summary: Side A: Battle scene. Side B: Erotic scene.
artifact.collection: Martin von Wagner Museum, University of Würzburg
artifact.collection_history: A gift for Dr. Ludowici, from the owner E. Lieben
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Battle scene, with a group of three hoplites fighting on the right and a chariot with four horses driven by a charioteer. The fighting group consists of three hoplites. One of them, in the middle, is kneeling and seems to be defended by the hoplite at right. The hoplite at left seems to be attacking the fallen soldier. All the warriors wear greaves, short chitons, metal corslets and Corinthian helmets and all three carry spears and shields. The shield of the attacker is seen from the back. The only difference between the attacker and the other two hoplites is the color of the helmets — the attacker's is black, the enemy's red.

On the right is a four-horse chariot driven by a charioteer towards the right, as if leaving the scene. The charioteer is dressed in a short purple chiton and is turning his head back to look at the fighters. The four horses are superimposed by pairs. The two behind hold their heads up, while the two before have them down. They have white manes. The details of the bodies of the horses are well rendered: the nose, the bridles and bit, dotted and white, and the hair over the forehead, also white. Behind their necks the yoke is in the shape of a head of a snake looking backwards.

Side B: Erotic scene. Three couples and a group of three, two men and a woman, in erotic attitudes. On the left, a couple making love lying on a couch or bed.
