Below both handles are large palmettes. The groundline on both exterior scenes is a band of crossed squares and meanders that circles the vessel. The lip bears a frieze of ivy and berries.

In the tondo, Apollo is killing Tityos. Apollo stands in right profile on the left, naked except for a cloak draped over his left shoulder and hanging on his back. A strap over his right shoulder holds his striped scabbard at his left side. He has a rich floral wreath on his head, with applied gilded berries, and a bracelet on his left wrist. His hair is long down his back. In his right hand he holds his sword high over his head. In his left hand are his bow and two arrows. Tityos is on his knees in the center of the scene, in frontal position with his head raised to the left to look at Apollo. He too is naked except for a cloak over his shoulders, decorated with a stripe around its border. He has a headband in his hair. His right arm is raised in empty defence while his left is crossed over his chest to guard against the brandished sword. His eyes are wide in fear. Behind Tityos on the right is a female, probably a goddess, in belted peplos and veil. She is lifting the dotted veil from her face with her right hand, revealing a patterned headband underneath. With her left hand she lifts the overfall of her garment as she moves away from the scene. This figure is taken to be the mother of Tityos, the goddess Ge, revealing herself at the moment of his death. At least one scholar, however, has suggested that she is really the mother of Apollo, Leto, who is being saved from Tityos.

On the exterior, both sides depict one seated and five standing figures. All the standing figures are draped to their knees or below. On side A, the first and fourth from the left lean on staffs, while the righthand standing figure carries a lyre. The third figure from the left is seated on a stool facing right, with his draped garment pulled up over his head. Scattered in the background are a number of objects difficult to recognize individually.

On side B, the same figures have changed position slightly. Here the second and sixth from the left lean on staffs, while the third holds a lyre and the fourth is seated facing left.
artifact.inscriptions: Above Tityos in the tondo are the words &epig-rough;*O *P*A*I*S *K*A*L*O*S (the boy is beautiful), and behind Apollo is another fragmentary inscription.

artifact.name: Munich 2423
artifact.summary: Panel: Three Amazons<lb>Shoulder: Chariot, and two boys on horseback
artifact.other_bibliography: Klein, Die griechischen Vasen mit Meistersignaturen 198 (Hypsis); Robinson and Fluck, A study of the Greek love-names 170.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.comparanda: Hydria in Rome, Collection Torlonia; ARV2, 30, 2. A modern copy of the hydria, now in the Musée Revillod in Geneva, was presented as a gift in 1847 by the Bavarian king Ludwig I to the dancer Lola Montez.
artifact.decoration_description:
Panel: Three Amazons prepare for battle. The central Amazon is testing a salpinx. She is wearing a short, belted chiton and helmet, and is equipped with greaves, sword, and a spear. The Amazon to her right turns back to her at the sound of the instrument, while lifting her shield. Her spear is leaning behind her. A third Amazon is looking on from the left holding her helmet and spear, her shield leaning against her left thigh. In the field behind her is the inscription painted in dark red *A*N*D*R*O*M*A*X*E ("Andromache"), the central Amazon is marked *A*N*T*I*O*P*E*A ("Antiopea"), and the one on the right &epig-rough;*U*P*O*P*U*L*E ("Hypopyle"). Above the central Amazon is the additional inscription *X*E*U*X*E ("Cheuche"), and along the right border &epig-rough;*U*F*S*I*S *E*G*R*A*P*S*E*N ("Hyphsis painted it"). The scene is framed around the bottom and side borders by a frieze of encircled red palmettes, on the top by a band of meanders.

Shoulder: The image on the shoulders extends the size of the panel. It shows on the right a quadriga preparing for departure: the bearded driver is mounting the chariot, holding the reigns of the horses and a kentron in his hands. To the left are two naked youths on horseback, each carrying a short whip. Several red inscriptions mark the field around the group: in front of the horses is written *k*a*i*r*e, in front of the charioteer *k*a*l*o*s ("[he is] beautiful"), in front of the first horseman *N*e*d*i*o*s or &epig-rough;*e*r*i*a*s?, below the tail of the horse *S*i*m*o*s or *S*i*m*o*n ("Simos" or "Simon").
artifact.inscriptions: *A*N*D*R*O*M*A*X*E; *A*N*T*I*O*P*E*A; &epig-rough;*U*P*O*P*U*L*E; *X*E*U*X*E; &epig-rough;*U*F*S*I*S *E*G*R*A*P*S*E*N; *k*a*i*r*e; *k*a*l*o*s; *N*e*d*i*o*s or *H*e*r*i*a*s?; *S*i*m*o*s or *S*i*m*o*n.

artifact.name: Munich 2421
artifact.summary: Panel: Music lesson<lb>Shoulder: Symposium of two hetairai
artifact.other_bibliography: <bibl>Lullies 1953, 10, 14f., 31, pls. 33-35</bibl>; <bibl>Marrou, Histoire de l' éducation dans l'antiquité</bibl>; <bibl>Richter 1958, 56.</bibl>
artifact.dimensions: H. to rim 0.47 m; H. to handle 0.515 m.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.decoration_description:
Panel: Music lesson. The main panel is framed on the bottom by a frieze of scrolls with alternating palmettes, at the sides by framed palmettes, and on the top by a maeander key. The music teacher is seated in an armchair on the right playing the lyre in a rather stiff posture. An older student, starting to grow a beard, sits on a stool with patterned pillow in front of him, also playing the lyre. A younger boy, wrapped tightly in a long mantle, stands between them and narrates a text. They are watched on the left by an older man leaning on a gnarled stick, his right hand resting on his hip. All figures are wearing red wreaths. Several red inscriptions identify the figures: behind the teacher is noted *S*m*i*k*u*d*o*s ("Smikydos"), in front of the seated student *E*u*d*u*m*i*d*e*s ("Eudymides"), in front of the young boy *T*l*e*m*p*o*m*e*n*o*s ("Tlempomenos"), in front of the bearded spectator is written [*D]*e*m*e*t*r*i*o*s ("Demetrios"), behind his back *n*a*i*z*w*n. Painted in red are also the knobs of the teacher's lyre, a ribbon decorating one of its arms, and the right wrist of the teacher. The muscles and the folds of the clothes are indicated in diluted brown varnish. The image shows few outline incisions and preliminary sketching.

Shoulder: The panel on the shoulder of the vessel extends to the same width as the image decorating the belly. It is a symposium scene with two reclining hetairai. Both women are bare breasted. Their muscles and the folds of their clothes are clearly incised. Both women are holding skyphoi. There is an inscription, *K*A*L*O*I ("[they are] beautiful"), retrograde to the left of the left woman, another, *S*O*I*T*E*H*D*I (?), between the two women, and a third, *E*U*Y*U*M*I*D*E*I ("Euthymides"), to the right of the right woman.
artifact.inscriptions: On Side A next to the warrior's helmet is inscribed in white *K*A*L*O*S, below it *K*A*L*E. In front of the old man's head is again written *K*A*L*O*S ("[he is] beautiful"), above the mother's head *K*A*L*E ("[she is] beautiful"). On the shoulder, *K*A*L*O*I ("[they are] beautiful") is inscribed retrograde to the left of the left woman. *S*O*I*T*E*N*D*I (?) is inscribed between the two women. To the right of the right most woman is inscribed *E*U*Y*U*M*I*D*E*I ("Euthymides").

artifact.name: Munich 2415
artifact.summary: Side A: Warrior leaving home. Side B: Three standing youths.
artifact.other_bibliography: <bibl>Buschor, Griechische Vasen, 209</bibl>; <bibl>Das Kriegertum der Parthenonzeit, 47</bibl>; <bibl>Richter, Attic Red Figure Vases, 1958, 143</bibl>
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A warrior is leaving home. His equipment consists of a sword, a spear, and a shield decorated with a large eye. He is wearing a short chiton and loin cloth, and he is raising a phiale to toast his wife standing in front of him. She is dressed in a peplos, a taenia decorated with two blossoms, and earrings. Her head is bowed and she lifts a part of her peplos in a gesture of grief. The warrior's old father is looking on from the left and his mother from the right, her hand raised in farewell. Next to the crest of the warrior's helmet is the white inscription *K*A*L*O*S ("[he is] beautiful"), below it *K*A*L*E ("[she is] beautiful"). In front of the old man's head is again *K*A*L*O*S, above the mother's head *K*A*L*E. Buschor, Griechische Vasen, 209 and Das Kriegertum der Parthenonzeit, 47 interprets the scene as the last encounter of Hektor and Andromache in the presence of Priam and Hekabe.

Side B: Three youths dressed in mantles are standing turned to each other, one of them is resting on a long stick.

The areas above and below the handles are decorated with large palmette scrolls painted in red.
artifact.inscriptions: On Side A next to the warrior's helmet is inscribed in white *K*A*L*O*S, below it *K*A*L*E. In front of the old man's head is again written *K*A*L*O*S, above the mother's head *K*A*L*E.

artifact.name: Munich 2413
artifact.summary: Side A: Birth of Erichthonius<lb>Side B: Zeus and Nike
artifact.other_bibliography: Cook 1914-1940, vol. 3, 181 ff.; Arias & Hirmer 1962, pl. 182 f., and p. 87.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.comparanda: For the Erotes compare the loutrophoros in the Agora Museum, ARV1, 489, no. 96.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Athena receives the baby Erichthonius from the hands of the earthmother Ge and proceeds to wrap him in her mantle. Hephaistos is watching from the left, his right arm resting on his hip, his left holding a staff. A mantle with many folds is draped around his shoulders. Two Erotes are flanking the scene on either side, balancing on delicate scrolls. The one on the left is holding on to a floral scroll for support and looks at the newborn child, the other is holding both a lyre and a scroll.

Side B: Zeus is seated on a folding chair, his right hand extended offering a libation bowl to the infant Erichthonius. The father of the gods is dressed in a long chiton with sleeves, a mantle, a taenia, and he is holding his scepter. A gorgoneion decorates the two joints where the seat is connected to the chair. In front of him stands Iris, who has just filled the bowl. She is also wearing a long chiton with sleeves and a mantle, her hair held up with a ribbon. Similar to the previous image, the scene is flanked by two Erotes. The one on the left is playing a lyre with seven strings, the one on the right extends his hand toward the seated Zeus.

All figures show delicate rendering lines and incised contours.

artifact.name: Munich 2411
artifact.summary: Side A: Three nude women bathing themselves at a basin<lb>Side B: three women
artifact.other_bibliography: See CVA entry for extensive bibliography.
artifact.dimensions: H. 42 cm., D. of outer rim 25 cm.
artifact.graffiti: There is a graffito on the underside of the foot.
artifact.decoration_description:
The profiled foot is glazed black on its upper part, while its lower wall is clay-colored. It is set off from the body of the vessel by an incised line that circles it. The handles are round and point upward. At the handle attachments are half-circle bands of eggs. Above the handles are large palmette ornaments, and on the shoulder at the body-neck join is a band of tongues. On the rim is a bordered band of eggs. Both scenes are bordered below by a crossed square and key meander.

On side A, three naked women are standing at a large louter or washbasin, which itself stands on a low foot whose stem attaches to the round basin with a volute-shaped connecting piece. Along the top of the upper basin rim, the words *K*A*L*O*S *P*O*L*E*M*A*N*E (Polemane is beautiful) are painted in dilute glaze. The woman on the left, with long loose hair held by a wide headband with three feathers or leaves stuck in it, stands in profile to the right. She holds in both hands her clothing in a bundle. In front of her are her shoes. The woman in the center stands behind the washbasin in full frontal pose. Her hair is also long and loose, and she dries it or applies oil to it with a mop-like implement on a staff held in her left hand. In her right hand she holds a leather strap attached to an alabastron which hangs below. The woman on the right stands in profile to the left. Her hair is held up by a wide headband with three feathers or leaves in it. She wears an earring, as well as a thread amulet around her left thigh. She dips both hands into the washbasin.

On side B, two women bring a mirror and a salt vessel to their mistress. The mistress, standing upright, is wearing a long chiton, mantle, headband, and earring. The woman carrying the mirror wears a longsleeved chiton, mantle, and cap, while the third woman has a mantle and earring. The pupil of the mistress's eye is not depicted, as are the pupils of the other two. The surface of this figure is covered with dark flecks. On both sides, relief outlines are used.

The scene on side B is generally understood to be sepulchral in nature, with the lonely stance and empty gaze of the mistress representing one who has died, and the two women representing gift bearers.
artifact.inscriptions: On side A, the washbasin bears the inscription *K*A*L*O*S *P*O*L*E*M*A*N*E (Polemane is beautiful).

artifact.name: Munich 2406
artifact.summary: Side A: Athena between two fighters (Achilles and Hector?)<lb>Side B: arming. Early. The ghost of another vase by the same painter.
artifact.other_bibliography: Gerhard 1840-1858, Taf. 201, Text 3, 108 ff.; Beazley, Journal of Hellenic Studies 31 (1911): 282, no. 15; Beazley, Journal of Hellenic Studies 42 (1922): 94, no. 77; Pfuhl 1923, 3, fig. 775.
artifact.condit: A small piece of the body near the handle attachment, as well as a piece of the handle itself, have been restored.
artifact.graffiti: A graffito appears on the underside of the foot.
artifact.decoration_description:
The inside of the handles, as well as a space between the handle attachments are clay-colored. On the shoulder just below the body-neck join is a band of tongues. All the figures are standing on a clay-colored groundline.

On side A, Athena presides in the center over a battle between two hoplites. The warrior on the left is unbearded and appears to be the aggressor. He is wearing a short chiton, breast plate, and low-crested helmet, and a sword in its scabbard suspended from two dark red straps over the shoulder. In his left hand he holds his shield with the skull of a steer as its device. In his right hand he wields his spear in a threatening manner at the second warrior. The second, bearded warrior has fallen back to a squatting position as blood flows from two wounds, one in the torso, one in the thigh. He is naked except for his high-crested helmet and a mantle which has slipped from his shoulders and hangs over his arms. His helmet is high-crested and his sword scabbard hangs from a dark red double strap over his shoulder. In his right hand he holds his sword, attempting to defend himself. His shield is in his left hand, which is flung rather uselessly behind him. In the center Athena strides right, wearing a long sleeved chiton with broad horizontal patterned stripes on its lower part, a mantle, aegis, and dark red bracelets. Her hair is tied with a dark red band. In her left hand she holds her helmet, in her right her spear. She turns her head to the left to look at the warrior whom she has deemed the victor. Added reddish brown emphasizes the warriors' muscles, as well as the breast plate and the lefthand warrior's beard shadow.

On side B, three warriors are preparing for combat. In the center, a young warrior, naked except for his helmet and a mantle tied around his thighs, pulls on his greaves. The warrior to the left is also unbearded, wearing a short chiton, a mantle slung over his arms, and a helmet and holding in his left hand a spear and shield with a rooster as its device, as he watches his companion arming. The bearded warrior on the right is dressed similarly to the one on the left. He holds his spear in his right hand and his shield, with a triskelis for its device, in his left. The round shields have been drawn with a compass. Added red is used for musculature, the folds of the chiton, the beard shadow of the middle warrior, and the end of the righthand warrior's beard. On both sides the figures are outlined in light relief.

artifact.name: Munich 2362
artifact.summary: A, Apollo and Muse. B, woman fleeing.
artifact.other_bibliography: Beazley 1925, p. 439, no. 7.
artifact.collection_history: From Lipona.
artifact.condit: Under one handle an area of finish has misfired to red.
artifact.decoration_description:
The edge of the foot is clay-colored. Under each handle is a palmette decoration. Above and below the scene on side A are interrupted bands of meander and crossed squares. In the same places, side B bears simple meander bands.

On side A, Apollo stands in right profile on the left, wearing a mantle, a red wreath in his hair. In his left hand he holds a laurel branch upright. In front of him a Muse sits in left profile on a rock. She is wearing a chiton, mantle and headband, and she holds a lyre in her right hand. The figures are outlined in relief.

On side B, a woman is running to the right, turning her head to look behind her as she moves. She is wearing a chiton and mantle. Her figure is outlined in sketch form, but no relief is used.
artifact.shape_description: The vessel has triple handles.

artifact.name: Munich 2361
artifact.summary: Side A: The return of Hephaistos<lb>Side B: An old man and women
artifact.decoration_description:
Under the handles large palmette designs occur. Above the scene on side A is a bordered lotus-palmette band. Over side B's scene appears a bordered, diagonal rightward-pointing band of palmettes. Under the scenes an interrupted meander of keys and cross squares continues around the whole vessel.

In the middle of the scene on side A, a bearded Dionysos hurries to the right, while looking around to the left. He is wearing a long chiton, ependytes, a belted animal skin over his left shoulder, a mantle over his left arm, an ivy wreath and a headband. In his right hand Dionysos carries a kantharos, in his left a thyrsos. Following him on the left is Hephaistos in a belted chiton, a mantle over his left shoulder, an ivy wreath and a headband. He is holding his upraised hammer in his left hand, against his left shoulder. In his right he carries his tongs with a glowing ember gripped in them, its white color mostly worn away. Hephaistos's right arm is slung around the shoulders of a naked, bearded, wreathed silen. In front of Dionysos on the right are hurrying a maenad in belted peplos and wreath and a wreathed, bearded silen. The maenad is holding a cymbal in her left hand and hitting it with her right, while the silen has a spotted pelt over his left shoulder and carries a burning torch in his left hand. The figures are outlined in light relief.

On side B, a bearded man stands in the center, leaning on a staff in his right hand and wearing a long mantle and a white headband. On either side of him stands a woman in chiton and mantle. The woman on the left is wreathed, while the woman on the right wears a cap on her head. The figures are outlined, but no relief is used.
artifact.inscriptions: Between Hephaistos and Dionysos on side A, the word &epig-rough;*E*F*A*S*T*O*S (Hephaistos) is written. Above the maenad is the word *K*A*L*O*S (beautiful).
artifact.shape_description: The vessel has strap handles. Between the body and the foot is a disc-shaped attachment. The edge of the foot has a flattened profile.

artifact.name: Munich 2360
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles on Oita (the pyre, with satyrs; and Herakles driving to Olympus)<lb>Side B: satyrs and maenads
artifact.condit: Many of the breaks and small pieces are painted over.
artifact.material_description: The exterior layer of the clay is spotted light and dark reddish brown.
artifact.decoration_description:
Under the scenes runs an interrupted checkerboard-and-key meander pattern. Above side A is a bordered palmette-lotus band, while above side B is a bordered band of right-tilted palmettes and tendrils.

On side A, Athena, as charioteer, conducts the wreathed Herakles to Olympia. Athena is wearing a chiton, an aegis with a checkerboard pattern, and a helmet, and she is holding a spear in her left hand while she holds the reins in her right. Herakles is naked except for the cloak draped over his left arm, and he holds his club in his left hand. The quadriga races to the right. A tree is growing behind the horse team, and the terrain is depicted by added white rising and dipping arcs near the horses' feet. Below is the flaming funeral pyre where Herakles's breast armor lies. On the right, two nymphs in chitons hurry up carrying hydriae, to put out the flames. To the left, two naked bearded silens with wreaths are shown, the nearer one carrying a club in his right hand and running to the fire to look into it, the other with a spear in his right hand running away.

On side B, a naked, bearded silen stands in the center left, holding a thyrsos, his body frontal, his head turned left to look at a seated woman on the far left. She is facing the silen and wearing chiton, mantle, and cap, and she holds an ivy branch in her hand. On the far right, a naked, bearded, infibulated silen prances with outstretched right arm before a draped woman standing in the center right. She wears a chiton and mantle pulled up like a veil over the back of her head. Except for this woman, the figures stand on white ground lines. Outlines are traced, but no relief is used.
artifact.inscriptions: Next to Athena's head on side A is the inscription *A*Q*H*N*A*A, and underneath is Herakles's name, &epig-rough;*H*R*A*K*L*H*S. Above the lefthand female is the name *A*R*E*Q*O*S*A (Arethosa), and above the righthand female is *P*R*E*M*N*O*S*I*A (Premnosia). To the right of the righthand silen is written *S*K*O*P*A, and to the right of the lefthand silen is *U*B*R*I*S.
artifact.shape_description: The handles are triple. The edge of the foot is profiled.

artifact.name: Munich 2345
artifact.summary: The wind god, Boreas, abucting Oreithyia; Herse, Pandrosos, Kekrops, Erechtheus, and Aglauros surround them
artifact.condit: Several breaks and small pieces have been overpainted.
artifact.graffiti: There is a dipinto on the underside of the foot.
artifact.decoration_description:
Between the body and the neck is a plastic ring painted dark red. A similar ring exists, painted clay-colored, between the neck and the rim. On the neck are opposing palmettes attached to looping tendrils. The mouth is painted black outside and inside; its top rim is clay-colored. A meander-checkerboard band runs around the lower border of the main scene. The upper border is a band of tongues.

In the scene itself, Boreas is kidnapping Oreithyia. Boreas is short and stocky, winged, with wrinkled forehead and neck and spiked hair on his head and beard. He is wearing a belted chiton, mantle, and a spiked diadem in his hair. With a strong grip he clasps Oreithyia, who is dressed in a long, windblown chiton, mantle, spiked diadem, bracelets, and earrings. The edge of her mantle bears a black stripe. She has raised her left forearm in distress, as one of her companions, Herse, runs from the left to help her. Herse is wearing a long chiton, mantle, cap, and earrings. On the right, Pandrosos runs in fear away from the group, wearing a long chiton, mantle, and headband. With her left hand she holds her chiton, and she turns her head to look back at the action. To the right of Pandrosos runs a third, unnamed companion of Oreithyia, also dressed in chiton, mantle, and cap. With her left hand lifting her chiton, she hurries to Kekrops, the father of all the female companions, to report the incident. Kekrops, in a long chiton and mantle and holding a scepter, stands with his feet pointing left, but looking back to the right at Aglauros, also in long chiton, mantle and cap. Aglauros has run to Erechtheus, the father of Oreithyia, and she reaches frantically for his chin. Erechtheus is wearing a long chiton and mantle and holding a scepter, whose tip is not preserved. There are abundant tracing marks and relief lines in the scene.
artifact.inscriptions: Painted in dark red are the names of the figures: behind Boreas, *B*O*R*E*A*S, over Oreithyia's head *O*R*E*I*Q*U*A, behind Herse, *R*S*E, above Pandrosos's head, *P*A*N*D*R*O*S*O*S, over Kekrops's head, *K*E*K*R*O*S, behind Aglauros, *A*G*L*A*U*R*O*S, between Aglauros and Erechtheus (running vertically) *E*R*E*X*S*E*S, and between Kekrops and the daughter running to him, a set of five illegible characters.

artifact.name: Munich 2325
artifact.summary: A, Theseus and Procrustes. B, woman.
artifact.decoration_description:
At the foot-body join a red and a white line circle the vase. Below the scenes runs a right-facing meander band.

On side A, Theseus and Prokrustes are pictured. Theseus is wearing a short, belted chiton. His sword in its scabbard hangs from a strap over his right shoulder, and on his head is a wreath. With his left hand he grips the fleeing Prokrustes by the shoulder, and with his right hand he holds his double-bladed axe ready for use. Prokrustes is bearded and naked. Between the two figures stands the bed, and in the field above it the inscription *A*L*K*I*M*A*X*O*S *K*A*L*O*S. The figures are outlined in light relief.

On side B, a woman wearing a chiton, mantle, and sakkos-like cap holds a phiale decorated with black stripes in her outstretched right hand. Her sleeve shows a double black stripe. On the lower part of her chiton two vertical black stripes are visible. The woman is hurrying to the right. No relief is used on this figure.
artifact.inscriptions: On side A is the inscription, *A*L*K*I*M*A*X*O*S *K*A*L*O*S.
artifact.shape_description: The handles are round in cross section. Below the lower handle attachments horizontal plastic knobs appear, and the lower attachments themselves are dented. The foot and the rim are profiled.

artifact.name: Munich 2322
artifact.summary: Side A: Odysseus and Nausicaa<lb>Side B: servants doing laundry
artifact.other_bibliography: See CVA for extensive bibliography.
artifact.dimensions: H. 51 cm., d. of exterior rim 16.8 cm.
artifact.condit: Small areas of the lower body near the foot have been restored.
artifact.comparanda: Odysseus's head here resembles that of a beggar on a fragment in Athens, Athens, Agora P 18538 (Hesperia 17 (1948): 189 f. Taf. 68, 5; Van Hoorn 1951, 93, no. 245 bis, Abb. 388g).
artifact.graffiti: On the underside of the foot is a graffito.
artifact.decoration_description:
The lower, rounded part of the foot is glazed, while the upper profile is clay-colored. The exterior of the vessel's rim is also clay-colored. There is a band of tongues running from handle to handle just under the neck-body join. On the neck a band of ivy with added red tendrils (almost obliterated today) and clay-colored leaves runs around both sides. Both main scenes are bordered below by an egg pattern.

On side A, a naked Odysseus confronts the fleeing Nausicaa and her companions, whose game of ball has awakened him. His left foot is raised slightly on a low rock. In his hair, as well as clutched in his hands, are short branches with added red leaves. A leafless tree stands behind him, with items of laundry spread on its branches to dry. In front of him stands Athena, encouraging him, wearing a long peplos, helmet, and aegis with a crescent moon decoration, and holding a spear in her right hand. On the right two young women flee in fright. They are wearing short, belted chitons and long wraps over their shoulders, and their hair is decorated with diadems. The first woman, who looks back at Odysseus and is perhaps intended as Nausicaa, has her hair done up in the rear, while the second woman's hair hangs loose behind her.

On side B three female servants busy themselves with laundry while they talk together. All three wear belted chitons. The lefthand servant has her hair tied in back, the middle figure loose short hair, and the righthand woman a sakkos-like cap. All three have items of clothing in their hands and appear to be wringing them or preparing to hang them out to dry. Between the middle and the righthand servant is a small rock. On both sides relief outlines are used.
artifact.shape_description: The foot is in two parts, a short convex profiled disk on the bottom and a taller concave profiled disk above. The handle are spiral-shaped.

artifact.name: Munich 2314
artifact.summary: Side A: Athena with tablets and stylus. Side B: Acontist.
artifact.other_bibliography: Poland-Reisinger-Wagner, Die antike Kultur, 1925, 212, pl. 113; Chase 1902, 101, pl. 75.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.comparanda: A comparable image of Athena can be found on the amphora of the Oionokles Painter, Paris, Cab. Méd. 369, ARV2, 648, 31.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Athena is depicted standing to the right, holding a writing tablet opened in her left hand and a stylos raised in her right. A red ribbon hangs from the opened lid of the tablet. The goddess is wearing a long chiton with a red belt, the aegis, helmet and earrings. Her large shield embellished with a club is leaning against her right thigh.

Side B: An infibulated athlete is standing frontally, his head turned to the right. He holds a spear in his right hand, his left is resting against his hip.

Both figures are standing on a short band of meanders, interrupted by fields decorated with a cross. Poland-Reisinger-Wagner suggest that Athena is depicted contemplating what to write onto the tablet. Lullies interprets the gesture of the raised hand holding the stylus as an indication that Athena has already conceived of an idea and is now beginning to write it down.

artifact.name: Munich 2313
artifact.summary: Side A: Discus-thrower. Side B: Youth.
artifact.other_bibliography: Beazley, Der Berliner Maler, 16, no. 10, pl. 7,3.; Hussong, Zur Technik der attischen Gefässkeramik 22, pl. 7. For the kalos-name Sokrates see Robinson and Fluck, A study of the Greek love-names, 179, no. 250.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.condit: The vessel is in good condition, except for a few areas where the glaze is beginning to flake off. Hussong (p. 22) suggests that the vase was already too dry when the glaze was applied, preventing a better bond.
artifact.comparanda: St. Petersburg 635, ARV2, 138, 104.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A nude athlete crowned with a myrrh wreath is depicted standing to the left, holding a discus raised behind his head. Below his right arm is the vertical inscription painted retrograde in red: *S*O*K*R*A*T*E*S*K*A*L*O*S ("Socrates is beautiful").

Side B: A youth dressed in a red mantle is standing to the left, holding a burled stick in his right hand. His left hand is stretched out in front of him.

Both figures are standing on a short band of red meanders. The vase is an early work of the Berlin painter. The name Sokrates appears only once more on another, even earlier, vase of this artist, which is now in St. Petersburg (St. Petersburg 635).
artifact.inscriptions: *S*O*K*R*A*T*E*S*K*A*L*O*S, "Sokrates is beautiful" appears retrograde below the left arm of the youth on side B.

artifact.name: Munich 2312
artifact.summary: Side A: running Perseus<lb>Side B: running Gorgon
artifact.other_bibliography: Woodward, Perseus, 57ff., pl. 16, a-c.; Lullies and Hirmer, Griechische Vasen der reifarchaischen Zeit, 18, 23, 31, pls. 56-58.; Beazley 1974, 16, 9, pl. 9,1.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Perseus is here depicted running to the right, wearing a short chiton with decorative borders, a skin, and winged boots. His cap of invisibility is tied underneath his cheek with a red ribbon; he also is equipped with a kibisis and harpe.

Side B: this side shows a running Gorgon, apparently in pursuit of Perseus. She is wearing a long dress with sleeves and dotted decoration, a short mantle slung over her right shoulder, winged boots, earrings, and a red bracelet.

artifact.name: Munich 2243
artifact.summary: Side A: The Calydonian boar hunt<lb>Side B: Theseus and the Minotaur<lb>At each handle, sphinxes
artifact.other_bibliography: See CVA entry above for extensive bibliography.
artifact.dimensions: H. 18.7 cm., d. 26.8 cm., h. of foot 8.5 cm., d. of foot 12.0 cm.
artifact.condit: In the process of restoration, the broken edges have been smoothed. There are several missing pieces at breaks. On the foot there are several patches of altered color, and several added red figures in the frieze now appear olive green, as their color has faded.
artifact.decoration_description:
The vessel has black glaze on exterior and interior, the latter more diffuse. There are areas of clay color showing on the foot and handle attachments.

Side A depicts the Calydonian Boar Hunt. In the center stands the boar, being attacked from both sides. His lowered head and legs planted forward bespeak his defensive position. On his back a white hunting hound is crouching with grinning fangs. Underneath the boar a second hound lies dead, with its entrails, represented in dilute glaze, ripped out. From the left, five naked, bearded hunters are attacking, with their upper bodies turned frontally even though their heads and lower bodies are in right profile. Two hounds are at their sides. The figures are arranged in three overlapping levels. The first hunter, Kastor, has stuck one spear in the boar's eye and a second in its shoulder; the spear points stick out the other side of the bloody wounds. One hound, Charon, is biting the boar's snout. The second hunter, Polydeukes, stabs a trident with his left hand into the boar's forehead, while with his right he holds a spear ready. The following three hunters do the same, the first, Mofsos, with a second lance in his left hand, the second and third, Jason and Idasos, with their left weapons raised as well as those on the right. Between them the second hound is running hard. On the right, two more hounds and four naked companions proceed to attack as well. Only the first and third hunter are bearded, and all are pictured with their upper bodies turned to the back. The first, his name not completely clear, with his arms painted on backwards, leads the attack with a trident gripped in both hands, ramming it into the boar's hindquarters. One dog, a female, has gotten a biting grip on the boar's rear flank, where blood flows from the wound. The second and third hunters, Peleus and Melanion, correspond in their positions and weapons to Jason and Idasos, while the last, Kimon, with his hound corresponds to Mofsos and his hound on the left. On both sides of the scene a sphinx appears among the palmettes in the handle zone.

Side B depicts Theseus fighting the Minotaur. In the center of the scene Theseus leans forward, facing right, wearing a short chiton and belted nebris. At his side his scabbard, as well as his hair, both of which fly out behind him, demonstrate the force of his lunge. He grips the Minotaur's horn with his left hand, while with his right he holds his sword. The Minotaur is covered with hair, shown by white marks, and it bleeds from a wound in its midsection, as it tries to flee. It has fallen to its right knee even as it tries to run with its left, but it grips the blade of Theseus's sword in its right hand, turns its head toward him, and tries with its left to free its horn from his grip. With Athena in the lead, a group of four Athenian maidens and three youths watch the fight. The goddess, her upper body partly obliterated by a break, wears a peplos decorated above with spiral patterns. She holds in her right hand Theseus's lyre with its plektron hanging from it, while she gestures with her upraised left hand. Behind her the first female of the Minotaur's sacrificial victims, Euanthe, wears a long chiton with a rosette-decorated mantle over her shoulders and arms. The second figure, a youth named Lykinos, is dressed similarly, with a knee-length mantle thrown over him, a part of which he holds in his left hand. To the left follow the similarly clad Anthula, Antias, Glyke, and the bearded Simon and Engedo. The males' mantles are red, while the females' are black with large red dots. To the right of the struggle stands Ariadne in a peplos decorated with a fishbone border. In her outstretched right hand she holds a ball of wool, in her left a wreath. Ariadne's wet nurse, Throphos, stands behind her in a striped and rosette-decorated peplos. With her arms outstretched and her legs stepping nervously, she shows her unease at the spectacle. Behind her stand more calmly the Athenian youths and maidens, Lykios, Eunike, Solon, and the badly damaged Syon, all dressed similarly to those on the left. On both sides near the handles are sphinxes.

Red is used on both sides for hairbands, wide stripes and musculature on the thighs of the sphinxes, on the head and beard hair of the maidens and youths (except for the wet nurse), the females' long chitons and peploi except in the decorative zones, Theseus's short chiton and the stripes on his scabbard, the snout, throat, horn and blood of the Minotaur, the central dots in the rosettes of the females' mantles and the wet nurse's peplos, the necks, ribs and musculature of the hunting hounds and the boar, the boar's trunk, belly stripes and blood, the body of the lyre, and Ariadne's ball of wool. White is used for the females' skin, the face,neck and narrow wing stripes of the sphinxes, the rosettes on the females' mantles and the wet nurse's peplos, the youths' chitons, the lyre's arms, the hound on top of the boar, the belly and neck stripes of the other hounds, and spots on the body of one of the hounds. The females' and sphinxes' eyes are depicted with added white, now worn off the shinx on the right of side B.
artifact.inscriptions:
On side A, above the boar, its name is inscribed, *S*U*H (pig). The white hound on its back is :*L*E*U*K*I*O*S: (Leukios). The hound lying dead is, in retrograde, *P*O*D*E*S (feet). The first hunter on the left is [*K]*A*S*T*O*R: (Kastor). The hound next to him is *X*A*R*O*N (Charon). The second hunter is *P*O*L*U*D[*E]*U*K*E*S (Polydeukes). The last three hunters are *M*O*F*S*O*S (Mofsos), *I*A*S*O*N (Jason), and (retrograde) *I*D*A*S*O*S (Idasos). The hound next to them is *G[*O]*R*G*O[*S]. The first hunter on the right is (retrograde) :*M*E*L*E*A*G*R*O*S (Meleagros). The dog biting the boar's flank is (retrograde) *Q*E*R*O (Thero). The two companions following on this side are *P*E*L*E*U*S (Peleus) and *M*E*L*A*N*I*O*N (Melanion). The last two companions are *K*I*N*O (Kimon) and (retrograde) *P*O*D*A*R*G*O*S (Podargos). The sphinxes to right and left are *S*F*I*X*S (sphinx) and (retrograde) *S*F*I*X*S (sphinx). Between the forelegs of the sphinxes are &epig-rough;*E*D*E (Hede) and (retrograde) &epig-rough;*E*D*E (Hede), and above their heads are *X*A*I*R*E (greeting) and (retrograde) *X*A*I*R*E (greeting).

On side B, Theseus's name is inscribed in retrograde, *Q*E*S*E*U*S. By the Minotaur is inscribed in retrograde *M*I*N*O*T*A*U*R*O*S. Athena's name is inscribed *A*Q*E*N*A*I*A. Theseus's instrument, which she holds, is inscribed *L*U*R*A (lyre). The first female behind Athena has the inscription *E*U*A*N*Q*E (Euanthe). The next youth is *L*U*K*I*N*O*S (Lykinos). The next five young people are *A*N*Q*U*L*A (Anthyla), *A*N*T*I*A*S (Antias), *G*L*U*K*E (Glyke), *S*I*M*O*N (Simon), and *E*N*P*E*D*O (Enpedo). To the right, Ariadne's name is inscribed in retrograde *A*R*I*A*D*N*E. Her wet nurse's name is written, also in retrograde, *Q*R*O*F*O*S: (Throphos). Behind her stand the five young people, (retrograde) :*L*U*K*I*O*S (Lykios), (retrograde) *E*U*N*I*K*E (Eunike), (retrograde) *S*O[*L*O]*N (Solon), (retrograde) *T*I*M*O (Timo) and (retrograde) *S*U[*O]*N (Syon). The sphinxes to right and left have inscriptions *S*F[*I*X*S] (sphinx) and (retrograde) *S*F*I*X*S (sphinx). Above their forepaws are *X*A*I*R*E (greeting) and *X*A*I*R*E (greeting). Under them are the nonsense inscriptions *H*U[..] (hu...) and (retrograde) *E*U*L*S*P (Eulsp), as well as under the lefthand sphinx's tail the nonsense (retrograde) *E*U*S*I (Eusi). Above Theseus is written *E*U*T*I*L*A*S: (Eutilas). Above Ariadne's right arm is written *T*E*S (the), and above the wet nurse's hands *K*A*L*E (beautiful). Above the youths and maidens are written the nonsense inscriptions *I*U*S*U (Iusu), *P*N*S*U (Pnsu), *N*E*R*N (Nern), *N*E*R*N*S (Nerns), *E*N*O*P*S (Enops), *N*E*T*N*S (Netns), *M*I*P*O (Mipo), *E*U*T*I*S (Eutis), *P*I*P*O*I (Pipoi), and *E*P*N*S (Epns).

Between the handle attachments are the signatures of the potters, *A*R*X*K*L*E*S *E*P*O*I*S*E*N (Archikles made it), and *G*L*A*U*K*U*T*E*S *M*E*P*O*I*S*E*N (Glaukytes made me).

artifact.name: Munich 1468
artifact.summary: Side A, man courting boy. Side B, frontal chariot. On the shoulder: A, wrestlers; B, the like.
artifact.other_bibliography: Gerhard, Annali del Istituto 3 (1821): 123 (50), 232; Monumenti Inediti Pubblicati dall'Instituto Archeologico I, Taf. 26,9; Gardiner, Journal of Hellenic Studies 25 (1905): 281, Taf. 12 a and b; Gardiner 1910, 391, App. 121; Gardiner 1930, 193, Abb. 165a.
artifact.dimensions: H. 36.8 cm., d. of rim 16.4 cm., w. of lip 1.3 cm., d. of foot 13.1 cm.
artifact.decoration_description:
The edge of the foot is clay-colored, while its top is glazed with a red edge and a red stripe in the center. The body-foot join is painted red. The strap handles are glazed on top and bottom, decorated laterally with rosettes, and their upper edges bearing a red stripe. A delicate red bulge appears at the neck attachment. The neck is glazed on its exterior and interior, while the rim itself is decorated outside and inside with red stripes. There are two more red stripes on the neck interior. On the lower body of the vessel is a glazed zone bordered above and below by red stripes. In this area on both sides are the scenes, interrupted at the shoulder by a band of rosettes with red dots in the center. A band of red and black tongues borders the shoulder scenes at the body-neck join. The main scene on side A is bordered laterally by ivy leaves, on side B by diagonal zigzag marks. On both sides of the neck is a chain of opposed lotuses and palmettes, elaborately rendered, with red center leaves on the lotuses. The upper half of the decoration is repeated at the rim.

On side A, a bearded man beckons favor of a youth, while bearded men dance on either side of them. All four figures are naked. The youth holds a wreath with white dots on its edge in his left hand, and with his right he clasps the left hand of the man who is courting him. Both center figures, as well as the dancer on the left, wear white chain necklaces. The lefthand dancer hops on his right leg with lively upraised left leg and left arm, while the right arm punches the air behind him. The righthand dancer is in the midst of a leap, with both feet off the ground. Over his left shoulder, presumably as a love gift, he carries a deer with red throat and white belly stripes. All four figures have red hair, and the two on the left have red beards. In the background are nonsense inscriptions.

On side B a frontal chariot is depicted, with a bird flying to the left above the two horses on the right. Red is used for the four horses' breast bands, as well as the three lefthand horses' manes, two stripes on the chariot, the charioteer's throat, and two wing stripes on the bird. The horses' breast bands were decorated with rows of white dots. The two horses on the outsides have their forelocks tied into a tuft.

Both shoulder scenes depict two wrestlers flanked by two onlookers. Here the drawing is noticeably more careless than in the main scenes. On both sides the lefthand wrestler has his opponent locked in a firm grip. The spectators all lean on staffs, although the staff of the lefthand spectator on side A is so thinly painted that it is hardly visible. All are holding mantles over one arm. Both wrestlers on side B and the righthand wrestler on side A are bearded. All beard and head hair is red. Both mantles on side A and the lefthand mantle on side B are striped in red, while the righthand mantle on side B is dotted in red. Above each righthand wrestler a garment is hanging at the upper edge of the scenes.
artifact.inscriptions: There are nonsense inscriptions on side A.
artifact.shape_description: The foot is flat with a vaulted edge. There is a plastic ringlike attachment between foot and body. The belly of the vase is broad and low, with a sharp bend at the shoulder that resembles the shape of a hydria.

artifact.name: Munich 1442
artifact.summary: Side A: Warrior setting out<lb>Side B: same
artifact.other_bibliography: Burkhardt, Reitertypen auf griechischen Vasen, 16; Buschor 1969, Griechische Vasen 124, pl. 134.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori.
artifact.comparanda: Oxford 509, ABV, 239, no. 5 for the image of Hermes in front of Zeus.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: a young warrior on horseback is riding to the right. The horse is depicted at a slow trot, its mane tied up into two hair knots and its tail is pointing straight backwards. The muscles along the chest and back are delineated in red, the teeth and bridle are indicated with white dots. The horseman, who is holding the reins in one hand and a spear in the other, wears a headband with white decoration. His red chiton has short sleeves and white dotted decoration along the seams.

Side B: The horseman on this side is, with a few exceptions, similar to the one on the opposite side. His profile is lost; the headband does not show white decoration. The chest of the horse is entirely painted in red.

Shoulder B: The image decorating the neck on Side B shows a better state of preservation and is therefore discussed first. Hermes is depicted standing in front of Zeus, flanked on either side by a bearded man. Zeus is seated on a stool, his left hand raised in greeting, his right holding a scepter. He is wearing a red chiton with decorated seams and a black mantle with red dots and rosettes dotted in white. Hermes, with a red beard, is leaving to the right, his head turned back to Zeus. He raises his right hand in greeting while holding the kerykeion in his left. On his head he wears a petasos. His legs are almost entirely lost; only a faint trace of a winged boot is visible. A fawn skin is tied over his chiton and he has a black mantle draped around his shoulders, which is similarly decorated to that worn by Zeus. The two flanking figures each hold a scepter in one hand and have the other raised in greeting. Both men are wearing a long red chiton with decorated seams, and a mantle similar to those worn by the two gods.

Shoulder A: The image is largely destroyed. A bearded man is seated between two men in long mantles facing right. A nude youth is facing the one furthest to the right; both men are raising their right in greeting. The youth holds his left hand slightly raised, the palm pointing forward. He has red hair, a ribbon across his chest, and he wears a white beaded necklace.

Linear scrolls with spiral tendrils are decorating the areas below the handles. The frieze on the belly is framed by a band of dentils above a garland of buds and arches.

artifact.name: Munich 1404
artifact.summary: Side A: quadriga moving right<lb>Side B: the same
artifact.decoration_description:
On the clay-colored edge of the mouth is a band of rays. The insides of the handles are clay-colored. Above the scenes are chains of opposed lotuses and palmettes. Most details of the chain are red and black, while the lotus buds, outlines of the palmette leaves, and dots in the links are white. A red line runs around the vase on the foot profile, others on the neck above the handles, on the neck-mouth join, two above the band of rays, and two below the scenes.

On side A, a charioteer stands on his quadriga, wearing a long chiton decorated with white and red flowers, and a headband. Behind the horse team, three hoplites are moving left. Their helmets are low-crested, and the device on the near hoplite's shield is a white amphora with two red dots on its rim. In front of the team on the far right sits an old man on a stool. He is wearing a chiton and mantle and holding in his right hand an upright, curved staff. Above the horses a bird is flying left, while below them a salamander crawls upwards. Red is used for the mane, forelock, and tail of the near horse, the pupils of the third horse, the chariot wheel, the charioteer's headband, the near hoplite's helmet and shield rim, and the old man's cloak. White is used for the third horse, the breast band of the first horse, the second horse's teeth, dots on the helmet crest of the near hoplite, the other two hoplites' shield rims and helmet crests, and the old man's hair, beard, and chiton.

The scene on side B is similar to that of A. Behind the team, but in front of the charioteer and quadriga is a warrior facing right, putting on his greaves. He is wearing a chiton, chest armor, and a high-crested helmet. On the far right in front of the team is a running man, naked except for a mantle draped over his right forearm and left shoulder. He is moving in the same direction as the others. Above the team two birds fly, one to the right behind the warrior, the other to the left behind the running figure. Red is used for the mane, tail, belly stripe, and marks on the belly and breast band of the first horse, the mane of the third horse, the wheel of the chariot, the charioteer's hair, and the warrior's helmet. White is used for the fourth horse, dots on the upper part of the charioteer's chiton, the warrior's chiton, armor, and helmet crest.
artifact.shape_description: The handles are round, in three parts. The foot is disc-shaped with a vertically profiled rim.

artifact.name: Munich 1397
artifact.summary: Side A: Theseus and the Minotaur<lb>Side B: Herakles and the Lion
artifact.condit: In places the finish has misfired to red and worn away.
artifact.graffiti: Under the foot are three red dipinti.
artifact.decoration_description:
Above the scene on side A is a lotus-palmette frieze, and above side B's scene is a chain of opposing lotuses and palmettes. The lower body bears a band of rays. Three red lines circle the vase on its foot, two above the band of rays and under the scenes, and one above the handles. Two red lines provide the upper borders of the scenes. The outer edge of the lip is red.

On side A, Theseus is shown fighting the Minotaur, sticking his sword in its neck. Theseus is wearing a short-sleeved chitoniskos with broad red vertical stripes, white dots on the sleeves, and a white wave pattern with dots on the lower border. With his left hand he grips the Minotaur's head, while with his right he plunges his sword in. The Minotaur has fallen to his left knee; he holds a stone in his left hand. Blood flows out of his wound. Two women in red striped chitons and peploi stand to the right and left of the action. Their garments have white dots on the lower borders and sleeve edges, as well as white cross and dot patterns on the sleeves. Each has a necklace and earrings, and the lefthand woman wears a headband. On the far left and far right, behind the two women stand two naked youths, also watching the action. Red is used for the hair, beard, and stripes on the chiton of Theseus, the pupils and stripes on the peploi of the women, the lefthand woman's headband, and the youths' hair. White is used for the women's skin, Theseus's scabbard strap and sword blade, and the dots on Theseus's and the womens' garment borders.

On side B, Herakles is in the process of killing the lion by stabbing it in the neck. Herakles is naked; in a position similar to that of Theseus on other side, he grips the lion's head with his left arm and hand and plunges in his sword with his right hand. Blood streams out of the lion's wound. On the left stands a woman in chiton, peplos, and headband, and on the right is the naked Iolaos; both are watching the struggle. Red is used for vertical stripes on the woman's peplos and lower chiton edge, her headband, Herakles's hair, beard, and sword blade, the lion's mane, and Iolaos's hair. White is used for the woman's skin and Herakles's scabbard strap.

artifact.name: Munich 1396
artifact.summary: Side A, men in chariot, with warrior<lb>Side B, frontal chariot
artifact.graffiti: On the bottom of the base are red dipinti.
artifact.decoration_description:
Above the scene on side A is a lotus-palmette band, while over side B's scene is a chain of opposing lotuses and palmettes. A band of rays appears on the lower body. Three red lines circle the foot of the vessel, and two each above the band of rays and beneath the scenes, as well as one each on the neck above the handles and on the upper edge of the rim. Two red lines are visible above the scenes, extending from handle attachment to handle attachment.

On side A, a charioteer stands on a quadriga, wearing a long chiton and holding a kentron as well as the reins. Next to him in the chariot is a bearded man wearing chiton and mantle. Behind the team of horses stand a woman and a hoplite facing each other. The woman is dressed in a peplos decorated with white lines and dots and two broad red areas, one one her chest and one at the garment's lower border, as well as a necklace and headband. The bearded hoplite wears a high-crested helmet that covers his face and holds a spear and shield, both partially visible behind the horses. On the far right, in front of the horses, stands a second woman in chiton, peplos, necklace, and headband. She is facing the others, and her garments are red striped, with white lines as decoration. Red is used on side A for the mane, forelock, tail, and breastband of the horse farthest forward, two horizontal stripes on the quadriga, the charioteer's beard and the hair, beard, and part of the mantle of the man next to him, the pupils, headbands, and stripes on the peploi of the women, and the helmet of the hoplite. White is used for the women's skin, the hindmost horse, dots on the edge of the peplos overfall of the righthand woman, and the lower edge of hoplite's helmet crest.

On side B a quadriga is shown frontally. The charioteer wears a white himation and holds a kentron. Red is used for a broad horizontal stripe on the chariot, the charioteer's hair, and the manes, forelocks, and breastbands of the horses.

artifact.name: Munich 1392
artifact.summary: Side A: The judgement of Paris<lb>Side B: Recovery of Helen
artifact.condit: On side A there is a red firing mark in the middle of the scene.
artifact.decoration_description:
Above both scenes runs a frieze of lotus buds. Below the scenes is a band of rays. Red lines circle the vase on the foot, above the band of rays, on the neck above the top handle attachments, on the upper edge of the rim, and two just under the main scenes. In addition, a red line extends just above both scenes from right to left handle attachment.

Side A depicts the judgement of Paris. On the far right Paris himself is seated. In front of him is growing a shrub; his seat is shown only by a black line that curves with his body. Paris is wearing a mantle and holding a six-stringed lyre. He raises his right hand as if in greeting or amazement. In front of Paris and facing him stands Hermes, wearing a chlamys, winged shoes, and a pilos, and holding a wreath in his left hand and a kerykeion in his right. Hermes is leading the draped goddesses Aphrodite, Athena, and Hera into the presence of Paris. The first and last goddesses' chitons are decorated with white flowers, while Athena's peplos has red dots and white crosses as well. The first and third goddesses wear red-striped cloaks over their shoulders and down their backs, as well as headbands, while Athena wears an aegis and a high-crested helmet and holds a spear in her right hand. Red is used for parts of the garments as described, Paris's frontal hair and beard, Hermes's beard and wreath, the goddesses' headbands and the pupils of their eyes, the lower border of the first goddess's chiton, and the upper border of Athena's helmet crest. White is used for the goddesses' skins and the edge of Hermes' pilos, as well as dots on Athena's helmet crest.

On side B, Menelaos, armed as a hoplite, is leading Helen. Menelaos is wearing a short sleeved chitoniskos, greaves, and a high-crested helmet, and he carries a shield with a tripod as its device in his left hand. His sword in its scabbard hangs from a strap over his right shoulder. With his right hand, he grasps the left hand of Helen to pull her along. Helen is wearing a peplos decorated with white blossoms and red dots, a mantle pulled up over the back of her head and a necklace. Behind her on the far left is another hoplite, walking away from the pair but turning his head to look back at them. He is dressed similarly to Menelaos, except that his helmet has a low crest, and no strap is visible on his shoulder or back. His shield, which he carries in his left hand, has the skull of a steer for its device. Red is used on this side for the chitoniskoi of the hoplites, the shield and greave edges, Helen's pupils, the lower edge of her peplos, and the folds in her mantle. White is used for Helen's skin, the scabbard straps and the sword handles and tips of the scabbards, as well as portions of the helmet crests.

artifact.name: Munich 1381
artifact.summary: Side A: Warrior in chariot leaving home. Side B: Two fighting hoplites.
artifact.other_bibliography: Wrede, AM 41, 1916, 225, 16 and pl. 21.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori (?)
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: the farewell of a warrior. The rather crowded panel shows the warrior in full armor to the far left, surrounded by his two children. The boy on the right is wearing a mantle, the little girl a chiton with white floral decoration. Nearby stands a charioteer in a quadriga. Behind the chariot wait several figures, all looking toward the warrior: a woman in a peplos with incised decoration, a hoplite, a second woman, another hoplite, a bearded man, and a third hoplite. The shields of the warrior and the last hoplite both show a tripod as shield device. The shield of the second hoplite is decorated with white and red dots.

Side B: two hoplites fighting over a corpse. The one on the left wears a chiton with white floral decoration and a chlamys with ornamental flowers and red dots, the one on the left a chlamys with red dots along the seam. His shield shows a white bird as a shield device. Between them lies a dead hoplite on the ground.

artifact.name: Munich 1380
artifact.summary: Side A: Ajax and Cassandra<lb>Side B: Frontal chariot
artifact.other_bibliography: A. Schneider, Der troische Sagenkreis, 176 ff.; Technau, Exekias 23, 12; Hafner, Viergespanne in Vorderansicht, 8, 68.
artifact.collection_history: Collection Candelori (?)
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Ajax threatens Kassandra with his sword. His armor consists of a helmet and harness over a short chiton decorated with red dots and incised stars. Kassandra is kneeling in front of him turned to the right, her head facing Ajax. To her right stands Athena wearing a peplos with white floral decoration, ependytes, and a crested helmet. She is holding a spear in her raised left hand and a large shield decorated with a tripod in her right. A nude bearded man runs off to her right. The scene is observed on the far left by a woman dressed in a peplos.

Side B: A quadriga is depicted frontally. The charioteer wears a white himation and holds a kentron. The two central horses are facing each other, the other two outwards. Their manes and chest harnesses are painted in red.

Both panels are framed on the top by a frieze of alternating palmettes and lotus buds.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.99
artifact.summary: Side A: Hector (?) arming. Side B: Priam (?).
artifact.essay_text:
Collection of The University Museums, University of Mississippi Phase I Cultural Center (1977.3.99)Attributed to the Calliope Painter430-420 B.C.Height: 19.1 cm.Diameter: 16.1 cm.Side A: Hector (?) arming.Side B: Priam (?).

A young man stands pulling off his cloak with his right hand while with the left he takes the spear and helmet the woman holds for him. She carries his shield, which bears a lion as its device, and gazes at him over its rim. On the reverse, an older man stands holding a scepter and looking intently before him. He must belong with the two figures on side A, in the traditional grouping of a departing warrior between his parents. This was one of the longest-lived themes in Greek vase-painting, as well as in Greek life. War was endemic in the Greek world, with cities constantly quarreling among themselves, and every male citizen could expect to be in battle many times in the course of his life. This pelike was painted in the early years of the Peloponnesian War, when scenes like this one were being enacted frequently in Athenian homes. No names are given here; the young man looks like a contemporary Athenian whose wife or mother is helping him with his weapons and shield, all of which are conventional 5th-century heavy infantry equipment. If this were meant to be a contemporary scene, however, we would expect to see more armor; a breast-plate certainly, if not also a pair of greaves. A young man who goes out to battle wearing only a helmet and a sword belt is more likely to be a legendary hero, at least in vase-painting. The bearded man on side B gives another clue to the warrior's identity: from his wreath and scepter, he must be a king, and the hero leaving home is his son. In all probability he is Priam, and the young man Hector, while the woman may be his mother or his wife Andromache.

The painter has set his figures well apart, and has made the helmet the focal point of the picture by setting it at the crossing point of the vertical line of the spear and the diagonal lines of the two arms. These diagonals are extended and made more emphatic by the line of the cloak which Hector pulls off with his right hand and by the body of the lion on the shield. The helmet is held almost at eye level; are the figures looking at it or at each other? Perhaps we have here an echo of the touching scene in the Iliad (Hom. Il. 6.369-502) of Hector's farewell to his wife Andromache, who begs him not to go back to the battle, and to their baby son, who takes fright and begins to cry at the sight of his father's helmet, with its crest "nodding terribly, as he thought." The mood here is quiet and restrained, as in much of the art of the period, but there is something of poignancy in the two faces regarding each other over the crest of the helmet.

Bibliography: ARV2, 1262, 60.

Lucy Turnbull

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.98
artifact.summary: Two women
artifact.sources_used: D.M. Robinson "Unpublished Greek Vases in the Robinson Collection" AJA 60 (1956) 21-22, pl. 16, fig. 73
artifact.other_bibliography: Tillyard 1923, pl. 15, 111
artifact.collection_history: Formerly in the Hope collection, 102b. Sold at Sotheby's 14 Feb. 1955, no. 95 in Catalogue. Sold by Spink and Co. to D.M. Robinson. In the Robinson Collection, Harvard inv. 206. Gift of Helen Tudor Robinson, 1960.
artifact.condit: Almost perfect condition
artifact.decoration_description:
The vase has a tongue pattern on the rim, and an egg-and-dart pattern on the neck. Below the figures is a meander and cross pattern. In the figural scene are two women. On the far left is a klismos, or chair with curved legs, seen from the side. In front of it is a woman wearing a broad fillet in her hair, and a chiton and himation. Her arms, covered by the himation, are raised to greet the woman on the right. This woman stands with body frontal but her head in left profile. She is dressed similarly to the first woman, and holds a wide band in her right hand. Between them is the inscription *K*A*L*E *K*L*E*T*A*G*O*R*A ("Kleitagora is beautiful").

Kleitagora may have been an historical personage, perhaps an hetaira (Robinson, 22).
artifact.inscriptions: *K*A*L*E *K*L*E*T*A*G*O*R*A ("Kleitagora is beautiful").

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.97
artifact.summary: Side A: Theseus, Perithoos, and Amazon<lb>Side B: Three youths in mantles
artifact.essay_text:
Collection of The University Museums, University of Mississippi Phase I Cultural Center (1977.3.97)Attributed to the Group of Polygnotos440-430 B.C.Height: 42.2 cm.Diameter: 24.1 cm.Side A: Theseus, Peirithoos and Amazon.Side B: Three youths in mantles.

The Amazon on side A holds her bow in the left hand and retreats to the right, turning to strike with her battle-ax at Theseus, whose spear has already penetrated her side. Only the distinctive ax marks her as an Amazon; instead of the usual patterned tights she wears a Greek peplos. Behind Theseus his friend Peirithoos prepares to throw a stone. The figures are not named, but each is labeled "beautiful" — *K*A*L*O*S, *K*A*L*O*S, *K*A*L*E. This is one of six vases, all from the same circle of painters and all with the same three-figure composition, differing slightly in details of weaponry and costume, which probably go back to a common original. On one of the other vases the central figure is labeled "Theseus," and the identification should hold good for all six. Theseus is heroically nude except for his helmet; the painter has given Peirithoos a shaggy pilos and an animal-skin cloak, perhaps in reference to his rustic Thessalian homeland.

The combats of Achilles and Herakles against Amazons appear in vase painting after about 550 B.C., but Theseus' Amazonomachies begin in the last quarter of the century, when the Athenians were attempting to raise their national hero to equal status with Herakles. An epic poem, the Theseis was perhaps composed about 525, and illustrations of episodes from the epic appear soon afterward. The theme of Theseus' defeat of an Amazon army that invaded Attica to avenge his abduction of their queen became especially popular after the Athenian repulse of the Persian invasions of Attica in 490 and 480 B.C. Greek artists seldom represented historical events directly, preferring to look to the legendary past for a parallel event; thus for artists working in Athens, the Amazon invasion became a visual metaphor for the Persian ones, and Amazonomachies were chosen as the theme for decorating several public buildings. The common ancestor for the examples of this three-figure composition could be either a wall painting or another vase painting. Two large-scale Amazonomachies of Theseus were painted in Athenian buildings in the generation after the Persian Wars, one by Mikon and one by Polygnotos of Thasos (not the vase painter of the same name). No detailed description of either painting survives, but 5th-century vase painters are believed to have copied some of Polygnotos' innovations: many-figured compositions, the placement of figures at different levels rather than on a common ground line, and the use of trees and other landscape features. The Theseus-Amazon pair from this vase also occur on at least four other vases, as part of many-figured Amazonomachies with Polygnotan characteristics. Variations on the Peirithoos figure also occur in these pictures, and it is likely that this group was derived from a larger vase-painting that in turn was derived from a wall painting.

Bibliography: Robinson 1956, 1-25, pl. 16, 71-2; ARV2, 1058; von Bothmer 1957, 185-191; pl. 81, 4; For Theseus' significance in Attic art and politics: Ward 1970; for relationships between wall painting and vase painting: Simon 1963, 43-62.

Lucy Turnbull

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.96
artifact.summary: Side A: komos. Side B: komos.
artifact.sources_used: Mississippi museum archives. D.M. Robinson "Unpublished Greek Vases in the Robinson Collection" AJA 60 (1956) 19-20, pl. 15-16
artifact.collection_history: Gift of Helen Tudor Robinson, 1959. Formerly in the D.M. Robinson collection, Harvard inv. 204.
artifact.condit: Excellent condition; ancient repair of one handle with iron rivets. Slight surface wear.
artifact.comparanda: Robinson compared the shape of the vessel, and the decoration around the handles, to a signed stamnos by Polygnotos (London 96.7-16.5).
artifact.decoration_description:
Around the outside of the handles is an egg-and-dart pattern. Above and below at the sides of the handles are addorsed palmettes and spirals. Bordering the scene at the bottom is a cross and meander pattern, and at the top (near the neck) is a tongue pattern. The rim has an egg-and-dart pattern on it, as well. Robinson compared the shape of the vessel, and the decoration around the handles, to a signed stamnos by Polygnotos London 96.7-16.5, and further said "There can be no doubt that we must assign this very beautiful vase to Polygnotos himself" (19).

Side A: On the left is a tall bearded man, in profile to the right. He wears a fillet and a himation, and walks forward, supported by a flute girl. Near him is the inscription *D*E*M*O*N*I*K*O*S ("Demonikos"). The flute girl wears a broad fillet decorated with a row of angles and dots, and an Ionic chiton with an overfold. She plays the flute (puffing out her cheeks) while leaning back into the man's arms and lifting her left foot, toes pointed, off of the ground. Near her is the inscription *K*L*E*O*P*A*T*R*A ("Cleopatra"). Before her is a youth, nude except for a cloak hanging from his left shoulder and fillet, dancing to the right. He raises his right hand beyond the perimeter of the tongue decoration, and with the other hand balances a large column krater with ivy decoration on his left knee. Near him is the inscription *E*U*Q*I*P*P*O*S ("Euthippos"). The bearded man on the right is in profile to the left. He wears a cloak flung over his shoulders and a fillet. He strides to the left, holding his staff over his head with his left hand, and a barbiton over his back with the other hand. Robinson stated that this was a dance gesture, and that he was probably beating the time, and not the dancer before him (20). Near him is the inscription *K*A*L*L*I*M*A*X*O*S ("Callimachos").

Side B: Three draped youths stand together. The one on the left faces to the right, holding a skyphos in his left hand. His other hand is hidden under his himation. The middle youth, with himation wrapped around his waist and draped over his left arm, also faces right. He gestures with his right hand, and carries a torch of twigs in his left. Facing him on the right is the third youth, who looks back at him as he walks to the right. He raises his right hand to the center figure.
artifact.inscriptions: Robinson: traces of signature (19). Side A, near the appropriate figures: *D*E*M*O*N*I*K*O*S ("Demonikos"); *K*L*E*O*P*A*T*R*A ("Cleopatra"); *E*U*Q*I*P*P*O*S ("Euthippos"); *K*A*L*L*I*M*A*X*O*S ("Callimachos").

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.92
artifact.summary: Side A: Warrior and king. Side B: Youth in mantle.
artifact.sources_used: Mississippi museum archives. CVA, Robinson Collection 3, USA 7, 16, pl. 8.1
artifact.other_bibliography: Beazley 1925, 438, no. 7
artifact.collection_history: Formerly in the D.M. Robinson collection, Harvard inv. 198; gift of Helen Tudor Robinson.
artifact.condit: Much restored.
artifact.decoration_description:
The base of the vase is a plain torus, lipped at the top. The side of the base is reserved. Below the scenes, and all around the vase, is an egg-and-dart pattern.

Side A: A warrior and a king stand facing each other. At the right, the king stands in profile to the left, leaning on a spear which he holds in his right hand. He wears a laurel wreath in his hair, and is clad in a himation. At the left, stands a youth in a relaxed pose, frontally, with his weight on his left leg and right leg back. He wears the short chiton and cuirass of a hoplite, and carries a spear upright in his left hand. Both figures hang their heads, a characteristic detail of the artist.

Side B: A youth stands in profile to the left. He is enveloped in a himation.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.91
artifact.summary: Side A: Bride and two women<lb>Side B: the same
artifact.sources_used: Mississippi museum archives. CVA, Robinson Collection 2, USA 6, 36-38, pl. l and li, 1; C. Bérard "The Order of Women" A City of Images (Princeton, 1989): 89-108
artifact.other_bibliography: L. Deubner "Epaulia" JdI XV (1900)144-154
artifact.collection_history: Gift of Mrs. Frank S. Peddle, Jr., 1960. Formerly in the D.M. Robinson collection, Harvard inv. 196. Originally purchased in Western Europe.
artifact.condit: Broken and mended.
artifact.comparanda: On a pyxis in the Louvre Louvre CA 1857 a winged figure flying toward the bride is identified as a Nike.
artifact.decoration_description:
The pedestal is in one piece with the vase. The lid of the vase has a high knob. At the junction of the knob and lid, and near the outer edge of the top of the lid, there is a tongue pattern. On the body of the vase, an egg pattern is used around the edge of the rim, and around the base of the handles. There is a tongue pattern on the shoulder, above the scene and between the handles, and a meander and checker-square pattern runs all around below the scene, with a ray pattern at the base. On the conical pedestal a meander and checker-square pattern is used at the top. Below this, and above the scene, is a laurel wreath to the left, between narrow reserved bands. Below the scene are rays. The lower surface of the rim is reserved.

Side A: A bride and two friends are depicted. The bride is seated in the center of the composition on a high-backed chair (klismos) with curving legs. She wears a sleeved Ionic chiton and a himation wrapped about her legs. Her hair is done up in a knot at the back and held in place by a broad taenia. She is looking at herself in a hand mirror which she holds in her right hand. At the left behind the bride stands a woman wearing a Doric peplos, belted at the waist. She stands in a frontal pose with her weight on her left leg and her right knee bent. Her head is turned toward the bride. She holds out her hands in a gesture of admiration. Facing the bride at the right stands another friend, wearing a long Ionic chiton and a himation, a fold of which she pulls over her right shoulder with her raised right hand. Toward the group, from the right, flies the Dawn Goddess, to greet the bride. She is clad in a Doric peplos, similar to that worn by the figure at the left. Similar winged figures occur on most of the known examples of lebetes gamikoi. On a pyxis in the Louvre (Louvre CA 1857), a winged figure flying toward the bride is identified as a Nike (Bérard, 102, fig. 141).

Side B: The same as Side A. Here the bride is shown seated to the left, and wears her himation pulled higher over her shoulders. She holds in her right hand a small casket or chest, which has just been presented to her as a gift by the girl facing her at the left. She wears a Doric peplos and stands with her hands extended toward the bride to whom she has given the box. At the right stands an older and taller woman wearing a chiton and himation, who admires the gift. Though in a frontal position, she looks to the left and makes a gesture with her right hand toward the bride. Behind her is the hymeneal altar toward which a winged figure is flying. It is possible that the goddess is bringing the bridal veil, but it seems more likely that she is meant to be represented with her hands wrapped up inside her himation. On the wall above the bride hangs a taenia.

On the pedestal, a youth is pursuing a girl as an old man watches. The youth wears a mantle fastened at his shoulder, a petasos hanging from a cord around his neck, a wreath in his hair, and high laced sandals. He carries two spears in his right hand, and runs to the right, stretching out his left hand as though to grasp the girl by the shoulder. She wears a Doric peplos with a dark border around the bottom of the skirt and overblouse. She runs to the right, holding up her skirt with her left hand, her right arm bent and held across her breast, and her head turned back as if to ask for mercy. She is running toward an old man, probably her father, who stands at the right, leaning on a staff which he holds in his right hand. He is bearded, and wears a long chiton and himation, and a dark fillet in his white hair. To the left of the youth another woman runs away to the left, looking back at the central group. She wears a chiton and himation, and has her hair in a sakkos. In her right hand she carries a very stylized flower, in the form of palmette leaves and tendrils. Between her and the old man's back is a dolphin.

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.90
artifact.summary: Youth with spears (Theseus?) pursuing a woman.
artifact.sources_used: Mississippi museum archives CVA, Robinson Collection 2, USA 6, 32, pl. 44
artifact.collection_history: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank S. Peddle, Jr. Formerly in D.M. Robinson collection, Harvard inv. 192. Purchased in Western Europe.
artifact.condit: Broken and mended, with slight restorations at the cracks.
artifact.decoration_description:
The mouth of the vase is lipped at the top and bottom, and reserved above. There is a fillet at the base, and the lower edge of the base is reserved. An egg-and-dart pattern is used around the rim and at the base of the handles. Above the scene is an upright palmette and lotus pattern, and below is a meander in threes with cross-squares.

An armed youth is depicted pursuing a woman. The youth is dressed as a hunter, with a black-bordered chlamys over his left shoulder, a petasos hanging at his neck, and two spears in his left hand. He strides to the right and places his outstretched right hand on the shoulder of the fleeing woman. She wears a Doric peplos and a stephane in her hair. She looks back at the youth and raises her hands in a startled gesture. At the left of these two is another woman wearing similar clothes, with a sakkos in her hair. She runs to the left and looks back, gesturing to the youth with her left hand. With her right hand she lifts her peplos at the shoulder.

This might possibly represent Theseus pursuing one of his loves (Helen?).

artifact.name: Mississippi 1977.3.88
artifact.summary: Sides A & B: Dionysiac scenes.
artifact.sources_used: Mississippi museum archives; CVA, Robinson Collection 2, USA 6, 28, pls. 36-37; D.M. Robinson "Illustrations of Aeschylus' Choephoroi and of a Satyr-Play on Hydrias by the Niobid Painter"AJA 36 (1932) 406-407; Webster 1935, 18, fn. 32
artifact.collection_history: Formerly in D.M. Robinson collection, Harvard inv. 189. Purchased in Western Europe.
artifact.condit: Broken and restored, a few fragments missing.
artifact.decoration_description:
The vase has a cyma foot and is reserved around the mouth. The top and bottom surfaces of the rim are reserved. There is a band of egg-and-dart around the rim, and a meander and cross design below the figural panel. Above the panel, around the base of the neck, is a band of slanting double palmettes.
