He holds a spear in his right hand and firmly grips the reins of his horse in his left. An elaborate stand is positioned between Helen and the horse, and an object hangs between Helen and her maid. Below, an Erotes checks a dog in pursuit of a duck. The Erotes, holding the dog's leash, has fallen while trying to control him.

Side B: youths. Five youths stand in conversational attitudes. Each of the youths wears a mantle, with the exception of the middle youth who is nude. Four of the youths wear diadems with three vertical points in front; the right-hand youth wears a wreath. The central youth holds a wreath in his right hand.
artifact.shape_description: In place of handles the vase has projections in the form of a double saddle.

artifact.name: London 1928.2-13.1
artifact.summary: Man and woman at a tomb.
artifact.other_bibliography: Walters 1928-29, 7-8, pl. 2, a; Wehgartner 1985, 17, fig. 12; Beazley Addenda 2, 284; Boardman 1989,130, fig. 253.
artifact.condit: Some of the added colors have faded.
artifact.decoration_description: Man and woman at a tomb. A man and woman stand on either side of a tomb. The focus of the scene is the tomb itself, which is painted in a more careful manner than are the figures. It sits in front of a tymbos resting on a low platform, and consists of a tall stele set on a high base of unusual structure. The high base ends in six 'steps' set on top of a narrow entablature decorated with a zig-zag pattern. Both the tomb and tymbos are painted in secondary white. Ribbons originally hung around the monument but have faded, as has the painted decoration. The woman stands on the left holding out a fillet in both hands, ready to hang it on the tomb. She is dressed in a chiton with an overfold, and wears her hair pulled back in a simple style. The bearded man on the right leans on his stick, wearing a long chiton over which is wrapped a red mantle. His arms are folded and hidden under his clothes. Both figures are barefoot.

artifact.name: London 1923.10-16.10
artifact.summary: Side A: Orestes at Delphi. Side B: komos.
artifact.other_bibliography: ILN 27 Oct. 1923; Lacroix 1946, pl. 8 I.; Simon 1953, 8 fig. 3; EAA, v 743 fig. 903; Prag 1985, pl. 30 fig. a; Vogt 1981, 150; Beazley Addenda 2, 330; Boardman 1989, fig. 198.
artifact.condit: The vase is in excellent condition.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Orestes at Delphi. Orestes takes refuge at an altar while Apollo holds back the pursuing Fury. Orestes has just reached the altar and has lunged forward to place his right foot on it. He leans forward onto this leg as he looks back over his shoulder toward his pursuer. Apollo, in the center of the scene, has interposed himself between Orestes and the Fury. He is moving toward Orestes, his head turned toward the Fury who he intends to hold back with the forked stick he holds in one hand. His other arm is raised, perhaps preparing to strike the Fury. The running Fury has stretched out an arm toward Orestes (pointing at him?). She is winged and has snakes in her hair, and is wearing a short chiton. Orestes wears chlamys and petasos, and carries two spears and a sword.

Side B: komos.

artifact.name: London 1923.1-18.1
artifact.summary: Side A: wedding. Side B: two women. Side A, neck: woman. Side B, neck: man.
artifact.condit: The vase is in good condition.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: wedding. The bride and groom, each accompanied by an attendant, stand facing one another, a wreath hanging between them. The groom is wrapped in a long mantle with a black border, and wears a fillet over his hair. He is shown is three-quarter view, his right arm reaching forward to take the arm of his bride. The bride, head modestly lowered, wears a sakkos and earrings, a long, sheer chiton, and a himation decorated with a black border and black crosses. The female attendant, wearing a simple chiton and sakkos, stands behind her tying the bride's sakkos. The attendant behind the groom, also wearing a chiton, is holding up a long sash in both hands.

Side B: two women.

Side A, neck: woman. A woman wearing a chiton and himation stands facing to the right.

Side B, neck: man.

artifact.name: London 1920.12-21.1
artifact.summary: Wedding Procession. Lid: Helios, Selene and Nyx.
artifact.other_bibliography: Cat. Sotheby Dec. 6, 1920, pl. 2; Rumpf 1928, fig. 174; Krauskopf 1977, 16, fig. 3; Richter 1970x, fig. 158; Lacroix 1974, pl. 32,1; LIMC, II, pl. 671, Astra 4; MedInstRome 4, 1977, pl. 23,2; Beazley Addenda 2, 357, 358; Boardman 1989, fig. 243.
artifact.dimensions: H 12.5; H with lid 17.2; D at rim 12.4; D of lid 17.6
artifact.collection_history: The pyxis was bought by the museum at a Sotheby's sale in December 1920.
artifact.condit: The pyxis is in good condition. The surface is somewhat worn.
artifact.comparanda: A Parallel for the scene on the lid may be found on the Sabouroff pyxis, Berlin No. 2519.
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: wedding procession. A wedding procession moves to the right, away from the bride's home, represented by a double door. One of the double doors is ajar, as a maid in a simple chiton peeks out to watch the departure of the procession. The bride and groom in their four horse chariot are the focal point of the scene. The bride stands in the chariot, her mantle draped over her head, one edge of it held in her right hand. The groom holds the reins with both hands and leans into the chariot on his left knee, his right foot still on the ground. He wears a short mantle and a wreath over his hair. Standing on the further side of the horses and facing the couple, is a woman holding a torch, dressed in a chiton and himation with a fillet over her hair. A young male wearing a wreath and a mantle walks behind the chariot, a burning torch held in his left hand as he gestures with his right. He is followed by a young woman balancing on her head a flat, square box with a checkerboard design, perhaps containing part of the bride's trousseau. In her other hand she holds a misshapen bundle, possibly other articles of costume or toilet. She wears a simple chiton and a fillet. The young woman behind her carries a large lebes gamikos and is dressed in a chiton and himation, her hair bound with a fillet. The procession is led by a male figure (the groomsman or herald) in chlamys, wreath and sandals, a petasos hanging down his back. He leads the horses with his right hand and looks back at the couple. With his other hand he gestures toward the door, which functions at this end as the groom's home, the destination of the procession.

Lid: Helios, Selene and Nyx. The figures move in a circle to the right. Helios is apparently driving a four horse chariot, although his legs are shown only from mid-thigh up and the chariot is therefore are not shown. Helios, carrying a stick or staff in his left hand, wears a short piece of fabric draped to fall over his left shoulder, cross his chest and wrap under his right arm. It flies behind him to indicate speed. Selene stands in front of a horse facing forward, her head turned to the left and her arms raised in the orans position. She wears a chiton and himation, and her hair is wrapped in a sakkos. Nyx drives a two-horse chariot, her arms held forward to grip the reins. She wears a simple chiton and sakkos.
artifact.shape_description: Type A pyxis.

artifact.name: London 1917.7-25.2
artifact.summary: Side A: Apollo on a swan, with two women (Muses?) and a satyr. Side B: Eros and two athletes.
artifact.other_bibliography: Tischbein, 1792, pl. 12; Lenormant and de Witte 2, pl. 42; Cook 1914-1940, Zeus ii, 461; Metzger 1951, pl. 24, 2; LIMC, II, 227, pl. 211, Apollo 343; Beazley Addenda 2, 374; Boardman 1989,168, fig. 335.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Apollo on a swan, with two women and a satyr. A palm tree with bunches of fruit rises from a small mound in the center of the scene. From the left, Apollo is descending to earth seated on a swan and playing a lyre. He wears a laurel-wreath in his hair, held by a broad fillet, a chlamys bordered with a broad stripe, and high, elaborately tied sandals. The swan flies with wings held high and legs outstretched as it prepares to land. To the right of the palm tree, a maenad sits facing right, but turns her head to the left to watch Apollo's approach. She is wearing a chiton with an embroidered hem and overfold, a spiked crown, and a necklace and bracelet, and holds a lyre in her left arm. To her right is a naked satyr facing left, holding a thyrsos at his side in his left hand. In his right hand is a fillet, which he holds over the head of the seated maenad. He wears a garland in his hair. Above the outstretched arm of the satyr is a broad semi-circle, perhaps a hanging garland. A second maenad occupies the left-hand side of the scene. She is leaning on her left foot which rests on a rock, and has picked up a fillet with her left hand. She is dressed similarly to the other maenad. A hare stands in front of her, just below the tail of the descending swan. Yellow is used for many of the ornaments and details in the scene.

Side B: Eros and two athletes.

artifact.name: London 1917.12-10.1
artifact.summary: Side A: Orestes at Delphi<lb>Side B: Dionysos, satyr and maenad
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Brit. Mus. II, Gr. Brit. II, IV E a, pl. 1a-b; Trendall 1987, no. 2/244, pl. 91.
artifact.other_bibliography: Hope Sale Cat., no 134; Tillyard 1923, 137-140, pls. 36-37; Trendall 1936, 61, pl. 17; Trendall 1952, no. 147; Bieber 1961a, fig. 97; Webster 1967, 141; Trendall & Webster 1971, no. III. 1, 11; Williams 1985, 64 fig. 74a; Trendall 1989, fig. 371.
artifact.collection_history: The vase was brought from Naples. It was formerly in the Hope collection, from whence it passed in 1917 to the British Museum.
artifact.condit: The vase is in very good condition.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Orestes at Delphi. Orestes is seen in the center, kneeling on an omphalos. Two spears rest against his left shoulder, and a drawn sword is clutched in his right hand. He wears sandals and a cape decorated with stars and a wide black border. His head is turned left to look up at Athena, who stands resting her bare left foot on a column-base, gazing at him with an air of compassion, her right hand resting on her upright spear. She is in full panoply, wearing a crested helmet with two tall plumes and the aegis over elaborate drapery. The huge Delphic tripod is behind Orestes, and to his right is Apollo himself, wearing a laurel wreath, a bracelet and elaborate sandals; there is a beaded band around his thigh, and a similar band worn diagonally across his chest. He holds a piece of drapery between his legs. To the right and partially hidden behind Apollo is a laurel-tree with fillets and two votive tablets hanging in its branches. On the far right, a Fury in hunting costume is squeezed into the picture beside Apollo. Her wings rise up behind her and she holds a large snake in her left hand. Above the tripod is the bust on another Fury, snakes hissing in her hair and round her shoulders. She looks down malevolently in the direction of Apollo, who turns to face the other Fury. In the corners above are the busts of a woman wearing a crown with a veil, possibly Leto, and of a youth with pilos and spear, probably Pylades. The sun is depicted at the top, above Apollo.

Side B: Dionysos, maenad and satyr. A young, unbearded Dionysos with long hair stands in the center facing right, his braceleted right arm lifted, holding a piece of fruit. In his left hand he holds a patera. A garment is draped over his left arm. He wears a wreath, sandals and a beaded band across his chest. To his right stands a satyr, facing forward with his head turned to look at Dionysos. A leopard skin is wrapped around his waist, and he wears a small jug on his right wrist. A wineskin is flung over his left shoulder. The maenad stands on the left, facing forward, her head turned toward Dionysos. She holds a thyrsos in her left hand, and is dressed in long chiton and mantle, with a wide band over her hair. Above Dionysos' head is a hanging wreath(?), and the corners are occupied by busts; on the left is a satyr with thyrsos, on the right a maenad with thyrsos wearing the same style chiton as the woman below.

artifact.name: London 1914.10-30.1
artifact.summary: Animal friezes.
artifact.other_bibliography: Payne 1931, 300 no. 770, Pl. 23,5; Arias & Hirmer 1962, 281, pl. 6; Benson 1953, 124 no. 828; Williams 1985, 23, fig. 28.
artifact.condit: The vase is in excellent condition.
artifact.decoration_description:
Neck: siren and wild boar. A siren occupies the neck on one side. On the other side is a wild boar with head lowered.

Body: animal friezes. Five animal friezes cover the body. On the shoulder, between the handles, sphinxes frame a siren. Below, roaring lions frame a wild boar to the left. Behind them are rams. Underneath are lions alternating with deer and rams. The frieze below shows lions and bulls. The bottom frieze contains lions, rams and boars. There is a ray motif above the foot. In all the friezes, all available space is filled with incised rosettes and irregular 'space-fillers' which are also incised.

artifact.name: London 1912.5-22.1
artifact.summary: Prothesis. Shoulder: agrimi and birds.
artifact.other_bibliography: Zschietzschmann 1928, 38 no. 10, suppl. pl. 8, 10; Tölle 1964, 96 no. 316; Rombos 1988, no. 334, pp. 40, 83, 87, 360, Tables 2, 12, 50, pl. Ic, IIb.
artifact.condit: The vase is in very good condition. There is some chipping on the surface, and some of the paint has worn away.
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: Prothesis. The prothesis is depicted four times around the body of the jug, the most elaborated version placed opposite the handle. Here, six mourning women surround the bier on which the male corpse has been laid out. The woman standing nearest the bier on the right holds a palm frond over the head of the corpse. The rest of the women hold both hands to their heads in the gesture of mourning, their two arms depicted as an unbroken arch. The sex of the women is made clear by the breasts projecting from each side of their triangular chests. The crosshatched shroud covering the corpse is depicted as an arch over the corpse rather than as covering it. A pillow, also crosshatched, supports the head. The bier itself, supported on four sturdy legs, is decorated with a checkerboard motif. A regardant agrimi rests underneath it. To the immediate right of the bier, is an unidentifiable oblong motif. Moving to the right, three women mourn a second dead male, laid out on an almost identical bier. His head is again supported by a pillow, but there is no shroud. Instead, two palm leaves, though shown above his body, are to be understood as having covered it. The women on the right side of the bier holds a palm frond over the corpse; the woman on the left also holds something over the corpse, but it cannot be identified. An agrimi is again shown resting under the bier. The third prothesis involves four? mourning women and a male corpse, once again covered by a crosshatched shroud drawn surrounding the body to leave it visible. Bier, pillow and agrimi are as before. All four women are mourning with both hands to their heads. A second regardant agrimi floats in the space between the bier and the nearest woman on the left. In the fourth prothesis, five full-sized women and a smaller female mourn a male corpse. The bier and shroud differ slightly from the others, in that the bier is crosshatched, no pillow is depicted, and the shroud is decorated with simple Parallel lines. Between the body and the arch of the shroud are three palm fronds, which can again be understood as having covered the body. The women standing on either side of the bier hold palm fronds over the corpse. The others mourn as usual, including the half-size female figure positioned to the right of the bier, between it and the full-sized women holding the palm. As in the other scenes, an agrimi rests under the bier. Blobby chevrons, dots and crosshatched triangles fill all available space.

Shoulder: agrimi and birds. A regardant agrimi is represented in the central panel of the shoulder decoration. To either side, a bird is shown perched on a projecting 'nipple.'
artifact.painter_mod: Attributed to the workshop of the

artifact.name: London 1903.2-17.1
artifact.summary: Side A: Athena<lb>Side B: javelin-throwing on horseback
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Gr. Brit. 1, Brit. Mus. 1, III H f, 3, pl. 1a-b; Gardiner 1930, fig. 12, 1
artifact.other_bibliography: Gardiner 1907, 271, pl. 20; Brauchitsch 1910, 45, pl. I, 6; Gardiner 1910, 357; Pfuhl 1923, 332; Alexander 1925, 19; Boardman 1974, fig. 304.2; Sparkes 1977, 11 pl. 5, fig. 2; Beck 1975, pl. 41.220; Swaddling 1980, 53 above; Yalouris 1977, 201 fig. 105; Patrucco 1972, 188 fig. 94; Mededelingenblad Amsterdam 37-38, 1986, 2 fig. 1; Olivova 1984, 129; Beazley 1986, pl. 98.3-4; Beazley Addenda 1, 107
artifact.collection_history: Given to the British Museum by Campbell-Bannerman in 1903.
artifact.condit: The surface of the amphora has suffered some wear and flaking, particularly on the areas of black glaze near the foot.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Athena, armed, stands to the left between two Doric columns surmounted by cocks. Her chiton is simple and undecorated. The shield device is a Nike holding a long sash in both hands. The inscription runs along the inside of the left-hand column.

Side B: javelin-throwing on horseback. Two epheboi ride to the right, a target centered between them. The rider in front has already thrown his javelin and is past the target, his javelin left sticking in the bull's-eye. His right hand is still raised behind his head after the throw. The rider on the left raises his javelin in his right hand as he prepares to throw. The target is a shield supported by a post. The shield device, a crown, forms the bull's-eye. Both epheboi are dressed in chlamys and petasos, although the petasos of the foremost rider has fallen behind his back. The horses are depicted in almost identical stances, their back legs together and firmly planted on the ground, while both front legs are staggered and raised off the ground.
artifact.inscriptions: An inscription runs along the inside of the left-hand column: *T*W*N*A*Q*H*N*H*Q*E*N*A*Q*L*W*N, from the games at Athens.

artifact.name: London 1901.5-14.1
artifact.summary: Interior: seated boy opening a bird-cage. Side A: youths and a seated boy. Side B: youths and a seated boy.
artifact.other_bibliography: Vente 18 mars 1901, 18; Le Musée 3, 78; Deubner 1930, pl. 18 d; EAA, iii, 753; Boardman 1975, 135, fig. 244; Deubner 1982, 832, pl. G, d; Beazley Addenda 2, 220.
artifact.collection_history: The cup was formerly in the Bourgnignon collection. It was acquired by the British Museum in 1901, and is listed as No. 52 in the Bourgnignon Sale Catalogue.
artifact.condit: The vase is in very good condition.
artifact.decoration_description:
Interior: seated boy opening a bird-cage. The boy is seated on a stool facing right holding a large bird-cage on his knees. He appears to be opening the cage with his right hand, for he tips the cage up with his left hand while the thumb and index finger of his right hand grasp the cage. The boy wears a fillet, and a mantle is draped over his left shoulder and around his legs. In the field above are a long-handled bird-clapper and an inscription.

Side A: youths and a seated boy. The middle boy sits on a stool facing right, while the two youths stand facing him, leaning on sticks. All wear cloaks, and the right-hand youth holds out an open set of tablets in his right hand. In the field are a bird-clapper, a writing-tablet with stylus, and an inscription.

Side B: youths and a seated boy. The scene is similar to that on side A. The seated boy in the center, again facing right, holds a stick in his left hand. On the left is a youth leaning on a stick and holding out an open tablet-case. He wears a cloak and is wreathed. The right-hand figure is missing. In the field above are a bird-clapper, tablets, and an inscription.
artifact.inscriptions: In the field above the boy in the tondo is the inscription, [*O *P]*A*I[*S] *K*A*L*O*S, the boy is beautiful. The exterior, side A, is also inscribed [*O *P]*A*I*S *K*A[*L]*O*S, the boy is beautiful. Side B carries a similar inscription, [*N]*A *O *P*A[*I]*S *K*A[*L*O*S], to the beautiful boy.

artifact.name: London 1899.7-21.5
artifact.summary: Theseus and the Amazons
artifact.sources_used: von Bothmer 1957, 162, 170-171, Pl. 77, 2; CVA, Gr. Brit 8, Brit. Mus. 6 (III I), p. 11, pl. 103; Williams 1985, 49 fig. 53.
artifact.other_bibliography: Forman Sale Cat. 1899, no 357; Gerhard AV, pl. 329-30; Benndorf 1889, 150, fig. 139; Farmakovskii 1929, pl. 18; FR, pl. 58; Studniczka 1915, 222, fig. 34; Pfuhl 1923, fig. 508a; JRIBA 1955, 8; von Bothmer 1957, pl. 77, 2; ph. Ma. 3232; Barron 1972, 36-37, pl. 5c; Kron 1976, pl. 25.1,2; LIMC, I pl. 339. Akamas et Demophon 22, pl. 471; Brommer 1982, 116-117, fig. 17; Birchall & Corbett 1974, fig. 44; Böhr & Martini 1986, pl. 21,1; Beazley Addenda 2, 322; Boardman 1989, fig. 159.
artifact.collection_history: The vase was found at Akragas in 1830. It passed through the Rogers, Stoddart and Forman collections before being bought by the British Museum at the Forman sale in 1899.
artifact.condit: The vase is in fine condition, although the black glaze has partly turned to red in places.
artifact.decoration_description: Theseus and the Amazons. There are fourteen combatants which can be divided into three groups, with Theseus and Andromache in the largest group, taking up more than half the vase. Theseus, followed by Peirithoos and a companion whose name cannot be read, rushes up to Andromache who has fallen to the right onto her left knee. Andromache looks back toward Theseus and has raised the axe in her right hand in a last effort of resistance. Blood pours from the wound in her right thigh. Theseus, holding a shield, will be able to defer the blow from the axe. To Andromache's right, Hippolyte and two other Amazons ride up to defend the fallen queen. Andromache wears a short, transparent chiton under a sort of apronned tunic/cuirass decorated with two rosettes. She wears a Scythian helmet with a diadem, and holds a bow in her lowered left hand. Hippolyte is similarly dressed, but wears a different helmet. She is carrying a spear. The two other Amazons are dressed in patterned chitons over spotted 'bodysuits.' The one in the foreground wears a quiver at her side and carries an axe in her left hand. The other carries a spear. Broken spears and a quiver litter the ground. On the opposite side of the dinos, an Amazon runs to the defense of a comrade who is being attacked by a naked Greek, his sword arm raised to strike. He is aided by Akamas, who crouches with his left foot set on a rock. Visible on Akamas' shield are the hind-quarters of a quadruped. The threatened Amazon is seen in three-quarter front view, her body visible under a transparent chiton held at the shoulder by straps. There are horns on her helmet and she wears heel-guards. She holds a pelta in her left hand, and in her right, a spear is posed nearly horizontally. A young sapling is positioned between her and the Amazon running to her rescue, who wears a short-sleeved, short, patterned tunic and a sakkos, and holds a bow and an axe. The naked Greek wears a crested helmet; his shield device is a griffin(?). In the third group, Megareus has been wounded by a spear, the shaft of which has broken with the point lodged in his right thigh. He is down on both knees, and an Amazon has seized him by the hair and steps on his hip while she plunges her sword in his neck; blood gushes from the wound. Megareus has picked up a stone with his right hand and holds his shield aloft, and Sthenelos draws his sword as he rushes up to help his companion, but their efforts come too late. The Amazon wears greaves, an unusual hat and a patterned 'bodysuit' and short tunic. Megareus has short curly hair and is naked. Sthenelos is bearded and wears a helmet. His shield device is a roaring lion.
artifact.inscriptions: The figures are identified by inscriptions: [*P*E*I]*R*I*Q*O*S, Peirithoos: *Q*E*S*E*U*S, Theseus; *A[*N*D]*R*O*M*A[*X*E], Andromache; in retrograde, &epig-rough;*I*P*P*O[*L*U]*T*E, Hippolyte; in retrograde, *A*K*A*M*A*S, Akamas; *M*E*G*A[*R*E]*U*S, Megareus; *S*Q*E[*N*E*L*O*S], Sthenelos; and an indecipherable inscription ... *A....

artifact.name: London 1899.7-21.4
artifact.summary: Troilos and Polyxena
artifact.sources_used: CVA, Gr. Brit. 7, Brit. Mus. 5, 13, pl. 78, 4; Boardman 1975, 113, fig. 190.
artifact.other_bibliography: Forman Sale Cat., 339; Hertz Sale Cat., 592; Fölzer 1906, pl. 10, no. 23; Beazley 1912, 171, pl. 2; ph. Ma. 3131 left; Boardman 1972, fig. 190; Henle 1973, 132 fig. 62; Birchall & Corbett 1974, fig. 66; Beazley Addenda 2, 211
artifact.collection_history: The vase formerly belonged to the Forman collection. It was acquired by the museum in 1899.
artifact.decoration_description: Troilos and Polyxena. Polyxena runs at full speed to the right followed by Troilos, on horseback. Polyxena holds a sash over her head in both hands, and is looking back over her shoulder as she runs. Troilos spurs his horse forward with a stick and also looks back over his shoulder. He is mounted on a stallion which plunges forward, forelegs off the ground. A second horse runs along side it in a similar pose. Under the horses' bellies is a falling hydria, liquid spilling from the top and from a crack through the middle of the body. Troilos wears a short chiton held at the waist with a wide sash, and a chlamys held by a fibula at his neck. His hair is worn in a roll at the back of his neck with bangs and long side locks framing his face. A narrow cord binds the hair in place. Polyxena is wearing a chiton with an overfold. The sheer, lower part of the chiton is decorated with a simple black band. A narrow crossed fillet is tied around Polyxena's hair. The horses' manes are represented in a distinctive manner, being divided into three distinct parts.

artifact.name: London 1897.7-27.2
artifact.summary: Side A: sacrifice of Polyxena. Side B: komos. Middle frieze: sirens, panthers, rams and swans. Lower frieze: panthers and rams.
artifact.other_bibliography: Walters 1893, 283, pl. 15; Perrot & Chipiez, 10, 113; Atena e Roma 10, 17; 27; Maas 1951, 94; Walters 1905, pl. 23; Homan-Wedeking 1938, Arch V., fig. 8; Stella 1956, 752; EAA, vii 1009; Scherer 1963, 125; Willcock 1970, pl. 1b; Boardman 1974, fig. 57; LIMC, I, pl. 253, Aias II 8; pl. 570 Amphilochus 3; Birchall & Corbett 1974, fig. 68; Robertson 1975, pl. 40b; Bruxelles, 159-161 no. 93; Moon 1983, 88 fig. 6.1; Carpenter 1984, 48 fig. 1; Antike Plastik 15, p. 108, fig. 15; Prag 1985, pl. 41 fig. B; Beazley Addenda 2, 26.
artifact.condit: The vase is in good condition, but shows much wear of the black varnish on the foot, handles and mouth.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: sacrifice of Polyxena. Polyxena is held over the tomb of Achilles as the sacrifice is performed. The rigid body of Polyxena, wrapped in a shroud decorated with crosses, is held horizontally and face downward to facilitate the sacrifice. It is supported by three armed warriors, Amphilochos, Antiphates and Aias Iliades. Neoptolemos, son of Achilles, performs the sacrifice. Standing with legs spread wide and flexed, he holds the head of the princess by the hair, pulling her head up slightly as he plunges a knife into her throat; a blood stream of blood gushes from her throat. Diomedes and Nestor stand watching on the left, while Phoinix is turning away on the right, one hand tightly clenched. Polyxena wears a necklace. Her hair hangs loose down her back and falls in short curls on her forehead. Diomedes carries two spears and a shield. He wears a close-fitting, short white chiton, purple cuirass, greaves and helmet. Nestor, dressed in a long white chiton with a black border and a black himation, holds a single spear resting on the ground. He is shown as a relatively young man, for his hair and beard are black rather than white. Phoinix also holds a spear, and is shown wearing a mantle without the chiton underneath. The three warriors carrying Polyxena are dressed identically in cuirass, helmet and greaves. All but Amphilochos wear swords in their belts. The tomb is depicted as a mound covered with a patterned fabric; the decoration is alternating purple and black squares, the latter incised with a cross with white dots between the arms. A tripod brazier spouting flames rests on top of the mound.

Side B: komos. Naked youths dancing between cocks. Two cocks as tall as men stand facing inward to frame the central scene. The two youths in the center dance facing one another. The left-hand youth has one knee raised and his supporting leg is bent. Both his arms are raised in the air and his head is turned so as to look at the youth behind him. The right-hand youth bends his left leg off the ground and points with both arms toward his raised foot, his head tipped downward. The other two youths stand facing the cocks, their heads turned back toward the dancing pair. Each holds one arm around the neck of the cock, the other arm held at his side.

Lower frieze: row of animals. Griffins, lions, bulls and a swan.

Lowest frieze: row of animals. Bulls? and panthers?
artifact.inscriptions: On side A, written retrograde above the body of Polyxena: *P*O*L*U*X*S*E*N*E, Polyxena. Her three bearers also have their names inscribed. The first on the right, written retrograde, is: *A*N*F*I*L*O*X*O*S, Amphilochos. The second, also written retrograde, is: *A*M*T*I*F*A*T*E*S, Antiphates. The third is *A*I*A*S *I*L*I*A*D*E[*S], an unusual form of Ajax Oïliades (the son of Oileus). The name *F*O*I*N*I*X*S, Phoenix, is inscribed retrograde over the figure on the extreme right. To the left, the man holding two spears and a shield is inscribed with his name, again written retrograde: *D*I*O*M*E*D*E*S, Diomedes. Next to him stands *N*E*S*T*O*R *P*U*L*I*O*S, Nestor of Pylos.
artifact.shape_description: The body is separated from the neck by a plastic ring.

artifact.name: Lemonopoulos Collection (Shapiro No. 2)
artifact.summary: Side A: Apollo kitharoidos and four goddesses. Side B: Scythian archer between horsemen.
artifact.collection: Collection of Costas Lemonopoulos, St. Petersburg
artifact.essay_text:
Collection of Costas Lemonopoulos, St. Petersburg, courtesy of the Museum of Fine Arts of St. PetersburgUnattributedCa. 515-505 B.C.Height: 39.4 cm.Side A: Apollo kitharoidos and four goddesses. Side B: Scythian archer between horsemen.

Apollo is the patron of the arts, and especially of music. He is closely associated with the nine Muses, whom he often leads in a dance at a gathering of the gods or a celebration for a hero. His favorite instrument is the kithara, or lyre, and whenever the god is shown making music, it is always on the lyre. Other figures are sometimes depicted with a lyre on Attic vases, such as Nike(Austin 1980.63, or the boy Tithonos, who was ravished by the goddess of the dawn, but a stately male lyre-player in a long garment is generally Apollo. Though sometimes portrayed as a nude athletic type, especially in sculpture of the fifth century, Apollo is always draped when he plays the lyre. On side A of the Lemonopoulos amphora he wears a chiton and, over it, a himation decorated with large red dots. He also has a red fillet in his hair, and a cord attached to the instrument hangs from his right hand. The god is surrounded by two pairs of female figures, all dressed alike in a long chiton, also decorated with red dots. Two hold an object which looks like krotala, or metal castanets. A graceful doe stands beside each pair of women. It is difficult to say who these might be. The presence both of Apollo and of the does makes one think of Artemis, the god's sister and goddess of the hunt, but presumably she would somehow be singled out from the others. Four of the Muses, perhaps, drawn by an artist concerned more with symmetry than completeness?

In contrast to this peaceful and musical scene, side B features three warriors preparing to depart. The standing figure in the center carries bow and quiver and wears a short chiton and a pointed leather cap with long ear flaps. The hat and his pointy beard mark him as a Scythian archer, a native of South Russia probably employed at Athens as a mercenary. In the fifth century, Scythians appear to have served as policemen in Athens, but their frequent earlier appearance on black-figure vases of the later sixth century may reflect a policy of the tyrant Peisistratos in hiring foreign mercenaries from the North. Before the time of the Persian Wars, the Athenians had had little experience of archery (see Chapel Hill 66.27.4), while the Scythian skill with the bow was proverbial. The other two warriors flanking the archer, both mounted, wear Corinthian helmets and appear to be standard Greek soldiers.

The vase belongs to the period of the Leagros Group, a large body of mostly neck-amphoras and hydriae produced by one or several closely related black-figure workshops contemporary with the red-figure "Pioneers."

Bibliography: Cat. Sotheby, lot 173, ill.. On Scythian archers:Vos 1963.

artifact.name: Jacksonville AP.66.28
artifact.summary: Side A: man courting a boy<lb>Side B: youth riding a hippolektryon
artifact.collection: Collection of the Cummer Museum of Art and Gardens
artifact.essay_text:
Collection of the Cummer Gallery of Art, Jacksonville (AP.66.28)Group of Courting Cups [Shapiro]Ca. 520-500 B.C.Height: 10 cm.Diameter: 21.25 cm.Side A: Man courting a boy.Side B: Youth riding a hippalektryon.

Scenes of homosexual courting between men and boys first appear on Attic black-figure vases soon before the middle of the sixth century. In the third and especially the last quarter of the century this becomes one of the often repeated genre scenes in vase-painting. After 500 the scene's popularity falls off sharply, and after about 475 it disappears entirely. Well over 100 representations are known in all.

Sir John Beazley distinguished three stages in the courtship, and all painted scenes illustrate one of the three: an initial encounter (type alpha); the giving of gifts by the older man to the youth (type beta); and the consummation, in which the pair are intertwined (type gamma; cf. Mississippi 1977.3.72). Type alpha is depicted most often, and the Jacksonville vase is a typical example.

On side A, the older lover (erastes) stands at the left and reaches out both hands to his beloved (eromenos). With his left hand he chucks the boy's chin, as if to distract him while the lowered right hand moves in on its target. The boy reaches out with his left, perhaps a gesture of diffidence. Both are entirely nude, as is the rule in black-figure; in red-figure versions one or both will often be at least partly draped. The boy's hair is long and flows freely in the back, while the man's is bound by a fillet. The wooer's knees are usually bent to compensate for his greater stature.

On side B, a youth rides a hippalektryon, a mythical creature, half horse and half cock. It is one of many hybrids - fantastic beasts composed of elements of two or more animals or, like the centaur and the siren, part animal, part human - who populate Archaic Greek vase-painting and sculpture. Most hybrids seem to have come into Greece from the East, but there is no prototype of the hippalektryon in Egyptian or Near Eastern Art. Nevertheless it appears regularly on Attic vases (and only Attic) from the second quarter of the sixth century down to the end of the century or a little later. The rider is usually, as here, an unarmed youth. The hippalektryon has no mythology and is in fact scarcely mentioned by Greek writers: once in a lost play of Aeschylus, as a device painted on a ship, and once by Aristophanes, who implies that by his time (late fifth century) the average Athenian had never heard of it. But the vase-painters are consistent in portraying it with the hind legs of a cock and the forelegs of a horse, though attached to a cock's breast.

This cup may be assigned to a group of nearly thirty vases assembled by Beazley in Paralipomena as the Group of Courting Cups. They are eye cups (see Shapiro 1981a, no. 13) of Type A (a shallow bowl, plain lip, short, splaying foot with a moulding separating it from the bowl). The whites of the eyes are filled in with white paint, unlike those of earlier eye cups, which are mostly left in outline. All but a few of the Courting Cups have a man and boy on one side, and many repeat the motif on both sides. One has a youth on a hippalektryon on both sides (Para., 83,22). The choice of the courtship to decorate drinking cups that would be used at all-male symposia is not surprising; the monotonous repetition of the same formula and the hasty draughtsmanship show that the motif is nearing the end of its artistic life.

Bibliography: Unpublished. On courtship scenes: J. D. Beazley, Some Attic Vases in the Cyprus Museum (London 1948) 6-31; Shapiro 1981b, 133-43. On the hippalektryon: D. von Bothmer, in Bulletin of the Metropolitan Museum of Art 11 (1953) 132-36. Group of Courting Cups: Para., 82-83.

artifact.name: Jacksonville AP.66.21
artifact.summary: Side A: Dionysos between dancing satyrs<lb>Side B: maenads
artifact.collection: Collection of the Cummer Museum of Art and Gardens
artifact.essay_text:
Collection of the Cummer Gallery of Art, JacksonvilleGroup of Toronto 305Ca. 520-510 B.C.Height: 40.6 cm.Side A: Dionysos between dancing satyrs. Side B: Maenads.

On side A, Dionysos stands in a rigid, statuesque pose, while two bearded satyrs dance about him. The god wears a long chiton with a pattern on the hem and, over it, a himation. His beard is long and thick, like those of the satyrs, and an ivy wreath crowns his head. He holds up a large kantharos in his left hand and a vine with three long tendrils in his right. The satyr at left wears a white ribbon hung from his right shoulder across his chest.

On side B, a group of women stands aligned in an orderly row. At left and right is an overlapping pair standing side by side; the woman in the center appears to be alone, though it is possible that she too has a companion, completely hidden from view, as Beazley assumed, for a total of six. All are dressed alike in embroidered chiton and himation, and all wear a fillet, with long tresses falling behind and over the shoulder.

Two carry a pair of castanets (krotala), and the woman in the center holds a spreading vine. Though they have none of the identifying attributes of maenads - animal skin, thyrsos - the presence of Dionysos on the other side leads us to suppose that they are his followers.

A small frieze of lions and boars runs beneath the figured scene, a feature more common on hydrias of this period than on amphoras.

This vase is one of a large number of amphoras and hydrias of the late sixth century related to the circle of the Antimenes Painter, the most prolific artist of the years ca. 530 - 510 (see Richmond 57.9). Among several groups distinguished by Beazley, the Group of Toronto 305 includes about 20 amphoras, most of them with a Dionysiac subject. Only one other, in Sydney (ABV, 283, 8 bis), includes the animal frieze.

Bibliography: Para., 125, 5bis; Sale Catalogue, Christie's London, April 28, 1964. Lot. 65, pl. 10.

artifact.name: Houston 80.95
artifact.summary: Women working wool.
artifact.essay_text:
Collection of The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, Museum Purchase with funds donated by General and Mrs. Maurice Hirsch (80.95)Attributed to the Painter of the Yale OinochoeCa. 470-460 B.C.Height: 34.8 cm.Diameter: 33.3 cm.Women working wool.

The scene is a charming and authentic image of Athenian domestic life, showing three young women and a pet heron. In the center, a woman stands over a kalathos, a wicker wool basket, about to place in it (or take from it) a large bundle of wool. (Compare the woman drawing skeins of wool from a kalathos on the Chapel Hill lekythos Chapel Hill 78.15.1). At the left a woman holds an alabastron, an unguent bottle, in one hand, and in the other reaches out a similar bottle over the stooping figure, toward a third woman at the right. The women at left and right wear plain chiton and himation, while the central figure's garment is gaily decorated with an all-over pattern and fringed hem. All three wear a fillet, and their hair is tied in a knot at the back.

A heron, standing on long spindly legs, faces and watches intently the woman in the center. The heron was sacred to Aphrodite and was a favorite pet of Athenian matrons. Hence it is seen not infrequently in domestic settings such as this one.

Scenes of women working wool, as well as other domestic occupations, become increasingly popular in Attic red-figure after about 500 B.C. Of six hydrias attributed to the Painter of the Yale Oinochoe, five, including this one, show women's scenes with common elements. A hydria in Copenhagen (ARV2, 503, 24) portrays another aspect of wool working, a woman holding spindle and distaff. Two others, in London (ARV2, 503, 23) and at Harvard (ARV2, 503, 22), include herons, one being fed by its mistress. On the Harvard vase, a kalathos hangs upside down on the wall. A hydria at San Simeon (ARV2, 503, 21) shows a rare scene of women working out of doors, picking apples. The painter also decorated many other shapes, but his drawing is seldom as fine as it is here.

Bibliography: Unpublished. On the Painter of the Yale Oinochoe: ARV2, 501-503; H. M. Fracchia, in California Studies in Classical Antiquity 5 (1972) 103-111. On herons: Beazley 1920, 60-61.

artifact.name: Houston 37-19
artifact.summary: Athena battling the giant Enkelados.
artifact.essay_text:
Collection of The Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, the Annette Finnigan Collection (37-19)Assigned to the Segment Class [H. Hoffmann]Ca. 520-510 B.C.Diameter: 23.5 cm.Athena battling the giant Enkelados.

The scene is an excerpt from the Battle of Gods and Giants, one of the most popular mythological scenes in Archaic Greek art. The Giants, children of Ge, Mother Earth, tried to storm Mount Olympos, but were repulsed by the combined effort of all the Olympian gods and goddesses, with the help of Herakles. By convention certain gods battle certain giants, and when Athena's opponent is named by inscription, he is Enkelados. Otherwise Enkelados has no distinguishing traits or attributes.

Athena wears a belted chiton, himation, and a high-crested Attic helmet. Her aegis is draped over her extended left arm, serving as a shield, and in her right hand, obscured by the drapery, she wields a spear. Enkelados, who has fallen to one knee, tries to protect himself with a shield whose device is a satyr's head. He wears a corselet over a short chiton, which has short sleeves and a patterned skirt. His helmet is of the Corinthian type, which is meant to be pulled down over nose and cheeks, but has been knocked askew and almost off by the force of Athena's blow. The Giant too holds a spear but is powerless to use it. In Archaic art, the Giants are not represented as monstrous, or even of great stature, but instead look no different from heavily armed Greek hoplites. Only in later art, as on the Pergamon Altar, do they sometimes take on a grotesque appearance, as the poet Hesiod imagined them.

Attic plates were not functional, but were rather plaques, made for dedicatory purposes. The Houston example has two suspension holes near the top, which suggests that it was perhaps intended to be hung up in a sanctuary. Quite possibly it was dedicated to the city goddess, Athena, on the Acropolis. Certainly the subject is appropriate for such a purpose and is one which occurs on a number of vases and fragments excavated on the Acropolis. The Gigantomachy, including the Athena-Enkelados group, was the subject of several large-scale architectural sculptures in the sixth and fifth centuries. One of the most notable of these is a marble pediment which decorated the Old Temple of Athena on the north side of the Acropolis, also called Doerpfeld's Temple or the Peisistratid Temple, because it was probably built in the time of Hippias and Hipparchos, sons of the Tyrant Peisistratos (ca. 527-510). The splendid striding Athena from that composition is well preserved, and her pose and dress are similar to those of the Athena on this plate. The traditional date for this pediment, about 520, has recently been questioned by some scholars who would push it toward the end of the Peisistratid tyranny, about 510, or even later, regarding it as a product of the young Athenian democracy after 510. If the earlier date is correct, however, it would be reasonable to ask whether the Houston plate could have been inspired by the central group of the pediment and have hung not far from it in Athena's sanctuary on the Acropolis.

The decoration of this plate is akin to that of the Segment Class, a group of stemless cups in which the picture fills the whole interior and there is often an exergue below the principal scene. Here two leaping dolphins occupy the exergue.

Bibliography: Hoffmann 1971b, 386-87. On the Gigantomachy: Vian 1952. On the Peisistratid pediment: Ridgway 1977, 205-206. Segment Class: ABV, 212-214.

artifact.name: Harvard 1977.216.2397
artifact.summary: Musical contests.
artifact.other_bibliography: CVA, Fogg-Gallatin, 38, pl. 21, 3; A. Shapiro, in Neils 1992, 71, fig. 49.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Henry W. Haynes.
artifact.condit: Upper half missing, including the mouth; heads and shoulders of all figures lost. The clay has turned gray from burning, probably in a pyre.
artifact.comparanda: For alabastra, see H. E. Angermeier, Das Alabastron (Giessen 1936). For musical contests at the Panathenaia, including full bibliography and several vase-paintings of kitharodes, aulodes, and auletes standing on platforms, see A. Shapiro, in Neils 1992. For a kitharode in the act of mounting a platform, cf. a red-figure pelike by the Pan Painter, formerly in the Embiricos collection, Lausanne; Christies, London, April 28, 1993; Christie's International magazine (March/April 1993) 43.
artifact.decoration_description:
The designs are executed in black-figure on a white ground. A kithara-player is mounted on a low platform decorated with egg pattern. He wears a chiton and himation, and cloth tassels hang from his instrument. At right, a man dressed in a himation leans on his staff to right. He is either a simple listener or a judge of these musical contests, which may be those held at the Panathenaia. The man faces a three-stepped platform on which two males dressed in himatia stand to the right. The male at right is fully wrapped in his himation, with both arms covered. We know from other representations of this subject that he is a singer and that the male behind him is playing the double flutes (auloi). The singer is thus an "aulode" and his accompanist an "aulete." To the right of the platform and behind the kitharist is a slender, fluted column, probably Doric.

The groundline is a slender black stripe, below which is a broader black band framed by reserved stripes. Lower body black.
artifact.inscriptions: Nonsense inscriptions in black letters, including several epsilons.
artifact.shape_description: Alabastron: a hollow cylinder with a rounded base.

artifact.name: Harvard 1977.216.2260
artifact.summary: Herakles and the Cretan Bull
artifact.other_bibliography: CVA, Fogg-Gallatin, 39, pl. 21, 9.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Henry W. Haynes. Former inventory no. 2260.
artifact.condit: Unbroken; minor abrasions; lower body misfired red.
artifact.comparanda: For the shape, see J. R. Green, "Oinochoe," BICS 19 (1972) 2-3 and 6-7. For Herakles and the Cretan bull, see L. Todisco, in LIMC, V, 59-67, pls. 73-81 (cf. esp. pl. 77, nos. 2340 and 2341.
artifact.decoration_description: The entire vase is black except for a panel on the front, which is coated with smooth white slip, over which the designs are executed in black-figure. The setting is Crete. Herakles is wrestling the Cretan bull, which he will capture and bring to Greece as the seventh of his Twelve Labors. The bull has fallen to its front knees, its head on the ground. Herakles bends over it from the left, his left leg advanced, both hands grasping the bull's shoulders. He is nude except for a red fillet and a red baldric, the latter supporting the sword on his left hip. His beard is red, as are the breast of the bull and three stripes on its hindquarters. Herakles' bow and quiver hang in the field behind him; the quiver has red stripes. Athena, Herakles' divine patron, sits on a folding stool at left. She holds out her left arm toward the hero and holds a spear in her right hand. Her aegis, red-striped and fringed with snakes, covers her left arm. She also wears a peplos, a red-striped himation, and a Corinthian helmet circled by a red fillet and having a stilted crest with a red stripe. The ivy vines that snake throughout the background do not have any Dionysiac meaning, but rather are a common filling motif on minor black-figure vases of this period. Framing the top of the panel is a broad band of lotus buds: pointing downward, linked by tendrils, and with dots in the interstices. Above the panel, a red stripe circles the neck.
artifact.shape_description: Oinochoe of shape 3, a.k.a. a chous: globular body, tapering above to a trefoil mouth; wide torus foot; ridged handle.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.47
artifact.summary: Plastic alabastron in shape of woman.
artifact.other_bibliography: Münzen und Medaillen, Liste E, 120 Antike Terrakotten (Basel 1962) 17, no. 41; J. Ducat, Les vases plastiques rhodiens archaïques en terre cuite (Paris 1966) 73, no. 8; Watkins 1973, 39, no. 15.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.
artifact.condit: Unbroken. Cracks down the right side, below the elbow, and through the right side of the face to the right hand; chip on rim. Incrustation on the left arm, the left side of the hair, and down the back left side.
artifact.comparanda: The necklace and wig-like hair of the woman and the limitation of the plastic portion to the upper third of the vessel show clearly that it is a ceramic version of carved alabaster vessels with their origins in Mesopotamian prototypes of the 7th century. Similar stone alabastra, with a bewigged woman holding a bird, were produced in Syria and the Egyptian delta during the late 7th and 6th centuries, and spawned imitations in Etruria and elsewhere; see; see P. J. Riis, "Sculptured Alabastra," ActaA 27 (1956) 23-33. Like similar alabastra of the more numerous "Aphrodite Group, which have legs and feet, Ducat identified ceramic alabastra of this type as having been made on Rhodes. Because the style and accouterments recall contemporary Cypriote votive statues, Ducat termed this class the "Cypriote Series," which he dated to the second quarter of the sixth century. See J. Ducat, Les vases plastiques rhodiens archaïques en terre cuite (Paris 1966) 72-74. For an additional example, see H. Cahn, Kunstwerke der Antike, Münzen und Medaillen Auktion 34 (Basel 1967) 52, pl. 28, no. 110.
artifact.decoration_description: Added red on the mouth.
artifact.shape_description: Plastic alabastron. The upper third is in the form of a woman wearing a long wig and a necklace with pendant. The body below is a long, hollow cylinder with rounded base, the usual alabastron shape. On top of the woman's head is a flattened, disk-shaped mouth, painted with added red. Vertical marks on the lower body resulted from the shaving and smoothing of the vessel when the body was joined to the moldmade upper part.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.46
artifact.summary: Youth between two women.
artifact.other_bibliography: Buitron 1972, 120-21, no. 66; Watkins 1973, 68-69, no. 27.
artifact.collection_history:
Jacob Hirsch collection. Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.

Said to be from Gela, but if this is the vase described by E. Peterson in "Funde," RM 8 (1893) 340, no. 26, then it is probably from Curti or Capua; see ARV2, 623, 62.
artifact.condit: Unbroken; some abrasion and chipping, particularly on the back of the lower body and foot, the groundline, and the legs of the youth and the woman at right.
artifact.comparanda:
The Villa Giulia Painter employed a series of stock figure types, which he adapted to meet particular requirements. To judge by their waving arms and the fact that one of them runs away, the women on this vase are upset and agitated, but the waving or upraised hand is a very common motif in the painter's repertoire, and his running woman sometimes seems to be fleeing for no reason. Cf. the scenes on two kalpides formerly in the London art market: on one (Sotheby's, December 9, 1974, no. 247), a woman flees the tumult of Zeus' pursuit of Aegina; on another (Sotheby's, July 12, 1971, no. 162), the identical woman flees a quiet tableau of a hunter and woman pouring a libation.

For the Villa Giulia Painter, see J. D. Beazley, "The Master of the Villa Giulia Calyx-Krater," RM 27 (1912) 286-97; and Robertson 1992, 169-173.
artifact.decoration_description:
A youth stands in profile to the right; except for the cloak draped over his left shoulder and arm, he is naked. In his left hand he holds a staff. His hair is tied in a krobylos with a fillet of added red; long curls, drawn with thinned glaze, hang from his temples. On either side of the youth are two gesticulating women, the left one running away to the left, the right one standing frontally, her head turned to face the youth. Both women wear chitons and himations. The woman at left has her hair tied up with a double fillet, the trailing ends of which are drawn with added red. The woman at right wears a sakkos, from which wispy curls, drawn with thinned glaze, escape over the brow and temples. Dilute glaze is used for the minor musculature on the youth and women. The subject is unexplained, but from the behavior of the women, who raise their hands in apparent consternation, they are upset to find a naked male in their midst; they are probably, therefore, not hetairai, but "respectable" women, whose only normally social intercourse with men is with husbands and kin (but see comments below).

The groundline and upper frame consist of groups of three maeanders to left alternating with cross-squares; egg and dot pattern around the rim. The top of the mouth and the lower two thirds of the torus on the foot is reserved; the rest of the vase is black.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by Frederick M. Watkins

Height: 10 7/8 in. (27.7 cm.)

Intact; some abrasion of glaze.

A youth between two women. A nude youth with his cloak over his left shoulder and a stick in one hand stands in the center. On the left a woman runs off, looking back; on the right is a woman with one hand raised. Above and below, triple meanders alternating with cross-squares; on the lip, egg and dot pattern.

Dilute glaze: anatomical markings, lines on the drapery.

Red: fillet of the youth and of the woman on the left.

Attributed to the Villa Giulia Painter [Beazley] ca. 460 - 450 B. C.

The Villa Giulia Painter stands in the tradition of Douris and, like him, prefers subdued and refined figures depicted with a polished technique. His harmonious compositions are in opposition to the ambitious efforts of his contemporary, the Niobid Painter (see Bowdoin 1908.3). Fond of scenes of everyday life, he employs certain stock types such as the women and youth on this vase. Although the figures appear serene, the air is tense. The subject, however, remains unexplained. The vase is said to be from Gela but may be the vase described by E. Peterson in "Funde," Mitteilungen des Deutschen archäologischen Instituts. Römische Abteilung 8 (1893) 340, no. 26, and if so, it is probably from Curti or Capua (ARV2, 623, no. 62).

Bibliography: ARV2, 623, no. 62.
artifact.shape_description: Kalpis hydria: small, rounded body; ogival foot with slender torus base; fillet between foot and body; slender torus mouth framed by fillets; side handles relatively large and tilted upward.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.45
artifact.summary: Side A: Man and seated woman; Side B: Man with staff.
artifact.other_bibliography: Watkins 1973, 64-65, no. 25.
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.318 m.; D. at mouth 0.142 m.; D. at handles 0.179 m.
artifact.collection_history: Jacob Hirsch collection. Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.
artifact.condit: Unbroken; glossy black glaze; slight flaking on surface, particularly on the kalathos and the man's legs on side A; crack in handle A/B.
artifact.comparanda: This approach to decorating Nolan amphora, with a continuous band of floral decoration below the figures, was apparently invented by the Berlin Painter, who passed it on to his pupils Hermonax and the Providence Painter; similar schemes were employed by the Pan Painter and the Dutuit Painter. For the Providence Painter, see E. Papoutsakis-Sermpetis, Ho zographos tes Providence (Athens 1983); and Robertson 1992, 173-74. For Nolan amphorae, see H. Euwe, "The Shape of a Nolan Amphora in Otterlo," in Enthousiasmos. Essays on Greek and Related Pottery presented to J.M. Hemelrijk (Amsterdam 1986) 141-45. For "spinning hetairai," see G. Rodenwaldt, "Spinnende Hetären," AA (1932) 7-21; M. Meyer, "Männer mit Geld: zu einer rotfigurigen Vase mit 'Altagszene'," JdI 108 (1988) 87-125; and Keuls 1983.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A woman is seated to right on a klismos. With both hands, she offers a wreath drawn with added red to a bearded man wearing a wreath and a himation, who stands at the right; both wreaths are drawn with added red. The man leans forward on the knotty staff in his left hand and holds out his right hand to accept the wreath, although he is already wearing one. His beard and hair are fringed with strokes of dilute glaze. The woman wears a chiton, himation, sakkos, earrings, and bracelets, the latter in added red. Dilute glaze is used for the folds of the chiton and the speckled ornament on the sakkos. The woman's hair is represented by numerous black dots on a ground of brown, dilute glaze. On the floor between the two figures, behind the man's staff, is a kalathos, a wool-basket, containing wool or yarn. The kalathos is decorated with two bands of running S's, and its vertical weave is drawn with dilute glaze; the yarn is painted with added red. The composition, and the presence of the kalathos, suggest that this may not be a simple domestic scene, but a visit to a hetaira, who are sometimes shown working wool as they wait for customers.

Side B: A man dressed in a himation stands to the left, a knotty staff held vertically in his outstretched right hand. His beard and hair are fringed with strokes of dilute glaze. The black dot on his upper himation is an accidental drip.

The groundline is a continuous band of slanted, addorsed palmettes, linked by tendrils. At the base of each handle is a single palmette, pointing down, with voluting tendrils. The rest of the vase is black, except for the lower edge and base of the foot.
artifact.inscriptions: Two inscriptions on side A, in red letters: between the heads of the man and woman: *K*A*L*E; below the man's arm (uncertain reading): *K*A*L*O*S.
artifact.shape_description: Nolan amphora, a type of neck-amphora named after the Campanian site of Nola: triple reeded handles; echinus mouth; slender, tapering body; disk foot; fillet between foot and body.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.44
artifact.summary: Dionysos.
artifact.other_bibliography: Watkins 1973, 62, no. 23.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired. Glaze slightly abraded.
artifact.comparanda:
The groundline of ivy leaves was used occasionally by the Berlin Painter on small vases; e.g. the neck-amphora Boulogne 656 (ARV2, 200, 48) and a lekythos once in the Swiss art market (Para., 345, 201 bis). The Tithonos Painter, a pupil of the Berlin Painter, also employed it, as did the Troilos Painter; cf. Gela 68 (ARV2, 216, 20) and Stockholm G.1700 (ARV2, 297, 18).

For the Berlin Painter, see J. D. Beazley, "The Master of the Berlin Amphora," JHS 31 (1911) 276-95; J. D. Beazley, "An Amphora by the Berlin Painter," AntK 4 (1961) 49-67; Beazley 1974; Kurtz 1983; and Robertson 1992, 66-83.
artifact.decoration_description:
Dionysos stands to the right dressed in a red wreath, chiton, and himation; his left foot is advanced but he does not seem to be walking. The folds of the chiton on his upper body are drawn with dilute glaze, but those above his feet are drawn with relief lines. The himation draped over his left arm hangs in long straight folds. In his right hand he carries a large black kantharos, the drinking cup that is his particular attribute. In his left hand he holds a long, knotty staff and a branch of ivy with red leaves. His long hair hangs down his back and in long, corkscrew tresses on his shoulders.

The groundline is a short band of ivy leaves framed by paired stripes; there are dots in the gaps between the leaves. A band of dotted egg-pattern nearly circles the base of the neck. Except for the side and base of the foot, the rest of the vase is black.
artifact.shape_description: Lekythos: broad echinus mouth; short concave neck; straight-sided body; disk foot; fillet between foot and body; vertical strap handle.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.43
artifact.summary: Woman and maid.
artifact.other_bibliography: Watkins 1973, 70-71, no. 28.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.
artifact.condit: Heavily eroded, with considerable loss of the painted design. The loss of added color has left the maid an ethereal ghost of her former self, with only the barest outline of her body remaining and little trace of her garments. The other woman's himation has fared better, but the former crimson color is now very pale. The added colors were not of clay slip, but rather mineral pigments added after firing, which are particularly prone to erosion.
artifact.comparanda: Beazley compared the shape and style to two other lekythoi by the Achilles Painter: Athens 12746 and Athens 12745 (ARV2, 999, 184-185). For a closely comparable composition, cf. the painter's lekythos in the Museo Artistico Industriale, Rome (ARV2, 996, 136). For the Achilles Painter, see J. D. Beazley, "The Master of the Achilles Amphora in the Vatican," JHS 34 (1914) 179-226; Robertson 1992, 193-208; and the forthcoming Kerameus volume, J. Oakley, The Achilles Painter. For the painter's white-ground oeuvre, see Beazley 1938, 13-16; Kurtz 1975, 41-48, pls. 33-38; D. Kurtz, "The Achilles Painter's Early White Lekythoi," in Eumousia. Ceramic and Iconographic Studies in Honour of Alexander Cambitoglou, ed. Jean-Paul Descoeudres (Sydney 1990) 107-114; and I. Wehgartner, Ein Grabbild des Achileusmalers (Berlin 1985).
artifact.decoration_description:
The designs are painted in dilute glaze on a ground of chalky white slip, which covers the shoulder and three quarters of the body. In the scene on the body, a woman stands at the right, her body frontal and her head turned to face a second woman, who stands at the left. The second woman, who is probably a maid, carries a shallow basket decorated with a battlement-pattern framed by stripes. The basket is the type used to bring offerings — wreaths, fillets, lekythoi — to the tomb of a loved one. This basket seems empty, but the offerings may have been represented in fugitive added color. The hair of both women is tied up in chignons; their hair was painted with thinned glaze, darker than the dilute glaze of the outlines. To judge by the remains of the outlines, the maid wore only a chiton, without himation. Her mistress, the woman at right, wore a chiton (of yellow?) and a red himation. A mirror hangs on the wall at upper right.

Above the figures and extending half way round the vase on either side is a band consisting of groups of three maeanders alternating with saltire squares. The grouped maeanders run alternately to the right and left. The paired stripes that frame the band extend all the way around the upper body. On the shoulder, below a band of egg-pattern at the base of the neck, are three palmettes enclosed and linked by coiling tendrils. The groundline is a narrow black stripe. The handle, mouth, neck, lower body, and top of the foot are glazed.
artifact.shape_description: Lekythos: tall neck, slightly concave; tall echinus mouth; body straight-sided but slightly convex; disk foot; fillet between foot and body; tall strap handle; false bottom in neck; vent hole in lower body. Vases such as this were buried with the dead; the false bottom was to economize on expensive olive oil. The vent hole allowed gases to escape the sealed inner body when the vessel was fired.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.42
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles and Geryon<lb>Side B: arming
artifact.other_bibliography: Buitron 1972, 28-29, no. 10; Watkins 1973, 44-45, no. 17; LIMC, IV, 115, pl. 61, Eurytion II 46.
artifact.collection_history: Jacob Hirsch collection; Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired; missing pieces restored, with moderate repainting; damage to Eurytion's face; some loss of added color, particularly the white of the women's flesh.
artifact.comparanda: Shape and ornament are standard for type-B amphorae of Group E. For the arming scene, cf. that on another amphora of Group E, Vatican 348 (ABV, 134, 16), with a similar, but not identical composition, including the helmet beneath the upraised leg. Herakles and Geryon were represented by painters of Group E no less than 14 times, most examples being on panel amphorae of type B and most following the same basic scheme as this vase, with Herakles attacking from the left, Eurytion on the ground, and one of Geryon's bodies wounded and turning away; Orthros may or may not be present. This representation is unique among Attic examples in showing Eurytion on his hands and knees instead of on his back or side, an affecting and naturalistic posture; cf. a Chalcidian neck-amphora with Eurytion in a similar position, but facing away from Herakles: Paris, Cab. Méd. 202; LIMC, V, pl. 84, no. 2464. For the subject, described by Apollodorus (Apollod. 2.5.10) and perhaps inspired by the Geryoneis of the early sixth-century poet Stesichoros, see P. Clement, "Geryon and others in Los Angeles," Hesperia 24 (1955) 1-12, pls. 1-5; P. Brize, Die Geryoneis des Stesichoros und die frühe griechische Kunst (Würzburg 1980); P. Brize, in LIMC, IV, 186-90, pls. 104-107; E. Zervoudaki, in LIMC, IV, 112-17, pls. 56-61; and P. Brize, in LIMC, V, 73-85, pls. 84-90.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Herakles is battling the triple-bodied Geryon, the tenth of his Twelve Labors. The setting is Erytheia, an island in the far West, land of the setting sun. Herakles has come to fetch the cattle of Geryon, the son of Chrysaor. Herakles has a red beard and wears a short chiton, also red. Over this he wears his lionskin, the head of which covers his own head like a hood. The paws are knotted at his throat and the middle of the skin is cinched tightly around his waist with a belt. Herakles advances his left leg; his left arm is hidden behind one of Geryon's shields, but in his right hand he holds the sword with which he has already dispatched Geryon's herdsman, Eurytion. The herdsman crawls on his hands and knees, his head bowed. He wears a rough cap of wool or skin, a short chiton, painted red, and a tunic of some kind, over which is a red belt. As usual, Geryon is represented as three overlapping warriors, joined at the waist, all of whom are dressed as hoplites, with greaves, bell-cuirasses, and Corinthian helmets. All three advance the left leg in unison; the farthest and nearest warriors wear red greaves, but not the middle one. The nearest warrior has been wounded; he turns his upper body all the way round to face backward, so that we see the inside of the round shield on his left arm. He holds a stone in his right hand instead of a spear or sword, a mark of his barbaric nature. He and the middle warrior have stilted crests on their helmets, which overlap the lotus and palmette frieze above. The helmets may once have been painted red. The helmet of the farthest warrior has a low crest, which is all one can see of his head, and his shield is advanced beyond that of the middle warrior. Because his head seems to incline forward, and because he seems to have dropped the point of his spear behind the body of Eurytion, the farthest warrior may already have become Herakles' next victim. Both his shield and that of the middle warrior have red rims; neither shield seems to have had a device, unless this was in added color and is now lost. The spear above the shields may be held by the middle warrior; like the nearest warrior, he is bearded, but is yet unwounded. At lower right, behind the monster's rear legs, is Geryon's two-headed hound, Orthros. Of the hound's heads, the near one is down, the far one raised up. The near dog wears a collar and has a red neck. Orthros was the son of Typhon and Echidna and thus the brother of Cerberus, the three-headed hound who guarded Hades. Herakles will spare Cerberus, when he fetches him as the last of his Twelve Labors, but Orthros he will kill.

Side B: A nude warrior is putting on his armor, watched by four onlookers, two on either side. The red-haired warrior stands to the right, his left leg raised as he prepares to don the greave which he holds in both hands. On the ground below his upraised leg is a Corinthian helmet with a stilted crest, the added color of which has worn off. Facing him at right is a woman, who gestures toward him with her right hand. She wears a peplos from which the added color has been lost, like the white that once tinted her flesh; of her eye, only a faint incision remains. Behind her, at right, stands a nude male with red hair and beard, his hands held at his sides. To the left of the warrior stands a bearded man with red hair, wearing a himation; he may be the warrior's father, come to see him off to war. At far stands a fourth man. He has a red beard and red hair, the latter tied in a queue on the nape. His himation has slipped down around his waist.

Above each scene is a lotus and palmette "festoon," framed by lines of dilute glaze; the palmettes have red cuffs. Band of rays of lower body. Stripes of added red circle the edge of the mouth, the lower edge of the foot, the top of the band of rays, and the lower body below the figure panels, which also have lateral frames of red stripes.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by Frederick M. Watkins

Height: 17 in. (43.2 cm.)

Broken and repaired; missing pieces restored and painted.

Side A: Herakles and Geryon. Herakles, dressed in lion skin over chitoniskos, fights Geryon, the triple bodied monster who lived in regions farthest west and was rich in cattle (Apollod. 2.10). Herakles was sent to fetch the cattle as his tenth labor and succeeded in killing not only Geryon's herdsman, Eurytion, shown fallen at Herakles' feet, but also the monster's two-headed dog, Orthros, at Geryon's feet, and Geryon himself. Geryon is conceived as having three bodies joined at the waist. Each wears greaves and a high crested Corinthian helmet (two are visible; the top of the third is partly hidden), and each carries a shield.

Side B: arming. In the center a man puts on a greave; at his feet is his Corinthian helmet. On either side are spectators: to the left a man in himation and a man in chiton and himation, to the right a woman in peplos and a nude man.

Above on side A, palmette festoon; on side B, palmette chain; at the base are rays.

Red, on side A: Herakles' chiton and the edge of the lion skin; Eurytion's beard and chiton; Geryon's greaves, helmets, and shield rims; Orthros' ruff. On side B: the men's hair and two beards, parts of their drapery, the woman's hair and parts of her peplos. The cuffs of the palmettes, the frames of the panels, the edge of the base, and the edge of the mouth.

Attributed to Group E [Beazley] ca. 550 - 530 B. C.

Group E is the name given by Beazley to "a large and compact group which is very closely related to the work of the painter Exekias, though earlier. . ., the soil from which the art of Exekias springs" (ABV, 133). The battle of Herakles and Geryon is one of their favorite subjects and is found on at least nine other amphorae with much the same composition. Compare Würzburg L 245 (Langlotz 1932, pl. 79) where the drawing is neater, the shepherd Eurytion is partly fallen and the dog Orthros is missing.

Bibliography: ABV, 133, no. 8; Hôtel Drouot, Collection Hirsch (June 30 - July 2, 1921) 20, no. 141, pl. 6.
artifact.shape_description: Amphora of type B, with cylindrical handles, echinus foot, and flaring mouth.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.41
artifact.summary: Exterior: Satyrs and maenads. Interior: Satyr and maenad.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins. In the Watkins catalogue of 1973, the cup is said to be from Athens, but in ARV2, Beazley said it was from Vulci.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired from numerous fragments, with some repainting of cracks and wide fissures. The edges of the fragments are worn and irregular. The painted surface is eroded in places, with loss of relief lines, particularly in the very center of the interior, where the right arms and hands of both figures are lost, and the satyr and maenad on the right of side B.
artifact.comparanda:
Makron represented satyrs and maenads on numerous cups, sometimes with Dionysos present, apparently delighting in the opportunity to depict swirling drapery, spotted leopard skins, and a variety of animated postures. A satyr and maenad appear in more than one of his cup tondos, but not in this same arrangement; cf. Louvre G 144 and Munich 2654 (ARV2, 462, 43 and 47). The pair in the Harvard tondo are best compared with a satyr and maenad on side A of the Munich cup. For the goat under the handle, cf. Baltimore, Hopkins AIA B10 (ARV2, 463, 51). For the satyr under the handle, cf. a cup by the Brygos Painter, London E 65 (ARV2, 370, 13).

For Makron see, Beazley 1989, 84-97 [lecture given in 1955]; J. D. Beazley, "A Cup by Hieron and Makron," BABesch 29 (1954) 12-15; D. von Bothmer, "Notes on Makron," in D. Kurtz and B. Sparkes, eds., The Eye of Greece (Cambridge 1982) 29-52; and Robertson 1992, 100-106.
artifact.decoration_description:
Interior: A satyr and maenad stand facing one another with bowed heads. They seem to be dancing rather than fighting. The maenad, at left, wears a belted chiton with voluminous sleeves and overfold. The folds of the chiton are drawn with relief lines, as is the outline of her body, visible through the diaphanous gown. She wears a red wreath, and her long hair, tied at the nape, hangs loosely in back. A spotted leopard or cheetah skin is draped over her upraised left arm. The satyr raises his left arm over his head, the elbow extending beyond the frame and thus unseen. His right arm is destroyed, but was lowered toward the right hand of the maenad, which is also effaced. His right leg is bent, the left one straight and extended. He wears a red wreath, and a single corkscrew curl hangs on his shoulder.

Around the exterior, five maenads are, with some success, fighting off the unwanted advances of seven satyrs. All of the satyrs are ithyphallic and all have a spotted leopard or cheetah skin draped over their extended left arm. Some of the skins have round or oblong spots with smaller dots between, others have irregular blobs with dots; it is not clear which is leopard and which is cheetah, but one of those with oblong spots, worn by the central satyr on side A, has a central stripe down the back, which may indicate it is a cheetah skin. Confusing the issue is the fact that on the skins worn by two of the maenads, there are round spots around the shoulder and irregular blobs on the back. All of the maenads wear belted chitons with voluminous sleeves and overfolds; the red belts of the first two maenads on side A are represented, but not the others. The folds of the chitons are drawn with relief lines, as are the outlines of the bodies, visible through the diaphanous gowns. The two sides are divided by the figures under the handles. A balding satyr wearing a red wreath and leaning on his left hand crouches under handle A/B, his head down and his right hand raised. He may be about to ambush the right-hand maenad on side A. Under the opposite handle (B/A), a shaggy goat with long horns and upright tail faces the action on Side B. The hairs of its beard and back are drawn with strokes of dilute glaze, which is also used to drawn the ribs and minor musculature of the satyrs.

Side A: Three pairs of satyrs and maenads are locked in combat, with the maenads facing left and the satyrs right. The first two satyrs are in nearly identical stances, with the right leg advanced, both knees bent, and both arms extended. The first one has a full head of hair, tied at the nape, and wears a red fillet; the second is balding and wears a red wreath. The two maenads are also in similar positions, leaning back, with the right arm extended and one leg overlapping that of the attacker, but the first maenad advances her right leg and the second one her left. Both carry thyrsoi, the butt of which they point toward the satyr; they hold the shaft with different grips. The first maenad wears a skin over her chiton, with two paws knotted at her throat. Her hair is tied in a krobylos by a red wreath. The satyr grabs the shaft of her thyrsos to ward off her blows. The second maenad wears a red fillet, wrapped twice around her head; her long hair flies out behind her as she jerks away from the satyr. The third satyr, at right, leans over toward his prey, so that his phallos hangs between his legs like a second tail. He wears a red wreath, and although balding, has long hair down his back. He reaches for the maenad with both hands, his left hand grasping the shaft of her thyrsos, which she holds like the preceding maenad. Her hair also flies back in a similar manner, but is circled by a wreath rather than a fillet.

Side B: On this side the arrangement of figures is more varied, as the maenads are outnumbered three to two. At left, a satyr advances to the right, his right leg planted straight out before him, his left leg drawn back. A wineskin hangs on the wall behind him. He wears a red wreath over his full head of hair, which hangs in ringlets down his back. He extends both arms toward the back of the maenad at right; in his right hand he holds a drinking horn. The maenad backs away from a second satyr at right, her left leg extended and her right leg drawn back. She extends both arms toward her attacker, and wields a thyrsos in her left hand. Her hair is tied in a krobylos by a red fillet that circles her head twice. The satyr advances toward her from the right, his cheetah skin hanging over both of his legs (the left one advanced, the right one drawn back). He is balding and wears a red wreath. A single, long, corkscrew curl hangs on his shoulder. Unlike the other satyrs, his long beard is unfringed. He bends over slightly as he parries the thyrsos with his upraised right arm. At right, a second maenad runs away from a third satyr, her legs in motion to the left but her head and upper body turned back toward her assailant.
