She wears a skin over her chiton, and a red wreath, which holds her hair in a krobylos. With he left hand she fends off the satyr and with her right hand raises her thyrsos to strike a blow. The satyr bends both knees and extends his right leg; both hands reach out toward his reluctant prey. Although balding, he has long hair, tied at the nape; a red fillet is wrapped twice around his head.

The tondo is framed by a band of interlocked maeanders. The exterior groundline is a single reserved stripe. Two narrow reserved stripes circle the rim inside and out. The inside of the handles and the areas between the handle roots are reserved, as are the side of the foot, the resting surface, and the interior of the stem.
artifact.shape_description: Kylix of type B, the type most often decorated by Makron. Broad, shallow bowl; tall concave stem; flattened foot with slight ridge about two-thirds oy from stem; two horizontal handles, tilted upward. The potter who produced most of Makron's cups, and who signs several of them, was Hieron, but it is not clear that he was responsible for this example; in particular, the band on the underside of the foot is rather wide compared to others signed by him.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.39
artifact.summary: Side A: Trainer and two hoplitodromoi<lb>Side B: Three hoplitodromoi<lb>Interior: Hoplitodromos.
artifact.other_bibliography: Watkins 1973, 58-61, no. 22; Neils 1992, 89, fig. 55.
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.099 m.; D. 0.239 m.; Diam. with handles 0.313 m.
artifact.collection_history: Joseph Brummer collection; Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.
artifact.condit: Broken into 42 pieces; mended with some repainting, now discolored. The greatest damage is to the shield in the tondo and the shield and lower legs of the left-hand athlete on side A. The different tonality of the fragments in the tondo are the result of different conditions of erosion and salt absorption. Uneven firing in places, resulting in reddish color or iridescence. A reddish arc running through the legs of the figures on side B is from the rim of another vessel which touched the cup during firing.
artifact.comparanda: Cf. the hoplitodromoi and trainer on another, earlier cup by Onesimos, formerly in the Schweitzer collection, Arlesheim (ARV2, 323, 56); cf. also a cup fragment in the Cabinet des Médailles (ARV2, 323, 57). Similar scenes were represented by other contemporary cup painters, such as the Brygos Painter; e.g. Copenhagen, Thorvaldsen Museum 111 (ARV2, 401, 10). Beazley compared the stance of the athlete practicing his start in the interior to that of a hoplitodromos on a kylix by the Triptolemos Painter, Oxford 1947.262 (ARV2, 364, 42); see J. D. Beazley, "A Hoplitodromos Cup," BSA 46 (1951) 10. The race in armor, doubtless an outgrowth of military training, became an event at the Olympian games in 520 B.C., and is represented on Panathenaic prize amphorae of about 520-480 and of the fourth century. For the hoplitodromos, see Beazley 1951 (supra), 7-15; Gardiner 1930, 140-42; and D. G. Kyle, in Neils 1992, 88-89. For Onesimos, see A. Ashmead, A Study of the Style of the Cup Painter Onesimos (Dissertation, Bryn Mawr, 1959); Sparkes 1985; D. Williams 1985; and Robertson 1992, 42-51.
artifact.decoration_description:
Interior: A nude athlete with a budding beard and moustache, drawn with dilute glaze, is practicing the start of the race in armor, the hoplitodromos, a name shared by the competitors themselves. He stands to the left with his feet slightly spread and the knees bent, his body bent over, and both arms fully extended. The left arm, which would hold the shield in the race, is extended a little farther than the right, so that the man's back is turned partially toward the viewer. His fringed hair is tied with both a reserved fillet and a more slender cord, the latter in added red. Dilute glaze is used for the ribs and minor muscles of the back, hip, and limbs. Behind the hoplitodromos, at right, one above the other, lie a pair of greaves. Before him, at left, his shield leans against an unseen support; the damaged device may be the same poplar or plane tree leaf that appears on the four shields on the exterior. On top of the shield sits a Chalcidian helmet with a horsehair crest. The pair of jumping weights (halteres) hanging at the upper right do not indicate that the athlete is practicing for the long jump; they simply contribute to the athletic ambiance, presumably that of the palaestra.

Side A: In the center, a trainer (paidotribes), wearing a himation and a red wreath, is instructing a hoplitodromos. The trainer leans on the knotty staff in his right hand and with his left hand holds a forked wand, the symbol of his authority and dispenser of corrective pokes and whacks to athletes not exhibiting proper form. The hoplitodromos bends to the right to pick up his shield; he is already wearing greaves and a helmet. The latter, like all the helmets on the cup, is of Chalcidian type, and the shield device, as on all the other shields, is a leaf from a poplar or plane tree. At right, a second hoplitodromos, fully equipped with helmet, shield, and greaves, is practicing his start. Although he also stands to the left, his stance is the reverse of the athlete in the interior, with the right leg advanced and the right arm farther forward. His shield differs from the others on the cup in that the leaf device is surrounded by a circle of feathery strokes of dilute glaze, perhaps an attempt at suggesting rotundity. Behind him is a pick, with one blade stuck in the ground. A pair of halteres hand from red cords above the trainer's right hand. Unlike the man in the interior, whose beard is beginning to grow, these athletes and the ones on side B are still beardless youths.

Side B: Three young athletes, all wearing greaves and helmets, are practicing for the hoplitodromos. The two at left are running to the right, without shields. The one at left leans over with head down, his right arm back, his left arm forward with fingers spread; his left foot rests on a shield lying flat on the ground. The middle runner leans backward, a stance popular in early 5th-century art. The runner at right faces left and carries a shield; his pose is a mirror image of the left-hand runner, but with both feet on the ground. As on the athletes on side A, dilute glaze is used for the ribs and wispy sideburns of the youths and for minor muscles of the limbs, neck, and abdomen.

The exterior groundline is a single, continuous reserved stripe; reserved stripes also circle the inside of the rim and the resting surface of the foot. The side of the foot, the interior of the stem, the insides of the handles, and the area between the handle roots are reserved.
artifact.inscriptions: Inscriptions with red letters in all three scenes. Interior: Diagonally and retrograde, from the athlete's hip to the helmet: &epig-rough;*O*P*A*I*S ("The boy"; i.e. "The boy is handsome," as on side A). Side A: From the face of the left-hand athlete to the lower fork of the wand: &epig-rough;*O*P*A*I*S; from the trainer's cloak to the top of the pick: *K*A*L*O*S. Side B: Below the left arm of the first runner: &epig-rough;*O*P*A*I*S.
artifact.shape_description: Kylix of type B, with continuous profile from bowl to foot; stem concave and relatively tall; offset ridge about a third of the way down the foot; two horizontal handles, roughly rectangular and tilted upward.

artifact.name: Harvard 1972.325
artifact.summary: Head in oriental cap rising from a flower
artifact.other_bibliography: Art of the Ancients, Emmerich Gallery (New York 1968) 37, no. 45; Fogg Art Museum, The Frederick M. Watkins Collection (Cambridge, Mass. 1973) 74-75, no. 30; RVAp, 2.608, no. 21/33 (as 1972.235).
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Frederick M. Watkins.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with minor restoration.
artifact.comparanda: Floral heads are common on Apulian vases, particularly on the necks of volute-kraters. Most are female, but there are many males as well. Many wear an oriental cap like this one, more like a Persian tiara than a Phrygian cap. It identifies the youth as an oriental, an eastern barbarian, but the sex is unclear. If female, she is probably an Amazon, or perhaps Artemis Bendis; if male, which is more likely, he is either Attis, Orpheus, Paris, or Adonis. Trendall (Trendall & Cambitoglou 1982, 648) believes such heads represent Orpheus, pointing out that neither Attis nor Adonis are otherwise represented in eastern garb before about 300 B.C., and that there is no reason for Paris to be represented this way, not being the object of a particular cult. Orpheus, on the other hand, was the object of worship throughout Magna Graecia. His head, cut off by the Thracian women and thrown into the sea, floated all the way to Lesbos, where it became an oracle. On the other hand, the luxuriant foliage which normally accompanies the heads symbolizes fertility, more the realm of Aphrodite than Orpheus. A connection with Aphrodite is reinforced by the fact that many vases of the Alabastra Group, and those associated with it, have Eros in the same position, on top of a flower and surrounded by florals; e.g. Trendall & Cambitoglou 1982, pl. 232, 5 and 8; and pl. 233, 1-3. One theory suggests that the elaborate florals are connected with the Sicyonian painter Pausias, who flourished in the second quarter of the fourth century and who developed the art of flower painting (Pliny, NH 35, 123-25); for a full discussion, see Trendall & Cambitoglou 1982, 189-90..
artifact.decoration_description:
A youthful head, facing left and wearing an oriental cap, is emerging from a large flower growing from the groundline below. Long ringlets of hair, drawn with thinned glaze, fall down the youth's shoulder beneath the trailing ends of the cap. On either side, growing from the same source, are long coiling and spiraling tendrils, flowers, buds, and acanthus leaves. Added white, tinted yellow with a wash of dilute glaze, is used to highlight numerous details of the foliage and to color the cap and the top of the central flower; additional spots and streaks of dilute glaze give the cap a leathery color.

On the back of the vase, beneath the handle, is a large upright palmette, flanked by vertical scrolls, buds, and half-palmettes; the palmettes have yellow cores, and yellow dots and highlights are sprinkled through the stylized foliage. On the shoulder is a band of eggs with white cores separated by black dots; the eggs circling the lower body are drawn with added white, as are the dots. Tall black tongues decorate the neck, and the groove between foot and body is tinted with a red wash. The foot is black; the irregular blacking of the mouth, handle, and upper neck are the result of careless dipping.
artifact.shape_description: Squat lekythos of typical late Apulian type: ovoid body; tall, tapering neck; tall trumpet mouth; grooved foot in three degrees; broad groove between foot and body.

artifact.name: Harvard 1970.108
artifact.summary: Side A: Komos, with three youths<lb>Side B: Three draped youths
artifact.other_bibliography: E. H. Dohan, "A Bell-Krater by the Christie Painter," The University Museum Bulletin, 6 (1936) 126-8, no. 4; Buitron 1972, 128-9, no. 71.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Mrs. Alfred Mansfield Brooks.
artifact.condit: Unbroken; surface worn and pitted in places, most noticeable on the handles and adjacent areas on the body, and on the right-hand figures on either side. The glaze misfired red beneath both handles.
artifact.comparanda: For another Harvard vase by the Christie Painter, a pot-painter in the Group of Polygnotos, cf. the stamnos Harvard 1925.30.42 (ARV2, 1048, 38). The artist painted variants of this theme, with a komos on one side and three draped youths on the other, several times: see ARV2, 1047, 16-24). The lead komast on Malibu 71.AE.250 (ARV2, 1047, 24) is nearly identical to the leader in this scene, but carries a skyphos instead of a torch. For the Christie Painter, see S. Pingiatoglou, AA (1989) 11-21; For the Group of Polygnotos, including the Christie Painter, see A. Bowtell, The Group of Polygnotos (Dissertation, Oxford University, 1990). For Polygnotos, see Matheson 1993.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: komos. Three nude young revelers are in procession to the right. All three have cloaks draped over their shoulders — that of the one at right has slipped off his right shoulder — and all three wear fillets in their short, curly hair. The komast at left throws his chest out and rests his right hand on his hip. In his left hand he holds a staff. Unlike the other two, he is infibulated. The middle youth is playing the double-flutes (auloi); his cheeks are puffed out as he blows. The leader of the procession turns his body frontal and looks back at his companions, gesturing with his lowered right hand. The torch in his left hand shows that the procession takes place at night; they have left one drinking party and are reeling toward another, like Plato's Alcibiades (Plat. Sym. 212d).

Side B: Two youths stand in conversation with a third youth at right; all three wear himations and have short hair fringed with curls of dilute glaze. The youth at left gestures with his right hand; his companion holds a staff with his right hand. The youth at right holds out his right hand, palm upward. In the field above hangs a pair of jumping weights, a common filling device, perhaps suggesting a setting in the palaestra.

A laurel wreath circles the vase beneath the rim. Bands of egg-pattern nearly circle the handle roots. The groundlines on either side consist of groups of three maeanders to right alternating with saltire-squares. The side of the foot is reserved, as is the space between the handle roots.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by the Fogg Art Museum, Harvard University; bequest of Ruth Steele Brooks (1970.108)

Height: 12 3/16 in. (30.9 cm.)

Intact.

Side A: komos. Three youths proceed to the right. The first carries a torch. He is shown with trunk and one leg frontal, head turned back to the left towards his companions, his left leg turned to the right. He wears a chlamys over one shoulder. In the center is a youth playing flutes. He advances to the right, chlamys draped over his shoulders. At the left is a third youth, also in chlamys, holding a staff in one hand.

Side B: three youths conversing. All three wear himatia; the central youth carries a staff. Suspended in the field is a pair of jumping weights, a common filling ornament.

Below, triple rightward meanders alternating with saltires; on the lip, laurel wreath; at the base of the handles, egg pattern.

Dilute glaze: strands of hair, anatomical details.

Red: leaves of wreaths on A.

Attributed to the Christie Painter [Dohan] ca. 440 - 430 B. C.

The Christie Painter was a member of the group of Polygnotos (Mount Holyoke 1929.BS.II.4). His style is characterized by the same fluid figures and naturalistic drawing.

Bibliography: E. H. Dohan, "A Bell-Krater by the Christie Painter," The University Museum Bulletin 6 (The University of Pennsylvania May 1936) no. 4, pp. 126-128, pl. VII; ARV2, 1047, no. 20.
artifact.shape_description: Bell-krater of standard type for the period: torus rim; body tapering to a stem; disk foot with groove at top of side; two handles tilted upward and rolled back slightly.

artifact.name: Harvard 1969.15
artifact.summary: Dionysos between eyes; cocks.
artifact.other_bibliography: Art Journal 29 (Fall 1969) 53, fig. 2; M. M. Eisman, "New Attributions of Attic Kyathoi," AJA 77 (1973) 71, no. 1; Kurtz & Boardman 1986, 39-42, fig. 6.
artifact.dimensions: H. without handle 0.073 m.; H. with handle 0.14 m.; D. 0.113 m.
artifact.collection_history: Gift: A Supporter of Sardis in Recognition of Mrs. Ilse Hanfmann and Eleven Seasons of Hospitality.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with moderate restoration of cracks and small gaps. Considerable erosion of added white.
artifact.comparanda: Kyathoi are dippers for ladling wine out of kraters and other large vessels and into drinking cups. The shape is related to that of certain Etruscan bucchero vessels, and the Attic examples, which are normally found in tombs in Italy, may have been made specifically for export to Etruria. For kyathoi, see M. M. Eisman, Attic Kyathos Painters (Dissertation, Univ. of Pennsylvania, 1971); M. M. Eismann, "Attic Kyathos Production," Archaeology 28 (1975) 76-83; and M. M. Eisman, "New Attributions of Attic Kyathoi," AJA 77 (1973) 71, no. 1. The Harvard kyathos is the name-vase of Eisman's Hanfmann Painter, to whom he attributes 5 other examples, all of this shape and all with eyes on the sides; four of these also have cocks by the handles (see Eisman 1977, 71). Eyes are common on kyathoi by other painters as well, as are cocks; the same subjects, including Dionysos, are represented on another kyathos at Harvard: Harvard 1970.34 (see below). Eisman compares the style of the Harvard kyathos to the earliest examples of Beazley's Group of Vatican G 57 (ABV, 610-614). For a discussion of the kyathoi of the Hanfmann Painter and a related example in the Getty Museum (Malibu 77.AE.102 and Malibu 78.AE.5, see Kurtz & Boardman 1986, 35-47. For cocks on Attic vases, see H. Hoffmann, "Hahnenkampf in Athen," RA (1974) 195-220.
artifact.decoration_description: The upper three quarters of the cup are coated outside with chalky white slip, over which the figures are painted in black-figure. On the front, opposite the handle, Dionysos is walking to the right but looking back to the left, his clenched fists held against his mid-section. He wears a white chiton with a red hem and dotted collar, a red ivy wreath, and a himation with at least two red stripes. His beard is long and red. He holds his hands as though he were clutching the ivy vine which emerges from his shoulder, but in fact he is not. The vine spreads to both right and left, trailing over and under the two large eyes which dominate either side of the vase. Each eye has an eyebrow and a pronounced canthus. The iris and pupil are represented by three compass-drawn incisions, with the outermost band painted white and the middle one red; a dot in the center of the black pupil marks the point where the compass pivoted. Beyond the eyes, flanking the handle, stand two cocks with several details of their anatomy picked out in added red: comb, hackle, wattles, and alternate tail feathers. From both cocks, a pair of sickle feathers arch back from the tail. Each holds his head high, as though they had just spotted each other across the vase and were about to do battle. A single lotus bud grows behind each cock, leaning over its back from a drooping tendril. The groundline is a single black stripe; below this a broader band and another, slender stripe. The interior, lower body, handle and foot are black.
artifact.shape_description: Kyathos (dipper): thin-walled body in the form of a truncated cone with convex sides; slender echinus foot; straight rim; single, high-swung strap handle with a central rib that extends half way down at either end, terminating inside in a mold-made palmette, with a snail-shaped knob on top of handle. Eisman calls this type of kyathos, painted by vases he assigns to the Hanfmann Painter, the Class of Munich 1963.

artifact.name: Harvard 1969.14
artifact.summary: Departure scene, with chariot.
artifact.other_bibliography: Parke-Bernet Galleries, January 24, 1969, no. 216A; Fogg Art Museum Newsletter 6:4 (April 1969) 107; Art Quarterly 32 (1969) 324; Art Journal 29 (fall 1969) 53, fig. 1; and J. G. Pedley, "A Black-Figure Hydria in the Fogg Art Museum," in Studies Presented to George M. A. Hanfmann, eds. D.G. Mitten, J.G. Pedley and J.A. Scott (Cambridge, Mass. 1971) 121-26, pls. 32-33.
artifact.collection_history: Gift: A Supporter of Sardis in Recognition of Prof. George Hanfmann and His Eleven Seasons as Field Director of the Harvard-Cornell Archaeological Exploration of Sardis.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with some repainting of cracks and small gaps, including parts of the following: the tongues below the neck, the ivy vine at left, both shields, the feet of the horses, gesturing man, and man at right, and the left arm and upper torso of the left runner on the shoulder.
artifact.comparanda: For the shape, cf. Louvre F 47 (ABV, 309, 100), by the Swing Painter. The vase is unattributed (it is not by the Swing Painter). Pedley compared the style to that of the Princeton Painter and the Painter of Berlin 1686; cf. the chariot scene on Munich 1375 (ABV, 297, 15). Although chariots were not used in warfare in this period, scenes of warriors departing in chariots are common in Attic black-figure of the second half of the sixth century. They may have funerary overtones, with the young hoplite leaving for death and the Underworld in a conveyance whose heroic associations were enshrined in the Homeric poems. The scene on the shoulder is interesting not only for depicting athletes — still uncommon in this period — but for one of the earliest representations of a Thracian zeira, a cloak adopted by Athenian cavalrymen which appears in many later depictions of horsemen; see J. M. Padgett, "Phineas and the Boreads on a Pelike by the Nausicaa Painter," Journal of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston 3 (1991) 22-23, and 31, note 33; and Knauer 1987, 22, n. 48, and 28-29.
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: A warrior is preparing to depart in a chariot. The charioteer stands in the box at left, holding the reins in both hands and a long goad in his left hand. He is dressed in the long, belted gown normally worn by charioteers; the front panel of the skirt is painted red and the back is decorated with rosettes (red dots circled by smaller white ones). The driver's Theban shield hangs on his back from three white cords, which cross the man's chest. The shield device is a bucranium in added white. Like the other men in the scene, the charioteer has a red beard and a red fillet in his hair. The warrior approaches the chariot box from the right, his body obscured by the large round "Argive" shield on his left arm, and by the bodies and legs of the horses standing before him. The shield is white, with a red rim; no device was ever added. We cannot tell if the warrior wore a bronze cuirass, but he does carry a spear and wears a Corinthian helmet with a red crest, and greaves with rows of white rivets along the edge (to hold the padded lining). A bearded man faces the warrior and gestures toward him with his left hand; he stands on the near side of the chariot, on the opposite from the hoplite. The man wears a red fillet, white chiton with incised folds, and a red himation draped over his shoulders. The incised line across his throat could be a necklace. He may be the father of the hoplite, come to bid his son farewell as he leaves for battle or, allegorically, death. A fourth man stands at right, dressed in a red chiton, red fillet, and a himation decorated with red and white rosettes. His hair is longer than the others and is tied in a queue. His hands are hidden by the heads of the two near horses, but he is probably holding the bridles of the two far horses, who rear their heads as though in need of steadying. The horses have red manes; the tails, which often are painted red in such scenes, are hidden behind the gesturing man.

Shoulder: A mounted youth rides to the right between two groups of males. The horse has a red mane and tail and a red stripe near the rump. The rider wears a red fillet and a Thracian cloak, a zeira, with woven designs of red and white. The reins are half red and half incised. To the left of the horse, two nude youths are running to the right, arms and legs pumping. Both have red hair, and the leader, on the right, has his tied in a krobylos with a fillet. Between the runners stands a youth in a himation decorated with red and black stripes and rosettes of red and white. He wears a red fillet and holds his left hand out as though holding a staff, though none is depicted; he may be judging the race or training the runners. Another youth in identical pose and costume stands on the other side of the horse, facing left. Beyond him, at far right, is a third young red-haired runner, racing to the left. Either more than one event is represented, or this is simply the daily activity in the palaestra, with a number of athletes practicing in different places and directions.

Band of tongues, alternately red and black, above the figures on the shoulder. Single black stripe between shoulder frieze and main panel. The main panel is framed laterally by ivy vines with berries and large leaves, and below by a single black stripe. Double stripes of added red circle the lower body below the main panel and above the rays on the base; single red stripes circle the middle of the foot, the top of the rim, and the inner edge of the brim. The mouth, neck, handles, and foot are black.

Top border: tongues of alternating red and black.

Shoulder scene: youth on horseback flanked by two standing draped and three running nude youths.

Panel scene: hero mounting chariot, departing for battle, with two spectators and charioteer.

Vertical borders: ivy leaves.

Above foot: rays. Foot black.
artifact.shape_description: Hydria: plump, ovoid body; relatively steep shoulder; short side handles, tilted upward but not curved; short vertical handle flanked by spurs at the juncture with the lip; tall concave neck; torus rim, flat on top; spreading foot with torus base.

artifact.name: Harvard 1965.82
artifact.summary: Three friezes. Shoulder: four geese. Middle: wild goats. Belly: floral.
artifact.other_bibliography: Fogg Art Museum Acquisitions, 1965 (Cambridge, Mass. 1966) 66.
artifact.collection_history: Purchase from the David M. Robinson Fund.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired; the handle is modern; some abrasion and chipping.
artifact.comparanda: For the Wild Goat style, see C. Kardara, Rhodiaki Angeiographia, (Athens 1963); Walter-Karydi 1973; Schiering 1954; and Cook 1972, 117-25; and R.M. Cook, "The Wild Goat and Fikellura Styles: Some Speculations," OJA 11 (1992) 255-66. As a result of clay analysis and new excavation, it is now recognized that the "classic" Wild Goat style oinochoai found on Rhodes were mostly made at Miletus. It has also become increasing clear that there were several centers of production for East Greek pottery outside of Ionia, particularly in Aeolis, Chios, and Caria; see E. A. Hemelrijk, "A Group of provincial East-Greek Vases from South Western Asia Minor," BABesch 62 (1987) 33-55; and E. A. Hemelrijk and J. M. Hemelrijk, "A Homeless Billy Goat in Missouri," Muse 23-24 (1989-90) 30-47. The Harvard oinochoe has been assigned to Milesian Middle Wild Goat Style II and dated to the last quarter of the 7th c. (see Cook, above, p. 257); cf. the goats, lotuses, filling ornaments, and general scheme of Amsterdam 784 (Hemelrijk and Hemelrijk 1989-90, 35, fig. 4) and Oxford 1966.1021 (Cook 1992, 259, fig. 2a).
artifact.ceramic_phase: Milesian Middle Wild Goat Style II
artifact.decoration_description: The decorated areas are coated with a pale, creamy slip, over which the designs are painted in dark brown slip, fired red or black in places. Covering the body are three decorative friezes separated by broad stripes. The first, which fills most of the shoulder, has four geese, nestled low on the groundline so that their feet are not represented. They are in two pairs, back to back, so that the middle two face each other on the front, separated by a large filling ornament in the form of a swastika with coiled tips. Throughout the background are other filling ornaments, including concentric circles surrounded by dots, dotted quatrefoils, and crosses with T-shaped crossbars on the arms. Pendant from the upper border and rising from the groundline are hatched semi-circles and cross-hatched triangles. In typical East Greek style, the birds are drawn in outline, with no use of incision as on Attic black-figure. In the middle frieze is a row of grazing goats, with black bodies and outlined heads, shoulders, and bellies. They are clearly billy goats (i.e. male), and have beards, long ears, short tails, and long arching horns. The background is cluttered with assorted filling ornaments like those in the upper frieze. The lower body of the vessel is filled with large lotus flowers alternating with lotus buds, all with dark centers and reserved edges. Around the neck is a broad cable pattern with dotted centers. Band of crude tongues around the upper shoulder. Mouth, foot, and handle are black.
artifact.shape_description: Oinochoe: trefoil mouth; flat, reeded handle; globular body with high, rounded shoulder; hollow, flaring foot; cylindrical neck with fillets at top and bottom.

artifact.name: Harvard 1964.8
artifact.summary: Exterior: Lions. Interior: Cock and snake.
artifact.collection_history: Purchase from the David M. Robinson Fund.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired; foot re-attached. Some flaking of glaze on the exterior, including the foot and some of the lions. The interior is much more eroded, with most of the glaze on the cock lost.
artifact.comparanda: Stibbe attrinutes the cup to the Chimaira Painter and says the cock is in the tradition of those of the Naukratis Painter: eg. a cup in a Dutch private collection (Stibbe 1972, no. 98, pl. 32.2). For the shape and ornament, particularly the treatment of the bud frieze, cf. a cup by the Chimaira Painter in the Grand Rapids Art Museum (Stibbe 1972, no. 354, pls. 129.1, 130.3, and 131.2). For cocks on Greek vases, see H. Hoffmann, "Hahnenkampf in Athen," RA (1974) 195-220; and Kurtz & Boardman 1986, 41-44.
artifact.decoration_description:
Interior: The tondo is filled by a large cock, standing to right, with a red comb and red tail feathers (there may have been additional added color, but most of the glaze has worn off). In the space at right is an undulating snake, its head near that of the cock. In the space above the cock is a stylized flower, probably a lotus. The cock symbolizes male pugnacity and fertility. The snake is a symbol of fertility and good luck, but in this case it may also be the cock's dinner.

Exterior: A continuous frieze of lions walk from right to left. Their long tails are alternately curled beneath them or over their backs, but otherwise they are nearly identical, with open, roaring mouths and added red on the bellies and manes; one lion also has a red tongue. Large black dots are placed throughout the frieze as fillers.

The tondo is framed by four stripes of varying width, with another reserved stripe farther out in the bowl. The handles, and foot are black; the lip is black except for a reserved stripe just inside the rim. The grooved area at the top of the stem is reserved except for a black stripe. In the handle zone on either side is a band of upright lotus buds, with dots in the interstices and a row of dots below. The lotuses are framed above by two narrow stripes and below by a broader one; below the latter, and above the lions, is a broad red stripe framed by groups of slender black stripes. The lions stand on a thick black stripe, and below this is another such stripe framed by groups of slender stripes.
artifact.shape_description: Kylix of Laconian type, a form of lip-cup: flaring lip, offset inside and out; hollow, tapering stem, grooved at the top; two horizontal handles, nearly V-shaped and tilted upward.

artifact.name: Harvard 1963.69
artifact.summary: Body: Theseus and the Minotaur; Shoulder: satyrs and nymphs.
artifact.other_bibliography: Fogg Art Museum Acquisitions 1962-1963 (before cleaning); Buitron 1972, 32-33, no. 12.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of Edith J. Purrington.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with some pieces missing, most from the black areas of the body but also a large section of the main scene, including the legs, chest, and neck of Theseus; the face, right leg, and right shoulder and arm of the Minotaur; and the right leg of one spectator. Details in added red are well preserved, but most added white has been lost. All previous repainting has been removed.
artifact.comparanda:
Buitron compared the shape and style of two hydriae signed by the potter Timagoras and attributed to the Taleides Painter: Louvre F 38 and Louvre F 39 (ABV, 174, 7 and 5). These examples, however, lack the ribbed handles and distinctive mouth and foot of this vase, for which cf. the unattributed Louvre F 8 (CVA, Louvre 6, pl. 60).

For Theseus and the Minotaur, see E. Young, Theseus and the Minotaur (Dissertation, Bryn Mawr, 1972); D. von Bothmer, "The Taleides Amphora," BMMA 5:9 (May 1947) 221-28; F. Brommer, Theseus: die Täten des griechischen Helden in der antiken Kunst und Literatur (Darmstadt 1982) 35-64; and S. Woodford, in LIMC, VI, 574-81, pls. 316-25.
artifact.graffiti: On the bottom of the foot: *A*L
artifact.decoration_description:
Body: In the center, Theseus holds the Minotaur by one of its horns and stabs it with the sword in his right hand. The monster has fallen to his right, on his right knee, and turns his head back toward Theseus. He holds a stone in his upraised left hand. Theseus has a scabbard at his waist and wears a white fillet (now nearly invisible) and a tunic with a red kilt. He has long red hair and a row of incised curls over his forehead. The Minotaur has added red on his neck and chest, and the hair on his head is indicated with short incisions. Watching the action from either side are two pairs of spectators, in each case a woman and a youth. The women, whose features have been lost with the added white that colored their faces and limbs, wear belted peploi with red overfolds and have himatia with red and white spots draped over their arms. Both wear red fillets and have their hair tied in queues. The youths are nude, but have cloaks with red and white dots and rosettes (now effaced) draped over their arms. Both youths have long red hair, and the one at right has added red around his nipples and on his chest, as on the Minotaur. All four figures hold one arm level at the waist and raise the other perpendicular, as though hailing the central event.

Shoulder: Four pairs of dancing satyrs and nymphs. The satyrs all have red hair and beards. The women all wear belted peploi with red overfolds and have their hair tied in a queue. Because they lack maenadic attributes — thyrsoi, snakes, etc. -the women are more accurately termed nymphs. Their features have been lost through flaking of the added white which colored their faces and limbs. The direction of the dance is to the right, but all of the women and one satyr (the second one) turn their heads to the left. The first satyr raises his left leg and left hand; his partner raises her left hand too. The second satyr holds a drinking horn, and although he looks back at the first pair, raises his left hand toward his own partner, who holds both of her hands low. The third satyr stands with legs together and knees bent, with one hand up and the other down; his partner holds both of her arms down on either side of her body. The fourth satyr raises his left leg and right hand and touches his belly with his other hand; the nymph touches her stomach also.

The scene on the body is framed laterally with ivy wreaths, with red vines and black leaves and berries. The figures on the shoulder stand on a slender line of dilute glaze; above them, below the neck, is a band of tongues, alternately red and black. There is a zone of rays on the lower body. The mouth, neck, handles, and foot are black. Stripes of added red circle the middle of the foot and its ribbed moldings, the top of the zone of rays, the lower body just below the figure panel, the upper and lower edges of the mouth, and the fillet between foot and body. The ends of the handles rotelles are also red.
artifact.essay_text:
Lent by the Fogg Art Museum, Harvard University; bequest of Edith J. Purrington (1963.69)

Height: 17 5/16 in. (44 cm.)

Broken and repaired; missing pieces restored and painted.

Theseus and the Minotaur. Theseus, dressed in loincloth with a fillet in his long hair, grasps the horn of the Minotaur with one hand and stabs him with a short sword. The Minotaur falls to one knee, raising one arm to throw a rock. On either side stand a youth and a girl, the companions of Theseus, raising their arms in alarm. Each youth is nude but for a chlamys over his arm; the girls wear peploi, mantles, and fillets in their hair.

On the shoulder: komos. Four pairs of dancing satyrs and maenads. The satyrs are nude and have bushy tails. The maenads wear peploi and have fillets in their hair. Double rows of ivy and corymboi (ivy berries) frame the main panel laterally. Above the shoulder scene, alternately red and black framed tongues.

Red is used in the design areas and to articulate parts of the shape.

Red: the men's hair, the Minotaur's mane, fillets, upper parts of peploi, traces on mantles of girls, loincloth of Theseus, breast of the Minotaur and youth to far right. Two lines running all around the vase at the base of the scene, narrow ridges on the upper and lower edges of the mouth, ends of the half spools attaching the vertical handle to the lip, three narrow mouldings on the foot, line on comes of foot, fillet between base and foot.

White: traces on female flesh.

Unattributed 550 - 530 B.C.

In shape and in style this hydria is close to two hydriai in the Louvre (Louvre F 38 and Louvre F 39) signed by Timagoras as potter and attributed to the Taleides Painter. The shape with broad belly and sloping shoulder, gently offset, is popular just after the middle of the sixth century. The mouth, handles, and foot which are sturdy and elaborate imply metal work prototypes. The subject, the legendary slaying of the Minotaur which ended the tribute Athens paid to Crete, reached its height of popularity with Attic vase painters during the third quarter of the sixth century. At this time a canonical scheme for its representation was established. This hydria is an excellent example of the canon. The action has lost its vigor and has acquired a ceremonial character. (Compare with Harvard 1960.312 which is more vigorous.)

Unpublished.
artifact.inscriptions: In red wash on the bottom of the foot, now quite pale, a ligature, possibly *P*R.
artifact.shape_description: Hydria: swollen, bulbous body; rounded shoulder; concave neck; slender rim, flattened on top, with grooves at top and bottom framing a torus molding; echinus foot with lower section grooved to create a reeded profile; fillet between foot and body; small horizontal handles with torus rib in center; low vertical handle, ribbed along the sides and framed at the upper juncture by spool-shaped rotelles.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.390
artifact.summary: Sides A-B: Deer hunt
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 57; CVA, Robinson 1, 42, pl. 22, 1.
artifact.dimensions: H. with handles 0.164 m.; Diam. 0.142 m.; Diam. with handles 0.23 m.
artifact.collection_history: David M. Robinson Bequest.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with repainting of wide cracks and gaps, including parts of the lower body, the central rider on side B, and all of his dog except the tail. Large chip in foot. Misfired red in parts, both inside and out.
artifact.comparanda:
Kilinski (ref. below) attributes this kantharos and two others to his Atalanta Painter, named for the huntress in a depiction of the Calydonian boar hunt on Athens, NM 432. On the reverse of the Athens vase are mounted hunters and hounds like those on this cup; similar riders, without hounds, occur on the third kantharos, New York 06.1021.28. The shape of all three cups is P. N. Ures's Group A of deep-bottomed kantharoi; see Kilinski 1990, 21 and 65, pls. 18-21.

Robinson said the deer on side A is a stag and that on side B a doe, but this is far from clear; neither have horns. For Greek hunters and their representation in art, see D. B. Hill, Hounds and Hunting in Ancient Greece (Berkeley 1961); and J.-L. Durand and A. Schnapp, in Bérard 1989, 59-70.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Two hunters on horseback pursue a deer to the left. The hunters are bearded and wear tunics of added red. They hold the reins with their right hands and hold a spear aloft in the left. The horses have red manes. Below the horse in the center is a hound, which like the deer and the horses on both sides, has both its forelegs in the air. The horse at the right has its weight back on its rear legs, as though rearing up, while the horse at center is stretched out in full gallop. The deer, possibly a stag, has already been hit by a spear, the point of which has pierced its back and emerged by its left shoulder. Added red is used to color the deer's breast and belly the spots on its rump.

Side B: The composition is nearly the same as on Side A, but the chase is to the right, and whatever added color may have been used has disappeared. The deer's head is damaged, but traces of added red remain on the body.
artifact.shape_description: Kantharos of Group A deep-bottomed type: thin-walled; high looping handles, concave in profile and with spurs above the juncture with the body; echinus foot; tapering lower body; tall rim, offset from the body and slanted outward; straight lip.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.368
artifact.summary: Side A: Two satyrs and two women. Side B: Three youths.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 144; Robinson AJA 60 (1956) 23-24, pl. 18, figs. 77-78.
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.385 m.; Diam. 0.32 m.; diam. mouth 0.385 m.
artifact.collection_history: Franz Trau collection, Vienna; Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Unbroken; moderate scratching and flaking of glaze.
artifact.comparanda: For the Amykos Painter, see Trendall 1967, 29-50, pls. 10-21; and Trendall 1989, 20-21, figs. 11-19.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Two pairs of figures, each consisting of a satyr speaking to a draped woman. The satyrs are nearly identical, with the left foot resting on a rock (its rough texture indicated with streaks of dilute glaze), a thyrsos held vertically in the left hand, and the right hand gesturing toward the woman, with the palm held open. The only difference is that the satyr at left is bald, but not the one at right. Dilute glaze is used for their moustaches and eyebrows, for the wispy fringe of their hair and beards, and for the line of hairs below the navel. The first woman wears a chiton and a himation which covers both arms, though one can tell that the left hand is resting on the hip. Her hair is held in a krobylos by a hairband with three upright points. The woman at right wears a belted chiton and a sakkos decorated with stripes, dots, and a wavy line of dilute glaze. She holds her left hand behind her waist and lets her right hand dangle beside the satyr's left hand.

Side B: Three youths, all dressed in himatia, stand in conversation. The himation of the central youth covers both his arms. He looks at the youth at left, who holds a staff in his right hand. As is often the case in such scenes, it may be that the middle youth is being accosted by the other two, although there is no indication he is younger than they. One suggestion that this may be so is the behavior of the youth at right, who reaches down to pat the rump of the central youth.

A laurel wreath circles the vase beneath the rim. The groundline on either side consists of groups of maeanders to right alternating with cross-squares (and one saltire-square on the reverse). Reserved stripes circle the interior just inside the lip and 6.5 mm. farther down. The side of the foot and the spaces between the handle roots are reserved. There are reserved grooves beneath the lip, between the foot and body, and around the outer edge of the top of the foot.
artifact.shape_description: Bell-krater: height and diameter of mouth the same; body tapering to a stem and slightly constricted above the handles; torus lip; tapering disk foot.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.360
artifact.summary: Side A: Profile of woman<lb>Side B: Draped youth
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 147; CVA, Robinson 3, 33, pl. 24, 2.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Unbroken; considerable chipping and pitting of the rim and interior. Lusterless glaze with a rough, granulated surface.
artifact.comparanda: For the CA Painter, whose workshop was at Cumae, see Trendall 1967, 450-77, pls. 175-183; and Trendall 1989, 167-69, figs. 312-317. Trendall notes that on the head vases of the CA Painter, the lips are slightly parted and the nostril may be indicated by a dot, as here; Trendall 1967, 472.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A woman's head in profile to the left. She wears earrings, a necklace, a radiate crown, and a sakkos drawn tight by a string, from which a bunch of hair emerges at the back. The sakkos is decorated with rows of dots and stripes, the latter, like the jewelry and crown, tinted yellow by coating added white with a wash of dilute glaze.

Side B: A youth stands in profile to the left. He wears a yellow apicate fillet, yellow sandals, and a himation, the latter covering both arms and drawn tight in front by the right arm. In the field before him is a rosette; behind him is a narrow "window." Both filling ornaments are touched with yellow, which is also used for the plants or branches on either side of the youth, and for the necklace or fillet which hangs from the window.

Below each handle is a large palmette; the groundline is a single reserved stripe, circling the vase. The upright florals framing the figures consist of coiling tendrils and half-palmettes, which on side B are partially outlined with yellow. Below the mouth on either side is a laurel wreath, which is interrupted over the handles by a continuation of the reserved spaces between the handles, extending almost to the edge of the rim. The foot and stem are all black.
artifact.shape_description: Bell-krater: body tapers to a tall stem; tall, concave foot; handles set high on body; rim not offset, but continuous with body.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.358
artifact.summary: Side A: Seated maenad and two satyrs. Side B: Three draped youths.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 142; CVA, Robinson 3, 26, pl. 18, 1.
artifact.collection_history: From Warren Coll. Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Unbroken. Uneven firing, partly due to careless application of glaze. Traces of incrustation.
artifact.comparanda: For the Amykos Painter, see Trendall 1967, 29-50, pls. 10-21; and Trendall 1989, 20-21, figs. 11-19.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A woman, probably a maenad, is seated on a rock to right between two dancing satyrs. She is playing the double flutes (auloi. She wears a chiton and a broad hair-band, which holds her hair in a krobylos. The rock is streaked with dilute glaze, perhaps indicating a rough surface. The satyrs are nude and balding. The one at left lifts his left leg in the air and extends his right arm for balance; in his left hand he holds a thyrsos. The satyr at right also raises his left leg, but it is his right arm he extends toward the flutist; his face is drawn in three-quarter view.

Side B: A pair of youths wearing himatia and holding staffs vertical in their right hands stand on either side of a third youth (or boy), who faces the youth at left. The arms of the central youth are covered by his himation.

A laurel wreath circles the vase below the rim, and inside there are two reserved stripes at the top and bottom of the mouth. The groundline on either side consists of groups of three maeanders to right alternating with cross-squares. The side of the foot is reserved, and there is a reserved groove between foot and body.
artifact.shape_description: Bell-krater: bulbous body, somewhat constricted below the rim, tapering to a broad stem; torus rim; tall disk foot.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.355
artifact.summary: Band of enclosed palmettes.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 117; CVA, Robinson 3, 21, pl. 12, 3.
artifact.dimensions: Max. H. 0.087 m.; Pres. W. o.118 m.
artifact.date_description: In addition to the style of the palmettes, that of the lettering and the arrangement of the inscription in two tiers, with the letters vertically aligned (stoichedon), are clues to the range of dates.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Single fragment preserving most of the spout, part of one trefoil lobe, the front of the neck, most of the upper frame of the picture panel, and part of the left frame. No figure-work preserved. Some abrasion, including a scratch across the palmette-band.
artifact.comparanda: For the shape, see J. R. Green, "Oinochoe," BICS 19 (1972) 2-3 and 6-7. For the iconography and possible cultic significance of painted choes, see R. Hamilton, Choes and Anthesteria: Athenian Iconography and Ritual (Ann Arbor 1991); and G. van Hoorn, Choes and Anthesteria (Leiden 1951). For the name Akryptos, see J. E. Kirchner, Prosopographia Attica I (Berlin 1901), 36, nos. 481-82. The band of palmettes on this fragment are similar to those on choes of the Eretria Painter and his associates; see Lezzi-Hafter 1988, pls. 135-36 and 138-39.
artifact.decoration_description: Narrow band of upright palmettes, enclosed by tendrils; it is part of the upper frame of the missing figure panel. Part of one lateral frame — a thin reserved line — is preserved at left. Inscription in added red letters at upper left.
artifact.inscriptions: *A*K*R*U*P*T*W*I *O *P*A*T*H*R ("His father (gave it) to Akryptos").
artifact.shape_description: Oinochoe of type 3, also known as a chous, with trefoil mouth and spherical body.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.352
artifact.summary: Seated traveller and his gear.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 114; CVA, Robinson 2, 29-39, pl. 38, 3.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with repainting of cracks. Misfired red in places. Handle chipped.
artifact.comparanda: For oinochoai of type 8, see J. R. Green, "Oinochoe," BICS 19 (1972) 8 and pl. II a, b, and e (the latter, type 8b); Green equates the shape with the kothon, a drinking cup for soldiers and travelers, an interpretation given added support by this representation. The shape also appears in black-glaze and in silver; see M. Vickers, et al., From Silver to Ceramic (Oxford 1986) pl. 2.
artifact.decoration_description: A bearded traveller sits on a rock, facing right. He holds his left knee in his hands. He wears a chlamys, petasos, and shoes with striped leggings. In front of him is his bundle of gear, tied to a stick; one item is clearly a mug like this one. The subject thus alludes to the intended use as a traveling cup. The groundline is a simple reserved stripe, which circles the lower body. The side of the foot is reserved.
artifact.shape_description: Attic "mugs" are normally classed as oinochoai, in this case type 8b, with a concave neck (offset), a simple strap handle, and a broad, slender disk foot.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.346
artifact.summary: Sides A and B: Komos
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 106; CVA, Robinson 3, 15-16, pls. 6-7.
artifact.collection_history: ex Branteghem coll; E. P. Warren coll.; Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with restoration and repainting in the cracks and gaps. Reserved areas, including parts of several figures, are damaged by pitting and erosion. Much of the neck on both sides is lost, including a large part of the lotus buds. Rim chipped.
artifact.comparanda: The Pig Painter was one of the Early Mannerists, a name given the group by Beazley, who saw in their lean, sometimes elegant but other times impossibly robust figures something of the mannerism of 16th-century Flemish art, an analogy that has subsequently proved difficult to support, even if one knows what he meant. The Mannerists might also be termed "sub-archaic," as they tended to adhere to older, Late Archaic subjects, compositions, and formulae at a time when more innovative painters were taking the first steps toward the development of the Early Classical style. The group's founder was Myson, and the Pig Painter must have been his main pupil; their styles are closely related. Other workshop members included the Leningrad Painter and, at some time in his career, the Pan Painter. The Mannerists were pot-painters, as opposed to cups, with column-kraters a particular specialty. The Pig Painter painted mostly column-kraters, but also amphorae, pelikai, and hydriai. He was particularly fond of drawing satyrs and maenads, as well as their human correspondents: bawdy, robust komasts and hetairae in full revel. Cf. the komoi on two other of his column-kraters with framed pictures: Cleveland 26.549 and Louvre G 355 (ARV2, 563, 9-10). Sometimes there are only two komasts on a side, either two males or a male and female. The female flute-player on Palermo V 789 (ARV2, 564, 20) is the performing counterpart of the hetaira on this vase, whose flutes either have been returned to their case now that dinner is over, or were left sheathed as their owner stripped down for immediate action; cf. also the way the man on the Palermo vase touches the girl's belly. For the Mannerists, see Robertson 1992, 143; and Boardman 1975, 179-80. For Myson and the Pig Painter, see Berge 1992. For hetairai on red-figure vases, see Peschel 1987; Reinsberg 1989; and Keuls 1985.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Two nude, ithyphallic komasts (revelers) are clutching and pawing a pair of nude hetairai (prostitutes). The women move away from the men, as though teasing them or expressing unwillingness to succumb; the latter is unlikely, considering their nudity and the fact that they have been hired for the evening. The man at left is bearded and balding, and wears a cloak over his shoulders. He gestures with his left hand and reaches with his right for the woman's right arm. She walks to the right but looks back at the man, a black skyphos in her left hand and a leopard-skin flute case (sybene) in her right. She wears a kekryphalos, dotted earrings, anklet, thigh-band, and a necklace with a chain drawn with dilute glaze. At right, the second komast, a beardless youth, extends his left hand to grab the second hetaira by the leg while reaching for her breast with his right hand. She walks to the right but looks back at the youth, a kylix in her left hand (which she expertly keeps level), her right hand raised to summon or ward off her suitor. The youth wears a padded fillet and kothornoi, tall boots with the tops rolled down. The hetaira wears a kekryphalos with trailing ends, earrings, and a necklace like her companion. On both women, the tuft of hair in back is rendered in dilute glaze, which on the first hetaira is also used for the hair around the brow and temples.

Side B: A hetaira is accosted on either side by two komasts, one a bearded man, the other a youth with budding sideburns drawn with dilute glaze. The woman walks to the left but looks back at the youth at right. She is nude except for a kekryphalos with trailing ends and a necklace with a chain of dilute glaze. Curls in dilute glaze emerge from her cap over the brows and temples. She raises her right hand and holds a black skyphos in her left. The youth seems to be capering or dancing, with his right leg in the air. He is nude and ithyphallic. He holds a small (empty?) wineskin in his left hand and reaches with his right hand for the woman's left arm. The man at left reaches out to touch the woman's belly with his left hand; in his right hand he holds a knotty staff. The man is nude but not (yet) ithyphallic.

The panels are framed below by a narrow reserved stripe, at the sides by ivy vines, and above by a band of black tongues. On the neck of side A is a band of inverted lotus buds and dots. There are rays on the lower body and ivy vines on the side of the rim. On each handle-plate is a single black palmette framed by coiling tendrils. On top of the rim are animals in black silhouette: on either side, two groups of a goat and leopard, and half of a goat inserted to fill the remaining space. Stripes of added red circle the vase above the rays, below the panels, and on the outer and inner edges of the mouth.
artifact.shape_description: Column-krater: tapering body; foot in two degrees (torus with rounded riser); relatively short neck.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.344
artifact.summary: Side A: torch race<lb>Side B: three draped youths.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 103; CVA, Robinson 2, 34-35, pls. 47, 2-48, 1; Neils 1992, 178-79.
artifact.collection_history: ex Hirsch collection, Geneva; Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with considerable surface damage effecting all of the figures and reserved areas; discolored re-painting of cracks and worn areas. The black-glaze is scratched and pitted, especially on side B and the handles.
artifact.comparanda: For torch-racers at the Panathenaic Festival and elsewhere, including this vase, see J. Neils and D. Kyle, in Neils 1992, 96, 178-79, and 207 notes 110-113. See also Parke 1977, 45-46 and 171-75; Deubner 1932, 211-13; and C. G. Giglioli, "La corsa della fiaccola ad Atene," Rendiconti della Classe di Scienze morali, storiche e filologiche dell'Accademia dei Lincei 31 (1922) 315-35. For the inscription listing a hydria among the prizes for the torch-race at Athens, see Neils 1992, 16, fig. 1. For another vase-painting of a hydria at an altar at a torch-race, see G. van Hoorn, Choes and Anthesteria (Leiden 1951) fig. 118. A miniature Panathenaic, New York 41.162.52, shows a victorious torch-racer seated on a hydria (CVA, New York 2, pl. 48, 3-4). For the priest wearing an ependytes, cf. Palermo 661a (ARV2, 472, 210). Beazley said the Harvard krater was "close to the Peleus Painter and may be from his hand" (ARV2, 1040).
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: A torch-race (lampadedromia), with two young runners heading for an altar at right. The racers are nude, but wear broad headbands, the first like a radiate crown, with vertical spikes, the second with two vertical spikes and a central upright with a tiny picture of a runner on it. Both youths have the right arm lowered and the left arm outstretched, holding the blazing torch by the handle beneath the drip-plate. The first runner, in the lead, has his right leg forward, which would be very awkward with the left arm extended; the second runner is drawn correctly, with the left leg forward. The altar is decorated with an ovolo molding, volutes, and a palmette akroterion; the wood on top will be kindled by the torch of the winning racer. Behind and to the right of the altar is an olive tree, and in the foreground at left sits a large kalpis-hydria, probably of metal. Behind the altar stands a bearded man gesturing to left and right and looking toward the advancing runners. He wears a laurel wreath and chiton, and over the chiton an ependytes, a type of long, sleeveless tunic with woven or embroidered designs. In the background to the right of the man is a wreath in added white, now largely destroyed.

Side B: A youth with long hair stands between two youths with shorter hair. Beazley called the central youth a boy, but he is the same height as the other two. The two youths at left face the third youth at right. All three wear himations, that of the central youth covering both his arms. The youth at left holds a strigil in his outstretched right hand; the youth at right holds a staff vertically in his right hand.

This torch-race is almost certainly the one at the Panathenaic Festival, for a 4th-century prize inscription states that individual winners in the torch-race were given 30 drachmas and a hydria; the hydria by the altar is the prize. The inscription also states that the races were organized by tribe, the winning tribe receiving 100 drachmas and a bull, and it has been suggested that the different headgear worn by these racers indicates a difference in tribes. The event was a relay race, and the winning team had to arrive with their torch still lit. The torches were lit at the altar of Prometheus in the Academy (Paus. 1.30.2) and the race ended at another altar at the foot of the Acropolis, where the winning torch lit the altar for the sacrifice to Athena Polias, a symbolic journey demonstrating the cultic roots of this and other athletic events. Aristotle says the Archon Basileus was in charge of all torch-races (Arist. Ath. Pol. 57.1), so he may be identified with the bearded man by the altar. The ependytes the man wears identifies him (in this context) as a priest. The altar may be that of Athena Polias herself, as the olive tree is doubtless the one that stood next to her temple on the Acropolis.

An olive wreath circles the vase under the rim. The groundlines on either side consist of groups of three maeanders to right alternating with saltire-squares (and a single cross-square on side A). Bands of egg-pattern nearly circle the handle roots. The space between the handle roots is reserved, and reserved stripes circle the side of the foot at top and bottom, the inside of the lip, and the top of the body inside.
artifact.shape_description: Bell-krater: disk foot with groove near the top; lower body tapering to a broad stem; torus rim narrowed to a ridge.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.342
artifact.summary: Domestic scene, with loom.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 101; CVA, Robinson 2, 31-32, pl. 43.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with repainting of cracks and small gaps. Hole in the bottom, perhaps intentional.
artifact.comparanda: Beazley, who knew this vase well, did not attribute it to a particular painter or group, apparently rejecting Robinson's attribution to the wider circle of Polygnotos. For children in ancient Greece, see A. Klein, Child Life in Greek Art (New York 1932); H. Rühfel, Kinderleben in klassischen Athen (Mainz 1984); and L. Beaumont, The Iconography of Children in 5th Century Attic Red-figure Pottery (Dissertation, Univ. of London, 1990). Similar scenes of seated women, nurses, and infants appear on other vases of the period; e.g. London 1907.7-10.10 (ARV2, 1227, 10), and Berlin F 2443 (ARV2, 995, 118). The subject also is found on marble tombstones; e.g. the stele of Ampharete, from the Kerameikos in Athens; (Boardman 1985a, fig. 150. On a stele from Phalanna, in Thessaly, a young man plays with the child on the mother's lap (Boardman 1985a, fig. 166). For sprang sakkoi, see I. Jenkins and D. Williams, "Sprang Hair Nets: Their Manufacture and Use in Ancient Greece," AJA 89 (1985) 411-418 and I. Jenkins and D. WIlliams, "A Bronze Portrait Head and its Hair Net," Record of The Art Museum, Princeton University 46:2 (1987) 8-15.. For Thracians and Thracian clothing, see W. Raeck, Zum Barbarenbild in der Kunst Athens im 6. und 5. Jahrhundert v. Chr. (Bonn 1981) 67-100 and 323-25; H. Cahn, "Dokimasia," RA (1973) 1-22; K. Zimmermann, "Thraker-Darstellungen auf griechischen Vasen," Actes du IIe Congrès International de Thracologie, vol. I (Bucharest 1980) 429-50; Knauer 1987, 22, n. 48, and 28-29; and J. M. Padgett, "Phineas and the Boreads on a Pelike by the Nausicaa Painter," Journal of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston 3 (1991) 22-23, and 31, note 33. For clothing, looms, and textile production in Greece, see M. Bieber, Griechische Kleidung (Berlin 1928); A. Pekridou-Gorecki, Mode in antiken Griechenland: Textile Fertigung und Kleidung (Munich 1989); H. L. Roth, Ancient Egyptian and Greek Looms, (Halifax 1913); and E. J. W. Barber, "The Peplos of Athena," in Neils 1992, 103-117 (particularly the diagram of a Greek loom on p. 109).
artifact.decoration_description:
A seated mother hands an infant boy to a standing woman, perhaps a nurse, who gazes across at the beardless youth standing at right, possibly the father. The mother sits to the left on a klismos, her feet resting on a low stool in the form of a rectangular block. She wears a chiton, himation, and sakkos. The latter, decorated with dotted lines and zigzags, has a small top-knot indicating it is made in the "sprang" technique. A laurel wreath hangs on the wall above the woman. The young man wears a himation and rests his weight on a tall staff, which he holds with his left hand; his right hand rests within the himation. His right leg is relaxed, with the foot drawn back. The nurse bends to receive the child, who reaches out to her with both hands. The string of charms across the infant's chest are to protect it from sickness. The nurse wears a chiton and a belted tunic of Thracian type, with long sleeves and dentilated borders; it indicates that she is of barbarian origin and is probably a slave. Behind and to the left of the nurse is a tall loom, consisting of a framework of slender poles, lashed together and well-braced. The threads of the warp are drawn with fine relief lines, and there are ten small weights at the ends. The cloth being produced is rolled up at the top, but enough is visible to see that it has a dark, sawtooth pattern along the sides, a motif common on Thracian garments, such as the long cloak called a zeira.

Egg pattern around the rim and part way around the roots of the handles; the area between the handle roots is reserved, as is the top of the mouth. Above the figures, framed by horizontal stripes, is a laurel wreath with berries. The groundline consists of groups of three maeanders to left alternating with saltire-squares.
artifact.shape_description: Kalpis hydria. This example has a rather tapering body and a cyma foot; the top of the mouth is flat, rather than beveled.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.341
artifact.summary: Three mourning women
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 100; CVA, Robinson 2, 27-28, pl. 35.
artifact.collection_history: Said to have been found in a grave at Vari with two other hydriae: Harvard 1960.340, by the Painter of the Yale Oinochoe (ARV2, 503, 22), and Univ. Mississippi, no number, in the manner of the Niobid Painter (ARV2, 611, 35).
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with discolored in-painting of cracks and some restoration.
artifact.comparanda: Both their behavior and their accouterments identify the women as mourners. Pulling the hair was a time-honored sign of mourning in Greece; cf. the women on a Protoattic hydria and a pair of Protoattic plaques in Boston: Boston 24.151, Boston 27.146, Boston 27.147; BMFA 25 (1927) 55. For an example contemporary with the Harvard vase, cf. the mourners on a loutrophoros formerly in the Schoen collection, now in Munich (ARV2, 1102, 1). The basket full of fillets, leythoi, and wreaths is frequently represented on white-ground lekythoi in scenes of mourners bringing offerings to a tomb; for several examples, see Kurtz 1975, pls. 18.2, 19.2-3, 20.1-2, 29.4, 36.3, 39.1, 40.3, 41.2b, 44.1, and 47.3a. Sometimes the tomb is omitted, and the subject is obviously the preparation for the visit or the setting out for the cemetery; e.g. Kurtz 1975, pl. 25.2-3. The hydria on the Harvard vase may be either the container for the cremated ashes of the dead, as is probably the case on the lekythos Athens 1975 (Kurtz 1975, pl. 20.3), or another article to take to the cemetery, as on the lekythos Karlsruhe 234 (Kurtz 1975, pl. 43.2), where a woman cleans a tomb monument with water from a hydria. The shape and subsidiary ornament of this kalpis are characteristic of the Painter of the Berlin Hydria, a close follower of the Niobid Painter; cf. the painter's name-vase, Berlin F 2381 (ARV2, 617, 11).
artifact.decoration_description:
Three female mourners wearing chitons and himations are standing around a kalpis hydria, which sits on the ground. The woman at left stands frontally, her head turned to the right. She is pulling her hair with her right hand and touching (or beating) her breast with her left. The woman at right, whose himation hangs open in front, pulls her hair with her left hand and extends right hand in an emphatic gesture. The woman in the center stands in profile to the right, carrying a broad, shallow basket filled with small lekythoi, two wreaths in added white, and at least one fillet in added red. The short, unadorned hair of the women might indicate that they are slaves, but because they have been pulling their hair, the artist may have been trying to portray the dishevelment of grief. Robinson and Pottier believed the scene might depict Electra, her sister Chrysothemis, and a servant, but there is nothing to indicate a mythological rather than generic meaning; see CVA, Robinson 2, 27-28. The hydria, which has a wreath or branch in added red in its mouth, may be an ash urn, or, like the offerings in the basket, is but another item to be taken to the tomb (see discussion below).

The ground line is a band of dotted egg-pattern; a similar pattern circles the rim. Bands of black tongues circle the roots of all three handles. Above the figures, at the base of the neck, is a band of enclosed palmettes alternating with lotuses.
artifact.shape_description: Kalpis hydria (cf. 1960.340, above) with cyma foot.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.340
artifact.summary: Women and herons.
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 99; CVA, Robinson 2, 27, pls. 34-34A; P. J. Holliday, "Red-figure Hydria: A Theme in Greek Vase Painting," Bulletin of the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston vol. 8, no. 3 (1984) 6, fig. 4.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of David M. Robinson. Said to have been found in a grave at Vari with two other hydriae: Harvard 1960.341, by the Painter of the Berlin Hydria (ARV2, 617, 13), and Mississippi 1977.3.88, in the manner of the Niobid Painter (ARV2, 611, 35).
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with some repainting of cracks and small missing pieces; e.g. parts of the himatia of the three women. The glaze is worn and scratched in many places, and there is discoloration from removal of incrustation. Large areas of the back and sides misfired a reddish color due to thinly applied slip.
artifact.comparanda: Herons were apparently popular household pets in Athens. They were sacred to Aphrodite and their behavior was considered a clue to changes in the weather; see J. D. Beazley, The Lewes House Collection of Gems (Oxford 1920) 60-61. Women and herons appear on two other kalpides by the Painter of the Yale Oinochoe: London 83.11-24.26 (ARV2, 503, 23), and Houston 80.95; P. J. Holliday, Bulletin of the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, vol. 8, no. 3 (winter 1984) 2-7. The women on the Houston vase wear their hair in the same way as those on the Harvard kalpis, with the queues secured in small cloth bags. For some other examples of women and herons, cf. Chicago 1916.140 (ARV2, 258, 18); Copenhagen 4997 (ARV2, 1214,4); Copenhagen 7359 (CVA, Copenhagen 4, pl. 156; and Louvre G 544, (CVA, Louvre 8, pl. 44, 5). See also H. Cahn, Kunstwerke der Antike, Münzen und Medaillen Auktion 56 (Basel 1980) pl. 47, no. 105. For the shape and subsidiary ornament of this kalpis are characteristic of the Painter of the Yale Oinochoe, a pot-specialist who painted at least seven hydriae, but also decorated stamnoi, kraters, and other large shapes; cf. the shape and ornament of kalpis London E 178, with the Judgement of Paris (ARV2, 503, 20).
artifact.decoration_description:
Three women wearing fillets, chitons and himations are gathered in an interior setting, probably the women's quarters of a home. All three have the queues of their hair tied up in small cloth bundles secured with crossed cords. The two women standing at left are facing the woman at right, who is seated on a klismos; she may be the mistress of the house and the other two either relations or slaves. A wool-basket (kalathos) hangs upside down on the wall above. On the ground, interspersed between the women, are two herons, probably pets. The heron at left looks up at the first woman, whose himation covers both arms and is pulled taut in front by the right arm, the hand of which emerges just below the face. The second heron faces the woman in the center, who holds a skyphos in her left hand and stretches her right hand forward with the thumb and index finger nearly touching; she appears to be dropping a piece of food to the heron, having just removed it from the skyphos. The bird raises its head in anticipation, lifting one foot off the floor. Behind it, the seated woman also extends a hand over the bird; it is not clear whether she is teasing it or trying to calm it.

The groundline consists of a band of paired maeanders to right alternating with cross-squares; the same pattern is used for a shorter band above the figures, at the base of the neck. A band of tongue pattern circles the lip.
artifact.shape_description: Hydria of kalpis type, with a continuous profile from neck to foot and a vertical handle from shoulder to neck. Two horizontal handles, tilted upward; depressed globular body with deep shoulder; torus foot with short, carinated riser; fillet between foot and body; overhanging rim with beveled top and groove around upper edge.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.333
artifact.summary: Hunter and stag.
artifact.other_bibliography: CVA, Robinson 3, 20-21, pl. 12, 2; Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 85.
artifact.collection_history: Purchased in Europe.
artifact.condit: Neck broken and repaired. Numerous scratches and abrasions; some wear of the white glaze.
artifact.comparanda: For lekythoi in the Six's technique, see Kurtz 1975, 116-120..
artifact.decoration_description:
A nude hunter is shown chasing a stag, which though unnaturally small, has a full rack of horns. Both are drawn in creamy, opaque white glaze directly on the black background, with no use of incision. The hunter wears a petasos and an object on his left arm. His spear is in his upraised right hand. A slender white stripe forms the groundline, and two more run above the scene but do not circle the vase.

Robinson called the object on the hunter's arm a pelt, but what looks like a pendant paw is actually closer to the leather apron often represented attached to the bottoms of shields; the part on the hunter's arm also resembles a foreshortened shield. There is no reason why anyone would carry a shield in a deer hunt, but it seems that is exactly what this minor, and somewhat confused artist has drawn, perhaps being more used to drawing that motif than one more appropriate.

The shoulder, neck, underside of the handle, side of the foot, and top of the mouth are reserved; the rest of the vase is black. Around the base of the neck is an unframed band of crude tongues; around this is an unframed band of rays, the noticeable slant of which attest to their hasty execution. A reserved stripe circles the vase just below the shoulder.
artifact.inscriptions: Three meaningless letters are scattered in the upper field: *A*I*L.
artifact.shape_description: Lekythos: tapering cylindrical body; grooves between body and disk foot; relatively broad, narrow mouth; vertical handle.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.327
artifact.summary: Black archer and palm tree
artifact.other_bibliography: Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 87; LIMC, I, 415, Aithiopes 8.
artifact.collection_history: Bequest of David M. Robinson.
artifact.condit: Unbroken. White ground worn in places. Black glaze worn on table and bottom of tree. Numerous root-marks.
artifact.comparanda: The Group of the Negro Alabastra may all have been painted by the Syriskos Painter, who otherwise worked only in red-figure. The Ethiopian archers on these alabastra are similar in style, differing only in minor details of dress and weaponry. The palm tree is a standard motif. A number of related white-ground alabastra are decorated with the figure of an Amazon, also in "barbarian" dress; e.g. Princeton 1984-12; Record of the Art Museum, Princeton University vol. 44, no. 1 (1985) p. 45. Cf. Berlin F 3382 (ABV, 269; LIMC, I, pl. 322, Aithiopes 7), on which both an Ethiopian and an Amazon appear. The meaning of these vase-paintings is not known, though the African archers find parallels among the squires of Memnon on earlier black-figure vases; e.g. an amphora by Exekias, Philadelphia MS4873 (ABV, 145, 16). For a discussion of the Group and additional parallels, see J. Neils, AntK 23 (1980) 13-23.
artifact.decoration_description: An "Aethiopian" (i.e. black African) archer, drawn in outline except for the face, hands, and cloak. There is no use of incision. The archer stands with his torso frontal, legs in profile to the right, head turned to the left, and arms outstretched on either side. He wears long trousers decorated with stripes and dots, a tunic with long, striped sleeves, and a cuirass with shoulder-flaps and black belt. In his left hand he holds a bow, in his right a battle-axe like those often carried by Amazons. A large quiver of gorytos type hangs at his waist. To the right is a small table, probably 3-legged. On the side opposite the archer is a tall palm tree with rippling trunk. The groundline is a slender stripe of thinned glaze. The lip and base are black. A black band framed by two narrow stripes circles the upper body.
artifact.shape_description: Alabastron: flattened disk mouth; swelling body tapering to a point; no lugs.

artifact.name: Harvard 1960.321 and 1958.19
artifact.summary: Potters' workshop.
artifact.other_bibliography: CVA, Robinson 3, 11-12, pls. 1-2; JHS 58 (1938) 153; Robinson exhibition catalogue 1961, no. 76; J. Z. Ziomecki, Les représentations d'artisans sur les vases attiques (Wrocaw 1975) 30 and 32, figs. 6-7; Munich 1983, 12 111, fig. 102.
artifact.date_description: The Theseus Painter's skyphoi date to his early period, before 500 B.C.
artifact.collection_history: David M. Robinson Bequest. Purchased in Rome. A fragment with a potter attaching an amphora handle, formerly in the Jacob Hirsch collection and not included in the CVA, of 1938, was recognized as joining by D. von Bothmer and donated by J. V. Noble (inv. 1958.19).
artifact.condit: Broken and repaired, with several pieces missing, particularly on side B, where the head of the herm and portions of all three figures are lost. Half of the foot, the center of the base, and parts of the lower body are also lost. Some missing contours have been restored, most noticeably the head of the herm and the top of the mound on side B. The added color has worn off in many places. At least one fragment present in the CVA, publication of 1938 is now lost: it gave the top of the head and part of the basket of the central man on side B.
artifact.comparanda: Although there are numerous scenes of potters at work, none parallels this example, where mounds of the raw material dominate the scenes. For related examples and some insight into the possible activities represented on this cup, see Noble 1988 and Scheibler 1983. The herms recall the masks on some representations of kilns; e.g. Munich 1717 (ABV, 362, 36).
artifact.decoration_description:
A potters' workshop. The subject is the same on both sides and continues under the handles. Under each handle is a bearded potter with his cloak around his waist. The potter under handle A/B sits on the base of a herm; the other sits or kneels behind the base of a second herm.
