artifact.decoration_description: White Nike (with frontal blue wings) flying 3/4-view to the right, wearing a white (or colored) chiton, a himation billowing at her side (?), a red taenia, a high pony tail, bead earrings, and a beaded necklace, reaches her arms out to Athena; white Athena, seated 3/4-view to the left, with her head profile to the right, tilted back, wearing a red, sleeveless chiton, a white himation, a Corinthian helmet, a beaded necklace, and two red bands on each wrist, rests her bent left arm on her shield, and holds upright in her right hand a scepter with a gold tip; Herakles, standing near frontal, with his weight on his left leg, his right leg relaxed, and his head profile to the left, wearing a himation over his back/left arm, and his lion's-head helmet, rests the back of his left hand on his hip, and holds his club under his right arm; Dionysos, seated or standing 3/4-view to the left, wearing a short-sleeved oriental tunic over a long-sleeved oriental tunic, and an ivy wreath, holds a thyrsos (with a snake around its lower part ) upright in his right hand; Demeter, seated 3/4-view to the left, with her head 3/4-view to the right, wearing a short-sleeved chiton, a gold crown, and one gold bracelet on each wrist, holds her scepter in her upraised right hand, and holds her left hand in front of her body; small, white Ploutos, standing 3/4-view to the left, wearing a red oriental tunic, a blue himation on his back, and a red taenia, holds in both hands, to the right, an empty red keras with a gold rim; indistinct red objects fall on the ground beneath the keras; white Kore, standing nearly frontal, with her head 3/4-view to the left, wearing a white chiton, a blue himation, a gold taenia, a gold necklace, and two bracelets on her right wrist, raises a torch in each hand; Eumolpos, seated 3/4-view to the left, with his head profile to the right, wearing a long oriental tunic, rests his right hand on knee, and rests a gold scepter on his left shoulder; one Dioskouros on horseback, riding 3/4-view to the left (only the white head of the horse, and the head of the Dioskouros are evident); Iakchos, standing 3/4-view to the right, holds a torch to the right in his left hand (only the top half of his head and the top half of his torch are preserved); a second Dioskouros on a rearing horse, riding near profile to the left, enveloped in a chlamys. Behind him lie three boukrania on the ground (the center one has gold on the horns).

artifact.name: Athens, Fethiye Djami 1961-NAK 790
artifact.summary: Ploutos and Eleusinian divinities
artifact.sources_used: <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 7.416 s.v. Ploutos no. 6 (K. Clinton); <bibl>Clinton 1992</bibl>, 50, 83, 93-94, 103-104, 133 no. 5 fig. 3; <bibl>LIMC</bibl>, 4.877 s.v. Demeter no. 402, pl. 592 (L. Beschi); <bibl>Métzger 1965</bibl>, 37 no. 17, pl. 16.2.
artifact.decoration_description:
A seated (?) figure, perhaps Dionysos (only part of left arm [?] and diagonal thyrsos, remaining); Demeter, seated 3/4-view to the left on a cista (?), with her head profile to the right, wearing a peplos belted high over a long overfold, with two vertical striations (relief) down the front of her garment, a himation draped over her lower body, a polos with vegetal ornament, pendant earrings, a single band necklace with a central pendant, a beaded bracelet on her right hand, and a band bracelet on her left hand, leans her bent left arm on the back of her seat (the back is not visible), and holds a scepter in her upraised right hand; three stalks of grain; a white, nude boy, Ploutos, standing 3/4-view to the right, with his head turned 3/4-view to the left, and his weight on his left leg, with his right leg relaxed, wearing a grain crown, with a colored (or white?) himation, draped over his bent left arm, holds in both hands, slightly to the right, a gold keras filled with grain stalks; a white female figure, probably Kore (only right body preserved), standing near frontal, with her weight on her left leg, and her right leg relaxed, wearing a white (?), patterned himation with gilded relief border, probably over a chiton, and a band on her right wrist, bends her right arm above Ploutos.

According to Clinton (50) this Ploutos is a perfect parallel to the boy on the Great Eleusinian relief (Athens, NM 126), except for the keras, which, "... however, .. is not an essential attribute of Eleusinian Ploutos. The crucial element is the display of grain." In this painted representation, however, we can be more confident that Ploutos rather than Triptolemos is intended.

artifact.name: Hamilton 1476
artifact.summary: Ge, Hermes, and Dionysos?
artifact.sources_used: J.H.W. Tischbein, <hi rend="ital">Collection of Engravings from Ancient Vases of Greek Workmanship Discovered in Sepulchres in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies but Chiefly in the Neighbourhood of Naples during the Course of the Years MDCCLXXXIX and MDCCLXXXX Now in the Possession of Sir. Wm. Hamilton</hi> (Naples 1795) 3.14-15, pl. 8.
artifact.graffiti: Beazley notes that this plate may have the same story shown on <rs type="vase">St. Petersburg St. 1792</rs>. It is impossible to determine how much of the drawing reflects restoration and/or artist's embellishments, as the vase is now lost. If the attributes are all authentic, then the identity of Hermes (with boots, chlamys, petasos, and kerykeion) is secure. As Dionysos is the baby who was traditionally handed to Hermes, and this baby is shown with nebris and ivy leaves, as befits Dionysos, it is most likely that he, not Ploutos, is here represented. Although she does not emerge from the ground, according to the drawing), the female figure is closer to the image of Ge (particularly on <rs type="vase">Naples H 2883</rs>, <rs type="vase">Istanbul 2576</rs> and <rs type="vase">St. Petersburg St. 1792</rs>) than the nymphs, who traditionally receive Dionysos, on account of her attire and hair.
artifact.decoration_description: A female figure, surrounded by ivy leaves, perhaps Eirene or Ge, standing 3/4-view to the right, with weight on her left leg, wearing a belted peplos, and long hair cascading over her shoulders, holds an infant, on a nebris, towards Hermes; the infant, perhaps Ploutos or Dionysos, wearing a himation, reclines 3/4-view to the left, on the nebris, but turns near profile to the right and reaches both arms up to Hermes; Hermes, advancing 3/4-view to the left, with both legs bent, and his head bowed down, holds the child's right hand in his left hand, and his right hand on the child's head. He wears calf-length boots, a chlamys bucked in front, and a petasos. A kerykeion lies on the ground behind his right foot.

a young, white boy, Ploutos, standing near frontal, with his weight on his left leg, and his head turned profile to the left, wearing a blue chlamys on his back tied with red cross-straps, a short pony tail, and a gold taenia, rests his right elbow on a cista, and cradles in his left arm a keras; white Kore, standing near frontal, slightly to the right, with her head turned 3/4-view to the left, wearing a button-sleeved chiton, a himation, a laurel wreath, a gold band on her right wrist, a gold beaded necklace, and two-part pendant earrings, holds two torches, one in each hand, to the left; a female figure, Eleusis (or Rhea ?), seated profile to the left on an omphalos (otherwise interpreted as "the Mirthless rock"), wearing a himation veiled over her head and around her body, obscuring her left arm and her hand, draped over a sleeveless chiton (?), a stephane, a gold beaded necklace, pendant earrings, and one band on her right wrist, rests her feet on a footstool; Eros seated 3/4-view to the right, with his head profile to the left, and his (blue?) wings frontal, wearing a himation around his lower legs and waist and a red taenia.

artifact.decoration_description:
Antheia, standing 3/4-view to the left, with her head profile to the right, wears a white, belted chiton, a dark himation draped over both arms and held in both hands, and a sakkos. Peitho, standing profile to the right, with her weight on her left leg, and her right leg relaxed, wears a sleeveless, belted chiton with a long kolpos, a sphendone, and two bands on each wrist, holds a small baton in her left hand, and reaches her right hand to an unidentifiable object (a game for the child?). A female figure (Eukleia?), seated profile to the right on rock, wearing a medium-sleeved chiton, a dark himation wrapped around her legs, a sphendone, and earrings, raises her left hand thoughtfully toward her lowered head, and holds a small bird in her raised right hand. A young, nude boy, Kephimos?, runs profile to the left, wearing amulets around his chest, left foot, and wrist, reaches both arms to the bird. In front of a laurel (?) tree stands Eunomia, in 3/4-view to the left, wearing a sleeveless, belted chiton with a kolpos and long hair. She reaches her right hand to the tree, and holds a plate of fruit in her left hand, at waist level. Paidia, standing profile to the left, wears a sleeved chiton, a himation draped over her left shoulder, a sphendone, and earrings, holds an unidentifiable object in her left hand, and dangles a beaded necklace from her right hand.

Machaira interprets Antheia as one of the Horai. Jucker (67) has interpreted the unlabelled character as Eukleia on the basis of her cult association with Eunomia, or Aphrodite (who is usually accompanied by Peitho); an alternate interpretation has been provided by Kron (291) who identified her as Herse, mother of Kephalos, on the incorrect assumption that the boy is the Attic hero Kephalos, rather than Kephimos. On the speculative basis that this white-ground lekythos served a distinctly funerary purpose, the unidentified mother, and the child Kephimos may represent merely a mortal mother and son, as paralleled on grave stelai. Although Paidia and Peitho are both laden with erotic overtones, the innocent nature of this scene discourages us from ascribing particular erotic connotations in this context.
artifact.inscriptions: In the main scene several figures are labelled: Anthea (<Foreign lang=Greek>*A*N*Q*E[*I]*A</Foreign>), Peitho (<Foreign lang=Greek>*P*E[*I]*Q*W</Foreign>), the infant, Kephimos (?) (<Foreign lang=Greek>*K*E**F[*H]*M*O*[*S]</Foreign>), Eunomia (<Foreign lang=Greek>*E[*U*N]*O[*M]*I*A </Foreign>), and Paidia (<Foreign lang=Greek>*P*A*I*D*I*A</Foreign>)

artifact.date_description: Beazley believed that the Kleophrades Painter's (9) Panathenaic amphorae were created early in his career, and that they show signs of the influence of his teacher, Euthymides (broad figures, large heads, and relaxed poses).
artifact.collection_history: Gift of Frederic W. Stevens, B.A. 1858.
artifact.condit: Some missing portions have been restored in plaster and clay. The surface, earlier overpainted, has been cleaned, while some of the restorations have been painted over.
artifact.decoration_description: On side A, helmeted Athena strides profile to the right, with her shield raised on her left arm and her spear in her upraised right arm. This is the typical Promachos ("Ready for war") pose in which she appears on Panathenaic amphorae. She is flanked by two colonettes supporting cocks (which is also customary). Her shield is here decorated with a white Pegasos (winged horse). The athlete shown on side B--a charioteer riding a quadriga, or four horse chariot profile to the right--indicates the event in which this vase (filled with oil) would have been given as a prize in the Panathenaic games.

artifact.collection_history: From the Rebecca Darlington Stoddard Collection.
artifact.condit: The surface has been dulled by salts. The area near the handle is chipped.
artifact.decoration_description: The black lip contrasts with the ray-decorated neck, divided from the shoulder by a narrow, raised, black band above a beaded frieze. The neck frieze illustrates a prowling panther (left) and lion (right), both shown in profile, approaching each other (the lion turns back to the right). They are divided by palmette from which two lotus buds emerge. The scene on the body illustrates the hero Herakles (with lion-skin helmet) fighting Kyknos (with Doric helmet), to punish him for robbing sacrificial cattle in the sanctuary of Apollo. Herakles is characteristically armed with his club, in his right hand, while his sword and quiver fall at his left side; Kyknos defends himself with shield and lance, and a sword also falls at his left side. Two men stand behind each combattant.
artifact.shape_description: A broad lekythos with a flat-topped mouth (unusual), flaring lip, narrow neck, and carinated shoulder tapering in towards the base.

artifact.name: Yale 1913.122
artifact.summary: Side A: Achilles pursuing Troilos<lb>Side B: An older man courting a boy (attended by other nude men)<lb>Side C: Woman surrounded by men (perhaps a betrothal scene)
artifact.other_bibliography: <bibl>Heldensage3, 361</bibl>; <hi rend="ital">MuM</hi> 40, 13 December 1969, 36<bibl>Beazley 1947a, 5, 8</bibl>; <bibl>Hofkes-Brukker 1935, pl. 5.11</bibl>; <bibl>Baur 1922, 82 pls. 3-4</bibl>
artifact.condit: The lid is missing. The body is comprised of rejoined fragments from which the black decoration has worn off, except where added white covered the surface and on the interior of the bowl of the vase.
artifact.decoration_description: On the pyxis foot taken traditionally to be "side A" appears a scene from the <hi rend="ital">Kypria</hi> (some of this story is also retained in Virgil's <hi rend="ital">Aeneid</hi> 1.474): Achilles, wearing the helmet, has ambushed the Trojan prince, Troilus, at the fountainhouse, where he has come with his sister, Polyxena, to fetch water. As Troilus flees on horseback, his sister, Polyxena, also flees on foot; she has just dropped her amphora, which appears on the ground behind Troilus' horse. The man at the far left is not identifiable.
artifact.shape_description: This shape--a bowl supported by three large, rectangular uprights--began to be used in Middle Corinthian pottery, but is used strictly in Attica in the sixth century.

artifact.name: Yale 1913.138
artifact.summary: Side A: Herakles in the Garden of the Hesperides<lb>Side B: A satyr pursuing a maenad, preceded by Eros
artifact.other_bibliography: <bibl>Baur 1922, 92-94 no. 138, fig. 26</bibl>; <bibl>Brommer 1973, 41 no. 15</bibl>; <bibl>Metzger 1951, 203 no. 20</bibl>; <bibl>Brommer 1942, 118, IIb8</bibl>; <bibl>Horn 1931, 90</bibl>; <bibl>Jacobsthal 1927, 202 no. 369</bibl>
artifact.collection_history: From the Rebecca Darlington Stoddard Collection.
artifact.condit: The broken handles have been repaired. The neck and mouth have been restored, incorrectly (so that the lip is rounded rather than overhanging and offset). Some chips from the base of each handle are missing, and the surface is worn.
artifact.decoration_description:
Herakles sits, in 3/4-view to the left, just left of center. He is nude, but reclines on his himation, beneath an apple tree that indicates the locus of the scene in the garden of the Hesperides (the daughters of Hesperos), to where he has come to fetch the apples of immortality, as his last labor. At left stands a draped Hesperid, profile to the right; a second Hesperid sits on a rock, in 3/4-view to the right, although she turns her head profile to the left, to look at Herakles. A third Hesperid stands in a near frontal pose, with her head turned profile to the left. She is completely draped and veiled, while the seated Hesperid wears a dotted garment that only covers her lower torso, legs, and left arm. A Pan (woodland god) perches on a rock at the far right, and also turns his head profile to the left, to face the hero. The snake, Ladon, is coiled in the tree, above Herakles, and a winged Eros hovers above the seated Hesperid.

Additional decoration includes an egg-and-dot frieze above and below the figural scene on both sides (the lower frieze encircles the entire vase); a thin egg-and-dot frieze above the main egg-and-dot frieze on side A; and palmettes at bottom of each handle.
artifact.painter_mod: Attributed to the school of the

artifact.name: Yale 1913.139
artifact.summary: A nude man, between a woman and a draped figure with a laurel branch (Apollo?).
artifact.other_bibliography: <bibl>Hoorn 1951, 156</bibl>; S. Papaspyridi Karouzou, "Chous," <hi rend="ital">AJA</hi> 50 (1946) 123; <bibl>CVA, Robinson Collection 3 (Baltimore 1938) 19</bibl>; <bibl>FR, 3.316</bibl>; <bibl>Baur 1922, 94 fig. 32, pl. 9</bibl>; <bibl>Beazley 1918, 180</bibl>
artifact.collection_history: From the Rebecca Darlington Stoddard Collection.
artifact.condit: Reconstructed from many fragments and extensively restored: much of the lip and the base are modern. Losses include the face of the woman, the lower legs of the youth, and the head and shoulder of the figure on the right. The surface is worn, especially on relief lines and the arm of the central figure.
artifact.decoration_description: Possible identifications of the two figures on the left include Creusa and Ion (Baur), or Erigone and Orestes (Sears). The latter suggestion is particularly compelling. Apollo instructed Orestes to kill his mother and therefore defended him at his trial for matricide. When Orestes arrived at Athens for his trial, however, he found the city engaged in a festival. In order to participate in the festival without contaminating the populace, he was forced to drink from his own cup (see Euripides' <hi rend="ital">Iphigenia in Tauris</hi> 947-60 [<bibl n="Eur. IT 947">Eur. IT 947</bibl>]): this story became the aetion or cause for the tradition that each participant in the Anthesteria was required to drink from his own cup. Erigone, a daughter of Aegisthus and Clytaemnestra, came to Athens, on behalf of her father, to prosecute her brother Orestes. She lost the case, and consequently hanged herself: this hanging, in turn furnished the origin for the <hi rend="ital">Aiora</hi>, or swing ceremony, on the third day of the Anthesteria. Both stories are appropriate decoration for a chous, the particular shape of jug used on <hi rend="ital">Choes</hi>, the second day of the Anthesteria festival.
artifact.shape_description: Type III oinochoe

artifact.name: Yale 1913.144
artifact.summary: A sphinx seated on a three-stepped base, facing a stylized palmette.
artifact.other_bibliography: <bibl>Baur 1922, 97-98, fig. 31</bibl>
artifact.collection_history: From the Rebecca Darlington Stoddard Collection.
artifact.condit: The breaks have been repaired with large portions of the back and sides (including the tips of the wings) restored. The surface is scratched and pitted.
artifact.comparanda: <rs type="vase">Athens, NM 1938</rs> (<bibl>ARV2 685.166</bibl>)
artifact.decoration_description:
he base and palmette suggest that this sphinx serves here, as elsewhere, as a guardian of the dead, which is an appropriate decoration for an oil flask, or lekythos, which was customarily used as a grave offering.

The shoulder bears a reserved band with five black palmettes, below a tongue frieze. A short maeander frieze, between two red bands, serves as the ground line for the sphinx. Added red is used for the fillet worn by the sphinx.

Characteristics of the style of the Bowdoin Painter that are exhibited in this vase include the use of a continuous line to represent the nose and the forehead and a wide eye, with curved upper lid and straight lower lid.
artifact.shape_description: Type II lekythos

artifact.name: Yale 1913.163
artifact.summary: Symposium scene: A nude youth and a flute girl, entwined in love making, reclining on a couch with a large, banded pillow; a hanging basket appears at the left
artifact.other_bibliography: <bibl>CB, 1.10-11</bibl>; <bibl>Licht 1925, 57</bibl>; <bibl>Baur 1922, 108</bibl>; <bibl>Hambidge 1920, 122, fig. 12</bibl>
artifact.collection_history: From the Rebecca Darlington Stoddard Collection.
artifact.condit: Repaired from several fragments. THe left handle and part of the adjacent rim have been restored in plaster, painted black. The figural scene is intact, except for a slight loss on the right knee of the youth.
artifact.decoration_description: The exterior is not decorated. Preliminary sketch lines on the figural scenein the tondo (especially apparent where the painter did not follow these lines) indicate the degree to which the painter (perhaps a minor figure in the Pioneer Group) experimented (somewhat unsuccessfully) with rendering the figures in a naturalistic pose.
artifact.inscriptions: Side A: <Foreign lang=Greek>*H*O *P*A*I*S [*K]*A*L*O*S</Foreign> (along the column at the left)

artifact.name: Yale 1933.175
artifact.summary: Side A: Two pairs of male figures<lb>Side B: Two youths and a boy
artifact.other_bibliography: <hi rend="ital">YaleBull</hi> 7 (1935) 10-11; <bibl>Clarke 1917, no. 373</bibl>; <bibl>Morgan 1909, pl. 4.139</bibl>
artifact.dimensions: H. 0.39 m; Diam. (mouth) 0.26 m; Diam. (handles) 0.34 m
artifact.collection_history: Gift of Allison V. Armour, B.A. 1884. Formerly in the collection of Thomas B. Clarke.
artifact.condit: The vase remains without repairs or restorations, but the surface has been dulled by the effect of salts. A dark horizontal line--perhaps original--mars the lower right portion of the scene on side A.
artifact.decoration_description:
Side A: Two pairs of men and boys. The men, standing at left in each pair, are distinguished by their height and each wear a himation draped over the shoulder. The boys are entirely enveloped in their himatia. The first man, bearded, leans on a staff, gesticulates with his left hand, and in his right hand holds an apple, which he presumably gives to the boy. The third figure, a slightly younger (unbearded) man, also leans on a staff, holds his right hand on his hip, and raises a hare (another gift) in his left hand. A strigil (oil scraper) appears above, between the two pairs.

Side B: A boy, similarly wrapped in his himation, stands profile to the right. He is surrounded on both sides by unbearded youths, with himatia draped over their left shoulders, and staffs. The one on the left rests his right hand on his hip while the one on the right holds his right hand out to the boy.

Preliminary sketch lines are visible on the first and third figures on side A.
artifact.inscriptions: Kalos inscriptions between the third and fourth figures on side A and between the second and third figures on side B.
